rows.q: Seated over a fissure in the earth, the cryptic prophetess known as the Pythia delivered oracles inside a Delphi temple dedicated to which Greek god?
rows.n: Modern surveys revealed active faults beneath Delphi that could vent intoxicating hydrocarbon gases.

rows.q: In the ceremonial ballgame played across ancient Mesoamerica, players bounced a heavy rubber ball toward stone rings using primarily their elbows, knees, and what joint of the torso?
rows.n: The solid rubber ball could weigh upwards of eight pounds, making protective padding essential.

rows.q: When Alexander the Great offered to grant him any wish in the world, the philosopher Diogenes asked only that the conqueror stop blocking this.
rows.n: Alexander was impressed by the snub, remarking that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes.

rows.q: When King Philip of Macedon warned that if he brought his army into Laconia he would raze Sparta, Spartan magistrates sent back what one-word reply?
When Praetorian guards murdered Caligula, they found his uncle Claudius trembling behind one of these household furnishings and dragged him out to be made emperor.
rows.n: Claudius had survived family purges for decades by playing up his physical infirmities and stammer.

rows.q: Roman public latrines had no toilet paper; visitors instead wiped with a sea sponge on a stick called a tersorium, which was rinsed in a bucket of water mixed with this acidic liquid.
rows.n: Seneca recorded a German gladiator who died by suicide using a tersorium to avoid the arena.

rows.q: Nero blamed Christians for the Great Fire of Rome in 64 AD, notoriously coating them in pitch and tying them to poles in his gardens to serve as these night fixtures.
rows.n: Tacitus noted that even Roman citizens hardened to spectacle ended up pitying the victims.

rows.q: During mummification, embalmers spent over a month desiccation-treating royal corpses in this naturally occurring, sodium-rich salt harvested from dry Egyptian lakebeds.
rows.n: The word passed through Greek and Arabic and ultimately gave sodium its chemical symbol, Na.

rows.q: Domitian was so paranoid about palace plots that he lined the portico walls where he walked with phengite stone, which acted as these reflective household objects.
rows.n: The polished stone allowed him to see anyone approaching from behind, though he was still assassinated in 96 AD.

rows.q: Carved high on an Iranian cliff to boast of Darius the Great, the trilingual Behistun Inscription was the cuneiform equivalent of this Egyptian artifact.
rows.n: Its Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian texts let linguists finally crack the cuneiform code.

rows.q: Under Cyrus and Darius, the Achaemenid Persian Empire was divided into provinces ruled by regional governors known by this Greek-derived title.
rows.n: Satraps ran regional taxation and defenses, shadowed by traveling royal inspectors known as the King’s Eyes.

rows.q: Persian heralds sent by King Darius demanded Greek submission by asking for two symbolic tokens: water and what companion substance?
rows.n: The Spartans reportedly tossed Darius’s ambassadors down a deep well, telling them to dig out both.

rows.q: In 330 BC, Alexander the Great burned the ceremonial Persian capital of Persepolis, reportedly in revenge for the Persian burning of this Greek landmark 150 years earlier.
rows.n: Xerxes had torched the temples atop the Acropolis in 480 BC during his invasion of Greece.

rows.q: Halting a war between the Medes and Lydians, Thales of Miletus stunned the ancient Mediterranean in 585 BC by predicting which sky phenomenon?
rows.n: The sudden midday darkness terrified both armies into dropping their weapons and negotiating a peace treaty.

rows.q: The Sacred Band of Thebes, the elite infantry strike force that crushed Sparta at the Battle of Leuctra, was composed of 150 pairs of what?
rows.n: Commander Gorgidas believed pairs of lovers would fight harder to protect one another and avoid disgrace.

rows.q: The chronologically oldest spoken greeting on the record, wishing peace to the cosmos, was delivered in this extinct language of southern Mesopotamia.
rows.n: The speaker translates roughly as ‘May all be well,’ followed on the track by a greeting in ancient Greek.

rows.q: Diogenes was the most eccentric champion of the Cynics, an ascetic philosophical school named after the ancient Greek word for this domestic animal.
rows.n: It comes from ‘kynikos’ (dog-like); Diogenes embraced a feral, shameless lifestyle on the streets.

rows.q: To humiliate a senator who had criticized him, Caligula forced the man to march for miles alongside his chariot wearing only this formal woolen garment.
rows.n: Togas were heavy and strictly ceremonial; running in one was both exhausting and a massive loss of dignitas.

rows.q: Discovered in Java in 1891 by Eugène Dubois, what extinct hominin species holds a Latin binomial name translating directly to “upright man”?
rows.n: Dubois originally dubbed his fossil find Pithecanthropus erectus, popularly known as Java Man.

rows.q: Until decimalization in 1971, Britain used the lowercase letter ‘d’ as the standard abbreviation for a penny, borrowing the initial from what ancient Roman silver coin?
rows.n: The system came from the Carolingian currency model: librae, solidi, and denarii (£, s, d).

rows.q: Before excavating Abu Simbel and hauling giant pharaonic statues to England, 6-foot-7 Italian explorer Giovanni Belzoni performed in London circuses billed as this biblical strongman.
rows.n: Belzoni could hoist an iron frame supporting twelve people on his shoulders.

rows.q: Before magnetic steel needles were invented, Han dynasty diviners built early south-pointing spoons carved out of this naturally magnetic iron mineral.
rows.n: The spoon balanced atop a polished bronze plate inscribed with constellations and compass points.

rows.q: Before paper, Mesopotamian scribes pressed reed styluses into wet clay. The resulting script is called cuneiform after the Latin word for this shape.
rows.n: A cut reed naturally created a triangular indentation when pressed at an angle into soft clay.

rows.q: The elite 10,000-man royal infantry guard of the Achaemenid Persian kings earned this death-defying nickname because any fallen member was immediately replaced.
rows.n: Herodotus recorded that their spears ended in silver or gold pomegranates instead of standard counterweights.

rows.q: When ancient Athenians voted to banish a dangerous politician, they scratched their verdict onto broken shards of this ubiquitous household material.
rows.n: An ostrakon was a broken piece of ceramic urn—ancient scrap paper reused for casting political ballots.

rows.q: Emperor Elagabalus shocked Rome by replacing Jupiter with a Syrian sun god whose sacred relic was not a statue, but a large black one of these fallen from the sky.
rows.n: The conical black stone of Emesa was paraded through Rome on a chariot before Elagabalus was assassinated in 222.

rows.q: The narrow pass of Thermopylae translates directly to English as the ‘Hot Gates’, taking its name from the local presence of these geological features.
rows.n: The sulfur-rich geothermal springs that gave the pass its name are still bubbling along the roadway today.

rows.q: Tutankhamun’s gold funerary mask features royal eyebrows and eye borders inlaid with this prized, deep-blue metamorphic rock, imported all the way from modern Afghanistan.
rows.n: The ancient Egyptians called it ‘khesbed’ and considered its starry blue hue sacred to the gods.

rows.q: The 6th-century Indian board game chaturanga, ancestor of modern chess, derived its name from a Sanskrit word meaning the four traditional divisions of this institution.
rows.n: Those divisions were infantry, cavalry, chariots, and war elephants, mirrored in modern chess pieces.

rows.q: To warm the rooms and plunge pools of Roman baths, furnaces forced hot air through hollow terracotta tiles beneath a raised floor, an engineering system called a what?
rows.n: The system was also adopted in wealthy northern villas to heat bedchambers during winter.

rows.q: Han dynasty expeditions across Central Asia sought the prized “Heavenly Horses” of the Fergana Valley, renowned for an affliction that made them appear to sweat this fluid.
rows.n: Skin parasites caused the horses to bleed when galloping, inspiring legends of divine steeds.

rows.q: For over 3,800 years, the Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest man-made structure on Earth, until finally surpassed in 1311 by a soaring cathedral in this English city.
rows.n: Lincoln Cathedral’s 525-foot central spire held the title until it blew down in a 1548 storm.

rows.q: Terracotta versions of this stringed bobbin toy, dating back to 440 BC, were dedicated to the gods by ancient Greek adolescents as an offering upon reaching adulthood.
rows.n: Greek vase paintings from the period show children dangling the toy from their fingers.

rows.q: Rather than private houses, the vast majority of ancient Rome’s working poor lived in multi-story, fire-prone tenement blocks known by the Latin word for what geographic feature?
rows.n: Augustus eventually set a height limit of seventy Roman feet to keep the timber-framed blocks from collapsing.

rows.q: Spartan men were able to train for war full-time because agricultural manual labor was forced onto which subjugated, state-owned underclass?
rows.n: Helots vastly outnumbered full Spartan citizens, prompting Sparta to declare ritual war on them each year.

rows.q: Marcus Licinius Crassus, who brutally crucified 6,000 rebellious slaves along the Appian Way, built much of his fortune running Rome’s first private one of these emergency crews.
rows.n: Crassus’s men would only douse burning buildings after the desperate owner agreed to sell the property at a discount.

rows.q: Long before his legendary adventures were etched in stone, the historical King Gilgamesh ruled this southern Mesopotamian city-state, famous for its massive mudbrick walls.
rows.n: Flourishing around 3200 BC, Uruk is often considered by historians to be the world’s very first true city.

rows.q: To arm millions of soldiers efficiently, Qin dynasty state foundries mass-produced this projectile weapon with standardized, interchangeable bronze trigger locks.
Sumerians drank their cloudy, unfiltered barley beer through long versions of this dining tool, crafted from hollow reeds or gold to bypass the mash floating on top.
Discovered in a walled-up library cave in Dunhuang, an 868 CE scroll of this sacred Buddhist work stands as the world’s oldest surviving dated, complete printed book.
rows.n: The text was block-printed on seven sheets of paper glued together into a sixteen-foot scroll.

rows.q: Concluded around 1259 BC following the Battle of Kadesh, the world’s earliest known parity peace treaty was struck between pharaoh Ramesses II and the king of this Anatolian empire.
rows.n: A replica of the treaty tablet hangs at the United Nations headquarters as a symbol of diplomacy.

rows.q: Beyond right angles and math, Pythagoras ran a secretive sect that strictly forbade its initiates from touching or eating this common legume.
rows.n: Pythagoras reportedly believed fava beans contained the souls of the dead because of their fleshy shape.

rows.q: Built by Pharaoh Sneferu at Dahshur after his workers miscalculated the Bent Pyramid, this rust-tinted monument was the first successful smooth-sided pyramid ever built.
rows.n: It owes its color to reddish limestone exposed after its white Tura limestone casing was stripped.

rows.q: Before Pericles famously moved its funds to Athens, the mutual defense pact against Persia kept its treasury on which sacred island, its namesake?
rows.n: The Delian League treasury funded Pericles’s lavish rebuilding of the Acropolis, sparking Spartan outrage.

rows.q: Ancient Mediterranean merchants tested the purity of gold coins without melting them by rubbing them against this dark slate-like mineral and inspecting the colored streak.
rows.n: The streak left on the stone was compared against needles of known alloy purity.

rows.q: Didius Julianus briefly ruled the Roman Empire in 193 AD by winning this kind of commercial event held by the Praetorian Guard after they murdered Pertinax.
rows.n: He promised each soldier 25,000 sesterces, outbidding the city prefect Titus Flavius Sulpicianus.

rows.q: At Saqqara in 1851, French archaeologist Auguste Mariette discovered the Serapeum, an underground necropolis holding twenty-four colossal stone sarcophagi for sacred specimens of this animal.
rows.n: Only one sacred Apis bull lived at a time, pampered as an earthly incarnation of the god Ptah.

rows.q: To discourage hoarding and luxury trade, Spartan lawmaker Lycurgus decreed that Sparta’s official currency be heavy rods forged from this cheap metal.
rows.n: Plutarch recorded that even a modest sum of iron spit-coins required an ox-cart to haul.

rows.q: Carved into the cliffs of Nubia, the smaller temple at Abu Simbel was dedicated to the goddess Hathor and this beloved chief queen of Ramesses II.
rows.n: Her tomb in the Valley of the Queens is famed for having some of Egypt’s best-preserved paintings.

rows.q: Dating to around 1208 BC, the black granite victory stele of Pharaoh Merneptah is renowned among biblical historians for containing the earliest known outside reference to this group.
rows.n: The hieroglyphic text boasts of Egyptian military triumphs, claiming ‘Israel is laid waste.’

rows.q: The Latin phrase ‘ab ovo usque ad mala’ referred to a complete Roman formal banquet from start to finish, translating literally as ‘from eggs all the way to’ what fruit?
rows.n: The phrase entered English as an idiom meaning from beginning to end, much like soup to nuts.

rows.q: Court inventor Zhang Heng built an earthquake detector in 132 CE that dropped a bronze ball from a dragon’s mouth into the open jaws of this amphibian waiting below.
rows.n: Eight dragons faced the cardinal directions, each perched over a matching toad to show the quake’s direction.

rows.q: Agatha Christie drew inspiration for her 1937 mystery Death on the Nile from years spent on Middle Eastern excavation digs alongside this prominent British archaeologist, her husband.
rows.n: Christie helped clean and photograph artifacts on his digs in Iraq and Syria, once using cold cream.

rows.q: When the teenage pharaoh Tutankhamun died suddenly without heirs, he was succeeded by this elderly grand vizier, whose two-letter name is the shortest of any pharaoh.
rows.n: Ay ruled for just four years and was buried in a tomb originally prepared for Tutankhamun.

rows.q: Centuries before the book of Exodus, the birth legend of this first Mesopotamian emperor tells of his mother placing him in a reed basket adrift on the Euphrates River.
rows.n: Fished out of the water by an irrigator, Sargon rose from royal cupbearer to ruler of history’s first empire.

rows.q: Julius Caesar once seized 1,500 pounds of this now-extinct giant fennel from the Roman treasury to fund the civil war, prized as both a gourmet seasoning and a contraceptive.
rows.n: It grew only along a narrow coastal strip of modern-day Libya and vanished by the first century AD.

rows.q: After working out in the palaestra, ancient Greek and Roman athletes scraped dirt, sweat, and olive oil off their skin using a curved bronze tool known by what name?
rows.n: Slaves collected the scraped-off mixture, called gloios, to sell to bathers as a medicinal rub.

rows.q: Convened in 1545 to push back against the Reformation, this Catholic church council met across eighteen years in northern Italy.
rows.n: The council standardized the Latin Tridentine Mass, which remained in use until the 1960s.

rows.q: Rallying her troops against the Spanish Armada at Tilbury, Elizabeth I famously claimed she had the heart and stomach of this kind of ruler.
rows.n: She declared: ‘I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman, but I have the heart and stomach of a king.’

rows.q: About a quarter of Johannes Gutenberg’s 42-line Bibles were printed on this calfskin material rather than paper.
rows.n: Producing a single vellum copy required the hides of over one hundred calves.

rows.q: While in hiding at Wartburg Castle disguised as Junker Jörg, Martin Luther spent ten weeks translating this part of the Bible into German.
rows.n: His translation of Erasmus’s Greek text helped standardize the modern German language.

rows.q: Baroque master Peter Paul Rubens painted The Descent from the Cross for the Cathedral of Our Lady in what Flemish port, famed for its diamond district?
rows.n: During its sixteenth-century peak, an estimated eighty percent of all European maritime trade passed through Antwerp.

rows.q: In 1212, thousands of unarmed youths marched across Europe expecting the Mediterranean Sea to part, in a doomed movement known by this name.
rows.n: Modern historians believe many participants weren’t actual children, but marginalized rural poor people.

rows.q: Byzantine ships defended Constantinople using this incendiary weapon, pumped through bronze siphons, which famously continued to burn on top of seawater.
rows.n: Its precise chemical recipe was a closely guarded state secret and remains unknown today.

rows.q: The Fourth Crusade went wildly off script in 1204 when Crusaders, heavily indebted to this maritime Italian republic, sacked Christian Constantinople instead.
rows.n: Doge Enrico Dandolo was in his nineties and blind when he directed the fleet against Constantinople.

rows.q: Overlooking Granada, this fortified palace complex with its iconic Court of the Lions was the last Moorish stronghold to fall in Spain in 1492.
rows.n: Its Arabic name translates to ‘the red one,’ likely due to the reddish clay bricks of its ramparts.

rows.q: In 1572, targeted assassinations of these French Protestants in Paris sparked the nationwide St. Bartholomew’s Day massacre.
rows.n: The killings began five days after the royal wedding of Protestant leader Henry of Navarre.

rows.q: Renaissance Florence’s Medici family rose to political influence through the Arte del Cambio, the powerful guild representing this profession.
rows.n: The guild operated from benches, or ‘banchi,’ in the Mercato Vecchio, giving us the modern word bank.

rows.q: Medieval town bells warned residents to bank their hearth fires each evening, creating this word from Old French for ‘cover the fire.’
rows.n: From ‘couvre-feu,’ it was strictly enforced because timber-and-thatch buildings burned easily.

rows.q: To ward off the Black Death, doctors carried pomanders filled with herbs to counteract this supposedly disease-spreading ‘bad air.’
rows.n: This theory persisted well into the 19th century until germ theory proved microbes caused infections.

rows.q: Named after the Hellenistic city of Pergamon, where production flourished after Egypt cut off papyrus supplies, what writing surface was made from stretched sheepskin?
rows.n: Finer grades made from calfskin were called vellum, preferred for luxury illuminated manuscripts.

rows.q: Henry VIII agreed to wed Anne of Cleves based on a flattering miniature portrait painted by this German-born court artist.
Before her lengthy marriage to Henry VIII, Catherine of Aragon was briefly married to this older Tudor prince who died in 1502.
rows.n: Arthur’s early death at Ludlow Castle at age 15 made ten-year-old Henry the heir apparent.

rows.q: Heavily refined in medieval Islamic astronomy, this handheld brass disc allowed sailors and scholars to calculate time and latitude using the stars.
rows.n: Geoffrey Chaucer even wrote an instruction manual on how to use one for his ten-year-old son, Lewis.

rows.q: He managed Henry VIII’s break with Rome and dissolved the monasteries, but this chief minister was beheaded after arranging the Cleves match.
rows.n: Henry later lamented Cromwell’s death, blaming his councillors for lying to him.

rows.q: Derived from the French word for a day’s work, this title belonged to a guild tradesman who earned daily wages while saving up to become a master.
rows.n: It comes from the Old French ‘journée,’ referring to the day’s wage earned before opening their own shop.

rows.q: After retaking Jerusalem in 1187, this chivalrous Kurdish sultan sent Richard the Lionheart fresh fruit, snow from Mount Hermon, and his own physician.
rows.n: Dante gave Saladin a surprisingly light sentence in the Inferno, placing him with virtuous pagans in Limbo.

rows.q: During the bloody Nika riots of 532, this Byzantine empress refused to flee, famously asserting that royal purple made a fine burial shroud.
rows.n: Before marrying Justinian, she worked as an actress, dancer, and mime in the Hippodrome.

rows.q: Heading home from the Third Crusade in disguise, this English king was captured near Vienna by Duke Leopold V and held for a massive ransom.
rows.n: Leopold was furious because Richard had cast Leopold’s banner into a ditch at Acre.

rows.q: Preaching to crowds at the Council of Clermont in 1095, this pope launched the First Crusade with the rallying cry ‘Deus vult!’ or ‘God wills it!’
rows.n: Byzantine Emperor Alexios I had only asked for a few mercenaries, not an invading wave of crusaders.

rows.q: First minted in 1252, this gold coin featuring the city’s heraldic lily became Europe’s trusted trade standard, named directly for Florence itself.
rows.n: It was struck with virtually 100 percent pure 24-carat gold, ensuring widespread trust across trade routes.

rows.q: Too poor for beeswax, medieval peasants lit their homes with smelly, smoky candles made from this rendered animal fat.
rows.n: Guilds for candlemakers were even split in two: the aristocratic Waxchandlers and the humble Tallowchandlers.

rows.q: In 1070, William the Conqueror founded Battle Abbey on the exact hill where this rival English monarch was slain during the Battle of Hastings.
rows.n: The high altar of the abbey church was placed directly over the spot where Harold allegedly fell.

rows.q: Before marrying England’s Henry II, this formidable queen took the cross on the Second Crusade alongside her first husband, King Louis VII of France.
rows.n: She brought along 300 of her own vassals, insisting on joining the military campaign in person.

rows.q: Born in the wake of the Black Death, this macabre artistic genre depicted dancing skeletons dragging mortals of every social rank to the grave.
rows.n: One of the earliest known murals of it was painted in 1424 at the Holy Innocents’ Cemetery in Paris.

rows.q: Founded by Norse settlers in 930 at Thingvellir, this national assembly of Iceland is often cited as the world’s oldest surviving parliament.
rows.n: The Lawspeaker had to recite one-third of the commonwealth’s legal code from memory each summer.

rows.q: Believing the Black Death was divine punishment, bands of penitents roved European towns whipping themselves raw under this Latinate name.
rows.n: Pope Clement VI outlawed them in 1349, alarmed by their anticlerical fervor and violent attacks on Jewish communities.

rows.q: For centuries, Italian city politics were torn between rival factions: the Ghibellines, who backed the Holy Roman Emperor, and the Guelfs, who backed this leader.
rows.n: Dante Alighieri was exiled from Florence due to internal factional infighting between White and Black Guelfs.

rows.q: Early printers created a folio by folding a sheet of paper once; folding it a second time produced this four-leaf book size.
rows.n: Most of Shakespeare’s plays were first sold in inexpensive quarto editions.

rows.q: To forge an alliance with Spain, Mary I married this monarch in 1554, briefly making him co-ruler and king consort of England.
rows.n: Three decades later, Philip sent the Spanish Armada against Mary’s half-sister Elizabeth.

rows.q: The Mongols’ westward blitz across the Levant was finally broken in 1260 at the Battle of Ain Jalut by this Cairo-based sultanate of former slave soldiers.
rows.n: Ain Jalut translates to the Spring of Goliath, fought in modern-day Israel.

rows.q: King John II coined the hopeful name Cape of Good Hope, replacing this gloomier, weather-beaten name Bartolomeu Dias had given it.
rows.n: Dias died twelve years later in 1500 when his ship sank in a storm off that very cape.

rows.q: Before dying at Stamford Bridge in 1066, this future king of Norway spent a decade in Constantinople commanding the Byzantine emperor’s Varangian Guard.
rows.n: He supposedly used the loot he carried back from Byzantium to claim the Norwegian throne.

rows.q: To stop raids on Paris, French king Charles the Simple signed the 911 Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, granting lands that became Normandy to this Viking leader.
rows.n: In legend, one of Rollo’s men pulled the king over backward rather than kneel to kiss his foot.

rows.q: Though displayed as a tapestry, the 11th-century Bayeux Tapestry depicting the Norman Conquest is actually an example of this textile art technique.
rows.n: It was stitched with wool yarn onto linen cloth, likely commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux.

rows.q: This first Protestant Archbishop of Canterbury put liturgy into English by compiling the landmark 1549 Book of Common Prayer.
rows.n: When burned at the stake by Mary I, he held the right hand that signed his recantations in the fire first.

rows.q: Securing their newly conquered English lands, the Normans rapidly threw up dozens of these two-part earthen mound and courtyard castles.
rows.n: The motte was the artificial hill topped with a wooden keep; the bailey held stables and quarters.

rows.q: Advocating for adult rather than infant baptism, this radical Reformation sect seized the German city of Münster in 1534.
rows.n: After retaking the city, Catholic authorities displayed the leaders’ corpses in cages hung from a church steeple.

rows.q: Strangled and burned at the stake in 1536, this scholar produced the first English Bible translated directly from Greek and Hebrew.
rows.n: Much of his phrasing survived unchanged into the 1611 King James Version.

rows.q: Starting from Tangier in 1325, this medieval Islamic scholar logged over 70,000 miles across Africa and Asia, dictating his travels in the Rihla.
rows.n: His journey took roughly thirty years, covering three times the distance Marco Polo traveled.

rows.q: Late medieval English towns employed laborers to muck out cesspits by night, known colloquially by this rhythmic title from an Old English word for privy.
rows.n: They could only work between 9 p.m. and 5 a.m., hauling human waste outside town walls to sell as fertilizer.

rows.q: Magellan got the glory, but this Basque navigator actually brought the battered Victoria and its 18 survivors home to Spain in 1522.
rows.n: Charles I granted him a coat of arms bearing a globe and the motto ‘You first encircled me.’

rows.q: Ruling England, Denmark, and Norway all at once in the early 11th century, this monarch forged what historians call the North Sea Empire.
rows.n: The famous legend of him commanding the incoming tide to stop was meant to show the limits of royal power.

rows.q: In damp harvests, rye fungus often caused agonizing burning sensations and hallucinations in an outbreak known as this saint’s fire.
rows.n: The Order of St. Anthony ran specialized hospitals to care for victims of ergotism across Europe.

rows.q: Aiming to fit classical poetry into pocket-sized volumes, Venetian printer Aldus Manutius debuted this slanted typeface around 1500.
rows.n: Manutius also popularized the modern use of the comma and the semicolon.

rows.q: When the Great Heathen Army seized it in 866, the English city of York became the Norse-ruled center of northern trade under this historical name.
rows.n: Coppergate excavations in the 1970s unearthed thousands of preserved Viking leather and wooden relics.

rows.q: The Portuguese Age of Discovery is traditionally dated to 1415, when Prince Henry the Navigator helped capture what Moroccan coastal city, later ceded to Spain?
rows.n: Portugal recognized Spanish control over the strategic Mediterranean port in the 1668 Treaty of Lisbon.

rows.q: Elizabeth I finally ordered the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, after Mary was caught plotting her assassination in this 1586 conspiracy.
rows.n: Spymaster Francis Walsingham used a double agent to intercept and decode Mary’s letters.

rows.q: Medieval Norse sagas mention this mysterious navigation aid, widely believed by modern researchers to be a polarizing crystal of Iceland spar.
rows.n: By finding the polarization rings of sunlight, navigators could locate the sun even on overcast days.

rows.q: After crushing Hungarian and Polish armies in 1241, Mongol forces abruptly withdrew from Europe due to the sudden death of this second Great Khan.
rows.n: Mongol princes returned home to Karakorum to take part in the kurultai to elect his successor.

rows.q: Crowned at thirteen and forced to ride into battle with bandages covering his skin, this ‘Leper King’ of Jerusalem held off Saladin for over a decade.
rows.n: He scored a stunning victory over Saladin at Montgisard in 1177 when he was just sixteen years old.

rows.q: To mislead the Axis about Mediterranean targets, British intelligence dropped a corpse carrying bogus invasion plans off the coast of this neutral country.
rows.n: The body was of a Welsh homeless man named Glyndwr Michael, who had died from eating rat poison.

rows.q: In 1957, pan-African leader Kwame Nkrumah led which former British colony to independence, making it the first sub-Saharan nation to break free?
rows.n: Nkrumah chose the name to honor a medieval trading empire located hundreds of miles to the northwest.

rows.q: A tearful Lee Kuan Yew announced Singapore’s sovereignty in 1965 after the island was unanimously voted out of this federation by its parliament.
rows.n: Singapore had joined the federation just two years earlier to escape British colonial rule.

rows.q: Codenamed Operation Ironclad, a 1942 British campaign aimed to seize this massive, Vichy-held Indian Ocean island before Japan could use it as a naval base.
rows.n: It was the first large-scale amphibious assault carried out by Allied forces during the war.

rows.q: The passive Soviet bug found hidden inside a wooden U.S. seal in Moscow was invented by this man, better known for an eerie electronic musical instrument.
rows.n: Dubbed The Thing by American intelligence, it was powered remotely by an external radio beam, needing no battery.

rows.q: New Zealand-born surgeon Harold Gillies pioneered this medical specialty after operating on the shattered jaws and faces of thousands of trench casualties.
rows.n: He opened a dedicated ward at Queen’s Hospital in Sidcup, developing the tubed pedicle skin graft.

rows.q: Convicted and executed by France as a German spy in 1917, the exotic dancer known as Mata Hari was actually born Margaretha Zelle in this neutral country.
rows.n: As a Dutch citizen, she had been able to travel freely across national borders during wartime.

rows.q: Brokering the 2015 Minsk II ceasefire agreement alongside France and Germany, this authoritarian president served as host in his nation’s capital, which he has ruled since 1994.
rows.n: The marathon talks lasted sixteen continuous hours overnight at Minsk’s Independence Palace.

rows.q: Enlisted as a private to receive rations, a Syrian brown bear named Wojtek famously helped carry artillery shells for this nation’s exiled army.
rows.n: Wojtek lived out his retirement eating fruit and smoking cigarettes at the Edinburgh Zoo.

rows.q: Flying a skull above crossed cutlasses, what 18th-century pirate captain sailed alongside Anne Bonny and Mary Read until his capture in Jamaica in 1720?
rows.n: He earned his nickname from his fondness for flamboyant white-and-patterned calico cotton coats and trousers.

rows.q: When the supertanker Torrey Canyon ran aground off England in 1967, the British military attempted to burn off the massive oil spill by dropping dozens of canisters of this incendiary jelly.
rows.n: Royal Air Force and Navy jets dropped high explosives, aviation fuel, and napalm in an effort to ignite the slick.

rows.q: Allied transport planes landed around the clock during the 1948 Berlin Airlift at this inner-city airport, famous for its massive semicircular Nazi-era terminal.
rows.n: The airfield was decommissioned in 2008 and transformed into one of the world’s largest public city parks.

rows.q: Led by the Kenya Land and Freedom Army, this violent 1950s anti-colonial rebellion prompted the British Empire to declare an eight-year emergency.
rows.n: Future Kenyan president Jomo Kenyatta was imprisoned for nearly a decade on charges of managing the uprising.

rows.q: When Emperor Akihito abdicated in 2019, he stepped down from a hereditary imperial seat poetically named for which autumnal flower?
rows.n: The imperial seal of Japan is a stylized 16-petal chrysanthemum.

rows.q: In a 1905 work, this German sociologist argued that Calvinist notions of predestination and worldly calling helped spur the rise of modern capitalism.
rows.n: The book, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, remains a sociology cornerstone.

rows.q: The Treaty of Versailles was formally signed on June 28, 1919, a date chosen because it was the exact fifth anniversary of what triggering event?
rows.n: The signing took place in the Hall of Mirrors, where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871.

rows.q: Norwegian commandos skied into the remote Vemork hydroelectric plant in 1943 to sabotage Nazi production of this substance needed for atomic research.
rows.n: Operation Gunnerside destroyed the electrolysis chambers without firing a single shot or losing a man.

rows.q: Jean-Bedel Bokassa’s lavish 1977 coronation as Central African Emperor was patterned after which French ruler’s 1804 ceremony?
rows.n: The ceremony consumed roughly a third of the impoverished country’s annual national budget.

rows.q: In 1953, the satirical Nova Scotia micronation of Outer Baldonia declared war on this superpower after its state newspaper attacked the island’s pro-fishing constitution.
rows.n: Outer Baldonia was founded by an American Pepsi executive who bought the island for bluefin tuna fishing.

rows.q: China’s last emperor, Pu Yi, abdicated as a child in 1912, only to be installed twenty years later as the puppet ruler of Manchukuo by this occupying nation.
rows.n: After World War II, Pu Yi was pardoned and spent his final years working as a gardener in Beijing.

rows.q: In East Africa, German general Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck waged a four-year guerrilla campaign, finally surrendering in Zambia nearly two weeks after what 1918 event?
rows.n: He only learned the war was over when a British magistrate delivered a telegram under a white flag.

rows.q: On Christmas Eve 1914 along the Western Front, British troops were stunned when German soldiers placed thousands of these festive objects atop their parapets.
rows.n: The German high command had shipped over 100,000 miniature trees and candles to the front lines.

rows.q: Under cover of mining the seafloor for manganese nodules, the CIA hired this eccentric billionaire in 1974 to build a salvage ship to raise a sunken Soviet submarine.
rows.n: Project Azorian recovered two nuclear torpedoes and several Soviet bodies, who received a proper burial at sea.

rows.q: Warren G. Harding’s presidency was rocked by the Teapot Dome scandal, named for a naval oil reserve located north of Casper in this U.S. state.
rows.n: Interior Secretary Albert Fall was sent to prison for taking bribes to lease the government lands to oil tycoons.

rows.q: Alderney, Jersey, and Guernsey were among this archipelago of British Crown dependencies, the only British territory occupied by German forces.
rows.n: Alderney was home to the only Nazi concentration camps built on British soil during the occupation.

rows.q: The 1962 peace accords that ended the Algerian War of Independence were signed in this French resort town, better known on supermarket shelves for water.
rows.n: Secret talks were held at the Hotel Royal on Lake Geneva under heavy guard due to right-wing terror plots.

rows.q: Surveyor of the Queen’s Pictures Anthony Blunt was stripped of his knighthood in 1979 after Margaret Thatcher unmasked him as the fourth man in this spy ring.
rows.n: Blunt had actually confessed to MI5 back in 1964 in exchange for immunity, but it was kept hidden for 15 years.

rows.q: Soviet lieutenant Viktor Belenko delivered a massive intelligence prize to the West in 1976 by flying an advanced Foxbat from this jet series to Japan.
rows.n: Western analysts were stunned to discover the advanced MiG-25 relied on vacuum tubes rather than transistors.

rows.q: Using inflatable rubber tanks, dummy planes, and massive sound recordings, the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops were an American deception unit nicknamed this.
rows.n: Their staged illusions tricked German forces about troop movements more than twenty times in Europe.

rows.q: Officially neutral Spain sent nearly 50,000 volunteers to fight for the Axis on the Eastern Front, organized into a force known by this colorful name.
rows.n: They wore the blue shirts of the Spanish Falange under standard German Army uniforms.

rows.q: When 18-year-old Victoria ascended the British throne in 1837, she succeeded this uncle, the Sailor King whose legitimate children had died in infancy.
rows.n: Victoria’s accession also ended the personal union between Great Britain and the Kingdom of Hanover.

rows.q: British artist Norman Wilkinson designed warship paint schemes not to hide vessels, but to confuse submarine aim using bold geometric stripes called what?
rows.n: Vorticist and cubist artists helped paint thousands of Allied vessels in high-contrast zigzag patterns.

rows.q: This German newsweekly paid millions of marks in 1983 for the forged Hitler Diaries, only to learn modern synthetic whiteners were laced into the paper.
rows.n: Reporter Gerd Heidemann bought them from forger Konrad Kujau, who claimed they were salvaged from a plane crash.

rows.q: While raiding Allied shipping across the Indian Ocean in 1914, the cruiser SMS Emden disguised herself as British by rigging a fake fourth one of these features.
rows.n: British cruisers in the region had four funnels, so the dummy stack tricked lookouts at a distance.

rows.q: A bust of Lenin overlooks the Arctic ghost town of Pyramiden, a Soviet coal-mining settlement deserted in 1998 on what Norwegian archipelago?
rows.n: The 1920 Svalbard Treaty granted Soviet Russia mining rights on Norwegian Arctic territory.

rows.q: Allied pilots flew treacherous supply missions from India to China over the Himalayas, an airlift route nicknamed this after its jagged profile.
rows.n: Flying over the eastern end of the mountain range claimed nearly 600 transport planes during the war.

rows.q: At the 1962 Glienicke Bridge swap dramatized in Bridge of Spies, downed U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers was traded for this Soviet intelligence officer.
rows.n: Abel was a pseudonym; his real name was Vilyam Fisher, and he was born in Newcastle upon Tyne.

rows.q: Thousands died when Mount Pelée erupted in 1902, but one of the few survivors in Saint-Pierre was spared by the thick stone walls of this specific room.
rows.n: Convict Ludger Sylbaris survived the deadly pyroclastic surge and was later pardoned, touring with Barnum & Bailey.

rows.q: During the 1910 Dreadnought hoax, a prankster troupe in turbans fooled the Royal Navy into touring its flagship, led in part by this future modernist author.
rows.n: Woolf and her Bloomsbury circle companions disguised themselves with stage paint to play an Abyssinian delegation.

rows.q: Catastrophe struck a Welsh mining community in 1966 when a mountain of colliery waste collapsed onto a school in this village, killing 116 children.
rows.n: The disaster prompted Parliament to pass the Mines and Quarries (Tips) Act to regulate industrial spoil heaps.

rows.q: A 1970s sex scandal that toppled British Liberal leader Jeremy Thorpe began when a botched hit on his former lover killed nothing except a family pet of this massive breed.
rows.n: Hitman Andrew Newton shot Norman Scott’s dog, Rinka, on a foggy moor before his gun jammed.

rows.q: Serving over eight years before her surprise 2023 resignation, who was the first woman and longest-tenured First Minister of Scotland?
rows.n: She joined the pro-independence Scottish National Party at just 16 years old.

rows.q: In Operation Bernhard, Nazi counterfeiters forced concentration camp inmates to forge millions of banknotes denominated in this Allied currency.
rows.n: By 1945, about ten percent of all British banknotes in circulation were thought to be Nazi forgeries.

rows.q: Captured in 1968, the crew of this U.S. Navy surveillance ship subtly flashed middle fingers in North Korean propaganda photos, claiming it was a Hawaiian good luck sign.
rows.n: The ship remains commissioned in the U.S. Navy today, though it is moored as a museum trophy in Pyongyang.

rows.q: The 1979 partial meltdown of the Unit 2 reactor at Pennsylvania’s Three Mile Island nuclear facility took place along this lengthy river named after an indigenous tribe.
rows.n: Twelve days before the disaster, the nuclear accident thriller The China Syndrome had opened in theaters.

rows.q: The only civilian casualties from enemy action on the continental U.S. during World War II died from a Japanese balloon bomb in this state.
rows.n: A pregnant woman and five children on a church picnic near Bly were killed when they moved the device.

rows.q: Facing execution for Nazi collaboration after World War II, Dutch painter Han van Meegeren saved his life by confessing he was an art forger who had faked works by this 17th-century master.
rows.n: To prove he wasn’t a traitor, he painted another ‘Vermeer’ under the watchful eyes of police guards in his cell.

rows.q: Despite pop culture depicting it as a red telephone, the famous 1963 Moscow-Washington hotline originally transmitted all messages using this text-based machine.
rows.n: Leaders chose text over voice to reduce the chance of misinterpretation or rushed emotional responses.

rows.q: Idling their engines to glide silently over German targets at night, the all-female Soviet 588th Night Bomber Regiment earned this sinister German nickname.
rows.n: They flew Polikarpov Po-2 biplanes, vintage wood-and-canvas aircraft originally built for crop dusting.

rows.q: Before war erupted, Kaiser Wilhelm II and Tsar Nicholas II exchanged urgent telegrams trying to stop it. Despite ruling Germany and Russia, they wrote in this shared language.
During the first spacewalk in 1965, this Soviet cosmonaut had to deliberately vent oxygen from his stiffened suit just to squeeze back through the airlock hatch.
rows.n: Ten years later he commanded the Soviet side of the joint Apollo-Soyuz mission.

rows.q: Before becoming the first woman in space aboard Vostok 6 in 1963, Valentina Tereshkova had no pilot training, but excelled in this extreme hobby.
rows.n: Her jumping skill was crucial because Vostok cosmonauts had to eject at 20,000 feet before landing.

rows.q: Deposed in 1952, King Farouk of Egypt famously predicted that in the end, only five kings would remain: the King of England and the kings of these objects.
rows.n: Farouk lived out his post-abdication exile in Italy and Monaco, notorious for his extravagant dining.

rows.q: Project Greek Island was a secret Cold War bunker built under the luxurious Greenbrier resort in West Virginia to protect this entire branch of government.
rows.n: The facility was maintained in constant readiness for 30 years until a Washington Post exposé revealed it in 1992.

rows.q: To build a US military base on Diego Garcia, Britain excised this archipelago from Mauritius just three years before granting Mauritius independence.
rows.n: In 2024, the UK government agreed to begin transferring sovereignty over the archipelago back to Mauritius.

rows.q: Seeking to shed the public stigma of Britain’s worst nuclear disaster—a raging graphite fire in 1957—the government renamed the Windscale reprocessing complex to this new moniker in 1981.
rows.n: The three-day blaze released radioactive iodine and polonium that contaminated farmlands across northern England.

rows.q: After taking Grenada to independence in 1974, Prime Minister Eric Gairy repeatedly urged the United Nations to launch a global study of these phenomena.
rows.n: Gairy was deposed in a 1979 coup while visiting New York to lobby the UN about unidentified flying objects.

rows.q: The Royal Navy dragged two motorboats through African bush to fight German gunboats on Lake Tanganyika, naming the vessels Toutou and this other French pet name.
rows.n: Commander Geoffrey Spicer-Simson claimed the names were Parisian slang for dog and cat.

rows.q: Months before Apollo 8 carried humans around the far side of the moon, the Soviet Zond 5 spacecraft flew two living specimens of this reptile around it and home.
rows.n: They survived the trip with only minor weight loss, becoming the first Earth creatures to circle the moon.

rows.q: Free French naval forces defied U.S. wishes in 1941 by liberating this tiny archipelago near Newfoundland from Vichy control.
rows.n: A local plebiscite backed de Gaulle by over 98%, embarrassing Washington which favored Vichy ties.

rows.q: Bricks were found stuffed into the pockets of Roberto Calvi, the Vatican’s ‘God’s Banker,’ when his body was discovered hanging beneath this London bridge in 1982.
rows.n: Five members of the Italian mafia and the secret P2 Masonic lodge were later tried for his murder but acquitted.

rows.q: A catastrophic nuclear exchange was avoided in September 1983 when this Soviet duty officer correctly dismissed a satellite alert of five U.S. ICBMs as a computer glitch.
rows.n: The false alarms were caused by unusual solar reflections off the tops of high-altitude clouds.

rows.q: John Paul Jones named his flagship, the Bonhomme Richard, in honor of the French translation of an almanac character created by which founding father?
rows.n: Franklin had published his Poor Richard’s Almanack under the pseudonym Richard Saunders.

rows.q: FBI director J. Edgar Hoover branded this 1969 Black Panther community initiative a grave propaganda threat because it fed thousands of impoverished schoolchildren daily.
rows.n: Hoover feared the wholesome service would win sympathy from moderate Black citizens and undermine the bureau.

rows.q: Nathan Leopold and Richard Loeb thought they committed the perfect 1924 Chicago murder, until detectives found this personal accessory with a rare patented hinge near the body.
rows.n: The unique hinge was sold to only three people in Chicago, quickly leading investigators straight to Leopold.

rows.q: Before moving its capital to Richmond to be closer to the front lines, the Confederate government was established and inaugurated in this Deep South city.
rows.n: Jefferson Davis took the oath of office on the portico of the Alabama State Capitol in February 1861.

rows.q: Blown off course on their voyage to Virginia, the Pilgrims drafted and signed the Mayflower Compact while anchored off the hook of what peninsula?
rows.n: They dropped anchor in Provincetown Harbor before sending scouting parties across the bay to modern-day Plymouth.

rows.q: In December 1942, Enrico Fermi and his team produced the world’s first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction under the abandoned football stands of this Midwestern university.
rows.n: The makeshift reactor, Chicago Pile-1, was assembled out of graphite blocks and raw uranium under Stagg Field.

rows.q: Twelve days after fleeing Ford’s Theatre, presidential assassin John Wilkes Booth was trapped and fatally shot in a burning tobacco barn in this state.
rows.n: Sergeant Boston Corbett fired the fatal shot against orders, claiming God commanded him to pull the trigger.

rows.q: Robber barons Jay Gould and Jim Fisk triggered the Black Friday panic of 1869 by attempting to corner the market on this asset, until the U.S. Treasury broke their scheme.
rows.n: President Ulysses S. Grant thwarted the syndicate by unexpectedly dumping $4 million in federal gold into Wall Street.

rows.q: When asked who owned the patent on his revolutionary polio vaccine in 1955, Jonas Salk famously replied: ‘Could you patent’ this celestial body?
rows.n: Salk’s decision not to patent the vaccine forfeited an estimated seven billion dollars in personal royalties.

rows.q: Eighteen Boston dignitaries met in 1772 to formally interrogate which enslaved teenage girl and verify she had actually written her poems?
rows.n: John Hancock signed the certificate confirming her authorship, which was published in her 1773 London edition.

rows.q: Watching the British flag lowered as Ghana gained independence in 1957, this American civil rights leader was moved to tears, later preaching his famous sermon ‘The Birth of a New Nation.’
rows.n: It was King’s first trip outside the United States, funded by his Montgomery congregation.

rows.q: The Culper Ring’s invisible ink was invented by physician James Jay, whose younger brother became the first person to hold what federal office?
rows.n: John Jay served as the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court from 1789 until 1795.

rows.q: Samuel Morse sent the first intercity telegraph message from the Capitol in 1844, transmitting ‘What hath God wrought’ to an engineer in this Maryland city.
rows.n: The receiver was Alfred Vail, Morse’s collaborator, stationed at the Mount Clare railroad depot.

rows.q: Opening in 1825, the Erie Canal transformed commerce by connecting Lake Erie to this major river, creating an all-water commercial route straight to Manhattan.
rows.n: Governor DeWitt Clinton marked the opening by pouring Lake Erie water into the Atlantic in the Wedding of the Waters.

rows.q: Theodore Roosevelt was awarded the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize for mediating the Treaty of Portsmouth, which ended a war between Russia and this nation.
rows.n: Roosevelt held the peace negotiations at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, Maine.

rows.q: During his brazen 1934 escape from an Indiana county jail, John Dillinger bluffed armed guards using a fake pistol whittled from a block of this common material.
rows.n: Dillinger rubbed black shoe polish over the whittled wooden gun to make it look like blued steel.

rows.q: Passed in 1733 and 1764, British trade acts sparked outrage in New England by heavily taxing imports of which sweet byproduct used to distill rum?
rows.n: Distillers routinely bribed customs officials or smuggled French West Indian molasses to avoid the duties.

rows.q: Cornelius Vanderbilt II flaunted his Gilded Age wealth by hiring architect Richard Morris Hunt to design this 70-room Newport ‘cottage,’ named for waves crashing on nearby cliffs.
rows.n: The Renaissance-style mansion covers 125,000 square feet, built for a family that used it about six weeks a year.

rows.q: While nearly every artist played the 1967 Monterey Pop Festival for free, organizers paid a standard $3,000 fee to this Indian sitar master for a four-hour afternoon set.
In 1918, Walter L. Jacobs founded a Chicago car rental outfit with twelve Model Ts, later selling to this transport mogul whose name remains on the fleet.
rows.n: Buyer John Hertz also founded the Yellow Cab Company in Chicago.

rows.q: A forestry expert provided crucial testimony in the Lindbergh kidnapping trial by tracing the wood grain of this homemade piece of equipment back to the suspect’s attic.
rows.n: Technologist Arthur Koehler matched saw marks and nail holes from a ladder rail directly to Hauptmann’s attic floor.

rows.q: To ensure its owner could never return, Quartermaster General Montgomery Meigs ordered Union dead buried around Robert E. Lee’s confiscated plantation, creating what cemetery?
rows.n: Meigs had dozens of officers buried in Mrs. Lee’s rose garden, just yards from the mansion’s front door.

rows.q: Alan Shepard’s 1961 suborbital flight aboard Freedom 7 made him the first American in space under this inaugural NASA crewed program named for a Roman god.
rows.n: Shepard spent over four hours on the pad before launch, famously telling controllers to ‘light this candle.’

rows.q: Refusing to enter a plea during the 1692 Salem witch trials, this 81-year-old farmer was pressed to death under heavy stones, famously demanding ‘more weight’.
rows.n: Because he never entered a plea, his estate could not be confiscated by the colony and passed to his sons-in-law.

rows.q: Boston surgeons made medical history in 1954 by performing the first successful organ transplant between identical twin brothers, swapping this organ.
rows.n: Surgeon Joseph Murray went on to win the 1990 Nobel Prize in Medicine for pioneering organ transplantation.

rows.q: Hanged at London’s Execution Dock in 1701, Scottish-born William Kidd insisted he was not a pirate, but a government-commissioned one of these wartime sea raiders.
rows.n: Kidd carried a Letter of Marque from King William III authorizing him to capture French ships and piratical craft.

rows.q: In 1901, J.P. Morgan bought out Andrew Carnegie to forge this leviathan, the first corporation in world history with a market capitalization exceeding one billion dollars.
rows.n: Carnegie scribbled his selling price on a scrap of paper; Morgan accepted without haggling over a single dollar.

rows.q: An ambiguous boundary in the 1783 Treaty of Paris created what geographic curiosity, the northernmost part of the contiguous United States, in Minnesota?
rows.n: British and American negotiators relied on John Mitchell’s flawed 1755 map, which misplaced the Lake of the Woods.

rows.q: The thirteen original Freedom Riders departed Washington, D.C. in May 1961 on commercial buses, intending to conclude their journey in this southern port city.
Before leading a 1794 uprising in Poland, which military engineer designed the formidable American fortifications at Saratoga and West Point?
rows.n: His river defenses and redoubts at Saratoga forced British General Burgoyne to surrender in 1777.

rows.q: Whose farm in Manassas was shelled during First Bull Run, prompting him to move to Appomattox Court House where Lee surrendered in his parlor four years later?
rows.n: Union officers ransacked McLean’s home after the surrender, walking away with his tables and chairs as souvenirs.

rows.q: Pioneering the aggressive tactics of modern single-issue lobbying, Wayne Wheeler spearheaded the push for Prohibition as the de facto leader of this powerful group.
rows.n: Wheeler’s coercive pressure tactic of mobilizing church voters against uncooperative lawmakers was called Wheelerism.

rows.q: Imprisoned at Dry Tortugas for aiding John Wilkes Booth, Dr. Samuel Mudd won an 1869 presidential pardon after heroic work treating this mosquito-borne viral outbreak.
rows.n: Mudd took charge of the prison hospital when the post physician died of yellow fever, saving dozens of lives.

rows.q: Subtitled “access to tools,” this counterculture catalog founded by Stewart Brand in 1968 provided communal homesteaders with everything from log-cabin guides to synthesizers.
rows.n: Steve Jobs famously praised it as a paper-and-typewriter precursor to Google, decades before the search engine.

rows.q: In their controversial 1921 murder trial, Nicola Sacco was an Italian immigrant shoemaker, while co-defendant Bartolomeo Vanzetti peddled this food from a cart.
rows.n: Vanzetti claimed he was selling cod and eels in Plymouth at the exact hour the Braintree robbery occurred.

rows.q: When Jacob Coxey led the first major protest march on Washington in 1894, police arrested him on the Capitol grounds for the trivial offense of walking on what?
rows.n: Coxey had brought over 500 unemployed men to D.C., but spent 20 days in jail purely for damaging the newly seeded lawn.

rows.q: Fleeing criminal charges in 1875, Boss Tweed was recognized in Spain because local police matched him to a Thomas Nast caricature published in this magazine.
rows.n: Spanish police believed the cartoon showed a kidnapper because Nast had drawn Tweed dragging little children.

rows.q: After being abducted in 1974 by the Symbionese Liberation Army, heiress Patty Hearst shocked the public by renouncing her family and adopting this codename from a Cuban revolutionary.
rows.n: The alias honored Tamara Bunke, known as Tania, an Argentine-born guerrilla who fought and died alongside Che Guevara.

rows.q: John Adams insisted that future Americans would celebrate which specific summer date with fireworks, the day Congress actually voted for independence?
rows.n: Congress approved the resolution of independence on July 2, but the formal text wasn’t adopted until July 4.

rows.q: When hijacker D.B. Cooper commandeered a Boeing 727 in 1971, he demanded four parachutes and $200,000 paid exclusively in bills of this denomination.
rows.n: The bundle of 10,000 twenties weighed roughly 21 pounds and had been pre-photographed by the FBI for serial numbers.

rows.q: During the bloody 1892 Homestead Strike, Andrew Carnegie retreated to a remote Scottish estate, leaving this ruthless manager to break the union and survive an assassin’s bullet.
rows.n: Anarchist Alexander Berkman shot Frick twice and stabbed him four times, but Frick was back at work within a week.

rows.q: Standing on the street watching workers leap from the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist fire convinced this social reformer to enter public life, later becoming FDR’s Secretary of Labor.
rows.n: Perkins became the first woman to hold a U.S. cabinet post, serving throughout FDR’s entire twelve-year presidency.

rows.q: Abraham Lincoln spoke for just over two minutes at Gettysburg. The crowd’s main event was a two-hour, 13,000-word oration by this Massachusetts diplomat.
rows.n: Everett wrote to Lincoln afterward, admitting Lincoln captured the battlefield’s spirit far better in two minutes.

rows.q: On October 12, 1492, lookout Rodrigo de Triana cried “Tierra!” after spotting land from the deck of this fastest of Columbus’s three ships.
rows.n: Columbus claimed he had seen a light hours earlier to keep the lifetime pension promised to Triana.

rows.q: To enforce court-ordered integration at Little Rock Central High in 1957, President Eisenhower bypassed local authorities by deploying 1,000 troops from this famed Army airborne division.
rows.n: Troops from the Screaming Eagles patrolled school hallways and escorted each of the Little Rock Nine individually.

rows.q: Titusville became the birthplace of the modern petroleum boom in 1859 when Edwin Drake struck oil at a depth of 69 feet in this northeastern state.
rows.n: Drake pioneered the use of an iron pipe casing to keep the borehole from collapsing as his team drilled.

rows.q: In 1898, future president Theodore Roosevelt earned fame leading the Rough Riders up Kettle and San Juan Hills just outside this historic eastern Cuban city.
rows.n: Roosevelt was nominated for the Medal of Honor for the charge, but it was not awarded until 2001 by Bill Clinton.

rows.q: The sensational press moniker given to 1947 murder victim Elizabeth Short was a nod to a film noir released the prior year, penned by this hard-boiled detective novelist.
rows.n: Chandler wrote the screenplay for The Blue Dahlia, starring Alan Ladd, which inspired reporters who covered the case.

rows.q: Promoted to brigadier general in 1864, Stand Watie became the highest-ranking Native American in the Confederate army and represented this Southeast nation.
rows.n: Watie was also the last Confederate general to formally surrender in the field, laying down his arms in June 1865.

rows.q: Though it served as the unofficial anthem of the Confederacy, the song ‘Dixie’ was composed in 1859 for a minstrel show based in this northern city.
rows.n: Lincoln loved the song and had a Union band play it at the White House right after Lee surrendered at Appomattox.

rows.q: Charles Hires marketed his root beer as ‘The Temperance Drink’ to teetotalers after debuting the commercial recipe in Philadelphia at this 1876 world’s fair.
rows.n: Hires, a Quaker pharmacist, discovered the herbal tea formula at a New Jersey boarding house while on his honeymoon.

rows.q: Wyatt is the legend, but this older brother was the actual town marshal who led the lawmen into the 1881 Gunfight at the O.K. Corral.
rows.n: Virgil took a bullet to the calf during the thirty-second shootout, while Wyatt emerged without a scratch.

rows.q: The Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction by handing the presidency to Rutherford B. Hayes over this New Yorker, who actually won the popular vote.
rows.n: Tilden needed just one disputed electoral vote to win, but a bipartisan commission awarded all twenty to Hayes.

rows.q: During the 1920s, foreign ships packed with liquor lingered three miles off the U.S. coast in an offshore black market corridor known by this nautical alliteration.
rows.n: Federal authorities eventually renegotiated maritime treaties to extend their boarding jurisdiction out to 12 miles.

rows.q: Benjamin Franklin was an ardent Patriot, but his estranged son William spent the Revolution loyal to the King as royal governor of what colony?
In 1863, Harriet Tubman became the first woman to lead an armed U.S. military assault when she guided Union gunboats up the Combahee River in this state.
rows.n: The raid destroyed several wealthy plantations and successfully liberated over seven hundred enslaved laborers.

rows.q: In April 1865, three of the four boilers exploded on this severely overcrowded Mississippi steamboat, killing around 1,200 returning Union prisoners of war.
In 1941, this head of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters pressured FDR into banning defense-industry discrimination by threatening a massive March on Washington.
rows.n: FDR issued Executive Order 8802 to avert the march, though Randolph eventually helped lead the 1963 rally anyway.

rows.q: Locked out of their WPA theater in 1937, the cast of Marc Blitzstein’s pro-union musical The Cradle Will Rock performed the show from this unusual location to dodge union bans.
rows.n: Union rules barred them from stepping on stage, so actors stood up from paid seats across the house to sing.

rows.q: The four freshmen who launched the 1960 Greensboro sit-in at a Woolworth’s lunch counter were all enrolled at this historically Black North Carolina university.
rows.n: Joseph McNeil, Franklin McCain, Ezell Blair Jr., and David Richmond were inspired by Gandhi’s nonviolent protests.

rows.q: When Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters drove their acid-fueled bus Furthur across America in 1964, the man behind the wheel was this real-life muse for Jack Kerouac.
rows.n: Cassady was the manic, fast-talking inspiration for Dean Moriarty in Kerouac’s 1957 classic On the Road.

rows.q: Prompted by wartime religious sentiment, the motto ‘In God We Trust’ appeared on American money for the first time in 1864, stamped onto this bronze coin.
rows.n: The coin didn’t last long; Congress discontinued the odd two-cent denomination less than a decade later in 1873.

rows.q: While serving an eleven-year sentence on Alcatraz, Al Capone passed the time by playing this stringed instrument in the inmate band, the Rock Islanders.
rows.n: He was granted permission to practice in the shower room to avoid conflicts with inmates who hated his playing.

rows.q: Captured and held as a Confederate POW in Richmond, this pioneering battlefield surgeon remains the only woman to ever receive the Medal of Honor.
rows.n: Congress revoked hundreds of Medals of Honor in 1917, including hers, but President Jimmy Carter restored it in 1977.

rows.q: A former classics professor with a knack for numbers, James A. Garfield published an original, trapezoid-based proof of what ancient mathematical theorem in 1876?
rows.n: Garfield worked out the proof in a math chat with other congressmen, later publishing it in a math journal.

rows.q: Originally founded under the name Lancaster, this Midwestern state capital was rebranded in 1867 to honor a recently assassinated commander-in-chief.
rows.n: Confederate sympathizers had opposed moving the capital from Omaha, so rivals named it after Lincoln to spite them.

rows.q: Set in place in 1884, the lightning-defying pyramid at the very apex of the Washington Monument is made of this metal, which was as costly as silver at the time.
rows.n: Before the Hall-Héroult smelting process made it cheap, aluminum was considered an exotic luxury.

rows.q: At age 36, he electrified the 1896 Democratic convention with his “Cross of Gold” speech, capturing the first of his three presidential nominations.
rows.n: Bryan lost all three of his general election campaigns, falling twice to McKinley and once to Taft.

rows.q: Fulfilling a campaign promise to get a hypoallergenic dog for their daughters, the Obamas welcomed a Portuguese Water Dog named Bo, a gift from which long-serving Massachusetts senator?
rows.n: Kennedy, who owned several Portuguese Water Dogs himself, had endorsed Obama early in 2008.

rows.q: Carved into the granite pediment above the entrance to Grant’s Tomb in Manhattan is this simple three-word phrase, lifted from his 1868 campaign letter: ‘Let Us Have _____.’
rows.n: The phrase became a national healing slogan in the turbulent years of early Reconstruction.

rows.q: In the summer of 1864, Lincoln’s sitting vice president Hannibal Hamlin reported for two months of active coastal defense duty in Maine, serving at this humble enlisted rank.
rows.n: Hamlin spent his summer peeling potatoes and doing guard duty at Fort McClary instead of campaigning.

rows.q: After her husband suffered a massive, debilitating stroke in October 1919, this first lady effectively ran the executive branch for over a year, deciding which matters reached his bedside.
rows.n: Her secretive period at the helm was later nicknamed the “petticoat presidency.”

rows.q: In 1977, the president’s colorful, brew-loving younger brother licensed his name to this short-lived commercial lager, marketed with the tagline, “I had it brewed up just for me.”
rows.n: Billy Carter earned an estimated $500,000 in royalties before sales abruptly dried up in 1978.

rows.q: Before serving as the sixth U.S. president, which Massachusetts statesman headed the American commission that negotiated the 1814 Treaty of Ghent?
rows.n: His delegation included future Whig leader Henry Clay, who clashed frequently with the austere, early-rising Adams.

rows.q: While fishing alone in his hometown of Plains, Georgia in 1979, Jimmy Carter was startled when this unlikely swimming animal aggressively approached his boat, forcing him to paddle it away.
Seeking relief from the paralysis caused by polio, Franklin D. Roosevelt spent years rehabilitating in the mineral waters of this Georgia town, where he died in 1945.
rows.n: FDR bought the entire run-down resort in 1926 and turned it into a world-renowned polio treatment center.

rows.q: Ratified under Carter to return the Canal Zone to Panama, the 1977 treaties abolished the U.S. territory where this 2008 Republican presidential nominee was born at Coco Solo Naval Air Station.
rows.n: Congress passed a bipartisan resolution in 2008 confirming he was a natural-born citizen eligible for office.

rows.q: Five days before dying of acute gastroenteritis in 1850, Zachary Taylor reportedly binged on raw cherries and iced glasses of this beverage during a July 4th celebration.
rows.n: His body was exhumed in 1991 to test rumors of arsenic poisoning, but forensic tests found only normal trace levels.

rows.q: “Who am I? Why am I here?” Ross Perot’s running mate opened the 1992 vice-presidential debate with that memorable line. Name this decorated vice admiral.
rows.n: Stockdale spent over seven years as a prisoner of war in Vietnam and received the Medal of Honor.

rows.q: Franklin D. Roosevelt was placed on the American dime in 1946 largely to honor his role in founding this charity, originally created to battle polio.
rows.n: Comedian Eddie Cantor coined the charity’s name in 1938 as a pun on the newsreel series ‘The March of Time.’

rows.q: In 1837, Martin Van Buren’s running mate Richard Mentor Johnson became the only vice president ever chosen by this legislative body after electors balked at his personal life.
rows.n: Electors objected to his open, lifelong relationship with Julia Chinn, an enslaved woman who managed his estate.

rows.q: Section 2 of the 25th Amendment, which allows a president to fill a vice-presidential vacancy, was used for the first time in 1973 after the resignation of this politician.
rows.n: Agnew resigned after pleading no contest to tax fraud stemming from kickbacks he accepted while in Maryland politics.

rows.q: Long before his scandal-plagued administration, Warren G. Harding built his wealth and local influence as the owner and publisher of The Marion Star, a newspaper in what state?
rows.n: Harding bought the struggling paper for just $300 in 1884 with two partners and turned it around.

rows.q: Dying of throat cancer and penniless after a Wall Street swindle, Ulysses S. Grant raced to finish his memoirs, published posthumously in 1885 by what legendary American author?
rows.n: Twain gave Julia Grant a 70% royalty, generating about $450,000 for the president’s widow.

rows.q: Best remembered for an 1890 antitrust law, this Ohio politician served as Treasury secretary and Secretary of State while his brother William fought as a famous Union general.
rows.n: His older brother, General William Tecumseh Sherman, famously marched Union troops through Georgia to the sea.

rows.q: Both John F. Kennedy and his assassin Lee Harvey Oswald were treated and pronounced dead inside the emergency facilities of this Dallas hospital.
rows.n: Jack Ruby, who fatally shot Oswald, also died at Parkland three years later from a pulmonary embolism.

rows.q: Calvin Coolidge was sent this masked mammal by a supporter intending it for Thanksgiving dinner, but the family adopted it as a White House pet named Rebecca.
rows.n: Rebecca was walked on a leash around the grounds and had her own house built in a South Lawn tree.

rows.q: Harry Truman’s number two, Alben Barkley, popularized this informal four-letter moniker for the vice presidency after his grandson coined it from his official title.
rows.n: Barkley loved the nickname and used it widely, though his successor Richard Nixon disliked it and banned its use.

rows.q: Lincoln was not the only target on April 14, 1865. Conspirator Lewis Powell invaded the home of this Secretary of State, who survived despite being repeatedly stabbed.
rows.n: Seward was already bedridden from a carriage crash, and an iron surgical collar helped deflect Powell’s knife blows.

rows.q: Alf Landon’s lopsided defeat in 1936 was so severe that the Kansas governor carried only Vermont and this other New England state.
rows.n: The wipeout inspired the wry political slogan: “As Maine goes, so goes Vermont.”

rows.q: Hillary Clinton scored a Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album in 1997 for the audio recording of this bestselling book on child-rearing, titled after an African proverb.
rows.n: She donated all royalties from the book to children’s hospitals across the country.

rows.q: Following the 1981 attempt on Ronald Reagan’s life, this Secretary of State sparked controversy by telling reporters in the press room, “As of now, I am in control here.”
rows.n: Haig spoke inaccurately; under the Presidential Succession Act, the Speaker of the House and Senate pro tem came first.

rows.q: Long before taking the oath of office, a 28-year-old Gerald Ford appeared in uniform on the April 1942 cover of what iconic women’s magazine alongside his model girlfriend?
rows.n: Ford worked as a male model while attending Yale Law School, earning about $10 an hour.

rows.q: Hoping to attract War Democrats in 1864, Abraham Lincoln ran for reelection under the banner of this temporary coalition party rather than the Republican label.
rows.n: The coalition chose Tennessee Democrat Andrew Johnson as Lincoln’s running mate to balance the ticket.

rows.q: In 1886, he became the only U.S. president to wed inside the White House, marrying 21-year-old Frances Folsom in the Blue Room.
rows.n: Frances was the youngest First Lady in U.S. history and became an immediate fashion celebrity.

rows.q: LBJ made history in 1966 by appointing Robert C. Weaver as the first African American cabinet secretary, placing him in charge of this newly created department.
rows.a: Department of Housing and Urban Development
rows.n: Weaver held three degrees from Harvard, including an economics doctorate earned in 1934.

rows.q: James G. Blaine’s 1884 bid imploded in New York after he failed to condemn a supporter who smeared Democrats as the party of “Rum, Romanism, and” this third R-word.
rows.n: The insult incensed Irish Catholic voters, tipping New York and the presidency to Grover Cleveland.

rows.q: After losing his reelection bid and his party’s backing, Martin Van Buren made an 1848 comeback bid as the presidential nominee of what anti-slavery third party?
rows.n: Van Buren won no electoral votes, but his candidacy siphoned enough New York votes to defeat Democrat Lewis Cass.

rows.q: James K. Polk had the shortest post-presidency in American history, dying just 103 days after leaving office during an outbreak of this bacterial waterborne disease.
rows.n: Polk fell ill during an exhausting farewell tour of the American South following his single term.

rows.q: In 1861, Abraham Lincoln accepted honorary citizenship from what European republic, founded in 301 AD by a Christian stonemason?
rows.n: Lincoln wrote back praising the small nation as an enduring proof that government based on freedom can survive.

rows.q: While serving as sitting vice president, this future Confederate general ran for president in 1860 on the Southern Democratic ticket.
rows.n: At age 36, Breckinridge remains the youngest vice president in American history.

rows.q: Weeks before his sole face-off with Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan debated this independent candidate and former Illinois congressman in September 1980.
rows.n: Carter boycotted the debate because he refused to share a stage with a third-party contender.

rows.q: When William Henry Harrison died in 1841, John Tyler insisted he inherited the full office rather than an acting title, prompting bitter opponents to call him by this nickname.
rows.n: Tyler established the crucial precedent that the vice president fully assumes the presidency upon a vacancy.

rows.q: When George Wallace launched his 1968 third-party campaign, he alarmed voters by picking this retired Air Force general who casually suggested using nuclear weapons.
rows.n: Wallace’s aides spent the rest of the campaign trying to keep LeMay away from television cameras.

rows.q: Andrew Johnson’s 1868 impeachment was triggered when he breached the Tenure of Office Act by trying to dismiss this stubborn Secretary of War inherited from Lincoln.
rows.n: Stanton literally barricaded himself inside his War Department office for weeks to prevent his removal.

rows.q: At the 1901 Pan-American Exposition, Leon Czolgosz approached William McKinley and fired two shots from a revolver concealed beneath this ordinary cloth item.
rows.n: Guards mistook the wrapped handkerchief for a bandage and assumed Czolgosz was merely nursing an injured hand.

rows.q: To prevent household staff or guests from eavesdropping on private conversations, Herbert and Lou Henry Hoover frequently spoke this Asian language, which they learned while living abroad.
rows.n: The couple lived in Tianjin, China, during the 1899 Boxer Rebellion while Herbert worked as a mining engineer.

rows.q: Accused by Republicans of accidentally stranding his Scottish Terrier on the Aleutian Islands and sending a Navy destroyer to fetch him, FDR fired back in his famous 1944 “_____ speech.”
rows.n: FDR joked that while he and his family didn’t mind personal attacks, his dog’s “Scotch soul was furious.”

rows.q: Theodore Roosevelt once lamented, “I can either run the country or I can attend to” this headstrong eldest daughter, who famously smoked cigarettes on the White House roof.
rows.n: She carried a pet green snake named Emily Spinach in her purse and lived to age 96.

rows.q: He won an absolute majority of the popular vote in 1876, but lost the presidency by one electoral vote after a special commission awarded all disputed ballots to his rival.
rows.n: Tilden accepted the ruling peacefully to prevent a renewed constitutional crisis after the Civil War.

rows.q: Before shocking political insiders by winning the 1940 Republican nomination, this utility executive had never held elected public office or high military rank.
rows.n: Willkie had been an enrolled Democrat until late 1939, just months before launching his campaign.

rows.q: Calvin Coolidge learned of Warren G. Harding’s death while visiting Vermont, where his father administered the oath of office in his official capacity as this state official.
rows.n: Coolidge repeated the oath quietly in Washington to avoid any legal challenge over a state notary administering it.

rows.q: In a bold departure from his conservative father’s path, Ronald Reagan’s son Ron dropped out of Yale in 1976 to dance professionally with this acclaimed New York-based ballet company.
rows.n: The Secret Service accompanied him on tour, sitting quietly in the wings and backstage.

rows.q: Gravely ill with tuberculosis, Franklin Pierce’s running mate William R. King became the only vice president sworn into office on foreign soil, doing so on this island.
rows.n: King died just six weeks into his term after returning home to Alabama, having never presided over the Senate.

rows.q: Six days a week from 1935 to 1962, Eleanor Roosevelt published this syndicated daily newspaper column sharing her travels, opinions, and White House routine.
rows.n: The only times she missed her daily deadline were immediately following FDR’s death in 1945.

rows.q: Sitting alongside Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre was this Union Army major, who was severely slashed by John Wilkes Booth while attempting to stop him.
rows.n: Deeply traumatized by the night, Rathbone later went mad in 1883 and murdered his wife Clara, who was also in the box.

rows.q: In 1952, long before his presidency, young naval lieutenant Jimmy Carter led a hazardous cleanup of a partially melted down nuclear reactor in what country?
rows.n: The incident at Chalk River Laboratories near Ottawa was one of the world’s first major nuclear reactor accidents.

rows.q: Calvin Coolidge’s VP Charles Dawes won a Nobel Peace Prize, but pop charts know him for co-writing this 1958 number-one hit.
rows.n: Dawes composed the tune in 1911 as ‘Melody in A Major.’ Carl Sigman added lyrics decades later.

rows.q: Theodore Roosevelt only landed on the 1900 GOP ticket because William McKinley’s first vice president, this New Jersey politician, died of heart failure in 1899.
rows.n: New York bosses pushed TR into the VP spot to strip his power, not anticipating McKinley would be assassinated.

rows.q: Stretching 19,000 miles, the Pan-American Highway is interrupted only by this notoriously swampy 60-mile break between Panama and Colombia.
rows.n: Heavy rainforest and environmental concerns have blocked efforts to bridge the gap with asphalt since the 1970s.
