rows.q: Akrotiri and Dhekelia are military base areas retained by the UK after Cyprus became independent, making them the only British overseas territories to officially use this currency.
rows.n: They adopted the euro in 2008 alongside the Republic of Cyprus to simplify civilian trade and wages.

rows.q: Spoken by eighty million people across Indonesia’s most populous island, what is the world’s largest language lacking national official status?
rows.n: Bahasa Indonesia was chosen over Javanese as the official tongue in 1945 to avoid ethnic favoritism.

rows.q: Seeking a buffer against Venice, the Republic of Ragusa ceded a strip of land in 1699 to the Ottoman Empire, giving this modern Balkan country its only coastline.
rows.n: The 12-mile coastal strip around Neum divided Croatia’s mainland until the Peljesac Bridge opened in 2022.

rows.q: Named by French colonizers for a river network, Upper Volta changed its name in 1984 to this nation, whose moniker translates to “Land of Incorruptible People.”
rows.n: Thomas Sankara combined words from two indigenous languages, Moore and Dyula, to create the new national name.

rows.q: Liechtenstein’s national anthem, ‘Oben am jungen Rhein’, is sung to the exact same melody as the royal anthem of which European island nation?
rows.n: It shares the tune of God Save the King, which was once used by dozens of royal anthems across Europe.

rows.q: Known as the Triple Frontier, the busy border confluence of the Iguazu and Paraná rivers links Brazil, Argentina, and this landlocked third neighbor.
rows.n: The tripoint is marked by stone obelisks painted in each country’s national colors.

rows.q: Because catastrophic floods along its course frequently reshaped northern China, this silt-laden waterway was dubbed ‘China’s Sorrow.’
rows.n: Its distinct color comes from loose loess sediment eroded from the Loess Plateau.

rows.q: Though an autonomous archipelago belonging to Finland, the Åland Islands are entirely monolingual, designating this Scandinavian language as their only official tongue.
rows.n: The League of Nations affirmed Finnish sovereignty in 1921 on the condition that Swedish culture be protected.

rows.q: Once known as the British crown colony of Basutoland, this mountainous monarchy changed its name in 1966 and is entirely surrounded by which single country?
rows.n: It is one of only three enclaved sovereign states in the world, alongside San Marino and Vatican City.

rows.q: Reflecting Holy See tradition, automated teller machines operated by the Vatican Bank famously offer customer prompts in this classical language.
Ushuaia, often celebrated as the southernmost city in the world, overlooks a strait in Tierra del Fuego named after this historic British survey vessel.
rows.n: Robert FitzRoy mapped the passage before returning on the famous 1831 voyage that carried Charles Darwin.

rows.q: Faroese engineers made civil engineering history in 2020 by opening an undersea road tunnel featuring the world’s first underwater one of these circular junctions.
rows.n: The Eysturoyartunnilin roundabout features an illuminated central pillar resembling an enormous jellyfish.

rows.q: Discovered by Walter Raleigh, Pitch Lake on southwest Trinidad is the world’s largest natural deposit of this sticky black substance used to pave roads.
rows.n: Raleigh used the lake’s thick natural bitumen to caulk the hull of his ships during an expedition in 1595.

rows.q: Al Capone reportedly stayed at the Hotel Robert while coordinating bootlegging on this French archipelago just 12 miles off Newfoundland.
rows.n: France retained the territory after the 1763 Treaty of Paris ceded the rest of New France to Britain.

rows.q: Defying the usual rules of marine biology, Lake Nicaragua is home to a famous freshwater-tolerant population of this aggressive, stocky apex predator.
rows.n: They swim up the rapids of the San Juan River from the Caribbean Sea, leaping like salmon to reach the lake.

rows.q: To make sports jerseys and beer labels less crowded, the Czech Republic officially registered this shorter, one-word English alternative with the UN in 2016.
rows.n: Despite government promotion, the shorter moniker received mixed reactions at home, with many citizens preferring the full form.

rows.q: Notoriously stormy, this 14-mile strait separates the North and South Islands of New Zealand.
rows.n: Ferry crossings are often delayed or cancelled because strong winds are funneled through the gap.

rows.q: Connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans south of Cape Horn, this notoriously rough 500-mile-wide strait is named for an English Elizabethan privateer.
rows.n: Francis Drake was blown south of Tierra del Fuego in 1578, proving open water connected the two oceans.

rows.q: Led by Kwame Nkrumah in 1957, this became the first sub-Saharan colony to gain independence, dropping its precious-metal nickname to become Ghana.
rows.n: Nkrumah chose the name Ghana to evoke a medieval trading empire, even though it lay hundreds of miles to the northwest.

rows.q: Sharing a heavily fenced border with Morocco, this autonomous city sitting opposite Gibraltar gives Spain one of its two permanent footholds on mainland Africa.
rows.n: Portugal ceded Ceuta to Spain in 1668 under the Treaty of Lisbon.

rows.q: A Marxist military regime dumped the kingdom-linked name Dahomey in 1975, renaming the West African nation after which coastal bight?
rows.n: Ironically, the historic Kingdom of Benin was located in what is now modern southern Nigeria, not within Benin’s borders.

rows.q: The floodwaters that sustain Botswana’s vast inland Okavango Delta originate hundreds of miles away in the wet central highlands of this Portuguese-speaking nation.
rows.n: It begins as the Cubango River before cutting across Namibia’s Caprivi Strip into Botswana.

rows.q: Under the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, Norway was granted sovereignty over the Arctic archipelago, but this foreign power still operates an active coal mining settlement at Barentsburg.
rows.n: The treaty lets all 46 signatory states exploit mineral rights visa-free, which only Russia actively does.

rows.q: Flanked by the Sea of Okhotsk and the Bering Sea, this 780-mile Russian peninsula holds dozens of active volcanoes.
rows.n: Because of its submarine bases, the entire peninsula was sealed off to outsiders until 1990.

rows.q: Chile’s hyper-arid Atacama Desert owes its dryness partly to this cold ocean current, named for a Prussian naturalist, that sweeps up the coast.
rows.n: Alexander von Humboldt mapped the chilly northward flow along South America’s west coast in 1802.

rows.q: Presumed extinct for 170 years, the black-browed babbler was found in 2020 on Borneo, an island shared by Indonesia, Malaysia, and what tiny sultanate?
rows.n: Two local men caught the bird by chance in South Kalimantan, took photos, and released it back unharmed.

rows.q: Separated from the Russian mainland by Lithuania and Belarus, the exclave of Kaliningrad sits on roughly 90 percent of the world’s extractable reserves of this fossilized resin.
rows.n: The Baltic coastline around Kaliningrad has yielded amber since the days of ancient Roman trade routes.

rows.q: Grytviken’s cemetery on this mountainous British overseas territory holds the grave of polar explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton.
rows.n: His widow insisted he be laid to rest there rather than having his body brought back to England.

rows.q: Marking the British Empire’s final territorial annexation, the Royal Navy landed a party in 1955 to claim this isolated granite islet in the North Atlantic.
rows.n: London annexed the uninhabited rock to stop Soviet vessels from observing missile tests off the Hebrides.

rows.q: In 1986, a lethal limnic eruption at this Cameroonian crater lake silently released a massive cloud of carbon dioxide, suffocating more than 1,700 people.
rows.n: Engineers later installed degassing pipes extending to the lake floor to bleed off CO2 safely.

rows.q: Enjoying self-governing monastic status within Greece, Mount Athos has enforced an imperial decree since 1060 that strictly bars what group of living beings from its shores?
rows.n: The ban applies to domestic animals too, though female cats are quietly tolerated to hunt mice.

rows.q: Nocturnal thunderstorms ignite thousands of times per hour over this large, brackish Venezuelan lake connected to the Caribbean by a narrow strait.
Captain Cook named an archipelago after a blustery group of Scottish islands. In 1980, that Pacific chain declared independence under what four-syllable name?
rows.n: Before independence as Vanuatu, the New Hebrides was jointly administered by Britain and France as a condominium.

rows.q: Under British pressure in the late 1960s, the entire Chagossian population was evicted to make way for a military base on this Indian Ocean atoll.
Alongside the Gold, Slave, and Ivory Coasts, historic West African trade maps included this culinary-named coastline corresponding to modern Liberia.
rows.n: It was named for melegueta pepper seeds, which traders also called ‘grains of paradise.’

rows.q: Military leader Phibunsongkhram transformed Siam into Thailand in 1939, adopting a root word that famously translates into English as what adjective?
rows.n: The rename underscored that it was the only Southeast Asian nation never colonized by a European power.

rows.q: Shared by Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, this large Alpine lake is the only body of water in Europe with no agreed-upon international borders across its main basin.
rows.n: Each country holds a different legal view on where its borders lie in the middle of the lake.

rows.q: Across the border-riddled enclave town of Baarle, a house that straddles the Dutch and Belgian frontier determines its nationality by the location of this exterior feature.
rows.n: If the boundary line passes straight through the front door, the building gets two separate street numbers.

rows.q: Great Britain first captured Gibraltar in 1704, but Spain formally ceded the strategic territory nine years later under this landmark European peace treaty.
rows.n: The same 1713 treaty also ended the War of the Spanish Succession.

rows.q: Polish explorer Paul Strzelecki named this highest peak on mainland Australia in 1840 after a leader of the American Revolution.
rows.n: Strzelecki thought the summit resembled the memorial mound built for Tadeusz Kosciuszko in Krakow.

rows.q: Towering over the borders of Venezuela, Brazil, and Guyana, the tabletop mountain Mount Roraima inspired this 1912 Arthur Conan Doyle prehistoric adventure novel.
rows.n: Botanist Everard im Thurn’s 1884 summit expedition sparked Conan Doyle’s tale of surviving dinosaurs on a plateau.

rows.q: Though geographically an extension of the Horn of Africa, this alien-looking island known for dragon’s blood trees is sovereign territory of Yemen.
rows.n: Roughly a third of its plant life is found nowhere else on the planet.

rows.q: In 1961, a volcanic eruption forced the complete evacuation of Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, the lone settlement on this British Atlantic island.
rows.n: Nearly the whole population returned two years later after geologists declared the volcano dormant.

rows.q: Governed for over four centuries by a hereditary Seigneur, this car-free Channel Island was widely called Europe’s last feudal state until its first democratic election in 2008.
rows.n: Cars remain banned; residents get around by bicycle, horse-drawn carriage, or tractor.

rows.q: Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across an expansive lake-like widening of the Congo River that was once named for this Welsh-American explorer.
rows.n: Now called Pool Malebo, it spans roughly 14 miles across between the twin capitals.

rows.q: An expedition in 1964 discovered an abandoned, mystery-shrouded lifeboat on this glacier-capped Norwegian island, the world’s most remote landmass.
rows.n: It lies over 1,600 kilometers from the nearest land, Gough Island, and has never had permanent residents.

rows.q: Resembling a giant 25-mile bullseye when seen from orbit, the enigmatic geological dome known as the Eye of the Sahara lies in this desert-heavy West African nation.
rows.n: Known formally as the Richat Structure, geologists believe it is an eroded volcanic dome.

rows.q: Located 340 miles off the mainland, this uninhabited, rain-drenched Costa Rican island served as the real-world visual inspiration for Isla Nublar in Jurassic Park.
rows.n: The island gets over 275 inches of rain per year, fostering cloud forests unlike anywhere else in the region.

rows.q: Wedged between Belgium and Prussia, the pocket-sized territory of Neutral Moresnet existed for over a century so both powers could exploit a lucrative mine producing this metal.
rows.n: Local enthusiasts in 1908 attempted to turn the mining territory into the world’s first Esperanto-speaking state.

rows.q: Unlike most coastal nations, Equatorial Guinea kept its capital, Malabo, offshore on this volcanic island once known to European sailors as Fernando Po.
rows.n: The mainland portion of Equatorial Guinea is known as Rio Muni.

rows.q: Topped by the active Mawson Peak, the highest summit in any territory governed by Canberra sits on this subantarctic island.
rows.n: Mawson Peak stands 2,745 meters high, significantly taller than any peak on the Australian mainland.

rows.q: Descending from the HMS Bounty mutineers, nearly two hundred Pitcairn Islanders relocated in 1856 to this now-Australian external territory.
rows.n: The island was previously used as one of the British Empire’s harshest penal settlements.

rows.q: Rusting fishing trawlers sit marooned in the desert at Moynaq, a former port stranded when Soviet irrigation projects drained what inland sea?
rows.n: Diverting the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers shrunk the Aral Sea to roughly 10% of its original size.

rows.q: The cast-iron Ha’penny Bridge, named for its original pedestrian toll, arches over this dark river that cuts straight through central Dublin.
rows.n: James Joyce personified the river as the character Anna Livia Plurabelle in Finnegans Wake.

rows.q: Express commuter boats weave past Wat Arun and the Grand Palace on this “River of Kings,” the bustling waterway coursing through Bangkok.
rows.n: King Rama I moved the Siamese capital across the river in 1782 to defend against Burmese attacks.

rows.q: Stretching between Spain and France, the Bay of Biscay takes its English name from a Spanish province primarily inhabited by what unique ethnic group?
rows.n: The province of Bizkaia forms part of Spain’s autonomous Basque Country, centered on Bilbao.

rows.q: Separating Victoria on the Australian mainland from Tasmania, this storm-tossed strait is named for the British surgeon and explorer who proved Tasmania was an island.
rows.n: George Bass circumnavigated Tasmania with fellow explorer Matthew Flinders in 1798.

rows.q: Jacques Cousteau popularized the Great Blue Hole as a world-class scuba dive site in 1971. The submarine sinkhole lies off the coast of what nation?
rows.n: The underwater sinkhole spans nearly 1,000 feet across and plunges over 400 feet deep into an ancient cave system.

rows.q: Britain suffered a catastrophic naval blow in 1941 when the Bismarck sank this pride of the Royal Navy in the Denmark Strait in under ten minutes.
rows.n: Only three of the battlecruiser’s 1,418 crew members survived the catastrophic explosion.

rows.q: In 1872, the merchant brigantine Mary Celeste was discovered completely deserted in the Atlantic, roughly 400 miles east of this Portuguese archipelago.
rows.n: The ship’s cargo of 1,701 barrels of denatured alcohol was untouched, deepening the mystery.

rows.q: A major Dutch brewery and the city of Amsterdam both take their name from this canal-feeding river that was dammed in the 13th century.
rows.n: The river’s name is derived from Old Dutch words meaning “watery area” or “abundant moisture.”

rows.q: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle was so weary of his best-known creation that he marched him to Switzerland’s Reichenbach Falls to be killed off in this 1893 short story.
rows.n: Outraged readers canceled subscriptions and wore black armbands, forcing Doyle to bring him back.

rows.q: Before Fletcher Christian led his infamous 1789 mutiny aboard HMS Bounty, the crew spent five idyllic months gathering breadfruit on this French Polynesian island.
rows.n: Captain William Bligh subsequently navigated an overcrowded 23-foot launch over 3,600 miles to safety.

rows.q: The strait separating Alaska from Siberia honors Vitus Bering, a Danish explorer who charted it while sailing under the flag of this European empire.
rows.n: Peter the Great personally commissioned Bering’s first expedition shortly before dying.

rows.q: The colossal Motherland Monument overlooks this river as it cuts through Ukraine’s capital on its way south toward the Black Sea.
rows.n: Ancient Greeks called this trade-heavy river the Borysthenes.

rows.q: Ships moving between the South China Sea and East China Sea often transit the Taiwan Strait, formerly known on Western nautical charts by this Portuguese name.
rows.n: Portuguese sailors in the 16th century christened the island Ilha Formosa, meaning beautiful island.

rows.q: Near the western fringe of the Nile Delta, the ancient harbor of Alexandria was marked by a towering lighthouse constructed on this limestone island.
rows.n: The island gave rise to the word for lighthouse in many Romance languages, including French and Spanish.

rows.q: In 762 AD, the Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur laid out his circular “City of Peace” along this river, establishing the historic core of Baghdad.
rows.n: The Euphrates flows roughly 20 miles to the west of Baghdad at its nearest approach.

rows.q: Spanish conquerors derived the Caribbean Sea’s name from the native Carib people, whom Columbus falsely accused of practicing what dietary taboo?
rows.n: The Spanish word “caníbal” was originally a regional variant of “Carib.”

rows.q: Roughly a fifth of the world’s petroleum supply navigates this narrow crescent of water, which links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
rows.n: At its narrowest point, the shipping lanes are only two miles wide in each direction.

rows.q: In 1893, engineers sliced through four miles of solid rock to finish this narrow canal, turning the Peloponnese into an island.
rows.n: Roman emperor Nero tried to dig it in 67 AD, personally turning the first shovel of dirt.

rows.q: Ferdinand Magellan named this southern archipelago for the flickering campfires he spotted along the shoreline while navigating his namesake strait in 1520.
rows.n: The name means ‘Land of Fire’; Magellan initially thought the fires were set by hostile ambushers.

rows.q: Lord Byron swam between Europe and Asia in 1810, crossing this narrow Turkish strait to reenact the mythological journey of Leander visiting Hero.
rows.n: Byron completed the swim in just over an hour and bragged about it for the rest of his life.

rows.q: Situated north of Antarctica, the Scotia Sea was named in 1932 after an expedition vessel whose name is the Latin term for which nation?
rows.n: William Speirs Bruce led the Scottish National Antarctic Expedition aboard the ship from 1902 to 1904.

rows.q: Connecting the Coral Sea to the Arafura Sea, the shallow Torres Strait lies between Cape York Peninsula in Australia and this second-largest island on Earth.
rows.n: The strait is dotted with nearly 300 islands, of which fewer than 20 are permanently inhabited.

rows.q: Narrowing to just 1.5 miles at the Phillips Channel, this strait between Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula handles over 80,000 ships a year.
rows.n: Named after the 15th-century Malacca Sultanate, it links the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea.

rows.q: Where the Volga River empties into the Caspian Sea, its sprawling delta has long served as the historic harvesting center for this briny, luxury culinary treat.
rows.n: The delta city of Astrakhan long served as the empire’s main hub for processing sturgeon roe.

rows.q: Because its distributaries reach out into the Gulf of Mexico like extended claws, the Mississippi River’s mouth is commonly described by geologists as this animal’s foot.
rows.n: Extensive levee construction has starved the delta of sediment, causing rapid land loss.

rows.q: Depending on who you ask, it’s either an estuary or the widest river in the world, separating Buenos Aires from this Uruguayan capital.
rows.n: At its mouth on the Atlantic, the Río de la Plata expands to an incredible 140 miles across.

rows.q: The Blue Nile, rushing from Lake Tana, merges with the White Nile at the “Elephant’s Trunk” peninsula in this North African capital.
rows.n: Khartoum is the capital of Sudan; its name derives from the Arabic word for an elephant’s trunk.

rows.q: Dividing Siberia from Alaska, the Bering Strait takes its name from an 18th-century explorer born in this Scandinavian kingdom.
rows.n: Vitus Bering was born in Horsens, Denmark, but spent decades leading northern exploration voyages.

rows.q: Adria, the ancient Etruscan port that gave the Adriatic Sea its name, now sits twelve miles inland thanks to millennia of silt deposited by which Italian river?
rows.n: The river’s expanding delta steadily pushed the coastline outward, stranding the old harbor.

rows.q: Oregon’s Crater Lake, the deepest lake in the United States, formed roughly 7,700 years ago when which violent volcano collapsed in on itself?
rows.n: The collapse left a caldera over five miles wide that filled entirely with accumulated rain and snow.

rows.q: In 1611, the starving, mutinous crew of the Discovery cast explorer Henry Hudson and his son adrift in a small open boat in what shallow southern extension of Hudson Bay?
rows.n: Hudson was never seen again; the eight mutineers who survived the voyage home were tried for murder but acquitted.

rows.q: The heavily trafficked Bab-el-Mandeb strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, its name translating from Arabic as the ‘Gate of’ this sorrowful word.
rows.n: The ominous name refers to the dangerous navigation reefs that wrecked countless early merchant dhows.

rows.q: The Tyrrhenian Sea off Italy’s western coast takes its name from the ancient Greek term for this pre-Roman civilization of Tuscany.
rows.n: The Greeks called them Tyrrhenoi; Romans called them Tusci, which gave Tuscany its name.

rows.q: Modern Mexico City largely sits on the drained bed of what historic endorheic lake, where the island capital Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325?
rows.n: Draining the lake caused Mexico City’s soft clay basin to subside by up to thirty feet over a century.

rows.q: In 1967, former army major Roy Bates seized an abandoned naval anti-aircraft tower in the Thames Estuary and proclaimed the founding of this tiny micronation.
rows.n: The fort was located in international waters at the time, providing a loophole for Bates.

rows.q: Turkey’s saline Lake Van gave its name to an indigenous breed of what domestic animal, unusual for its white coat, odd-colored eyes, and love of swimming?
rows.n: Unlike most domestic cats, Turkish Vans have a water-resistant coat and readily paddle in the lake.

rows.q: Sir Ernest Shackleton’s ship Endurance was crushed by pack ice in 1915 in this chilly Antarctic sea, named for the British explorer who penetrated it in 1823.
rows.n: The wreckage of Endurance was finally discovered largely intact in 2022.

rows.q: Dividing Isla Grande from smaller islands near Cape Horn, which 150-mile strait was the center of a tense 1978 border dispute between Chile and Argentina?
rows.n: Mediation by Pope John Paul II in early 1979 narrowly averted a shooting war over its islands.

rows.q: Vietnam’s Gulf of Tonkin gets its Western moniker from “Dông Kinh,” an older name for which modern Southeast Asian capital that translates as “Eastern Capital”?
rows.n: Just like Tokyo in Japanese, the Vietnamese characters for Dông Kinh literally mean “eastern capital.”

rows.q: Formed as a giant drowned river valley during the last Ice Age, Chesapeake Bay is primarily the swollen, tidal mouth of this 444-mile Pennsylvania river.
rows.n: The Susquehanna provides roughly half of the entire bay’s freshwater inflow.

rows.q: During the WWII Siege of Leningrad, the frozen surface of which immense lake served as the “Road of Life,” the surrounded city’s sole supply corridor?
rows.n: It is the largest lake located entirely in Europe, covering nearly 7,000 square miles.

rows.q: In 1858, which British explorer reached the southern shore of Africa’s largest lake and named it Lake Victoria, triggering a bitter feud with Richard Burton?
rows.n: Burton disputed Speke’s claim that the lake was the source of the Nile until Speke died in 1864.

rows.q: South Korea’s rapid postwar economic boom was dubbed a “miracle” on this river, which splits modern Seoul into northern and southern halves.
rows.n: Gangnam, the ritzy district made famous by Psy, literally translates to “south of the river.”

rows.q: Lisbon’s 25 de Abril suspension bridge, famously painted the same international orange as the Golden Gate, spans this longest Iberian river.
rows.n: It was built by the American Bridge Company, the same outfit behind San Francisco’s Bay Bridge.

rows.q: Jacques Cartier named the Gulf of Saint Lawrence after arriving on the feast day of Lawrence, a Roman martyr legendarily roasted alive on what cooking device?
rows.n: Saint Lawrence is the patron saint of cooks; tradition says he told his executioners to flip him.

rows.q: Filling the caldera of a supervolcano that erupted 74,000 years ago, what Indonesian lake on the island of Sumatra is the largest volcanic lake on Earth?
rows.n: The eruption was the largest known explosive event in two million years, creating a global volcanic winter.

rows.q: The Barents Sea is named for Willem Barentsz, a 16th-century explorer who died while trying to find which long-sought northern sea route to China?
rows.n: His stranded crew survived the Arctic winter on Novaya Zemlya by building a cabin from their ship.

rows.q: Straddling the border of Rwanda and the DRC, which African rift lake poses a severe limnic eruption threat due to vast pockets of trapped carbon dioxide?
rows.n: Rwanda has tapped the lake’s depths to extract methane gas, converting a disaster hazard into electricity.

rows.q: At 509 feet below sea level, Africa’s lowest point is this saline crater lake in Djibouti, which has an even higher salt concentration than the Dead Sea.
rows.n: Its shores are mined for salt, which Afar nomads have transported by camel caravan for centuries.

rows.q: Rising in the Tibetan Plateau, the Mekong River flows southward to define nearly 600 miles of international boundary between landlocked Laos and which neighbor?
rows.n: The border along the river is crossed by several “Thai-Lao Friendship Bridges.”

rows.q: Spanning the blue ocean field of Nauru’s flag is a thin yellow stripe, representing this major geographic line that runs just 26 miles north of the island.
rows.n: The twelve-pointed star just beneath the line represents the island’s twelve original indigenous tribes.

rows.q: Monarch, the captive grizzly bear that served as the model for California’s flag, was captured in 1889 on orders from this flamboyant newspaper tycoon.
rows.n: Hearst kept Monarch at San Francisco’s Woodward’s Gardens and Golden Gate Park until the bear died in 1911.

rows.q: Mozambique’s flag famously features an AK-47 assault rifle crossed with a hoe, but sitting behind both is this quiet symbol of education.
rows.n: The three central symbols on the flag collectively represent defense, agriculture, and education.

rows.q: Colored a distinct brownish-orange, the map on the flag of Cyprus symbolizes this metal, whose Latin name derives from the island itself.
rows.n: Ancient Romans dubbed the metal cyprium, later shortened to cuprum, because Cyprus was their chief mining hub.

rows.q: A flat-topped tepui in South America, Mount Roraima serves as a tripoint between Brazil, Guyana, and this third country that claims the Essequibo.
rows.n: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle used 19th-century accounts of Mount Roraima to inspire The Lost World.

rows.q: Mexico’s flag features an eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus devouring a snake, an omen that told the Aztecs where to build this legendary island capital.
rows.n: The modern Mexican presidential palace sits directly atop the ruins of the palace of Moctezuma II.

rows.q: Nourishing her three chicks with droplets of her own blood, a mother one of these state birds anchors the official flag of Louisiana.
rows.n: The motif is known in Christian heraldry as the ‘pelican in her piety.’

rows.q: In the center of Kenya’s flag, crossed spears sit behind a traditional defensive item painted in black, red, and white, carried by warriors of which ethnic group?
rows.n: The shield and two spears also appear on Kenya’s coat of arms, flanked by two supporting lions.

rows.q: Known as the Spice Isle of the Caribbean, Grenada places a small split pod on the left side of its national flag containing what aromatic baking spice?
rows.n: Grenada is one of the world’s top producers of nutmeg, second only to Indonesia.

rows.q: Virginia’s flag depicts the goddess Virtus standing victorious over a fallen tyrant, illustrating this Latin state motto that John Wilkes Booth later shouted.
rows.n: The phrase translates to ‘thus always to tyrants.’ Booth shouted it from the stage at Ford’s Theatre in 1865.

rows.q: Guatemala’s coat of arms on its flag includes two crossed rifles and two swords, over which perches this vibrantly colored national bird that also names its currency.
rows.n: In pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, quetzal tail feathers were so valuable they were used as currency.

rows.q: Oklahoma’s skinny panhandle exists because Texas ceded all territory north of latitude 36°30’ in 1850 to avoid violating this 1820 congressional compromise.
rows.n: The detached sliver went without any territorial government for decades and was called “No Man’s Land.”

rows.q: Across the celestial globe on Brazil’s flag stretches a white banner bearing an Auguste Comte-inspired motto: “Ordem e…” what Portuguese word?
rows.n: Comte’s full Positivist motto was ‘Love as a principle, order as the basis, progress as the goal.’

rows.q: Beneath the Union Jack on Australia’s flag, the Commonwealth Star’s first six points represent the founding states, while the seventh was added in 1908 for these.
rows.n: The seventh point was originally added to represent the Territory of Papua, which Australia then administered.

rows.q: Sri Lanka’s flag displays a golden lion for the Sinhalese majority, while its green and orange vertical stripes represent Muslims and which other minority community?
rows.n: The four leaves in the corners of the lion panel are bo leaves, representing the four Buddhist virtues.

rows.q: Carrying over a quarter of all commercial trade between the US and Canada, the Ambassador suspension bridge links Detroit with this Ontario city.
rows.n: Billionaire Matty Moroun bought the bridge in 1979, making it a rare privately owned international border crossing.

rows.q: Dividing its flag diagonally, Papua New Guinea placed the Southern Cross on the black half and this exotic, famously flamboyant feathered creature on the red half.
rows.n: The silhouette specifically depicts the Raggiana bird of paradise in mid-display.

rows.q: Completely surrounded on land by the Malaysian state of Sarawak, the sultanate of Brunei is located entirely on what third-largest island in the world?
rows.n: Brunei accounts for just one percent of Borneo’s land area, with Indonesia holding the vast majority.

rows.q: Claimed by Haiti since 1804, tiny Navassa Island became the first overseas territory seized by the US under an 1856 act aimed at mining this fertilizer.
rows.n: The Guano Islands Act allowed US citizens to claim any unoccupied island containing bird excrement.

rows.q: Penned off from the rest of its state by the 49th parallel, Point Roberts is an American pene-exclave attached by land only to this Canadian province.
rows.n: During pandemic border closures, local children had to take a ferry to attend school on the US mainland.

rows.q: An 1859 border dispute between the US and Britain in the San Juan Islands was sparked by the shooting of this domestic animal, the spat’s only casualty.
rows.n: The standoff dragged on until 1872, when Kaiser Wilhelm I arbitrated the boundary in favor of the US.

rows.q: Flanked by two indigenous Taino figures, the red cross on Jamaica’s coat of arms is studded with five specimens of this spiky tropical fruit.
rows.n: Christopher Columbus first encountered the fruit in Guadeloupe in 1493 and called it the ‘pine of the Indies.’

rows.q: The yellow triangle on the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina outlines the country’s map while its three points honor Bosniaks, Croats, and which third ethnic group?
rows.n: The diagonal row of stars running beside the triangle represents Europe and is cut off to suggest infinity.

rows.q: Legend says a Dutchman drinking gin and a Frenchman sipping wine walked around this Caribbean island in 1648 to split it between their two empires.
In 2020, Mississippi retired its Confederate-themed banner and adopted a new flag centered on the blossom of this official state tree.
In an 1890 treaty, Germany acquired Namibia’s Caprivi Strip hoping to reach the Indian Ocean along this river, only to realize Victoria Falls was in the way.
rows.n: Germany traded away its claims on Zanzibar in the same agreement to secure the corridor.

rows.q: The Welsh flag features a fierce red dragon, but the background stripes of white and green were the livery colors of which English royal house with Welsh roots?
rows.n: Henry VII flew the red dragon standard at the Battle of Bosworth Field before taking the English throne in 1485.

rows.q: In 2012, archaeologists in Gorham’s Cave found a crosshatched engraving hailed as the first abstract Neanderthal art, located in what British territory?
rows.n: Carved into bedrock, the geometric grid proved Neanderthals were capable of abstract artistic expression.

rows.q: When Barbados became independent in 1966, it placed Neptune’s trident on its flag, but removed this specific part to signify breaking away from British colonial rule.
rows.n: The symbol is known locally as the Broken Trident, and the three points represent three principles of democracy.

rows.q: Symbolizing the pope’s triple office as teacher, priest, and shepherd, this three-tiered headpiece appears above the crossed keys on the flag of Vatican City.
In the medieval lore that placed the red dragon on Wales’s flag, the beast fights an underground battle against a white dragon that symbolizes these Germanic invaders.
rows.n: The myth appears in the ninth-century Historia Brittonum and Geoffrey of Monmouth’s Arthurian tales.

rows.q: Above the sagebrush wreath on Nevada’s flag sits a ribbon bearing this two-word state motto, celebrating its admission during the Civil War.
rows.n: Nevada was rushed into statehood on October 31, 1864, just in time to support Abraham Lincoln’s reelection.

rows.q: Because neither country wants to compromise its claim to the coastal Hala’ib Triangle, Egypt and Sudan both disown this 800-square-mile wedge of desert terra nullius.
rows.n: American eccentric Jeremiah Heaton traveled there in 2014 to claim it so his daughter could be a “princess.”

rows.q: The lone black star at the center of Ghana’s flag was adopted from the name of a 1919 shipping line established by this Jamaican-born Black nationalist leader.
rows.n: The Black Star Line was formed to link Black economies and carry passengers between the Americas and Africa.

rows.q: Emblazoned on the presidential standard of the Czech Republic, the motto ‘Truth Prevails’ traces back to this Bohemian reformer burned at the stake in 1415.
rows.n: Hus was promised safe conduct to the Council of Constance, but church authorities arrested and executed him anyway.

rows.q: Reflecting its strategic position at the entrance to the Mediterranean, the flag of Gibraltar features a three-towered castle with what object dangling from a chain?
rows.n: Queen Isabella I of Castile originally granted Gibraltar this heraldic castle and key coat of arms in 1502.

rows.q: In adopting Beethoven’s ‘Ode to Joy’ melody as its official anthem, the European Union dropped the original German lyrics penned by which 18th-century poet?
rows.n: The EU intentionally uses no words, keeping the anthem neutral across its dozens of official member languages.

rows.q: Because the 1846 Oregon Treaty drew the border along the 49th parallel, what Washington community on the Tsawwassen peninsula is reachable by car only through Canada?
rows.n: Local high school students must cross the international border four times each day on their bus commute to Blaine.

rows.q: First raised upon the territory’s creation in 1999, Nunavut’s flag pairs the North Star with a red silhouette of this traditional Inuit stone landmark.
rows.n: Inuksuit were built as navigational aids, hunting guides, and markers across the treeless Arctic landscape.

rows.q: Boasting a mining heritage that minted silver kings, which western U.S. state features the Spanish motto ‘Oro y Plata’ on its flag and seal?
rows.n: Montana is the only U.S. state with an official motto in Spanish.

rows.q: Though written during the War of 1812, ‘The Star-Spangled Banner’ did not become the official U.S. national anthem until this president signed a bill in 1931.
rows.n: Before 1931, the U.S. military generally used ‘Hail, Columbia’ or ‘My Country, ‘Tis of Thee’ for official honors.

rows.q: Brokered by Teddy Roosevelt in New Hampshire, the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth split this large Pacific island between Russia and Japan along the 50th parallel.
rows.n: Roosevelt was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906 largely for mediating the negotiations.

rows.q: Ireland’s official emblem, the medieval harp, is modeled on a preserved instrument named for which High King who routed the Vikings at Clontarf in 1014?
rows.n: The Trinity College harp is actually from the 14th or 15th century, centuries after Brian Boru’s death.

rows.q: Ending the decades-long “Whisky War” in 2022, Canada and Denmark peacefully agreed to partition this tiny, uninhabited Arctic island.
rows.n: For years, visiting military patrols left behind bottles of Canadian Club or Danish schnapps for each other.

rows.q: The bloodless 1839 “Aroostook War” along the Maine-Canada border was settled by an 1842 treaty named for Lord Ashburton and which legendary US Secretary of State?
rows.n: Webster famously used a map marked with a red line by Benjamin Franklin to convince Maine to accept the deal.

rows.q: Brazil’s green and yellow flag features a blue globe bearing the motto “Order and Progress,” a phrase borrowed from this French philosopher’s Positivism.
rows.n: Comte’s original maxim was “Love as a principle and order as the basis; progress as the goal.”

rows.q: Behind two woodcutters bearing an axe and an oar, the shield on Belize’s flag sits before this valuable hardwood tree that formed the backbone of its early economy.
rows.n: Belize’s flag is the only national banner in the world featuring humans as its primary decorative focus.

rows.q: Drawn in 1893 between British India and Afghanistan, the contentious Durand Line famously cuts right through the traditional homeland of which ethnic group?
When the Comoros archipelago voted for independence in 1974, this single island voted against it, choosing to remain under French sovereignty instead.
rows.n: Comoros still claims Mayotte, but France made it an official overseas department in 2011.

rows.q: Rising in the center of Saint Lucia’s flag, two stacked triangles represent racial harmony and this pair of volcanic spires that dominate the island’s southwest coast.
rows.n: The yellow triangle beneath them symbolizes the tropical sunshine that draws tourists to the island.

rows.q: Delaware’s curved northern border is an arc drawn with a 12-mile radius centered on the colonial courthouse cupola in which historic riverfront city?
rows.n: Surveyed in 1701, it remains the only circular state border in the United States.

rows.q: Between Quebec and Vermont, the boundary slices straight through this cultural institution, where the stage is in Canada and the seats are in the US.
rows.a: Haskell Free Library and Opera House
rows.n: Visitors enter through the US door, but Canadians can visit without passing border control if they stay inside.

rows.q: Dubbed “Auld Reekie” for its coal soot, this seat of Scots law and enlightenment philosophy is well short of Glasgow in population.
rows.n: Its Royal Mile connects the cliffside castle with the Palace of Holyroodhouse, the monarch’s official residence.

rows.q: Emperor Franz Joseph ordered the creation of Vienna’s grand Ringstraße boulevard in 1857 to replace the city’s obsolete medieval what?
rows.n: The broad circular avenue was built partly to allow the military to maneuver quickly during civil unrest.

rows.q: New Orleans’ Bourbon Street was named in 1721 to honor a French royal dynasty that was also ruling which other European kingdom at the time?
rows.n: Philip V, a grandson of France’s King Louis XIV, founded the Spanish branch of the House of Bourbon in 1700.

rows.q: Nestled beneath the Margalla Hills, this planned 1960s grid city houses the tent-shaped Faisal Mosque, replacing coastal Karachi as capital.
rows.n: The Turkish-designed Faisal Mosque was built without a dome, inspired instead by a nomadic Bedouin tent.

rows.q: Just before its grand opening in 2010, the skyscraper Burj Dubai was renamed to Burj Khalifa to thank the leader of this neighboring, debt-relieving emirate.
rows.n: Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan provided billions of dollars to rescue Dubai from financial crisis.

rows.q: Outside the Forbidden City, Beijing’s Tiananmen Square takes its name from the monumental northern gate, translating into English as the Gate of Heavenly what?
rows.n: The gate has stood since the early Ming dynasty, though it was rebuilt in 1651 following wartime destruction.

rows.q: A bronze plaque set into the pavement of Madrid’s Puerta del Sol marks Kilometre Zero, the starting point for Spain’s national network of what?
rows.n: Radial highways are numbered clockwise from A-1 to A-6, all originating from this single central spot.

rows.q: Nestled along the Oos River in the Black Forest, this grand German resort town was officially renamed in 1931 to distinguish it from its home state.
rows.n: Its historic Friedrichsbad Roman-Irish bath complex was praised by Mark Twain, who claimed it cured his rheumatism.

rows.q: Sitting at over 13,000 feet above sea level, El Alto International Airport requires extra-long runways because thin air hampers takeoff for flights serving this de facto capital.
rows.n: Due to the extreme altitude, the airport keeps medical oxygen on hand for arriving passengers.

rows.q: Spanish conquistadors founded Intramuros on the ruins of a burned Muslim settlement, establishing this bay city now outpopulated by Quezon City.
rows.n: Quezon City was actually the designated capital of the Philippines from 1948 until Ferdinand Marcos revoked it.

rows.q: Covering nearly 300 square miles in eastern Saudi Arabia, King Fahd International Airport occupies more land area than this entire neighboring Persian Gulf island nation.
rows.n: Despite its colossal footprint, commercial aviation operations occupy only a small fraction of the property.

rows.q: In 1912, French colonial administrators bypassed Casablanca and Fez to make this former Barbary pirate haven their Atlantic capital.
rows.n: The unfinished 12th-century Hassan Tower and the Kasbah of the Udayas still stand near its riverfront.

rows.q: Dutch colonists erected a 1653 wooden palisade along what is now Wall Street to defend New Amsterdam from settlers arriving from which rival European nation?
rows.n: The wall never repelled an attack; an English fleet sailed into the harbor and seized the colony in 1664.

rows.q: One of the shortest-lived Wonders of the Ancient World, the bronze Colossus of Rhodes stood at the harbor for only 54 years before being toppled by this natural disaster.
rows.n: An oracle warned the Rhodians against rebuilding it, leaving the shattered bronze lying where it fell for centuries.

rows.q: In 1968, American industrialist Robert McCulloch bought a dismantled 1830s London Bridge and reassembled it over an inlet in this desert U.S. state.
rows.n: The bridge remains a major tourist draw in Lake Havasu City, connecting an island to the mainland.

rows.q: Rome’s Colosseum actually took its popular nickname not from its massive size, but from a nearby 100-foot bronze statue depicting this notorious, lyre-loving emperor.
rows.n: After Nero’s death, the Colossus was remodeled with a crown of sun rays to depict the solar god Sol.

rows.q: Riders on this isolated Asian capital’s subway system board at stations bearing revolutionary slogans like Glory, Triumph, and Red Star rather than neighborhood landmarks.
rows.n: Built over 300 feet underground, the network was engineered to double as a nuclear fallout shelter.

rows.q: Venetian locals historically avoided walking between the two columns on the edge of Saint Mark’s Square, as that space was reserved for what grim civic duty?
rows.n: Public hangings took place between the granite pillars carrying statues of St. Mark’s lion and St. Theodore.

rows.q: To outdo 40 Wall Street in 1930, architect William Van Alen secretly assembled a 125-foot stainless-steel spire inside this Art Deco skyscraper.
rows.n: The spire was hoisted into place in just 90 minutes, briefly making it the world’s tallest building.

rows.q: Built over Florence’s Ponte Vecchio, the elevated Vasari Corridor allowed this powerful banking dynasty to cross the Arno River without mingling with commoners.
rows.n: Grand Duke Ferdinando I evicted butchers from the bridge in 1593 because the smell bothered him on his walks.

rows.q: Antonio da Ponte won a 16th-century design contest over Michelangelo and Palladio to build this stone bridge spanning Venice’s Grand Canal.
rows.n: Critics predicted the heavy stone arch would collapse, but it remains the oldest bridge over the Grand Canal.

rows.q: Australian locals playfully call the Sydney Harbour Bridge by this mundane closet accessory nickname, inspired by its distinctive curved steel arch.
rows.n: It took 272,000 liters of gray paint to give the bridge its opening three coats in 1932.

rows.q: Unlike nearly every other major Khmer temple, which faces east toward the dawn, Angkor Wat uniquely faces this cardinal direction, traditionally associated with death.
rows.n: Because it faces west, Angkor Wat is famously illuminated by the golden rays of sunset rather than sunrise.

rows.q: Passengers stuck on long layovers at Amsterdam Airport Schiphol can admire 17th-century Dutch masters at an on-site outpost of this famed national museum.
rows.n: Opened in 2002, it was the first museum annex in an airport terminal to display authentic historical masterworks.

rows.q: The towering highway bypass bridge over the Colorado River near Hoover Dam shares its name with former Nevada governor Mike O’Callaghan and this fallen NFL safety.
rows.n: Tillman walked away from a multimillion-dollar contract with the Arizona Cardinals to enlist as an Army Ranger.

rows.q: Bavaria’s fairy-tale Neuschwanstein Castle was conceived by the eccentric King Ludwig II largely as a personal theatrical tribute to the dramatic operas of this composer.
rows.n: Ludwig covered the interior with murals depicting scenes from Wagnerian operas like Lohengrin and Tannhäuser.

rows.q: Leading down to Rome’s Piazza di Spagna, the Spanish Steps take their name from Spain’s historic embassy not to Italy, but to which sovereign entity?
rows.n: The Palazzo di Spagna has housed the Spanish ambassador to the Vatican continuously since 1647.

rows.q: Long before tourists crossed its tidal causeway, the island abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel spent decades following the French Revolution repurposed as this grim institution.
rows.n: Nicknamed the “Bastille of the sea,” its inmates included political prisoners until closure in 1863.

rows.q: Golfers at the Kantarat Golf Course must pause their swings for taxiing jetliners, as the 18-hole course sits between two active runways at Don Mueang Airport in this capital.
rows.n: The Royal Thai Air Force built the course in 1952 and still maintains the unique layout today.

rows.q: Bedridden with caisson disease, chief engineer Washington Roebling relied on this woman, his wife, to direct the daily construction of the Brooklyn Bridge.
rows.n: She was the first person to ride across the completed bridge, carrying a rooster as a sign of victory.

rows.q: South Africa’s judicial capital, which claims J.R.R. Tolkien as a native son, is this “City of Roses” in the Free State.
rows.n: Tolkien was born there in 1892 while his father managed a local bank branch, but returned to England as a toddler.

rows.q: Long before a certain newspaper moved there in 1904, New York’s Times Square was a horse-trading hub that shared a name with which equine London street?
rows.n: London’s Long Acre was the British capital’s carriage-building center for more than two centuries.

rows.q: Laid out over the 1st-century Stadium of Domitian, this elongated Rome public square features Gian Lorenzo Bernini’s famous Fountain of the Four Rivers.
rows.n: Until the 19th century, the square was deliberately flooded on August weekends for cooling aquatic games.

rows.q: Rising above Paris, the hilltop of Montmartre takes its name from the martyrdom of which patron saint of France, said to have walked with his severed head?
rows.n: Denis reportedly walked several miles north while preaching a sermon before finally collapsing.

rows.q: Moscow’s Red Square has nothing to do with communism or brickwork; the Russian adjective ‘krasnaya’ originally meant this compliment.
rows.n: Over the centuries, the word’s primary meaning drifted from beautiful to the color red.

rows.q: In 2001, Liverpool’s airport became the first in the UK named for an individual, adopting what four-word line from a 1971 John Lennon anthem as its official motto?
rows.n: The phrase comes from Lennon’s peace anthem “Imagine”, and the airport’s logo includes his self-portrait sketch.

rows.q: Myanmar’s military junta spent billions secretly carving this surreal, twenty-lane-highway administrative city out of the jungle in 2005.
rows.n: The name translates poetically to “Abode of the King,” despite its vast, sparsely populated ghost-town avenues.

rows.q: Once known as Tselinograd and Akmola, this frigid steppe city replaced Almaty as capital in 1997 and features a massive Norman Foster pyramid.
rows.n: Foster’s 200-foot-tall Palace of Peace and Reconciliation was designed to host congresses of world religions.

rows.q: Commuters waiting for high-speed trains in Madrid can wander among thousands of tropical plants inside this primary terminus, which converted its old train shed into a greenhouse in 1992.
rows.n: The indoor jungle covers an entire acre beneath the station’s original 1892 wrought-iron canopy.

rows.q: During his presidency, Richard Nixon frequently escaped Washington to his private “Florida White House” compound on what barrier island?
rows.n: Nixon visited the Key Biscayne residence more than 50 times during his presidency, often cruising with Bebe Rebozo.

rows.q: Julius Nyerere initiated a plan in 1973 to shift government functions away from coastal Dar es Salaam to this central dry-farming city.
rows.n: Though designated the capital five decades ago, the president’s office did not fully relocate there until 2019.

rows.q: After Hurricane Hattie wiped out coastal infrastructure in 1961, British Honduras built this Mayan-temple-inspired capital fifty miles inland.
rows.n: With around 25,000 residents, it is one of the smallest national capitals by population in the Americas.

rows.q: Petra’s famous rock-cut architecture was carved by this ancient Arab nomadic civilization, which grew fabulously wealthy taxing the desert frankincense trade.
rows.n: They mastered arid hydraulics, storing seasonal flash-flood runoff in hidden cisterns throughout the canyons.

rows.q: Sir George Gilbert Scott’s high-Gothic Midland Grand Hotel forms the stunning street facade of which Victorian London railway terminus, now the departure point for continental trains?
rows.n: The train shed behind the hotel was the largest single-span roof in the world when it opened in 1868.

rows.q: Now carrying London Overground trains, this 1843 engineering wonder beneath the riverbed was the world’s first known tunnel successfully constructed under a navigable river.
rows.n: Marc Isambard Brunel patented the revolutionary tunnelling shield specifically to burrow through the soft mud.

rows.q: Gold coins were minted elsewhere, but Tokyo’s upscale Ginza district owes its name to a 1612 government facility that minted coins of which metal?
rows.n: The Japanese word ‘gin’ means silver, while ‘za’ refers to a guild or chartered monopoly.

rows.q: Charles IV originally established Prague’s Wenceslas Square in the 14th century as a bustling market dedicated to trading which farm animal?
rows.n: The space was called the Horse Market until Czech nationalists renamed it for Saint Wenceslas in 1848.

rows.q: Four colossal granite giants holding glowing globes flank the main entrance of the central railway station in this Nordic capital.
rows.n: The Finnish granite figures, sculpted by Emil Wikström, are affectionately nicknamed the Lantern Carriers.

rows.q: This Canadian provincial capital dropped its original, muddy-sounding moniker of Pile O’ Bones in 1882 to flatter Queen Victoria instead.
rows.n: The original Cree name referred to mounds of buffalo bones left along the creek.

rows.q: Following Egypt’s 1952 revolution, Cairo’s Ismailia Square was stripped of its royal name and rechristened Tahrir Square, an Arabic word meaning what?
rows.n: The square was originally built by Khedive Ismail, who modeled 19th-century downtown Cairo on Paris.

rows.q: In 1978, UNESCO named its first two World Cultural Heritage cities: Krakow, Poland, and this Andean high-altitude capital south of the equator.
rows.n: Perched at over 9,000 feet, it was founded on the ruins of a northern Inca hub after the Spanish conquest.

rows.q: Rising bizarrely from the savannah, the world’s largest Christian church, modeled after St. Peter’s, dominates this Ivorian inland capital.
rows.n: President Félix Houphouët-Boigny poured over $300 million of state funds into building it in his home village.

rows.q: Opened in 1897 on Coney Island by George C. Tilyou, what historic amusement park was named for an attraction featuring mechanical horses on parallel rails?
rows.n: Its grinning ‘Funny Face’ mascot remained an iconic symbol of Brooklyn long after the park closed.

rows.q: In 1905, representatives of the Five Civilized Tribes met in Muskogee to propose a Native-led U.S. state named for this Cherokee silversmith.
rows.n: Congress rejected the plan, instead merging Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory into a single state in 1907.

rows.q: Before collapsing in 1789, an unrecognized breakaway republic in modern East Tennessee sought legitimacy by naming itself after this elder statesman.
rows.n: Originally called Frankland, organizers changed it to flatter Franklin into backing their bid for statehood.

rows.q: Resolving a bitter harbor dispute in 1998, the Supreme Court ruled that most of Ellis Island belongs to this state, not New York.
rows.n: Artificial landfill added over decades put roughly 80 percent of the island under Garden State jurisdiction.

rows.q: Near the town of Hancock, this Mid-Atlantic state narrows to less than two miles wide, pinned between the Mason-Dixon Line and the Potomac River.
rows.n: The narrow neck separates the state’s Appalachian panhandle from the Washington, D.C., suburbs.

rows.q: A bloodless 1835 border dispute between Ohio and Michigan ended with Michigan ceding this port city strip in exchange for the Upper Peninsula.
rows.n: The conflict is remembered as the Toledo War; the only casualty was a deputy sheriff stabbed with a penknife.

rows.q: Created by the massive 1912 eruption of Novarupta, the ash desert called the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes is protected in what state?
rows.n: The Novarupta event was the 20th century’s largest volcanic blast, ejecting 30 times more magma than Mount St. Helens.

rows.q: Stan Lee adopted it as his personal catchphrase, but this Latin word meaning ‘ever upward’ has served as New York’s state motto since 1778.
rows.n: It appears on the state seal beneath a shield supported by Liberty and Justice.

rows.q: Hoping to mold a lighter running shoe sole with superior traction, Oregon track coach Bill Bowerman ruined his wife’s kitchen in 1971 by pouring melted urethane into this appliance.
rows.n: His melted experiment yielded the famous Waffle Trainer sole, helping ignite Nike’s early success.

rows.q: Congress awarded this state its mineral-rich Upper Peninsula in 1836 as a consolation prize for surrendering the Toledo Strip to Ohio.
rows.n: At the time, Michiganders considered the rugged peninsula an uninhabitable, frozen wasteland.

rows.q: A Spanish duke and viceroy inspired the 1706 name of what New Mexico city, which later dropped the first “r” from its original spelling?
rows.n: The Spanish town of Alburquerque, near Portugal, was named for its white cork oak trees.

rows.q: Seeking to rebrand his digestive fountain beverage in 1898, New Bern pharmacist Caleb Bradham chose Pepsi-Cola, borrowing from the medical term for this common stomach ailment.
rows.n: Bradham believed the drink’s blend of pepsin and kola nuts aided digestion and boosted energy.

rows.q: Named in 1829 by a Mexican trader who found artesian springs in the desert, what Nevada gaming hub takes its name from the Spanish for “the meadows”?
rows.n: The springs made it an essential oasis on the Old Spanish Trail between Santa Fe and Los Angeles.

rows.q: Cadillac established Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit in 1701. The French word “détroit” describes what narrow body of water linking two lakes?
rows.n: The Detroit River connects Lake Saint Clair to Lake Erie.

rows.q: Built to whisk passengers between downtown and the 1962 Century 21 Exposition, what straddle-beam transit system became an enduring, iconic landmark of Seattle, Washington?
Brigham Young and fellow Mormon pioneers drafted an 1849 proposal for a giant provisional state with this honeybee-inspired name.
rows.n: Congress rejected the massive proposed borders, creating the much smaller Utah Territory instead.

rows.q: DuPont chemist Stephanie Kwolek developed this lightweight, ultra-rigid synthetic fiber at the company’s Wilmington, Delaware lab in 1965 while seeking better cords for radial tires.
rows.n: Kwolek’s invention became the gold standard for bullet-resistant body armor worldwide.

rows.q: Grand Detour blacksmith John Deere revolutionized Midwestern farming in 1837 by fashioning a self-scouring plow blade from a broken saw made of this metal instead of cast iron.
rows.n: The smooth steel surface allowed sticky prairie soil to slide off the blade instead of caking onto it.

rows.q: Entering the Union as the 37th state in 1867, it remains the only state with a unicameral, nonpartisan legislature.
rows.n: Promoted by U.S. Senator George Norris, the one-house system was adopted by voters during the Great Depression.

rows.q: Iowa’s capital takes its name from a nearby river that French traders assumed honored these religious men, though it likely came from an Algonquian word.
rows.n: They mistook the native name Moingona for “Rivière des Moines.”

rows.q: King Charles II named Pennsylvania in 1681 to honor not the colony’s Quaker founder, but rather this person, an English admiral.
rows.n: Charles II owed a massive debt to Admiral William Penn, repaid with the land grant.

rows.q: When seventeen-year-old Bud Hillerich turned the first Louisville Slugger bat in Kentucky in 1884, he carved it from this specific white timber, the game’s standard for over a century.
rows.n: Maple bats became widely popular after Barry Bonds adopted them in the late 1990s.

rows.q: In 1790, Arthur St. Clair renamed the settlement of Losantiville to honor a society of Revolutionary War officers named for this Roman farmer-statesman.
rows.n: George Washington was often compared to Cincinnatus for giving up power after the war.

rows.q: The ‘Old Man of the Lake,’ a 30-foot hemlock tree trunk that has bobbed vertically for over a century, floats in a caldera lake in this state.
rows.n: Crater Lake’s cold, pristine water has kept the hemlock trunk remarkably well preserved since its 1896 discovery.

rows.q: Brokered by Henry Clay, this sweeping legislative package admitted California directly as the 31st state without ever spending a day as an organized territory.
rows.n: The gold rush population boom had let California bypass the territorial phase required of most states.

rows.q: Guadalupe Mountains National Park in this state preserves the Capitan Reef, the world’s most extensive exposed fossil reef from the Permian era.
rows.n: The limestone reef formed underwater 260 million years ago before tectonic activity thrust it above the desert.

rows.q: In 1871, Reno tailor Jacob Davis came up with the idea of reinforcing miners’ denim work pants with these small copper fasteners, partnering with Levi Strauss to secure the patent.
rows.n: Davis could not afford the sixty-eight-dollar patent fee on his own, so he partnered with his cloth supplier.

rows.q: Sharing no land border with New York, this tiny state connects to the Empire State via a maritime boundary between Block Island and Long Island.
rows.n: Rhode Island shares land borders with only two states: Connecticut and Massachusetts.

rows.q: This state’s narrow western panhandle exists because Texas ceded all territory north of latitude 36°30’ in 1850 to keep slavery legal under federal law.
rows.n: For decades before statehood, the strip was an unorganized territory popularly dubbed No Man’s Land.

rows.q: Delaware took the inaugural spot on December 7, 1787, but this neighbor became the second state to ratify the Constitution just five days later.
rows.n: It was the first large state to ratify, voting 46 to 23 at the Pennsylvania State House.

rows.q: Distinctly bitter and flavored with gentian root, this vintage beverage was designated Maine’s official state soft drink in 2005.
rows.n: Created in 1876 as a patent medicine, it popularized the slang word for nerve and pluck.

rows.q: After an 1877 flood shifted the Missouri River, the city of Carter Lake ended up west of the river, entirely surrounded by Nebraska but legally part of this state.
rows.n: The Supreme Court ruled in 1892 that sudden river avulsion does not alter established state borders.

rows.q: Which southern capital was called Marthasville, after a governor’s daughter, before adopting its current railway-inspired name in 1845?
rows.n: Before Marthasville, the settlement was literally just called Terminus.

rows.q: Though forever branded as Hawaii’s unofficial welcoming cocktail, the rum-heavy Mai Tai was actually concocted in 1944 at Victor Bergeron’s original Polynesian tiki bar in this California city.
rows.n: Bergeron claimed a Tahitian guest drank it and shouted “Maita’i roa ae!”, meaning “the best!”

rows.q: Thirsty for access to the Tennessee River, lawmakers in this state have argued since 1818 that a botched survey placed its northern border one mile too far south.
rows.n: Gaining that single mile would allow metro Atlanta to pipe drinking water directly out of Nickajack Lake.

rows.q: A drop of rain falling on the summit of Triple Divide Peak can flow to the Atlantic, Pacific, or Arctic Ocean depending on the ridge in what state?
rows.n: The hydrological apex in Glacier National Park sends runoff to the Gulf of Mexico, the Columbia River, and Hudson Bay.

rows.q: Overwhelmed by thirsty patrons in 1971, Dallas restaurateur Mariano Martinez invented the frozen margarita machine by famously repurposing this existing piece of dessert equipment.
rows.n: Martinez was inspired by a 7-Eleven Slurpee machine; his original contraption now sits in the Smithsonian.

rows.q: The brand name Crayola was coined in 1903 by Alice Binney, wife of the Easton, Pennsylvania founder, by blending an oily suffix with “craie,” the French word for this substance.
rows.n: Before making wax crayons for children, Binney and Smith produced industrial slate pencils and carbon black.

rows.q: Four years after basketball was created in nearby Springfield, William G. Morgan invented volleyball at a Massachusetts YMCA in 1895, originally christening the sport with this name.
rows.n: Morgan sought a less punishing, non-contact sport for older businessmen who found basketball too rough.

rows.q: Elmer Cline coined the name Wonder Bread in Indianapolis in 1921 after being struck with childlike awe while watching an international race featuring these colorful aircraft.
rows.n: The bright balloons dotting the sky inspired the red, yellow, and blue polka dots on the wrapper.

rows.q: When North and South Dakota joined on the same day in 1889, this president shuffled the paperwork so no one knew which was admitted first.
rows.n: North Dakota is listed 39th and South Dakota 40th purely because of alphabetical order.

rows.q: In this state’s Red Desert, the Continental Divide splits into two branches that enclose a 4,000-square-mile basin with no outlet to any ocean.
rows.n: Precipitation falling inside the Great Divide Basin simply evaporates or pools in small alkaline lakes.

rows.q: Forty years before Yellowstone, Andrew Jackson created a federal reservation around a series of geothermal springs in this future state.
rows.n: The reservation became Hot Springs National Park in 1921, making it technically the oldest federal land reserve.

rows.q: Colonel Harland Sanders perfected his fried chicken recipe in Kentucky, but opened his very first franchise bearing the name Kentucky Fried Chicken in this western capital city in 1952.
rows.n: Salt Lake franchisee Pete Harman also pioneered the iconic red-and-white striped bucket.

rows.q: Corn flakes were accidentally developed at a Battle Creek, Michigan sanitarium run by John Harvey Kellogg, an adherent of this vegetarian, health-focused Protestant church.
rows.n: Kellogg believed bland grain foods would suppress sexual desire and promote moral purity.

rows.q: Created to commemorate the United States purchasing Alaska from Russia in 1867, the torched dessert Baked Alaska was debuted by pastry chef Charles Ranhofer at this legendary Manhattan steakhouse.
rows.n: Ranhofer dubbed the dessert “Alaska, Florida” to highlight the clash of frozen ice cream and warm meringue.

rows.q: Originally settled during an 1860 gold rush, what Rocky Mountain mining town sits at over 10,000 feet, making it the highest-elevation incorporated city in the U.S.?
rows.n: It boomed in 1877 when miners realized heavy black sand clogging their sluices was lead carbonate ore.

rows.q: In 1937, Oklahoma City supermarket mogul Sylvan Goldman invented the rolling shopping cart by mounting wheels and wire baskets onto this piece of folding furniture.
rows.n: Goldman hired models to push carts around the aisles because shoppers initially found them embarrassing.

rows.q: Non-sparking wrenches used on offshore oil rigs are alloyed from copper and this stiff, toxic alkaline earth metal, element number 4.
rows.n: Beryllium-copper alloys are non-magnetic and spark-free, making them safe for explosive atmospheres.

rows.q: The historic feldspar mine at Ytterby, which inspired the names of four separate chemical elements, sits on an island in which European country?
rows.n: Yttrium, terbium, erbium, and ytterbium were all isolated from gadolinite found in that one quarry.

rows.q: French chemist Georges Urbain named element 71 lutetium after Lutetia, the ancient Roman settlement that eventually became which modern European capital?
rows.n: It was the last naturally occurring rare-earth element discovered, after decades of separation efforts.

rows.q: Standard gasoline cars still rely on 12-volt starter batteries powered by sulfuric acid and plates of this dense ancient metal.
rows.n: Invented in 1859 by Gaston Planté, the lead-acid battery was the world’s first rechargeable battery design.

rows.q: Plated on shiny hot-rod bumpers and providing the rich yellow in school buses, this element takes its name from the Greek for ‘color’.
rows.n: Formulated in the early 1800s, chrome yellow became the official U.S. school bus color standard in 1939.

rows.q: Medieval miners cursed this metal as a goblin’s trick, but its blue pigment colored porcelain, and today it coats EV batteries.
rows.n: German silver miners blamed the goblin Kobold when arsenic-laden ore failed to yield precious metals.

rows.q: While burning seaweed to harvest saltpeter for Napoleon’s gunpowder, Bernard Courtois accidentally produced a dense violet cloud that revealed this heavy halogen.
rows.n: It was named from the Greek word ioeides, which translates to violet-colored.

rows.q: Clemens Winkler discovered element 32 in 1886 and named it after his homeland, fulfilling Mendeleev’s prediction of ‘eka-silicon.’ Name this metalloid.
rows.n: It was used to make the very first working transistor at Bell Labs in 1947 before silicon took over.

rows.q: Glenn Seaborg had to wait until 1997 for element 106 to be officially named seaborgium, because IUPAC historically forbade naming elements after whom?
rows.n: Albert Einstein had also received an element name, but only after his death in 1955.

rows.q: Chemists Ida Tacke and Walter Noddack discovered element 75 in 1925, naming it rhenium after this major European river that flows past Cologne.
rows.n: Rhenium was the last stable, non-radioactive element discovered in nature.

rows.q: Continuing the cosmic naming sequence initiated by uranium, this Berkeley creation discovered in 1940 became the very first synthetic transuranium element added to the table.
rows.n: Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson produced it by bombarding uranium with neutrons.

rows.q: Humphry Davy reportedly danced around his laboratory in delight after using electrolysis in 1807 to extract this violent alkali metal, whose letter K on the table nods to plant ashes.
rows.n: The K comes from kalium, derived from the Arabic al-qalyah, meaning calcined ashes.

rows.q: Discovered by Johan Gadolin in 1794, this transition metal with symbol Y was the very first element named after the village of Ytterby. Name it.
rows.n: Yttrium barium copper oxide was famous in the 1980s for achieving high-temperature superconductivity.

rows.q: Martin Heinrich Klaproth isolated a new metallic oxide from pitchblende in 1789, promptly naming the element after this celestial body discovered eight years earlier.
rows.n: William Herschel had discovered Uranus in 1781; Klaproth named uranium in its honor.

rows.q: Monochrome yellow streetlights that bathed highways in the late 20th century ran on vaporized atoms of this soft alkali metal.
rows.n: Low-pressure sodium lamps were highly energy-efficient, but their monochromatic output ruined color vision.

rows.q: Despite the five-cent coin’s nickname, a standard modern U.S. nickel is actually three-quarters composed of this reddish base metal.
rows.n: The only time nickels had zero nickel was during WWII, when they were minted from silver, copper, and manganese.

rows.q: Since 1967, international metrology has defined the precise length of a single second by counting 9,192,631,770 microwave cycles emitted by an isotope of this soft alkali metal.
rows.n: Bunsen and Kirchhoff named it from the Latin caesius, meaning sky blue, for its spectral lines.

rows.q: Its corrosive vapors smell so foul that its discoverer named it after the Greek word for “stench.” Identify this heavy, reddish-brown halogen that stays liquid at room temperature.
rows.n: Antoine Balard isolated it in 1826 from the brine of Montpelier salt marshes.

rows.q: Joining California in 2016, which southern state became only the second to have a chemical element named directly after it?
rows.n: Tennessine shares the -ine suffix with the halogens because it sits in group 17 on the table.

rows.q: Dmitri Mendeleev predicted it as ‘ekaboron,’ but when Lars Fredrik Nilson isolated it in 1879, he named it after his Nordic home region. Name the element.
rows.n: Scandium is lightweight and strong, making its alloys popular in high-end bicycle frames and baseball bats.

rows.q: Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered barium, chlorine, molybdenum, and tungsten, but died at 43 largely due to his habit of doing what with newly isolated substances?
rows.n: Scheele regularly tasted and smelled his chemical preparations, including hydrocyanic acid and arsenic.

rows.q: Ionization smoke alarms rely on tiny traces of this radioactive element, discovered in 1944 and named for a continent.
rows.n: It was synthesized at the University of Chicago during the Manhattan Project.

rows.q: Mendeleev left blank spots on his periodic table, predicting element 32 would behave like silicon. When Clemens Winkler found it, he named it after this homeland.
rows.n: Winkler named it germanium; Mendeleev had provisionally dubbed the gap eka-silicon.

rows.q: Unable to dissolve his new oxide in acid, Swedish chemist Anders Ekeberg named element 73 after which Greek mythical figure, condemned to stand in water that recedes whenever he drinks?
rows.n: Ekeberg wrote that the element tantalized his efforts to react it with acids, inspiring the name.

rows.q: Ramsay’s teenage son suggested the Latin word “novum” for this newly isolated crimson-glowing noble gas, but his father opted instead for this Greek word meaning “new.”
rows.n: Although neon signs come in many shades today, only reddish-orange signs contain pure neon.

rows.q: Pepto-Bismol gets both its soothing properties and half its brand name from the subsalicylate salt of this post-transition metal.
rows.n: Despite sitting next to toxic lead on the periodic table, bismuth is remarkably stable and safe to ingest.

rows.q: Medieval alchemists called sulfuric acid by this glassy name, which today mostly survives as an insult for caustic, bitter speech.
rows.n: It was distilled from green vitriol, the historical name for iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate crystals.

rows.q: Modern white paints and sunscreens get their stark brightness from the oxide of this metal named after Greek mythological giants.
rows.n: Discovered in Cornwall, it was named after the Titans of Greek mythology by Martin Heinrich Klaproth.

rows.q: The blue LED that made modern flatscreens and energy-saving lighting possible was unlocked using a nitride of this low-melting metal.
rows.n: The breakthrough earned Shuji Nakamura, Isamu Akasaki, and Hiroshi Amano the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

rows.q: When Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach split the supposed element didymium in 1885, he dubbed one fraction praseodymium and the other this “new twin” used in strong magnets.
rows.n: The name fuses the Greek words neos (new) and didymos (twin).

rows.q: Picher, Oklahoma was abandoned due to toxic chat piles and acid mine water after decades of extracting lead and what galvanizing transition metal?
rows.n: By the early 2000s, undermining left the town at risk of cave-ins, and 63% of local children had lead poisoning.

rows.q: Named from ancient Greek words meaning ‘light-bringer,’ which element shares its name with the mythological personification of the morning star, the dawn herald of Venus?
rows.n: White phosphorus emits a faint green glow in the dark due to chemiluminescence as it slowly oxidizes.

rows.q: Joseph Lister revolutionized surgery in the 1860s by soaking dressings in this antiseptic coal-tar acid, known systematically as phenol.
rows.n: Lister’s surgeons sprayed it as a mist during operations, often irritating their own lungs and skin.

rows.q: Prized for its extreme wear resistance, this densest naturally occurring element was long alloyed with iridium to tip fountain pen nibs.
rows.n: The alloy osmiridium resisted ink acidity and decades of abrasive friction against paper.

rows.q: Virtually all modern window glass is manufactured by floating molten silica over a perfectly flat bath of this molten metal.
rows.n: Invented by Pilkington in the 1950s, float glass eliminated the need to grind and polish flat plate glass.

rows.q: Before rare-earth magnets hit the market, the strongest permanent magnets were cast from this portmanteau alloy of aluminum, nickel, and cobalt.
rows.n: Guitar makers still prize Alnico magnets in pickups for producing smooth, vintage electric tones.

rows.q: Taking its name from the Greek word for “unstable,” this ephemeral halogen is the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth, with less than an ounce in the crust at any time.
rows.n: Because its most stable isotope has a half-life of only eight hours, it decays almost immediately.

rows.q: Per Teodor Cleve discovered two elements in 1879, naming one thulium and the other holmium, derived from the Latin name for which Swedish city?
rows.n: Cleve chose the name because he was born, raised, and educated in the Swedish capital.

rows.q: Ancient Egyptians lined their eyelids with kohl made from a sulfide of this toxic metalloid, whose modern chemical symbol Sb originates from the Latin word stibium.
rows.n: In medieval alchemy, it was nicknamed the “grey wolf” because it rapidly swallowed molten gold.

rows.q: In 1803, Smithson Tennant isolated two new metals from insoluble platinum residues, naming one osmium for its pungent smell and the other after this Greek goddess.
rows.n: He named iridium after Iris, the goddess of the rainbow, because its salts formed vibrant colors.

rows.q: In human blood, an iron ion anchors the center of the oxygen-binding heme ring. In plant chlorophyll, that exact central coordinating slot is occupied by this alkaline earth metal.
French chemist Henri Moissan earned the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for finally isolating this pale yellow, hyper-reactive halogen, surviving the poisonous fumes that killed others.
rows.n: The 19th-century chemists blinded or killed by its toxic vapors are known as the fluorine martyrs.

rows.q: Beloved by Van Gogh and Monet for radiant yellows and reds, this toxic heavy metal’s pigments were named for the founder of Thebes.
rows.n: Cadmium yellow was prized by Impressionists because, unlike older chrome yellows, it did not rapidly darken.

rows.q: Element 99 was secretly discovered in the fallout debris gathered on filter papers after the 1952 ‘Ivy Mike’ test of the first full-scale version of this weapon.
rows.n: The element was named einsteinium; the discovery was kept classified until 1955.

rows.q: Discovered in 1923 at Niels Bohr’s institute, element 72 was dubbed hafnium after Hafnia, the Latin name for which Scandinavian capital?
rows.n: Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy proved Bohr’s quantum model of electron shells by finding it where he predicted.

rows.q: Early Xerox photocopiers operated thanks to the light-sensitive conductivity of this nonmetal, named after the Greek goddess of the Moon.
