rows.n: Discovered in 1817 by Jöns Jacob Berzelius, it was named after Selene to complement tellurium, named for Earth.

rows.q: Lydia minted some of the Western world’s earliest coins from this naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver, named from the Greek for amber.
rows.n: Ancient Egyptians used it to cap the pyramidions atop obelisks to catch and reflect the morning sun.

rows.q: Isolated in 1844 from Ural platinum ores by Karl Ernst Claus, which platinum-group element takes its name from the Latin term for Russia?
rows.n: Claus worked at Kazan University and named the element to honor his adopted Russian homeland.

rows.q: Named after a Scottish mining village, this alkaline earth metal is what gives road flares and red fireworks their intense crimson hue.
rows.n: Strontian, Scotland, is the only place in the United Kingdom to have an element named after it.

rows.q: Discovered in Transylvanian gold ore in 1782, this brittle metalloid was eventually named after the Roman personification of the Earth, providing an astronomical sibling for selenium.
rows.n: Chemist Martin Klaproth coined the name from Tellus Mater, the Roman Earth goddess.

rows.q: Often applied to white gold jewelry to produce a mirror finish, this platinum-group metal derives its name from the Greek for ‘rose’.
rows.n: Discovered in 1803 by William Hyde Wollaston, its chloride solutions form a distinctive deep rose-red color.

rows.q: Before the IUPAC settled on niobium in 1950, American chemists spent over a century insisting on calling element 41 by this patriotic name.
rows.n: British chemist Charles Hatchett named it in 1801 after finding it in an American ore specimen.

rows.q: Surrounding the solar system out to roughly a light-year, the theoretical icy reservoir that spawns long-period comets is named for which Dutch astronomer?
rows.n: Estonian astronomer Ernst Opik proposed a similar shell in 1932, so it is sometimes called the Opik-Oort cloud.

rows.q: Telescope visionary George Ellery Hale led the construction of massive observatories on Mount Wilson and Palomar, and transformed a modest Pasadena trade school into which top university?
rows.n: Hale convinced chemist Arthur Noyes and physicist Robert Millikan to join him in building the institution.

rows.q: Percival Lowell founded the Arizona observatory where Pluto was found, largely driven by his obsession with spotting these alleged features on Mars.
rows.n: Lowell was misled by Giovanni Schiaparelli’s Italian word canali, which just meant channels.

rows.q: The jansky is a unit of radio wave flux density honoring Karl Jansky. He stumbled onto celestial radio emissions in 1931 while hunting down static for what iconic New Jersey telecom employer?
rows.n: Jansky built a 100-foot directional antenna mounted on Model T Ford wheels to track the mystery hiss.

rows.q: Jupiter’s volcanic moon Io is named for a mortal lover of Zeus, whom the king of the gods tried to hide from his wife Hera by turning her into this common farm animal.
rows.n: Hera saw through the trick and demanded the cow as a gift, placing it under guard by Argus.

rows.q: The metal cover shielding the Voyager Golden Record is etched with instructions for playback and electroplated with an ultra-pure sample of this element to act as a radioactive clock.
rows.n: Because uranium-238 decays at a known half-life of 4.5 billion years, alien finders can calculate when it launched.

rows.q: NASA’s Mars Pathfinder mission deployed the agency’s very first roving vehicle in 1997, naming the microwave-sized machine after which 19th-century abolitionist and women’s rights activist?
rows.n: The name was submitted by a 12-year-old student from Connecticut who won a year-long international essay contest.

rows.q: Caltech’s Zwicky Transient Facility honors Fritz Zwicky, who in 1937 became the first to suggest that massive galaxy clusters could act as what light-bending magnifying devices?
rows.n: Einstein had considered the effect for individual stars, but Zwicky realized whole clusters made it visible.

rows.q: Zeus concealed his lover Callisto by turning her into a bear, inspiring both the name of Jupiter’s second-largest moon and this prominent northern constellation.
rows.n: Callisto is the most heavily cratered moon in the solar system, with virtually no geological activity.

rows.q: When the Skylab space station plummeted to Earth over Western Australia in 1979, the local shire council cheekily billed NASA a 400-dollar fine for this minor infraction.
rows.n: NASA never paid the citation; a California radio host eventually raised the funds to settle the bill in 2009.

rows.q: Discovered in 1978, what largest moon of Pluto is so massive relative to the dwarf planet that the two tidally lock face-to-face?
rows.n: Discoverer James Christy coined the name by blending his wife Charlene’s nickname with the mythical ferryman.

rows.q: Found in 2003 in the deep, freezing reaches past Pluto, dwarf planet candidate Sedna is named after the sea goddess of this Arctic people.
rows.n: Astronomer Mike Brown picked Inuit mythology because Sedna’s frigid environment reflects the Arctic realm.

rows.q: Observing an unfamiliar yellow spectral line during an 1868 solar eclipse in India, astronomer Pierre Janssen discovered this chemical element.
rows.n: Named after the Greek sun god Helios, it was found in the Sun 27 years before being isolated on Earth.

rows.q: The primary mirror of the James Webb Space Telescope consists of 18 hexagonal segments of beryllium, each vapor-coated with a 100-nanometer layer of which reflective precious metal?
rows.n: Gold reflects infrared light far better than silver or aluminum, optimizing Webb for faint, distant heat.

rows.q: Pluto’s moons follow an underworld theme. While Charon and Kerberos guard it, this small moon shares its name with the mythical river of oaths encircling Hades.
rows.n: Styx was discovered in 2012 by Hubble astronomers searching for navigational hazards to New Horizons.

rows.q: Neptune might have been credited to Britain if Astronomer Royal George Airy had checked John Couch Adams’s math from this famous observatory.
rows.n: Airy was skeptical of mathematical astronomy and filed Adams’s predictions away for months.

rows.q: Pluto’s prominent heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice is named Tombaugh Regio. Discoverer Clyde Tombaugh spotted the dwarf planet in 1930 while working at which Arizona observatory?
rows.n: Percival Lowell established the Flagstaff facility in 1894 to hunt for Mars canals and Planet X.

rows.q: Serving as the dry run for Apollo 11, the Apollo 10 mission paid tribute to the Peanuts comic strip by naming its two spacecraft after these two characters.
rows.n: Snoopy became NASA’s official safety mascot, and the Silver Snoopy award is still given to exemplary staff today.

rows.q: Unlike wheeled rovers, NASA’s stationary InSight lander set down a sensitive dome-covered seismometer in 2018 to measure internal tremors known by what geologic portmanteau?
rows.n: InSight detected over 1,300 marsquakes before Martian dust accumulated on its solar panels, silencing it in 2022.

rows.q: Gerard Kuiper gave his name to the solar system’s icy outer debris ring, but in 1948 he also discovered the battered, cliff-strewn moon Miranda orbiting which tilted ice giant?
rows.n: Voyager 2 revealed Verona Rupes on Miranda, the tallest known cliff in the solar system at twelve miles high.

rows.q: Edward Maunder documented a stark 70-year dearth of sunspots between 1645 and 1715. This solar minimum closely coincided with which centuries-long period of bitter European winters?
rows.n: During the minimum, Londoners held regular frost fairs and rode sledges on a frozen River Thames.

rows.q: Fastened inside the New Horizons probe when it zipped past Pluto in 2015 was a small aluminum container holding the cremated ashes of which astronomer, Pluto’s discoverer?
rows.n: Tombaugh spotted Pluto in 1930 while working as a self-taught 24-year-old assistant at Lowell Observatory.

rows.q: Remembering how his Mercury capsule sank in the Atlantic, astronaut Gus Grissom cheekily nicknamed his two-man Gemini 3 capsule after this unsinkable Titanic survivor.
rows.n: NASA brass disliked the irreverence and banned astronauts from naming their capsules again until Apollo 9.

rows.q: Stranded in Jamaica in 1504, this explorer frightened the Indigenous Taino into feeding his crew by using a German almanac to forecast a total lunar eclipse.
rows.n: Columbus consulted the ephemeris tables computed by the astronomer Regiomontanus.

rows.q: Still communicating from interstellar space billions of miles out, the twin Voyager probes draw electrical power from radioisotope generators fueled by the decay of this transuranic element.
rows.n: Because sunlight beyond Jupiter is too feeble for early solar cells, each probe packed three plutonium generators.

rows.q: During their record-breaking Christmas Eve telecast from lunar orbit in 1968, the crew of Apollo 8 took turns reading the opening verses from this book of the Bible.
rows.n: Atheist activist Madalyn Murray O’Hair sued NASA over the reading, but the Supreme Court dismissed the suit.

rows.q: Built inside a natural limestone sinkhole in Puerto Rico, this 1,000-foot radio dish broadcast humanity’s famous 1974 interstellar greeting before its instrument platform collapsed in 2020.
rows.n: The dish famously served as a backdrop for the climactic battle in the 1995 James Bond film GoldenEye.

rows.q: While flying home from the Moon on Apollo 14, astronaut Edgar Mitchell conducted secret, unauthorized experiments to test for this three-letter psychic phenomenon.
rows.n: He tried transmitting symbols mentally to four colleagues back on Earth during his scheduled sleep periods.

rows.q: In May 1919, this British astronomer traveled to the island of Principe to photograph stars during a solar eclipse, providing early proof of general relativity.
rows.n: His team measured the gravitational deflection of starlight, matching Albert Einstein’s predictions.

rows.q: En route to the launch pad at Baikonur, cosmonauts always instruct their bus driver to stop so they can perform this crude personal ritual on the right rear tire.
rows.n: The tradition honors Yuri Gagarin, who had to relieve himself against his bus tire right before his 1961 flight.

rows.q: Parachuting into the Utah desert in 2023, NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission returned pristine gravel and dust from the surface of this near-Earth asteroid.
rows.n: The sample contained about 4.3 ounces of material, rich in carbon and water-bearing minerals.

rows.q: The Spitzer Space Telescope honoured Lyman Spitzer, who first championed orbital telescopes in 1946. Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum did this Great Observatory capture?
rows.n: To keep warm telescope hardware from blinding its detectors, Spitzer was chilled using liquid helium.

rows.q: Neptune’s innermost moon Naiad is named after the naiads of Greek myth, the aquatic nymphs who specifically presided over bodies of this type of water.
rows.n: Naiads were strictly associated with rivers, springs, and marshes, distinct from marine Nereids.

rows.q: Suckling the infant Zeus, the mythical creature Amalthea lent her name to a Jovian moon and was usually depicted as this horned farm animal.
rows.n: Discovered in 1892, Amalthea was the last jovian moon spotted through direct visual observation.

rows.q: The 1995 discovery of 51 Pegasi b upended planetary science, revealing a giant roasting close to its star and creating this two-word classification.
rows.n: It orbits its host star in roughly four days, with surface temperatures topping 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit.

rows.q: To honor early aviation, NASA engineers taped a tiny postage-stamp-sized swatch of muslin wing fabric from the Wright Brothers’ 1903 Flyer underneath which Mars vehicle?
rows.n: Originally planned for just five demonstration flights, the plucky four-pound rotorcraft completed 72 missions.

rows.q: Predating Stonehenge by centuries, which 5,200-year-old Irish passage tomb features an engineered roof-box that floods its inner burial chamber with sunlight only at the winter solstice dawn?
rows.n: Demand to be inside the chamber during the solstice is so high that access is decided by an annual global lottery.

rows.q: In 1982, the Soviet Venera 14 lander measured the compressibility of Venusian soil, only to find it strangely elastic because its spring-loaded tester landed squarely on its own discarded what?
rows.n: The camera lens cap popped off upon landing and bounced directly underneath the soil compressibility tester.

rows.q: Ganymede, Jupiter’s largest moon, is the only Galilean satellite named for a male consort of Zeus, abducted to serve in this thirsty domestic role.
rows.n: Ganymede is the solar system’s largest moon, edging out the planet Mercury in diameter.

rows.q: William Herschel built the reflector telescope that spotted Uranus with the help of this sister, who later discovered eight comets herself.
rows.n: She was the first woman in Britain to receive a royal salary for scientific work.

rows.q: The European probe that took the first close-up photos of Halley’s nucleus in 1986 honored this Italian artist, who painted the comet in a 1305 fresco.
rows.n: Giotto saw the comet in 1301 and used it as the model for the Star of Bethlehem in Padua’s Scrovegni Chapel.

rows.q: Deliberately slamming a spacecraft into the small asteroid moon Dimorphos in 2022, NASA successfully altered its orbit in this acronym-named test.
rows.n: The collision shortened Dimorphos’s orbital period around its parent asteroid Didymos by 32 minutes.

rows.q: Giving astronomers an impact scare in 2004 before being ruled out for 2029, a 1,100-foot near-Earth asteroid was named after this Egyptian god of chaos.
rows.n: Radar observations in 2021 finally confirmed it will not hit Earth for at least another hundred years.

rows.q: Derived from the Greek for ‘yoked together,’ this three-letter-repeating word describes a straight-line astronomical alignment of three celestial bodies.
rows.n: Solar and lunar eclipses are both examples of syzygy, as are unusually strong spring tides.

rows.q: The European Space Agency made the first soft landing on a comet in 2014 when the Rosetta spacecraft released this three-legged lander onto Comet 67P.
rows.n: Philae bounced twice after its harpoons failed to anchor, eventually lodging in the shadow of a cliff.

rows.q: In 1999, NASA broke a longstanding glass ceiling by appointing this veteran pilot as the first woman to command a Space Shuttle mission, aboard Columbia on STS-93.
rows.n: Collins later commanded STS-114, NASA’s crucial Return to Flight mission following the Columbia disaster.

rows.q: First confirmed in 1992, the earliest known exoplanets did not orbit a normal star, but this kind of rapidly spinning, dead stellar remnant.
rows.n: Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail detected them orbiting pulsar PSR B1257+12.

rows.q: NASA’s flagship X-ray space telescope honors the astrophysicist who proved that exceeding 1.4 solar masses causes the gravitational collapse of which common type of stellar ember?
rows.n: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar derived the limit at age 19 while aboard an ocean liner traveling from India to England.

rows.q: Peaking every August, the Perseid meteor shower is known in Catholic folklore as the ‘tears’ of which 3rd-century saint, famously roasted on a gridiron?
rows.n: His feast day falls on August 10, coinciding closely with the shower’s peak activity.

rows.q: Famous for co-discovering the comet that smashed into Jupiter in 1994, this planetary geologist is the only human whose ashes have been buried on the Moon.
In February 2013, an undetected 66-foot space rock exploded over this Russian city in the Ural Mountains, blowing out windows across six cities.
rows.n: It was the largest natural space object to enter Earth’s atmosphere since the 1908 Tunguska event.

rows.q: Two of Uranus’s moons break from the Shakespeare theme: Umbriel and Belinda were borrowed from ‘The Rape of the Lock,’ an 18th-century mock-epic by this English satirist.
rows.n: Ariel is the lone crossover character, appearing in both Pope’s poem and Shakespeare’s The Tempest.

rows.q: The Event Horizon Telescope produced the first direct image of a black hole in 2019, targeting the supermassive behemoth at the center of this giant elliptical galaxy in the Virgo cluster.
rows.n: The black hole’s shadow is larger than our entire solar system and harbors the mass of 6.5 billion suns.

rows.q: Stranded in orbit aboard Mir as his government dissolved below him, this cosmonaut launched from the USSR in 1991 and returned to Earth four months late as a citizen of Russia.
rows.n: During his unplanned 311 days in space, the Soviet Union fractured into fifteen independent nations.

rows.q: Months before Kathryn Sullivan became the first American woman to walk in space, this Soviet cosmonaut beat her to the milestone during a 1984 mission outside Salyut 7.
rows.n: During her three-hour EVA, Savitskaya tested a multipurpose tool used to cut and weld metals in a vacuum.

rows.q: Featuring Verona Rupes, the tallest known cliff in the solar system, this innermost round moon of Uranus is named for a Shakespearean heroine.
rows.n: If you stepped off Verona Rupes, its weak gravity means you would fall for over ten minutes before landing.

rows.q: Apollo 12 proved pinpoint lunar landing by setting down within walking distance of this uncrewed NASA probe, which had touched down on the Moon two years earlier.
rows.n: Astronauts removed its camera and brought it back to Earth to study long-term exposure to the lunar environment.

rows.q: Proving Galileo correct in the Moon’s vacuum, Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a geological hammer alongside a feather plucked from this bird of prey.
rows.n: The raptor matched the mission’s lunar module, named Falcon, which in turn honored the Air Force Academy mascot.

rows.q: Cassini made one of its greatest discoveries in 2005 when it imaged cryovolcanic geysers erupting from the “tiger stripe” fractures near the south pole of this brilliant icy moon of Saturn.
rows.n: The discovery proved Enceladus harbors a global subsurface liquid ocean, making it a prime astrobiology target.

rows.q: Embarrassed to press his ear directly to a female patient’s chest, French physician René Laennec rolled up paper in 1816 to invent this tool.
rows.n: Laennec soon carved a permanent wooden monaural version before the binaural tube design became standard.

rows.q: Controlling how much light hits your retina, the colored muscular ring of the eye gets its name from the Greek goddess of this atmospheric phenomenon.
rows.n: In Greek mythology, Iris traveled along rainbows as a personal messenger for the gods of Olympus.

rows.q: As humans grow up, blood-producing red bone marrow is gradually replaced in long bones by yellow marrow, which consists mostly of this storage tissue.
rows.n: In emergencies like severe hemorrhage, yellow marrow can convert back to red to make blood cells.

rows.q: Presbyopia, the age-related loss of near vision that requires reading glasses, shares its Greek root for ‘elder’ with which mainstream Protestant denomination?
rows.n: Both terms trace to ‘presbyteros,’ the ancient Greek word for elder, reflecting governance by church elders.

rows.q: King George III’s bouts of madness are often blamed on porphyria, an inherited blood disorder that famously turns what bodily fluid purple or reddish-black?
rows.n: Porphyria stems from a buildup of porphyrins, the chemical precursors to heme in red blood cells.

rows.q: Swelling visibly during a bout of the mumps, the parotids are the largest of the three major pairs of organs that produce this digestive fluid.
rows.n: The parotid glands alone produce up to a quarter of your total resting saliva each day.

rows.q: First described by Kinnier Wilson in 1912, Wilson’s disease causes dangerous tissue accumulation of this reddish metal, often forming dark golden rings around the cornea.
rows.n: Those dark corneal halos are known to eye doctors as Kayser-Fleischer rings.

rows.q: The autoimmune disorder lupus derives its name from the Latin word for this predator, as medieval doctors thought the distinctive facial butterfly rash resembled its bite.
rows.n: The full formal name, lupus erythematosus, translates roughly to ‘red wolf.’

rows.q: Deriving their name from the Greek words for ‘end’ and ‘part,’ these protective caps at the tips of chromosomes shorten each time a cell divides.
rows.n: Elizabeth Blackburn, Carol Greider, and Jack Szostak won the 2009 Nobel Prize for explaining how they function.

rows.q: A sudden wave of fainting, racing pulse, and panic caused by overwhelming artistic beauty is known as Stendhal syndrome, named after a French author who fell ill in this Italian city.
rows.n: Stendhal was overwhelmed in 1817 by the Giotto frescoes inside the Basilica of Santa Croce.

rows.q: Lifeguards famously coated their noses in what white mineral paste, which forms a reflective physical shield against UV rays rather than absorbing into the skin?
rows.n: Beyond sunscreens, the compound has long been used in calamine lotion and diaper rash ointments.

rows.q: Sitting atop the kidneys, the adrenal glands release this primary stress hormone, an excess of which leads to the fatty deposits of Cushing’s syndrome.
rows.n: High cortisol levels can cause a hallmark ‘moon face’ and a fatty pad between the shoulders.

rows.q: Positioned between the malleus and the stapes in the middle ear, what tiny auditory bone is commonly called the anvil?
rows.n: Together with the other two ossicles, it helps convert air vibrations in the ear canal into fluid waves.

rows.q: Barbara McClintock won a 1983 Nobel Prize for showing that genes can physically move on a chromosome, a phenomenon she discovered while studying the kernels of this crop.
rows.n: Her discovery of ‘jumping genes’ or transposons was dismissed for decades before molecular biology caught up.

rows.q: Butchers in old England hung slaughtered pigs by these rear leg tendons, giving this familiar muscle group its enduring pork-based name.
rows.n: In archaic English, “ham” simply referred to the hollow or crook behind the knee.

rows.q: Ancients believed this triangular bone at the base of the spine protected the soul, giving it a name that means “sacred bone”.
rows.n: It consists of five fused vertebrae wedged securely between the hip bones.

rows.q: Late in life, Claude Monet blamed this clouding of the eye’s natural lens for distorting his color perception and muddying his water lily paintings.
rows.n: After undergoing surgery to remove one in 1923, Monet could see ultraviolet light, which shifted his palette blue.

rows.q: The reconstructive “Tommy John surgery,” common among major league pitchers, replaces the torn ulnar collateral one of these tough connective tissues in the elbow.
rows.n: Dr. Frank Jobe took a tendon from Tommy John’s forearm to weave a new ligament in 1974.

rows.q: Groote Schuur Hospital was the site of the world’s first successful human heart transplant in 1967, located in this country.
rows.n: Recipient Louis Washkansky survived for 18 days after the landmark five-hour operation in Cape Town.

rows.q: One of the eight carpal bones in your wrist gets this celestial name from its crescent shape, derived from the Roman goddess of the moon.
rows.n: It shares its root with lunacy, from the old belief that moon phases caused madness.

rows.q: On the crime drama Bones, forensic anthropologist Dr. Temperance Brennan checks victims for strangulation by examining what U-shaped bone in the throat?
rows.n: The hyoid is the only bone in the human skeleton that does not articulate with any other bone.

rows.q: Worn-out red blood cells go to this fist-sized organ on your left side to be dismantled, earning it the nickname ‘the graveyard of red blood cells.’
rows.n: The spleen recycles the iron from aged erythrocytes while saving usable hemoglobin components.

rows.q: Borrowing its name from the Latin word for a flat cake, it is the only human organ grown entirely from scratch, used to nourish life, and then discarded.
rows.n: It acts as lungs, kidneys, and liver for the fetus, filtering nutrients and oxygen from maternal blood.

rows.q: Steve Jobs designed smooth, port-free Apple products partly because he harbored koumpounophobia, an irrational aversion to what small clothing fasteners?
rows.n: His distaste extended to clothing; Jobs virtually never wore shirts with buttons, favoring black turtlenecks instead.

rows.q: Forming a large diamond across your upper back and neck, this posture muscle is named for an irregular four-sided geometric shape.
rows.n: It shares its Greek root with “trapeze” as well as the geometric trapezoid.

rows.q: When sunlight strikes your skin, epidermal cells use ultraviolet-B rays to synthesize vitamin D from a chemical derivative of this waxy, often-maligned lipid.
rows.n: The precursor compound is 7-dehydrocholesterol, which converts to vitamin D3 after UVB exposure.

rows.q: Characterized by severe self-neglect and squalid domestic hoarding, this psychological syndrome is named after the ancient Greek philosopher who chose to live in a ceramic jar.
rows.n: Ironically, the real Diogenes practiced radical minimalism, rejecting possessions to live in public spaces.

rows.q: Whacking your “funny bone” does not hit bone at all, but rather this nerve running behind the elbow, named for an adjacent arm bone.
rows.n: It is entirely unprotected by muscle or bone at the elbow, making it vulnerable to bumps.

rows.q: Blood bank pioneer Charles Drew resigned as director of the American Red Cross blood program in 1941 to protest the military’s policy of doing what to donor blood?
rows.n: Drew insisted there was no scientific basis for separating blood, as human plasma is identical across races.

rows.q: To keep stomach acid from eating through your small intestine, this digestive organ pumps out a steady wash of sodium bicarbonate, the active chemical in baking soda.
rows.n: It secretes roughly a liter of alkaline fluid daily to neutralize acidic chyme leaving the stomach.

rows.q: First described as ‘the delirium of negation’ by a French neurologist in 1880, patients with Cotard delusion hold the unshakable belief that they are actually what?
rows.n: Also called Walking Corpse syndrome, severe cases lead patients to claim their organs are missing or putrefying.

rows.q: Dating back to ‘cingulum,’ the Latin word for this everyday accessory, the name for shingles reflects how its rash encircles one side of the torso.
rows.n: The disease is caused by a reactivation of the dormant varicella-zoster virus, which also causes chickenpox.

rows.q: Pound for pound the body’s strongest muscle, this jaw-closing powerhouse gets its name from the Greek word for “to chew”.
rows.n: By weight, it is widely considered the strongest muscle in the human body.

rows.q: Early European explorers treated malaria using quinine derived from the bark of this South American tree, named for a Spanish countess who allegedly survived an infection in Peru.
rows.n: The tree’s bitter bark was also known as ‘Jesuit’s bark’ because Spanish missionaries exported it.

rows.q: The medical term for hair loss, alopecia, derives from the ancient Greek word for which bushy-tailed wild canine, inspired by its mangy appearance while shedding?
rows.n: Ancient Greeks noticed that foxes regularly lost large, patchy clumps of fur to skin mites and seasonal molts.

rows.q: Human epigenetics gained vital proof from the 1944 ‘Hunger Winter,’ a wartime famine that altered the lifelong metabolism of unborn children in this European country.
rows.n: The famine was triggered by a German embargo that cut food rations to under 1,000 calories a day.

rows.q: The sartorius is the longest muscle in the human body, running diagonally down the thigh. Its name comes from the Latin word for what profession because it helps you sit cross-legged?
rows.n: Traditional tailors sat cross-legged on the floor all day to keep delicate fabrics out of the dust while sewing.

rows.q: At the lower tip of your sternum, the xiphoid process gets its name from the ancient Greek word for this bladed weapon.
rows.n: CPR instructors warn rescuers to avoid pressing it to prevent breaking it into the liver.

rows.q: Unlike most forms of asphyxiation that leave a victim pale or blue, carbon monoxide poisoning binds to hemoglobin so tightly that it turns the skin this vibrant color.
rows.n: Carboxyhemoglobin is bright ruby red, which often fools pulse oximeters into reading 100% saturation.

rows.q: An exaggerated startle reflex first observed in 1878 among Franco-Canadian lumberjacks in the Moosehead Lake region is known as the ‘Jumping Frenchmen of’ which U.S. state?
rows.n: When startled with a sudden shout, sufferers would automatically mimic sounds or obey dangerous commands.

rows.q: A dinner party guest who panics at the sight of a charcuterie board may have turophobia, a condition taking its name from the ancient Greek word for what food?
rows.n: The organic compound tyramine, abundant in aged cheddar and parmesan, shares the exact same Greek root.

rows.q: Generations of royal inbreeding culminated in the severe ‘Habsburg jaw’ of this sickly last Habsburg monarch of Spain, who died heirless in 1700.
When London doctor James Parkinson wrote the definitive 1817 account of the tremor-heavy condition now named for him, he titled his monograph ‘An Essay on the Shaking’ what?
rows.n: French neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot formally renamed the condition after Parkinson sixty years later.

rows.q: In 1909, Nobel laureate Paul Ehrlich developed the first targeted cure for syphilis, Salvarsan, relying on this notoriously lethal chemical element.
rows.n: Ehrlich dubbed Salvarsan a ‘magic bullet,’ though it still caused nasty side effects due to the toxic metal.

rows.q: On February 28, 1953, Francis Crick reportedly interrupted patrons at this Cambridge pub to announce that he and James Watson had found the secret of life.
rows.n: The pub still serves an ale called ‘Eagle’s DNA’ in honor of the announcement.

rows.q: Botulism takes its name from the Latin word for this ground meat casing food, which frequently spoiled and poisoned 18th-century German villagers.
rows.n: German physician Justinus Kerner called it ‘sausage poison’ after tracking outbreaks to bad blood sausages.

rows.q: Cyclists and marathoners have abused synthetic EPO to pack their blood with extra oxygen, but the human body naturally manufactures the hormone in this organ pair.
rows.n: When renal cells detect hypoxia, they boost EPO production to stimulate red cell growth in bone marrow.

rows.q: Coined during an 18th-century European outbreak, the name ‘influenza’ comes from an Italian phrase blaming the sickness on the unwholesome influence of these celestial bodies.
rows.n: Medieval astrologers believed the alignment of planets and heavenly bodies caused widespread epidemics.

rows.q: Sitting in front of your windpipe, the thyroid gland takes its name from the ancient Greek word for what defensive piece of armor, which anatomists thought it resembled?
rows.n: Specifically, it honors the ‘thyreos,’ an oblong door-shaped infantry shield with a notch for resting a spear.

rows.q: Dangling over the back of the throat to help block food from your nasal cavity, the uvula gets its anatomical name from the Latin diminutive for which small fruit?
rows.n: The Latin noun ‘uva’ means grape; ‘uvula’ translates literally as ‘little grape.’

rows.q: When captors unexpectedly develop sympathy and positive feelings toward their hostages, they display an inverse of Stockholm syndrome named for a 1996 crisis in which capital city?
rows.n: Tupac Amaru rebels held hundreds of dignitaries at the Japanese ambassador’s residence before releasing most unharmed.

rows.q: Tucked directly behind your calf, this flat postural muscle is named after the Latin word for a sandal, which also names a flatfish.
rows.n: The Dover sole fish gets its culinary name from the exact same flat sandal root.

rows.q: When Karl Landsteiner identified the first three human blood groups in 1901, he labeled them A, B, and this letter, later renamed O.
rows.n: Landsteiner changed it to O from the German ‘ohne,’ meaning ‘without’ antigens.

rows.q: In 1905, geneticist Nettie Stevens proved that sex is determined by X and Y chromosomes while examining the cells of this common pet-food beetle larva.
rows.n: Stevens published her discovery before E.B. Wilson, though her mentor Thomas Hunt Morgan long got the credit.

rows.q: Dismissed for centuries as fragmented abdominal tissue, this double-fold of peritoneum that anchors your intestines was finally reclassified as a continuous organ in 2016.
rows.n: Leonardo da Vinci drew it as a single structure, but anatomists ignored his sketch for five hundred years.

rows.q: Alexander Fleming’s moldy petri dish famously killed off colonies of this common bacterium, named for its grape-like clusters under a microscope.
rows.n: Fleming left his London lab messy in 1928, returning from vacation to find Penicillium mold killing the staph.

rows.q: Congenital central hypoventilation causes a person to stop breathing whenever they fall asleep. Clinicians often refer to it as the ‘curse’ of which mythological water nymph?
rows.n: In folklore, Ondine stripped her unfaithful mortal husband of automatic breathing, forcing him to stay awake to live.

rows.q: Cutaneous anthrax leaves patients with painless, pitch-black skin ulcers, earning the disease a name derived from the Greek word for this dark fossil fuel.
rows.n: The same Greek root gave geology the term anthracite, referring to hard, high-carbon coal.

rows.q: Georg Cantor proved that some infinities are strictly larger than others, using this ancient script’s first letter, aleph, to label their infinite sizes.
rows.n: Aleph-null denotes the cardinality of the natural numbers, which Cantor proved is the smallest infinite cardinal.

rows.q: In his 1202 book Liber Abaci, Leonardo of Pisa introduced his famous sequence by calculating the breeding cycles of what prolific mammals?
rows.n: He assumed an idealized scenario where no rabbits die and each pair breeds one new pair every single month.

rows.q: Equal to one ten-billionth of a meter, a unit of length used for atomic radii is named after Anders Jonas Ångström, a physicist from this country.
rows.n: Ångström made the first spectral analysis of the aurora borealis in 1867.

rows.q: Schrödinger’s morbid 1935 thought experiment put a cat in a steel chamber beside a decaying atom and a vial of this deadly poison.
rows.n: Schrödinger devised the scenario to mock quantum superposition on macroscopic scales, not celebrate it.

rows.q: In 1851, Léon Foucault demonstrated Earth’s rotation to the public using a 67-meter pendulum swung from the dome of this Parisian landmark.
rows.n: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte personally granted permission for Foucault to use the secularized mausoleum.

rows.q: Because ships flying off the top re-enter at the bottom and the sides wrap identically, the screen in the arcade classic Asteroids is topologically equivalent to this shape.
rows.n: In topology, identifying opposite edges of a flat sheet of paper produces the surface of a doughnut.

rows.q: Leonhard Euler laid the foundations of graph theory in 1736 by analyzing seven river bridges in Königsberg, a city now known by what Russian name?
rows.n: Renamed in 1946 for Bolshevik leader Mikhail Kalinin, the city sits on the Pregolya River along the Baltic coast.

rows.q: Arthur Eddington traveled to an island off West Africa in 1919 to photograph stars shifted behind the sun, possible only during this brief event.
rows.n: The bending of starlight around the sun made Einstein an overnight global celebrity on front-page newspapers.

rows.q: Claude Shannon’s landmark 1937 master’s thesis revolutionized computing by applying this 19th-century British logician’s binary algebra to electrical relay switches.
rows.n: Shannon was just 21 when he wrote the paper, hailed as one of the most important master’s theses of the 20th century.

rows.q: While recovering from illness in 1946, mathematician Stanislaw Ulam conceived the Monte Carlo method after pondering the odds of winning this solo card game.
rows.n: He realized playing hundreds of random hands on a computer was faster than calculating pure combinatorial odds.

rows.q: In 1901, the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics went to which German scientist, whose discovery of X-rays was later honored with a unit of radiation?
rows.n: He refused to take out patents on X-rays so that the entire medical world could use them freely.

rows.q: Long before his name became the SI unit of energy, this English physicist used thermometers and vats at his family’s brewery to study heat.
rows.n: He was trying to replace the brewery’s steam engines with electric motors to save money.

rows.q: Seeking a reliable zero for his temperature scale, which German instrument maker chose a freezing mixture of ice, water, and salt?
rows.n: He set 96 degrees as the human body temperature, which was later recalibrated to 98.6.

rows.q: Enrico Fermi won his 1938 Nobel believing he had synthesized new elements, but his experiments had actually split the nucleus—a process borrowing its name from this biological cell division.
rows.n: Physicist Otto Frisch coined the nuclear term in 1939 after asking a biologist how bacteria reproduce.

rows.q: Linus Pauling is the only person to win two unshared Nobel Prizes: his first for the nature of chemical bonds, and his second for campaigning against tests of these weapons.
rows.n: Pauling delivered a petition signed by more than 11,000 scientists to the United Nations in 1958.

rows.q: One radioactive disintegration per second equals one becquerel, named for Henri Becquerel, who found radioactivity in salts of this heavy metal.
rows.n: He discovered radioactivity accidentally when photographic plates wrapped in paper fogged inside a desk drawer.

rows.q: Often called the “Prince of Mathematicians,” which German polymath lent his name to both a magnetic unit and the bell-shaped normal distribution?
rows.n: Gauss also calculated the orbit of the newly discovered dwarf planet Ceres after astronomers lost track of it.

rows.q: Besides his 1972 prize for superconductivity, John Bardeen earned a 1956 physics Nobel for co-inventing this foundational semiconductor device.
rows.n: Bardeen co-invented the point-contact transistor at Bell Labs alongside Walter Brattain and William Shockley.

rows.q: Denoted by a Greek letter matching sculptor Phidias, the golden ratio of roughly 1.618 is represented by which twenty-first letter of that alphabet?
rows.n: Mathematician Mark Barr suggested the symbol phi in the early 1900s to honor Phidias’s Parthenon sculptures.

rows.q: Albert Tucker popularized a game theory puzzle about two conspirators weighing betrayal against silence, naming it after this type of captive.
rows.n: The paradox shows why two rational individuals might fail to cooperate, even when it is in their best interest.

rows.q: David Hilbert illustrated the weird mathematics of infinite sets in 1924 by imagining this commercial establishment, fully booked yet able to take guests.
rows.n: To fit one newcomer, the manager shifts the occupant of room 1 to room 2, room 2 to room 3, and so on ad infinitum.

rows.q: Harold Kroto and his team named their Nobel-winning, cage-like sixty-carbon molecule after Buckminster Fuller because its shape resembled these distinctive architectural domes.
rows.n: The structure consists of 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons, matching the geometry of a standard soccer ball.

rows.q: When Henry Cavendish measured Newton’s universal gravitational constant in 1798, newspapers famously described him as “weighing” what body?
rows.n: Cavendish’s calculation allowed scientists to determine Earth’s density to within one percent of its modern value.

rows.q: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar proved that a dying star heavier than 1.4 times this specific celestial body cannot become a stable white dwarf and must collapse.
rows.n: Exceeding the 1.4 solar mass threshold, known as the Chandrasekhar limit, leaves a neutron star or black hole.

rows.q: Felix Klein originally called his one-sided closed surface a “Kleinsche Fläche,” or Klein surface, which German-to-English translators confused with this domestic vessel.
rows.n: The German word “Fläche” (surface) was mistaken for “Flasche” (bottle), and the name stuck forever.

rows.q: To disprove Luigi Galvani’s theory of “animal electricity” in twitching frog legs, which Italian count built the first electric battery in 1800?
rows.n: Napoleon was so impressed by the battery that he made Volta a count and a senator.

rows.q: Greek mathematician Thales famously determined the height of which ancient royal tomb by measuring its shadow at the exact moment of day when his own shadow equaled his personal height?
rows.n: He used the geometry of similar triangles, measuring when a person’s shadow matched their physical height.

rows.q: The Chandrasekhar limit dictates that if one of these dense, pale stellar remnants exceeds 1.4 solar masses, it must collapse.
rows.n: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar derived the mathematical limit in 1930 while on a boat voyage from India to England.

rows.q: British twenty-pence and fifty-pence coins are shaped as Reuleaux heptagons so that they maintain a constant what as they roll through vending machines?
rows.n: Because their width is constant, the coins smoothly roll between parallel coin-testing sensors without jamming.

rows.q: Known as the father of nuclear physics, Ernest Rutherford quipped that his quickest transformation was switching from a physicist into this profession upon winning his 1908 Nobel.
rows.n: Rutherford famously claimed that all science is either physics or stamp collecting.

rows.q: To keep them from the Nazis occupying Copenhagen, chemist George de Hevesy hid two laureates’ gold Nobel medals by dissolving them in this corrosive nitric-and-hydrochloric acid cocktail.
rows.n: After the war, de Hevesy precipitated the hidden gold out and the Nobel Foundation restruck the medals.

rows.q: Formed by joining the ends of an everyday overhand knot, the simplest non-trivial knot in topology shares its name with this three-leaf plant symbol.
rows.n: Unlike a standard circle or unknot, the trefoil knot cannot be untied without physically cutting the strand.

rows.q: The Comte de Buffon showed in 1777 that dropping random needles across parallel floorboards can mathematically approximate this irrational constant.
rows.n: In 1901, an Italian mathematician dropped a needle 3,408 times and estimated pi accurately to six decimal places.

rows.q: Joseph Henry gave his name to the SI unit of inductance and in 1846 became the very first secretary of this Washington, D.C. institution.
rows.n: While heading the Smithsonian, Henry advised Alexander Graham Bell on the design of the telephone.

rows.q: On February 29, 1940, Ernest Lawrence accepted his Nobel Prize in Physics at UC Berkeley for inventing this circular particle accelerator.
rows.n: Because World War II had broken out in Europe, the ceremony was moved from Stockholm to California.

rows.q: According to ancient accounts, Archimedes considered the ratio between a sphere and this enclosing solid his greatest achievement, asking it be carved on his tomb.
rows.n: The Roman orator Cicero claimed to have tracked down and cleared the overgrown, forgotten tomb in Sicily in 75 BC.

rows.q: James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny gatekeeper sorting hot and cold gas molecules, but it was this temperature-scale physicist who dubbed it a “demon.”
rows.n: Maxwell objected to the supernatural label, originally calling his entity a “finite being.”

rows.q: Food scientists engineered the stackable Pringles potato crisp in the shape of a saddle, classified mathematically as a hyperbolic what?
rows.n: The saddle shape provides structural rigidity, making the thin crisps far less likely to break in the can.

rows.q: A decade before winning the 2010 physics Nobel for isolating graphene, Andre Geim won an Ig Nobel for using powerful magnets to levitate a living one of these amphibians.
rows.n: Geim remains the only individual scientist to win both a real Nobel Prize and an Ig Nobel Prize.

rows.q: Evangelista Torricelli analyzed a trumpet-shaped solid in 1644 with infinite surface area but finite volume, often named for this biblical archangel.
rows.n: The horn is created by rotating the curve y = 1/x about the x-axis for values of x greater than or equal to 1.

rows.q: Absolute zero anchors the temperature scale named for Lord Kelvin, who took his title from a river flowing past the university in this Scottish city.
rows.n: Born William Thomson, he was knighted for overseeing the laying of the first transatlantic telegraph cable.

rows.q: William Ramsay won the 1904 Chemistry Nobel for filling in an entire column of the periodic table, beginning with this inert gas he named after the Greek word for ‘lazy’.
rows.n: Ramsay chose the name from the Greek ‘argos’ because the element stubbornly refused to form compounds.

rows.q: Envisioning a universe of pure clockwork determinism in 1814, Pierre-Simon Laplace posited a hypothetical all-knowing intellect, later dubbed Laplace’s what?
rows.n: When Napoleon asked why his work never mentioned God, Laplace famously replied, ‘I had no need of that hypothesis.’

rows.q: Although named for Leonhard Euler, the constant e was discovered by Jacob Bernoulli while calculating continuous payouts of this financial return.
rows.n: Bernoulli explored what happens to an initial deposit if 100 percent annual interest is compounded continuously.

rows.q: Johannes Kepler’s early 1596 model of the solar system attempted to space the orbits of the six known planets using these five regular polyhedra.
Representing infinity as a sideways figure-eight, this ten-letter mathematical term is derived from the Latin word for ribbon.
rows.n: English mathematician John Wallis introduced the symbol in his 1655 treatise De Sectionibus Conicis.

rows.q: Often confused with a parabola, the curve traced by a heavy chain hanging freely between two supports under its own weight is known as what?
rows.n: The Gateway Arch in St. Louis is built as an inverted, weighted catenary to distribute its structural load.

rows.q: Famed as antiquity’s greatest female mathematician, this Alexandria scholar and head of the Neoplatonic school was brutally murdered by a mob of zealots in 415 AD.
rows.n: Her murder was politically charged; the Christian mob used sharpened oyster shells to scrape the flesh from her bones.

rows.q: In acoustics, circular walls that carry sound over long distances without dying out are named after this dome feature of London’s St. Paul’s Cathedral.
rows.n: Lord Rayleigh explained the math in 1910, proving sound waves cling to the curved masonry wall.

rows.q: Eratosthenes estimated the circumference of Earth around 240 BC by comparing midday shadows in Alexandria to a sunlit well in Syene, now this modern city.
rows.n: Syene was located nearly on the Tropic of Cancer, meaning the summer solstice sun shone straight down the well.

rows.q: When Albert Einstein divorced his first wife in 1919, he had so little cash on hand that he signed away the entire future purse of his yet-to-be-awarded Nobel Prize to her. Name her.
rows.n: The prize came in 1922; Maric used the Swedish kronor to purchase three apartment buildings in Zurich.

rows.q: Barred from faculty positions due to her gender, this German theorist lectured under David Hilbert’s name before publishing her landmark 1918 theorem linking symmetry to conservation laws.
rows.n: Her theorem established that the law of conservation of energy directly stems from the time symmetry of physical laws.

rows.q: Before lending his name to the standard unit of electrical capacitance, Michael Faraday began his working life as an apprentice in what trade?
rows.n: He got his break by binding his handwritten notes on Humphry Davy’s chemistry lectures and gifting them to him.

rows.q: Developed in 1960s California, this docile cat breed gets its playful toy-inspired name from its habit of going completely limp when held.
rows.n: Creator Ann Baker founded her own registry with strict rules to keep control of the breed.

rows.q: Horseshoe crabs have patrolled ocean shallows for 450 million years, kept alive by bright blue blood that relies on what metallic element rather than iron to bind oxygen?
An intact male donkey is a jack, but his female counterpart shares her five-letter name with Forrest Gump’s sweetheart and an iconic inverted airmail stamp.
rows.n: A jack and a mare yield a mule; a stallion and a jenny yield a hinny.

rows.q: Though their sloping backs and bone-crushing jaws make them look like oversized canines, hyenas are actually more closely related to what other domestic pet?
rows.n: Hyenas belong to the suborder Feliformia, placing them on the cat-like branch of carnivores.

rows.q: Driven to extinction in the 1880s, this South African equid had zebra stripes across its neck and head, but a solid brown coat over its rear.
rows.n: DNA analysis later confirmed the quagga was a subspecies of the plains zebra.

rows.q: Famous for locking prehistoric insects in golden tomb-like resin, roughly 90 percent of the world’s extractable amber is mined along the shores of this European sea.
rows.n: The vast deposits formed 40 million years ago from resin produced by ancient Scandinavian pine forests.

rows.q: Sharing its species name with a mythical beast, the narwhal is Monodon monoceros, Greek for ‘one-tooth’ and one what?
rows.n: European traders once sold washed-up narwhal tusks to royalty as genuine unicorn horns.

rows.q: To maintain traction at highway speeds, cheetahs are the only big cats whose paws lack the ability to fully perform what claw-hiding action?
rows.n: Their semi-retractable claws work like athletic cleats during high-speed sprints.

rows.q: After the Mines Act of 1842 banned women and small children from working underground in Britain, what sturdy Scottish pony breed replaced them as haulers?
rows.n: Their low center of gravity and immense strength let them pull twice their weight underground.

rows.q: Famed for absurdly fluffy coats shorn for soft wool, Angora rabbits trace their name back to the former moniker of which national capital?
rows.n: Angora goats and Angora cats also trace their historical names to the Turkish capital.

rows.q: Rarely standing over 16 inches tall, this tiny African dwarf antelope gets its repetitive name from the whistling alarm call made through its elongated snout.
rows.n: Dik-diks mate for life, and surviving partners often refuse to find a new mate when one dies.

rows.q: Living in underground mobs across the Kalahari, meerkats belong not to the cat family, but to this family of sleek, snake-fighting carnivores.
rows.n: A group of meerkats is officially known as a mob or a clan.

rows.q: Before scientist Nicolaus Steno recognized them in 1667 as giant shark teeth, fossilized Megalodon teeth were treasured in Europe as the petrified tongues of what mythical monster?
rows.n: Known as glossopetrae or tongue stones, nobles dipped them in wine believing they could neutralize poison.

rows.q: Pulling up a wrinkled, two-foot “snot otter” or “mud devil” might frighten an angler, but it is neither an eel nor a fish, but North America’s largest species of this amphibian.
rows.n: Hellbenders have lungs, but they absorb over 90% of their oxygen directly through folded, slimy skin flaps.

rows.q: Catching “lightning bugs” in a mason jar is a summer rite, but fireflies are not true dipteran flies. Their protective hardened wing cases reveal they belong to this largest insect order.
rows.n: Nearly 100% of the energy produced in a firefly’s chemical reaction is emitted as cold, efficient light.

rows.q: Seahorses belong to the genus Hippocampus, a name shared with a curved region of the human brain critical to which mental faculty?
rows.n: Anatomist Giulio Cesare Aranzi named the brain structure in 1587 after its curved shape.

rows.q: Originating in Central Africa, what hound breed is famously nicknamed the “barkless dog” because its shaped larynx produces a yodel instead?
rows.n: Ancient Egyptian tombs feature carvings of dogs bearing a striking resemblance to modern Basenjis.

rows.q: When Victorian sculptors built the famous Crystal Palace dinosaurs in the 1850s, they erroneously placed Iguanodon’s sharp thumb spike on what part of its face?
rows.n: Skeletons found later in a Belgian coal mine proved the spike belonged on the five-fingered hand, not the snout.

rows.q: A Siamese cat’s dark points on its face, paws, and tail are triggered by an enzyme that activates only in areas with a cooler what?
rows.n: Kittens are born pure white because the warm temperature inside the womb inhibits the pigment.

rows.q: An Alaskan king crab has only six walking legs instead of eight, tipping off biologists that it evolved not from true crabs, but from this spiral-shell-dwelling decapod.
rows.n: Evolutionary biologists call the repeated transition from lobster-like forms to crab shapes “carcinization.”

rows.q: Southeast Asia’s binturong is known as the “bearcat,” though it is neither. Visitors to nocturnal zoo exhibits recognize it immediately by its urine, which smells like this movie snack.
rows.n: The compound 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline gives both freshly popped buttered popcorn and binturong scent their odor.

rows.q: A cuttlefish is a cephalopod rather than a fish, but pet owners know it from the chalky white “cuttlebone” hung in birdcages to provide budgies and finches with this essential mineral.
rows.n: The cuttlebone is actually an internal, chambered aragonite shell that the cuttlefish uses to control buoyancy.

rows.q: Despite looking and slithering like a snake, the European slow worm reveals its true identity with blinking eyelids and an ear hole, proving it is this legless reptile.
rows.n: When attacked, it snaps off its own tail in a process called autotomy to distract the predator.

rows.q: Legends claim it arrived late to Noah’s Ark and lost its tail in the closing door. What cat breed actually evolved on a Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea?
rows.n: Completely tailless Manx cats are called “rumpies,” while those with tiny stubs are “stumpies.”

rows.q: According to Welsh folklore, these low-slung herding dogs were used by woodland fairies as stealthy mounts and war steeds.
rows.n: Welsh legend claimed the patches behind their shoulders were harness marks left by fairies.

rows.q: Famous for violent mating-season collisions that generate up to 800 pounds of force, this curly-horned mammal with the scientific name Ovis canadensis is the official state animal of Nevada.
rows.n: Thick double-layered bone cushions their skulls, preventing concussions during 20-mph head-on collisions.

rows.q: Distinguished by a golden coat paired with a white or flaxen mane and tail, this horse coloration gets its name from a Spanish word for a young dove.
rows.n: Genetically, the coloration is created by a single dilution gene on a chestnut base coat.

rows.q: A female swan is known as a pen, while her protective mate shares his three-letter name with a sturdy riding horse, an ear of maize, and a bread roll.
rows.n: The word likely derives from the Middle English cobbe, meaning a leader or big man.

rows.q: Boasting the longest legs and largest ears relative to body size of any cat, this slender spotted African feline hunts rodents by pouncing high in tall grass.
rows.n: Servals were bred with domestic cats in the 1980s to create the Savannah cat breed.

rows.q: Found in sharks, birds, and camels, this translucent ‘third eyelid’ sweeps horizontally across the cornea to clear debris while maintaining vision.
rows.n: In humans, the pink crescent in the inner corner of the eye, the plica semilunaris, is its vestige.

rows.q: The endangered bonobo, humanity’s peaceful, female-dominated ape relative, is native exclusively to the humid basin forests of what African nation?
Because of its scruffy neck crest, the cheetah was given the species name jubatus, which is Latin for having what hairy feature?
rows.n: Cheetah cubs sport this mane as camouflage to mimic the notoriously fierce honey badger.

rows.q: Karl Dobermann bred his namesake guard dog to protect him while walking town streets, a risky daily routine in his day job as what kind of municipal official?
rows.n: He was also Apolda’s dog catcher, giving him plenty of strays to crossbreed.

rows.q: While the fleshy lobe under a turkey’s chin is its wattle, the long, erectile flap of skin that drapes over the top of its bill shares its five-letter name with a knitted hairnet.
rows.n: During courtship displays, blood engorges the snood, causing it to lengthen and turn bright red.

rows.q: Often stereotyped as pampered French companions, poodles were originally bred in Germany as hunting retrievers for what kind of game bird?
rows.n: The distinctive pompom clips originally protected joints and vital organs from freezing water.

rows.q: Deep-sea Scotoplanes are nicknamed “sea pigs” for their fleshy pink appendages, but these abyssal mud-grazers are actually members of this leathery, tubular echinoderm class.
rows.n: Sea pigs march across the seabed using water-filled tube feet that function like hydraulic stilts.

rows.q: Popularized on film in 1990 by Dances with Wolves, this Lakota word translates literally as “great beast” and names the American bison.
rows.n: The Lakota considered tatanka sacred, utilizing every part of the animal for food, tools, clothing, and shelter.

rows.q: Nicknamed the “cow killer” for its agonizing sting, the fuzzy, wingless “velvet ant” scurrying through the dirt is actually a female member of this stinging insect family.
rows.n: While wingless females deliver the infamous sting, winged male velvet ants lack stingers entirely.

rows.q: The longest unbroken predator-prey study in wildlife history has documented the cycles of gray wolves and moose on what Lake Superior island?
rows.n: Inbreeding reduced the island wolf pack to just two severely deformed individuals before fresh wolves were brought in.

rows.q: Geologist Walter Alvarez proved an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs by discovering a worldwide layer of clay packed with this rare, platinum-group metal found in space rocks.
rows.n: The thin iridium-rich boundary marks the exact divide between the Cretaceous and Paleogene periods.

rows.q: Llamas were domesticated in the Andes from the wild guanaco, but the smaller alpaca traces its lineage back to which delicate wild camelid?
rows.n: Vicuña wool is among the rarest and most expensive in the world, once reserved only for Inca royalty.

rows.q: The basement creature called a “daddy longlegs” is dogged by myths about deadly venom, but it possesses neither fangs nor silk glands because it is this eight-legged arachnid, not a spider.
rows.n: Unlike spiders, which have a pinched waist separating two body segments, harvestmen have a single fused body.

rows.q: While a mule is the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse, what specific name is given to the reciprocal cross: a male horse and a female donkey?
rows.n: Hinnies are rarer and harder to breed than mules due to lower conception rates.

rows.q: Rhinos famously gather in a crash, but their massive, wallowing African neighbors take this unglamorous five-letter collective noun when resting together in river shallows.
rows.n: Hippos produce an oily pink fluid known as blood sweat that acts as natural sunscreen.

rows.q: Treasured by Chinese royalty in the Forbidden City, what small companion dog breed has a name that translates literally from Mandarin as “lion dog”?
It can shock predators with 860 volts, but South America’s electric eel is not an eel at all. It is the flagship species of this freshwater family named after a folding blade.
rows.n: Unlike true eels, electric eels are obligate air-breathers that must surface every ten minutes or drown.

rows.q: In 1572, Prince William the Silent of the Netherlands survived an assassination attempt after this breed of snub-nosed lapdog scratched at his tent.
rows.n: Pompey the pug became the official mascot of the royal Dutch House of Orange.

rows.q: During the late-19th-century fossil-hunting craze known as the Bone Wars, Edward Drinker Cope feuded bitterly with this Yale professor who named Stegosaurus and Triceratops.
rows.n: The rivalry saw both men spy on, bribe, and dynamite each other’s digs, exhausting their personal fortunes.

rows.q: Named for a river in Washington and Idaho, spotted Appaloosa horses were selectively bred for speed and endurance by what Native American tribe?
rows.n: Settlers originally called them “a Palouse horse,” which slurred into Appaloosa.

rows.q: Medieval falconers watching tall, gray waterbirds stand dead still in shallows like an army waiting out a fortress gave a flock of herons this military collective noun.
rows.n: The term was also spelled sedge, referring to the reed beds where herons naturally congregate.

rows.q: Prized by museum collectors who hastened its demise, the world’s last known pair of Great Auks was killed in 1844 on the rocky islet of Eldey, off the coast of this island nation.
rows.n: Sailors strangled the birds and crushed their single remaining egg; the species was never seen alive again.

rows.q: Once numbering in the billions, the passenger pigeon went extinct in September 1914 with the death of Martha, who lived out her days at the zoo in this Ohio city.
rows.n: Named after Martha Washington, her body was packed in a 300-pound block of ice and shipped to the Smithsonian.

rows.q: The 15th-century Book of Saint Albans coined collective nouns reflecting animal traits, giving a gathering of apes this word now used for sharp business sense.
rows.n: In medieval English, shrewd meant mischievous or malicious, matching the era’s view of mocking apes.

rows.q: Long before synthetic alternatives existed, luxury perfumers harvested a musky glandular secretion from this nocturnal, spotted African mammal to fix scents.
rows.n: Civet musk was prized for making floral perfumes last longer on human skin.

rows.q: DNA testing in 2002 confirmed that the closest living relative to the flightless, extinct dodo is a strikingly colorful pigeon named after this Indian island chain.
rows.n: The Nicobar pigeon roams remote forested atolls and is the only living member of its genus, Caloenas.

rows.q: Vienna’s Spanish Riding School is famed for Lipizzaner stallions, a breed that takes its name from Lipica, a historic stud farm located in what modern country?
rows.n: General George Patton helped rescue hundreds of Lipizzaners from the Nazis in 1945.

rows.q: Outlasting the construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza, the very last isolated herd of woolly mammoths died out around 2000 BCE on this remote Russian island in the Arctic Ocean.
Thought to have died out with the dinosaurs 66 million years ago, the lobe-finned coelacanth stunned science in 1938 when a trawler netted one off the coast of this country.
rows.n: Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted the five-foot blue fish on a boat dock in the port city of East London.

rows.q: Before humans colonized New Zealand, the giant, flightless moa was hunted by this terrifying bird of prey, the heaviest eagle known to have ever lived.
rows.n: Named after geologist Julius von Haast, it struck prey from above with talons as large as a tiger’s claws.

rows.q: The world’s most costly spice, saffron consists of the painstakingly hand-plucked crimson stigmas of an autumn-flowering species of this cup-shaped bulb.
rows.n: It requires about 75,000 individual crocus flowers to produce a single pound of dried saffron threads.

rows.q: Despised by 18th-century sailors for its windless equatorial calms, the Intertropical Convergence Zone took this colloquial name from an old word for low spirits.
rows.n: The word derived from dull and originally meant a state of sluggish depression or boredom.

rows.q: The cold, dry wind known as the Mistral blows down through the Rhône Valley toward the Mediterranean, chilling the vineyards of this famous southern French region.
rows.n: Old Provencal homes were built without north-facing windows to block the wind’s chill.

rows.q: While mythological Narcissus fell in love with his reflection, the flower’s name shares an ancient Greek root for numbness with this class of pain drugs.
rows.n: The root narke refers to the plant’s intoxicating alkaloids, which are toxic if ingested.

rows.q: Nicknamed the ‘snow eater’ for vaporizing foot-deep drifts in hours along the Rockies, this warm, dry downslope wind shares its name with a Boeing twin-rotor helicopter.
rows.n: In 1972, a Chinook wind in Loma, Montana, drove the temperature from -54°F to 49°F in a single day.

rows.q: Begun in 1950 by high school students building six snow statues in Odori Park, an annual winter Snow Festival takes place in what capital of Hokkaido?
rows.n: Over two million visitors now attend the annual festival to see hundreds of elaborate, building-sized ice sculptures.

rows.q: Matthias de l’Obel, namesake of the blue garden bloom Lobelia, served as personal physician to this English king who famously survived the Gunpowder Plot.
rows.n: De l’Obel also supervised botanical gardens in Hackney and cataloged thousands of plants.

rows.q: The chartreuse heads of Romanesco broccoli look surreal because each cone-shaped bud replicates the pattern of the whole head, forming this self-similar geometry.
rows.n: Romanesco also demonstrates the Fibonacci sequence in the spiraling arrangement of its conical buds.

rows.q: Deriving its name from the Latin word ‘creta’, the Cretaceous period is named after which soft white limestone that forms the White Cliffs of Dover?
rows.n: The cliffs consist of billions of microscopic skeleton plates from plankton called coccoliths.

rows.q: The fog-shrouded Skeleton Coast, famous for rusting shipwrecks stranded among desert sand dunes, forms the northern coastline of what African country?
rows.n: Early Portuguese navigators nicknamed the treacherous, fog-bound shoreline the ‘Gates of Hell.’

rows.q: In the Köppen climate system, groups A, C, D, and E are determined by temperature thresholds, while group B is defined exclusively by a severe lack of this.
rows.n: Group B covers arid and semiarid climates, which together cover nearly 30 percent of the Earth’s land area.

rows.q: Home to the nomadic gaucho and millions of grazing cattle, this fertile South American plain takes its common name from a Quechua word meaning ‘flat surface.’
rows.n: The biome is divided into the dry western pampa and the humid eastern pampa near Buenos Aires.

rows.q: Spanish explorers adopted the word ‘avocado’ from the Aztec Nahuatl word ahuacatl, which was also a slang term for this hanging male anatomical part.
Mawsynram, India, holds the world rainfall record thanks to monsoon moisture hitting the hills. Fittingly, its home state of Meghalaya translates as ‘abode of’ these.
rows.n: It receives over 460 inches of annual precipitation, nearly ten times that of New York City.

rows.q: Ancient Greeks carved wine goblets from this purple quartz variety in the superstitious belief that the stone would keep the drinker from getting drunk.
rows.n: Its name stems from the Greek ‘amethystos,’ meaning ‘not intoxicated.’

rows.q: Covering roughly a quarter of the Arabian Peninsula, the world’s largest continuous expanse of sand dunes is known in English by this two-word translation of Rub’ al Khali.
rows.n: It covers over 250,000 square miles, an area larger than the entire country of France.

rows.q: The blinding white crust of Bolivia’s Salar de Uyuni, the planet’s largest salt flat, sits atop roughly half of the world’s known reserves of this battery-powering metal.
rows.n: During the rainy season, standing surface water turns the flat into the world’s largest natural mirror.

rows.q: Before Nazi forces looted it during World War II, the legendary Amber Room stood in Russia as a 1716 diplomatic gift from King Frederick William I of this realm.
rows.n: Peter the Great sent 55 giant Russian grenadiers back to the Prussian king as a thank-you gift.

rows.q: Scouring the crumbling cliffs of Dorset in the early 1800s, which self-taught Englishwoman unearthed the first recognized complete ichthyosaur skeleton?
rows.n: Anning sold her seaside fossil discoveries to support her impoverished family in Lyme Regis.

rows.q: Okra is famous for the viscous mucilage it adds to gumbo, a trait shared by its close botanical cousin, this wetland plant that lent its name to a puffy candy.
rows.n: French confectioners originally boiled mallow root sap with sugar and egg whites to create the treat.

rows.q: Deriving from the Spanish word for ‘cauldron’, what massive volcanic depression forms when an emptied magma chamber collapses under its own weight?
rows.n: Crater Lake in Oregon is actually a caldera, formed around 7,700 years ago when Mount Mazama blew its top.

rows.q: Standing intact since 125 AD, the massive unreinforced concrete dome of the Roman Pantheon was lightened toward the top by using this frothy volcanic rock.
rows.n: Travertine aggregate was used at the heavy base, gradually transitioning to light pumice up top.

rows.q: Prized for baking extracts, vanilla is harvested from the cured seed pods of the only commercially cultivated edible member of this flashy floral family.
rows.n: In the wild, vanilla flowers open for just one morning and are pollinated by stingless Melipona bees.

rows.q: Female pigs were historically favored over dogs as truffle hunters because the underground fungi emit a steroid identical to the sex pheromone in the saliva of this animal.
rows.n: Sows required no training to find truffles, but farmers switched to dogs because pigs frequently ate the bounty.

rows.q: The pungent monster flower Rafflesia honors Sir Stamford Raffles, an amateur naturalist better known for founding this modern Asian city-state in 1819.
rows.n: The massive bloom was documented on an 1818 expedition into the rainforests of Sumatra.

rows.q: Deadliest of the nightshades, the genus Atropa takes its name from the Greek Fate responsible for ending human lives by doing this to their thread of destiny.
For centuries, Renaissance masters paid exorbitant sums for Afghan lapis lazuli to grind it down into this vivid blue pigment, often saved only for Mary’s robes.
rows.n: In 1828, a prize was awarded in France to synthesize it, giving rise to ‘French ultramarine.’

rows.q: Before names were standardized, Clement Wragge named tropical storms after politicians he disliked in this southern hemisphere country where he served as chief meteorologist.
rows.n: He also named pleasant tropical anticyclones after women he fancied.

rows.q: Spawned by collapsing thunderstorms in arid regions, these towering, wall-like dust storms carry a name derived from the Arabic verb meaning ‘to blow.’
rows.n: A haboob’s dust front can rise up to a mile high and travel at highway speeds.

rows.q: Emeralds and aquamarines belong to the very same mineral species, distinguished primarily by trace impurities. Name that parent cyclosilicate mineral.
rows.n: Chromium or vanadium creates the green of emerald, while iron creates aquamarine’s blue.

rows.q: In 2000, miners drained an underground chamber in Mexico’s Naica Mine, revealing 30-foot selenite pillars made of what common sulfate mineral?
rows.n: The subterranean crystal cave’s 136-degree heat required cavers to wear chilled suits packed with ice.

rows.q: Rather than emptying into an ocean, the Okavango River drains into an enormous inland oasis within this southern African desert named for a Tswana word for ‘great thirst.’
rows.n: The river’s waters never reach the sea, eventually evaporating under the desert sun.

rows.q: Native to the southern Andes, the monkey puzzle tree takes its genus name Araucaria from an indigenous territory in this South American nation.
rows.n: The tree’s edible seeds, piñones, were a crucial staple food for the indigenous Pehuenche.

rows.q: The sharp ‘berries’ that give gin its botanical punch are not true fruit, but the unusually fleshy, fused seed scales of this non-flowering plant structure.
rows.n: Because junipers are gymnosperms, their seeds sit exposed on the cone scales rather than enclosed in an ovary.

rows.q: Debunking a common kitchen myth, the fiery capsaicin in a jalapeño is concentrated primarily in this pale, spongy internal tissue, not the seeds.
rows.n: Birds lack the receptor that registers capsaicin heat, allowing them to disperse pepper seeds unharmed.

rows.q: The tobacco genus Nicotiana owes its name to Jean Nicot, a French diplomat who shipped seeds home to Catherine de’ Medici while posted to this Iberian country.
rows.n: Nicot had praised powdered tobacco as a miracle cure for persistent headaches and ulcers.

rows.q: Thin, heat-tolerant sheets of the ‘muscovite’ variety of this flaky silicate mineral were once used as an alternative to fragile glass in Russian windows.
rows.n: It was tough, did not crack in subzero Moscow winters, and was later used in woodstove windows.

rows.q: The birthstone peridot is merely the gem variety of this olive-green, iron-magnesium mineral that makes up much of Earth’s upper mantle.
rows.n: It is also found on the Moon, on Mars, and inside many stony-iron meteorites.

rows.q: Nicknamed ‘petrified lightning,’ these fragile, hollow tubes of fused glass form when a cloud-to-ground lightning strike superheats silica-rich beach sand.
rows.n: The name comes from the Latin ‘fulgur,’ meaning a flash of lightning.

rows.q: The 1900 Galveston hurricane killed thousands partly because U.S. forecasters ignored urgent telegraph warnings from weather officials in this Caribbean island nation.
rows.n: US Weather Bureau chief Willis Moore believed Cuban forecasters were overly alarmist and blocked their cables.

rows.q: Cashews are never sold in their raw shells because the outer hull contains this caustic resin, the exact same oily allergen that causes poison ivy rash.
rows.n: Cashew processing requires roasting or steaming the nuts outdoors to vaporize the resin without inhaling it.

rows.q: In 1979, meteorologists finally added male names to Atlantic hurricane lists. The first male name assigned was this one, starting with B.
rows.n: Bob made landfall as a Category 1 storm in Louisiana in July 1979.

rows.q: Often used as an ethical diamond alternative, moissanite was first identified in 1893 by chemist Henri Moissan inside a meteor crater in this U.S. state.
rows.n: Because natural moissanite is exceedingly rare, virtually all jewelry moissanite is lab-grown.

rows.q: Sunlight triggers raw potatoes to produce green chlorophyll, an event that simultaneously produces dangerous levels of this bitter, toxic nightshade alkaloid.
rows.n: Cooking, baking, and frying reduce solanine slightly, but boiling does not neutralize the toxic compound.

rows.q: In 1943, a sudden fissure in a Mexican cornfield birthed what cinder cone volcano, leaving only a church bell tower rising from the lava field?
rows.n: Parícutin gave volcanologists a rare chance to document the entire life cycle of a new volcano from day one.

rows.q: Wild lupines get their name from the Latin word for a wolf, reflecting the mistaken belief that the plants ravenously stripped this essential nutrient from soil.
rows.n: In reality, lupines are legumes that harbor bacteria that actually fix nitrogen into soil.

rows.q: Set in the Imperial State Crown of the United Kingdom, the famous 170-carat Black Prince’s Ruby is not a true ruby at all, but this red substitute.
rows.n: Henry V supposedly wore this very stone into battle atop his helmet at Agincourt in 1415.

rows.q: Despite starring in plastic dinosaur sets, the sail-backed Permian predator Dimetrodon is actually more closely related to which class of vertebrates?
rows.n: Dimetrodon was a synapsid, or stem-mammal, and went extinct millions of years before the first dinosaur.

rows.q: The fierce, freezing wind called the Bora blows off the Dinaric Alps into this arm of the Mediterranean Sea, often coating ships in ice.
rows.n: Wind speeds during a winter Bora along the Croatian coast can top 130 miles per hour.

rows.q: Fresh olives contain bitter compounds that make them unpalatable off the tree; commercial processors strip this bitterness by soaking them in a bath of this caustic alkali.
rows.n: The chemical bath breaks down oleuropein, the bitter compound that naturally protects raw olives on the branch.

rows.q: A pineapple is botanically a syncarp of fused berries, produced on the stalk of an exotic plant family familiar to terrarium keepers and air plant collectors.
rows.n: Spanish moss is also a bromeliad, making it a close botanical cousin of the supermarket pineapple.

rows.q: In 1893, this Japanese entrepreneur perfected a method to stimulate oysters into making cultured pearls, launching a luxury jewelry brand under his surname.
Highly prized for incense and perfumes, the fragrant aromatic heartwood of what parasitic tropical tree genus is among the world’s most expensive woods?
rows.n: Unlike most woods, sandalwood can retain its distinctive scent for decades.

rows.q: Quartz crystals keep precise time in wristwatches thanks to this electromechanical effect, discovered in 1880 by Jacques Curie and his brother Pierre.
rows.n: The word derives from the Greek ‘piezein,’ meaning to squeeze or press.

rows.q: Most of the world’s subtropical deserts sit around 30 degrees latitude where dry air descends, capping a massive atmospheric loop named for this 18th-century Englishman.
rows.n: Hadley published his circulation model in 1735 to explain the mechanics behind the trade winds.

rows.q: First recorded in 18th-century Barbados as the ‘forbidden fruit,’ the grapefruit originated as an accidental cross between the sweet orange and this massive citrus fruit.
rows.n: Botanists consider pomelos, citrons, and mandarins to be the three ancestral parents of modern citrus.

rows.q: The tea-family ornamental camellia honors Georg Joseph Kamel, a Jesuit pharmacist who spent decades documenting the flora of this Southeast Asian archipelago.
rows.n: Kamel ran a free apothecary in Manila and sent extensive plant drawings back to London.

rows.q: A banana plant can tower twenty feet high, but because its pseudostem consists entirely of tightly packed leaf sheaths with no true wood, it is technically a giant what?
rows.n: After producing a single crop of bananas, the main trunk dies back and is replaced by an underground sucker.

rows.q: Developed in 17th-century Scandinavia, the hardy rutabaga originated as an accidental, cold-tolerant hybrid between a turnip and this common leafy head vegetable.
rows.n: The Swedish turnip was shortened in American English to rutabaga, from the dialect word rotabagga.

rows.q: Earning director Sam Peckinpah the moniker “Bloody Sam,” this groundbreaking 1969 western stunned crowds with its slow-motion, blood-soaked border ambushes.
rows.n: The climactic shootout sequence alone used more than ninety thousand rounds of blank ammunition.
