rows.n: The band thought it was a temporary placeholder, but it stuck once they got signed to Warner Bros.

rows.q: Mick Jagger and Keith Richards wrote ‘Paint It Black’ while touring, but the track’s driving sitar riff was actually picked out in the studio by this versatile multi-instrumentalist bandmate.
rows.n: Jones also contributed dulcimer, recorder, and marimba to other mid-sixties Stones recordings.

rows.q: Arlo Guthrie’s rambling anti-draft monologue “Alice’s Restaurant” recounts how his arrest for littering occurred while visiting friends on which annual American holiday?
rows.n: The resulting criminal record made Guthrie ineligible for military service in Vietnam.

rows.q: Chaka Khan broke into the music industry as the powerhouse lead singer of this 1970s funk outfit behind “Sweet Thing.”
rows.n: Stevie Wonder wrote their breakout 1974 hit, “Tell Me Something Good.”

rows.q: Joe Strummer and Paul Simonon chose what punchy name for their punk band after noticing how often the word appeared in London newspaper headlines?
rows.n: Bassist Paul Simonon coined it after noticing the word constantly appearing in the Evening Standard.

rows.q: James Taylor landed his big break in London in 1968 when Paul McCartney and George Harrison signed him as the first non-British artist on which Beatles-founded label?
rows.n: McCartney and Harrison even sat in on the recording session for “Carolina in My Mind.”

rows.q: Before adopting the title of a 1963 Boris Karloff horror film, this Birmingham quartet played heavy blues under the moniker Earth.
rows.n: They changed the name after seeing people line up for a horror film and realizing scary themes sold.

rows.q: Known for their lush Philadelphia soul sound, production duo Gamble and Huff scored their biggest crossover hit with “Love Train” by this vocal trio.
rows.n: The group originally named themselves after Eddie O’Jay, a Cleveland radio disc jockey who championed them.

rows.q: Pink Floyd caused an aviation panic in 1976 when Algie, their 40-foot inflatable pig, broke free from its tether at which London landmark and drifted directly into Heathrow Airport’s flight path?
rows.n: Algie eventually landed safely in a farm field in Kent, where the farmer complained it frightened his cows.

rows.q: Aretha Franklin’s gospel roots ran deep: her father, C.L. Franklin, was a famous pastor who organized 1963’s Walk to Freedom alongside Martin Luther King Jr. in this city.
rows.n: Over 100,000 people marched down Woodward Avenue, where MLK gave an early version of his “I Have a Dream” speech.

rows.q: Though released as a Beach Boys single, the 1965 party track “Barbara Ann” features uncredited co-lead vocals by Dean Torrence, half of what rival surf duo?
Motown founder Berry Gordy modeled his label’s hit-making efficiency on his factory shift assembling car bodies for this Detroit automaker.
rows.n: Gordy hung chrome trim onto Lincoln-Mercury frames at Ford’s Wayne Assembly plant.

rows.q: David Byrne and company took what band name from a TV Guide term defining an onscreen shot that only shows a person speaking from the chest up?
rows.n: The band members liked the phrase because it sounded devoid of rock-and-roll pretense.

rows.q: Brian Eno ran into David Bowie’s Berlin studio in 1977 clutching Donna Summer’s ‘I Feel Love’ to announce that club music for the next fifteen years had just been invented by which Italian producer?
rows.n: Moroder sequenced the bassline using a Moog modular synthesizer, revolutionizing electronic dance music.

rows.q: Before recording his own hits, Marvin Gaye was a Motown session drummer who played the beat on this girl group’s 1961 chart-topper “Please Mr. Postman.”
rows.n: “Please Mr. Postman” was Motown’s first number-one single on the Billboard Hot 100.

rows.q: Pennie Smith’s iconic cover photo for The Clash’s 1979 album London Calling was paired with pink-and-green lettering that intentionally replicated the 1956 debut album by which rock-and-roll icon?
rows.n: Designer Ray Lowry pitched the homage to show that punk was returning rock and roll to its raw original roots.

rows.q: During 1970s arena shows, George Clinton’s Parliament-Funkadelic stunned crowds by landing this massive, smoke-billowing alien spacecraft prop onstage.
rows.n: The 1,200-pound aluminum prop was retired in 1977 and now resides in the Smithsonian.

rows.q: Mick Jones chose which arena-rock band name because half the lineup was British and half was American, meaning someone was an outsider wherever they went?
rows.n: They originally considered the name Trigger before Jones pointed out their unique nationality split.

rows.q: Kent State students Gerald Casale and Bob Lewis conceived which new wave band’s name as an abbreviation of their philosophy that mankind is regressing?
rows.n: Their concept of de-evolution was inspired in part by an anti-evolution pamphlet from the 1920s.

rows.q: In 1964, Jimi Hendrix honed his flamboyant stage moves while touring as a backing guitarist for this family group behind “Shout.”
rows.n: Hendrix played under the pseudonym Jimmy James during his brief stint with the brothers.

rows.q: Purchased in Hamburg in 1961, what German brand’s distinctive 500/1 violin-shaped electric bass was played by Paul McCartney throughout the Beatlemania era?
rows.n: Nicknamed the “Lost Bass” after vanishing from a van in 1972, McCartney’s original was finally returned in 2024.

rows.q: The serene front cover of Carole King’s landmark 1971 album Tapestry features her sitting barefoot by a window alongside Telemachus, who was what kind of pet?
rows.n: The ginger tabby belonged to King and wandered into the frame during Jim McCrary’s photo shoot.

rows.q: Mick Jagger was never formally credited on the sleeve of Carly Simon’s 1972 smash “You’re So Vain,” despite providing this prominent musical contribution.
rows.n: Jagger called the studio during recording and jumped into the vocal booth on the spot.

rows.q: Chrissie Hynde titled her band The Pretenders after hearing Sam Cooke’s soulful cover of “The Great Pretender,” originally a 1955 smash for which vocal group?
rows.n: Hynde was in a taxi listening to the song when the band name struck her.

rows.q: Alice Cooper’s 1975 theatrical concept album Welcome to My Nightmare featured eerie spoken-word narration from this legendary horror actor on the track “The Black Widow.”
rows.n: Cooper hired Price seven years before the actor delivered his famous rap on Michael Jackson’s “Thriller.”

rows.q: The Rolling Stones recorded their gritty classic ‘Brown Sugar’ in December 1969, not in London or New York, but at this famed Alabama recording landmark.
rows.n: They cut ‘Wild Horses’ and ‘You Gotta Move’ during the same three-day session in Sheffield, Alabama.

rows.q: The Yardbirds’ landmark psychedelic track ‘Happenings Ten Years Time Ago’ featured two future guitar gods playing together: Jimmy Page and this fellow legend.
rows.n: John Paul Jones also played bass on the session, two years before forming Led Zeppelin with Page.

rows.q: Before retreating to upstate New York to make Music from Big Pink, The Band backed Bob Dylan on his raucous 1966 world tour under what raptor-themed name?
rows.n: They originally formed in Canada to back rockabilly singer Ronnie Hawkins.

rows.q: Frontman Noddy Holder gave glam band Slade their most iconic visual when he began topping his mutton chops with a black top hat adorned with circular cutouts of which reflective material?
rows.n: Holder bought the hat in Kensington Market and glued small circular shaving mirrors to the band himself.

rows.q: The four-faced portrait on the cover of Queen II, famously recreated in the Bohemian Rhapsody video, was inspired by a 1932 photo of which screen siren in Shanghai Express?
rows.n: Photographer Mick Rock showed the band a Marlene Dietrich still; Freddie Mercury immediately loved the idea.

rows.q: Facing financial ruin and an imminent breakup in 1972, Mott the Hoople passed on David Bowie’s offer of ‘Suffragette City’ before scoring a huge glam-rock comeback with which song he wrote for them?
rows.n: Bowie played acoustic guitar on the track and produced their entire breakthrough album of the same name.

rows.q: Following the 1973 overdose death of her duet partner Gram Parsons, what silver-haired country-rock pioneer debuted as a solo superstar with the 1975 LP Pieces of the Sky?
rows.n: Over a five-decade career, she has won 14 Grammys and collaborated with Bob Dylan, Neil Young, and Dolly Parton.

rows.q: Sly and the Family Stone’s Larry Graham is widely credited with inventing this percussive bass technique, originally developed to replace a missing drummer.
rows.n: Graham referred to the percussive technique as “thumpin’ and pluckin’.”

rows.q: Before capturing Otis Redding and Booker T., the legendary Stax recording studio in Memphis was housed in a converted building of this type, giving it an acoustically sloped floor.
rows.n: The sloped floor gave the room unique acoustic decay, shaping the deep Stax drum sound.

rows.q: Running out of songs after opening Woodstock with an impromptu three-hour set, Richie Havens improvised his anthem “Freedom” around the melody of which traditional spiritual?
rows.n: The original 19th-century spiritual is often titled “Sometimes I Feel Like a Motherless Child.”

rows.q: Frank Sinatra founded this record label in 1960 to secure complete creative freedom, later adding legends like Jimi Hendrix and Joni Mitchell to its roster.
rows.n: Sinatra’s ownership of Reprise earned him his enduring nickname, The Chairman of the Board.

rows.q: Ray Davies wrote the Kinks’ breakthrough riff for ‘You Really Got Me’, but the distorted guitar sound came from his brother Dave slashing this piece of his amp with a razor blade.
rows.n: He pinned the slashed paper cone with knitting needles to achieve that buzzing proto-metal growl.

rows.q: Mick Fleetwood poses on the cover of 1977’s Rumours with two wooden balls dangling between his legs—odd trinkets he originally swiped from what venue bathroom fixture?
rows.n: Fleetwood nicked them from a club’s chain-pull toilet early in his career as good-luck charms.

rows.q: In 1964, the Zombies launched the British Invasion’s dreamier side with ‘She’s Not There’, written by this keyboardist who played its distinctive electric piano solo.
rows.n: Argent later went on to score a 1970s arena hit with ‘Hold Your Head Up’ under his own surname.

rows.q: For their 1969 debut cover, Crosby, Stills & Nash posed on a dilapidated sofa in reverse name order. When they returned to re-shoot it correctly, what had happened to the house?
rows.n: The house on Palm Avenue in West Hollywood was leveled just days after the original photo session.

rows.q: Peter Gabriel’s final tour as frontman of Genesis was a 102-date run supporting which 1974 double concept album, which followed a street youth named Rael through a bizarre New York underworld?
rows.a: The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway
rows.n: Gabriel announced his departure to the band before the tour began but agreed to see through the grueling schedule.

rows.q: Brothers Malcolm and Angus Young spotted the letters AC/DC, signifying electrical versatility, printed on their sister Margaret’s version of what home appliance?
rows.n: Margaret also suggested Angus wear his signature schoolboy uniform on stage.

rows.q: Joni Mitchell skipped performing at Woodstock on the advice of her manager, who feared she would miss a scheduled appearance on this sharp-witted late-night talk show.
rows.n: She penned the festival’s famous anthem from a New York hotel room while watching news coverage.

rows.q: The original die-cut sleeve for The Rolling Stones’ 1978 album Some Girls spoofed a wig catalog, drawing a lawsuit threat from this former First Lady whose photo appeared in a cutout.
rows.n: Atlantic Records hastily redesigned the sleeve to replace celebrity photos with plain colored blocks.

rows.q: Ray Davies centered The Kinks’ 1969 concept album Arthur (Or the Decline and Fall of the British Empire) on his real-life brother-in-law, who had emigrated to this Commonwealth nation.
rows.n: Arthur Anning moved to Australia in 1964 with Ray’s older sister Rose, inspiring the narrative.

rows.q: The Rolling Stones’ bluesy hit ‘Little Red Rooster’ topped the UK charts in 1964, penned by this towering Chicago bluesman and Chess Records bass player.
rows.n: It remains one of the few pure blues numbers to hit number one on the UK singles chart.

rows.q: Laura Nyro’s songs found massive pop success when recorded by others, notably when this vocal quintet reached the Top 5 with “Stoned Soul Picnic” and “Wedding Bell Blues.”
Beating the Sex Pistols’ debut to market by five weeks, this London band released ‘New Rose’ on Stiff Records in October 1976, marking the first commercially released British punk single.
rows.n: Fronted by the vampire-styled Dave Vanian, they were also the first British punk group to tour the United States.

rows.q: Eric Burdon sang lead on ‘San Franciscan Nights’ after the Animals reorganized, but his soulful voice originated from this tough industrial port city in northeast England.
rows.n: Burdon and keyboardist Alan Price initially bonded over blues records in Newcastle upon Tyne.

rows.q: Before scoring a 1982 smash with ‘It’s Raining Men’ as The Weather Girls, powerhouse vocalists Martha Wash and Izora Rhodes performed as backup singers for which flamboyant 1970s disco icon?
rows.n: Billing themselves as Two Tons o’ Fun, they sang prominent backing vocals on his 1978 anthem You Make Me Feel.

rows.q: Built in the Colorado Rockies at 8,600 feet by producer James William Guercio, this secluded high-altitude studio hosted Elton John, Chicago, and Supertramp before a 1985 fire.
rows.n: Elton John loved the alpine facility so much he named his 1974 album Caribou after it.

rows.q: Pete Townshend based the spiritual journey in The Who’s 1969 rock opera Tommy on the silent teachings of this Indian mystic, to whom the album is dedicated.
rows.n: Baba took a vow of public silence in 1925; his name also forms the first half of “Baba O’Riley.”

rows.q: Fighting deportation by the Nixon administration in 1973, John Lennon and Yoko Ono formed a borderless micronation with this name, a pun on a 1516 Thomas More work.
rows.n: Its national anthem, featured on Lennon’s album Mind Games, consists of four seconds of silence.

rows.q: Gladys Knight & the Pips topped the charts in 1973 with “Midnight Train to Georgia,” adapting a country demo that originally took a plane to this Texas city.
rows.n: Songwriter Jim Weatherly wrote it as “Midnight Plane to Houston” before Cissy Houston suggested the switch.

rows.q: The Sex Pistols became a notorious national front-page scandal in 1976 after an alcohol-fueled exchange on the live London television show Today with which baiting host?
rows.n: Grundy had drunkenly flirted on-air with guest Siouxsie Sioux, provoking the band to unleash swear words.

rows.q: David Bowie borrowed the surname of his Martian rock messiah Ziggy from Norman Carl Odam, an eccentric Texas novelty singer known by this celestial stage name.
rows.n: Bowie loved Odam’s outsider music and later covered his track “I Took a Trip on a Gemini Spaceship.”

rows.q: Barry Gibb discovered his trademark disco falsetto while improvising vocal harmonies during a 1975 Miami recording session for which hit single from the Bee Gees’ album Main Course?
rows.n: Producer Arif Mardin had asked if anyone could shriek in falsetto to add excitement to the track’s outro.

rows.q: On the sleek gatefold cover of Roxy Music’s 1973 album For Your Pleasure, model Amanda Lear struts down a city street in black leather, walking this predatory animal on a leash.
rows.n: Lear was dating David Bowie at the time, who recommended her to Bryan Ferry for the shoot.

rows.q: During a lengthy hiatus from Tool in 1999, frontman Maynard James Keenan joined forces with guitar tech Billy Howerdel to launch which alt-rock project?
rows.n: Their 2000 debut Mer de Noms scored the highest Billboard debut for a newly formed rock act up to that point.

rows.q: Weezer tapped new wave pedigree for their self-titled 1994 debut, recruiting which lead singer and rhythm guitarist of The Cars to produce the “Blue Album”?
rows.n: Ocasek returned to produce Weezer’s Green Album in 2001 and Everything Will Be Alright in the End in 2014.

rows.q: Long before Lollapalooza became a permanent festival in Chicago, Perry Farrell organized its inaugural 1991 tour primarily as a farewell trek for which of his bands?
rows.n: The original touring lineup included Siouxsie and the Banshees, Nine Inch Nails, and Ice-T.

rows.q: In 1992, Ice-T ignited a nationwide free-speech controversy and boycott against Time Warner over the track ‘Cop Killer,’ recorded with this heavy metal side project of his.
rows.n: Ice-T later pulled the track from the self-titled album and re-released it.

rows.q: Before his death in a 1990 helicopter crash, blues prodigy Stevie Ray Vaughan recorded four studio albums backed by this Texas rhythm section.
rows.n: Vaughan took the band’s name from a 1958 single by Chicago bluesman Otis Rush.

rows.q: Paula Abdul’s 1989 video for “Opposites Attract” features a tap-dancing cartoon feline who goes by this hip-hop-inspired moniker.
rows.n: The animated cat was voiced by Romany Malco, who later starred in The 40-Year-Old Virgin.

rows.q: Before leaving N.W.A to drop 1990’s AmeriKKKa’s Most Wanted, rapper Ice Cube answered to what birth name, later shared by his actor son?
rows.n: His son, O’Shea Jackson Jr., portrayed him on the big screen in the 2015 biopic Straight Outta Compton.

rows.q: Warren G and Nate Dogg’s 1994 G-funk anthem ‘Regulate’ heavily samples ‘I Keep Forgettin’ (Every Time You’re Near),’ a 1982 solo track by this former Doobie Brothers singer.
rows.n: McDonald later embraced the sample, noting it made him popular with a whole new generation.

rows.q: Long before his solo career took off, Brooklyn lyricist Big Daddy Kane worked as an uncredited ghostwriter for this comedic ‘clown prince of hip-hop,’ penning his 1988 hit ‘Vapors.’
rows.n: The two were tight friends and frequent collaborators in the Juice Crew.

rows.q: Screaming Trees scored their biggest crossover hit with “Nearly Lost You” thanks to its inclusion on the soundtrack of which 1992 Cameron Crowe romantic comedy?
rows.n: The film featured members of Pearl Jam as Matt Dillon’s fictional backing band, Citizen Dick.

rows.q: Salt-N-Pepa made their recording debut with ‘The Show Stoppa’, an answer record to ‘The Show’ by Doug E. Fresh and this eyepatch-wearing British-American MC.
rows.n: He was credited as MC Ricky D on the original 1985 release of ‘The Show.’

rows.q: LL Cool J’s 1985 debut Radio was the first full-length album released by this iconic label, founded inside an NYU dorm room by Rick Rubin and Russell Simmons.
rows.n: The album carried the catalog number DEF 400 and went platinum.

rows.q: Ousted from The Clash in 1983, guitarist Mick Jones embraced hip-hop breakbeats and samples by forming which explosive-sounding band?
rows.n: Clash videographer and reggae DJ Don Letts joined the group to handle sound effects and dialogue samples.

rows.q: Guns N’ Roses famously paid homage to an idol by covering ‘Mama Kin’ on their 1986 debut EP. Which Boston rock quintet wrote and recorded the original?
Prior to his 1980s solo fame and sneering MTV videos, Billy Idol fronted which London punk band that originally wrote and released “Dancing with Myself”?
rows.n: Idol re-recorded the track with producer Keith Forsey after moving to New York in 1981 to go solo.

rows.q: Producer Keith Forsey wrote “Don’t You (Forget About Me)” for The Breakfast Club with which former Generation X frontman in mind, though the rocker turned it down?
rows.n: Bryan Ferry also turned the song down before Simple Minds reluctantly agreed to record it.

rows.q: Will Smith launched his post-Fresh Prince solo career with 1997’s “Men in Black,” lifting its groove and chorus straight from which 1982 Patrice Rushen hit?
rows.n: George Michael had also sampled Rushen’s post-disco groove a year earlier on his hit “Fastlove.”

rows.q: The Wu-Tang Clan took their group name from a kung fu film, while adopting this traditional Chinese monastery’s name as a recurring alias for their home borough of Staten Island.
rows.n: The group’s debut was famously titled Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers).

rows.q: Before his solo breakthrough with ‘Brenda’s Got a Baby,’ 2Pac worked as a roadie and dancer for this Oakland crew, making his vocal debut on their 1991 track ‘Same Song.’
rows.n: Frontman Shock G co-produced 2Pac’s first hit solo single, ‘I Get Around.’

rows.q: Boyz II Men borrowed their name from a track on the 1988 album Heart Break by this earlier Massachusetts boy band featuring Bobby Brown.
rows.n: New Edition star Michael Bivins became their manager after the vocal quartet ambushed him backstage.

rows.q: Dexys Midnight Runners scored a global number-one in 1982 with “Come On Eileen.” Their band name referenced Dexedrine, a brand of what stimulant drug?
rows.n: Dexedrine was widely used by northern soul dancers to stay awake through weekend-long all-nighters.

rows.q: Stanley Burrell got his stage name MC Hammer while working as a batboy for this MLB franchise, because players thought he resembled all-time home run slugger Hank Aaron.
rows.n: Team owner Charlie Finley famously nicknamed him ‘Little Hammer’ in the 1970s.

rows.q: No Doubt keyboardist Eric Stefani walked away from the band just before Tragic Kingdom blew up, choosing to work as a full-time animator on which Fox sitcom?
rows.n: Gwen Stefani’s brother animated for the show from 1990 to 1998, working on classics like “Homer the Great.”

rows.q: Joe Esposito’s pump-up anthem “You’re the Best” made The Karate Kid roar, after Sylvester Stallone rejected it for which 1982 film in favor of “Eye of the Tiger”?
rows.n: Bill Conti and Allee Willis originally wrote the track specifically for Rocky’s rematch with Clubber Lang.

rows.q: Oxford quintet On a Friday changed their name when signing to Parlophone in 1991, lifting the moniker “Radiohead” from an album track by which American art-rock band?
rows.n: The song appeared on Talking Heads’ 1986 soundtrack album and film project True Stories.

rows.q: Queen Latifah took her 1993 feminist anthem ‘U.N.I.T.Y.’ to the top of the rap charts while signed to this iconic Detroit record label, which had just relaunched a hip-hop division.
rows.n: Latifah released her gold-certified third album, Black Reign, through Motown.

rows.q: Hard-rock supergroup Damn Yankees featured Styx guitarist Tommy Shaw, Night Ranger’s Jack Blades, and which outspoken Motor City guitarist?
rows.n: The group’s power ballad “High Enough” reached number three on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1991.

rows.q: After spending 55 weeks on the Hot 100 with his 1996 breakout “Barely Breathing,” which singer-songwriter pivoted to Broadway and won two Tonys for Spring Awakening?
rows.n: The 2006 rock musical swept the Tony Awards and launched the careers of Lea Michele and Jonathan Groff.

rows.q: Expanding beyond teen-pop fame, the three Oklahoma brothers of Hanson entered the craft beer business in 2013 with a pale ale named what?
rows.n: Produced with Mustang Brewing, the 7.5 percent alcohol brew donates a portion of sales to clean water charities.

rows.q: Black Francis drew from French surrealist cinema for the Pixies track “Debaser,” specifically describing a razor slicing an eyeball from this 1929 short by Dalí and Buñuel.
rows.n: The lyrics mispronounce the title on purpose, with Francis shouting “un chien andalusia.”

rows.q: A legal dispute forced The Verve to surrender all royalties for “Bitter Sweet Symphony” because its orchestral hook was adapted from which 1965 Rolling Stones song?
rows.n: Mick Jagger and Keith Richards finally signed their publishing rights back over to Richard Ashcroft in 2019.

rows.q: The duo OMC hit number one worldwide in 1996 with “How Bizarre.” The initials stood for Otara Millionaires Club, an ironic nod to a suburb of which southern city?
rows.n: Lead singer Pauly Fuemana was of Niuean and Maori descent, hailing from the working-class South Auckland suburb.

rows.q: Harvey Danger’s 1997 indie-rock hit “Flagpole Sitta” found a second life across the Atlantic as the opening theme for which cult British sitcom starring David Mitchell?
rows.n: The song replaced Daniel Pemberton’s original instrumental theme beginning in series two.

rows.q: The Notorious B.I.G. got his first national exposure after his demo tape was profiled in the ‘Unsigned Hype’ column of this influential hip-hop magazine, founded at Harvard in 1988.
rows.n: Sean Combs heard about Biggie after reading that issue and signed him to Bad Boy.

rows.q: Men Without Hats frontman Ivan Doroschuk wrote the 1982 new-wave anthem “The Safety Dance” after bouncers threw him out of a club for doing which bouncy punk dance?
rows.n: Venues frequently banned pogoing in the late 1970s and early 1980s, mistaking it for violent fighting.

rows.q: Beck revamped his acoustic slacker sound on 1996’s Odelay by teaming up with John King and Mike Simpson, the production duo known by which family-style name?
rows.n: The duo had previously produced the Beastie Boys’ 1989 sample-dense opus Paul’s Boutique.

rows.q: Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament launched Pearl Jam following the demise of which Seattle outfit, whose flamboyant frontman Andrew Wood died in 1990?
rows.n: Chris Cornell wrote the songs “Say Hello 2 Heaven” and “Reach Down” about Wood, launching Temple of the Dog.

rows.q: When Dave Grohl launched Foo Fighters in 1995, he recruited bassist Nate Mendel and drummer William Goldsmith from which pioneering Seattle emo band?
rows.n: Frontman Jeremy Enigk’s impassioned vocal delivery helped define the mid-1990s emo explosion.

rows.q: Rancid founders Tim Armstrong and Matt Freeman first made their mark in the late 1980s playing in which legendary East Bay ska-punk outfit?
rows.n: Operation Ivy called it quits at their 1989 album release party after playing fewer than 100 shows.

rows.q: Lisa Loeb topped the Hot 100 with “Stay” while unsigned, thanks to which next-door neighbor and actor who handed her demo tape directly to Ben Stiller?
Although fronted by Scottish singer Shirley Manson, 1990s alternative hitmakers Garbage formed and recorded their multi-platinum debut in which Midwestern state capital?
rows.n: Co-founder Butch Vig co-owned Madison’s Smart Studios, where Nirvana’s Nevermind was pre-produced.

rows.q: Long before finding solo stardom with “Orinoco Flow,” new-age singer Enya got her start playing synthesizer in which Celtic folk group formed by her family?
rows.n: Formed in County Donegal, Clannad featured her older sister Moya on vocals and her twin uncles on guitar.

rows.q: British crisis helpline the Samaritans set up emergency telephone support for teenagers in 1995 when this singer abruptly quit Take That.
rows.n: He launched a massive solo career soon after, highlighted by his 1997 arena anthem “Angels.”

rows.q: Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker became a tabloid folk hero at the 1996 Brit Awards when he stormed the stage to mock a messianic, choir-backed performance by which pop megastar?
rows.n: Cocker was arrested backstage after the protest, but charges were dropped after video footage cleared him.

rows.q: The tabloid-hyped Battle of Britpop in August 1995 went to Blur, whose single about an anxious city-dweller retreating to rural life beat Oasis to number one. Name it.
rows.n: Blur moved their release date to match Oasis’s “Roll With It” after Noel Gallagher insulted them in the press.

rows.q: Geri Halliwell’s famous Union Jack dress at the 1997 Brit Awards was created when her sister stitched this ordinary kitchen item to a black minidress.
rows.n: The original dress later sold at a charity auction at Sotheby’s for over forty thousand pounds.

rows.q: Bon Jovi’s 1986 blockbuster Slippery When Wet was famously named after the dancers at a strip club the band frequented in this western Canadian city.
rows.n: They recorded the album at Little Mountain Sound Studios and unwound at the No. 5 Orange club.

rows.q: On the eve of an American tour in 1995, lyricist and rhythm guitarist Richey Edwards disappeared near the Severn Bridge, leaving which Welsh rock band to carry on as a trio?
rows.n: His car was found abandoned at a motorway service station; he was legally presumed dead in 2008.

rows.q: D.C. post-hardcore band Fugazi was founded in 1987 by singer-guitarist Ian MacKaye, who had previously fronted which seminal straight-edge punk outfit?
rows.n: MacKaye also co-founded Dischord Records, which distributed all of Minor Threat and Fugazi’s albums.

rows.q: Years ahead of his big-beat reinvention as Fatboy Slim, Norman Cook played bass for which jangle-pop band known for the hit “Happy Hour”?
rows.n: Lead singer Paul Heaton found massive commercial success shortly after by forming The Beautiful South.

rows.q: Bruce Springsteen took home the 1994 Oscar for “Streets of Philadelphia,” topping which fellow folk-rock titan nominated for writing that same film’s closing ballad?
rows.n: Young’s track, titled simply “Philadelphia,” plays over home-movie footage of Tom Hanks’s character.

rows.q: Singer-songwriter Jeff Buckley drowned tragically in 1997 after taking a spontaneous, fully-clothed evening swim in the Wolf River harbor of which Tennessee city?
rows.n: Buckley was living in Memphis to record My Sweetheart the Drunk, playing a weekly local bar residency.

rows.q: The romantic love theme from 1984’s Footloose, “Almost Paradise,” paired Heart’s Ann Wilson with Mike Reno, the lead singer of which Canadian arena-rock band?
rows.n: Reno is best known for shouting the vocals on Loverboy’s 1981 smash “Working for the Weekend.”

rows.q: Soft Cell’s 1981 hit “Tainted Love” covered a 1964 single by Gloria Jones, who was the partner of which glam rock star and the driver in his fatal 1977 car crash?
rows.n: Bolan, the frontman of T. Rex, died instantly when their car struck a tree in southwest London.

rows.q: Before fronting Whitesnake through the 1980s, David Coverdale was a boutique clerk who got hired to replace Ian Gillan in this earlier British hard rock band.
rows.n: He sang lead on albums like Burn and Stormbringer before Ritchie Blackmore walked out.

rows.q: During a frantic stretch from 1982 to 1984, The Cure’s frontman Robert Smith pulled double duty as the official full-time lead guitarist for which other post-punk band?
Snoop Dogg’s commercial debut was not on The Chronic, but on the 1992 title track for this Laurence Fishburne film about an undercover cop infiltrating a drug ring.
rows.n: It marked Dr. Dre’s first solo single after his bitter split from N.W.A.

rows.q: Giorgio Moroder offered “Danger Zone” to several rock stars before Kenny Loggins. Which Canadian turned it down because he felt Top Gun was militaristic propaganda?
rows.n: Adams also refused to let his song “Only the Strong Survive” be included on the blockbuster soundtrack.

rows.q: Josh Homme formed Queens of the Stone Age following the 1995 breakup of which Palm Desert band, celebrated as pioneers of stoner rock?
rows.n: The band originally took their name from a monstrous undead creature in the Dungeons & Dragons manual.

rows.q: John Rzeznik of the Goo Goo Dolls named their 1998 City of Angels soundtrack smash “Iris” after spotting the name of which country-folk singer in a concert ad?
rows.n: Rzeznik had never heard her music at the time, but loved the sound of the name when skimming the LA Weekly.

rows.q: Famous for his smooth, polysyllabic flow, golden age pioneer Rakim has often credited this jazz saxophone icon, not other rappers, as the main rhythmic influence on his style.
rows.n: Rakim grew up playing the sax and aimed to duplicate Coltrane’s phrasing on the mic.

rows.q: Kim Carnes ruled the pop charts in 1981 with “Bette Davis Eyes,” which was originally co-written and recorded in 1974 by which “Put a Little Love in Your Heart” singer?
rows.n: DeShannon’s original version was a much more upbeat, countrified R&B track with heavy guitar.

rows.q: A Tribe Called Quest wanted a genuine jazz feel on The Low End Theory, hiring this legendary bassist from Miles Davis’s 1960s quintet to play upright bass on ‘Verses from the Abstract.’
rows.n: Carter agreed to do the session only if the group promised not to curse.

rows.q: Kim Deal formed the alt-rock band The Breeders with guitarist Tanya Donelly, who was already playing in which Rhode Island indie group?
rows.n: Donelly left both acts in 1991 to front her own band, Belly, scoring a hit with “Feed the Tree.”

rows.q: Chumbawamba’s 1997 anarchist bar-room chant “Tubthumping” opens with a monologue by Pete Postlethwaite sampled from which 1996 British comedy-drama?
In 1989, New Order frontman Bernard Sumner and former Smiths guitarist Johnny Marr united to form an alt-dance duo with what genre-defining name?
rows.n: Pet Shop Boys singer Neil Tennant contributed guest vocals to their debut hit, “Getting Away with It.”

rows.q: Guns N’ Roses guitarist Slash got his stage name from a family friend, but was born in London under what biblical first name?
rows.n: Character actor Seymour Cassel nicknamed him Slash because the hyperactive kid was always darting around.

rows.q: The Black Eyed Peas built their 2006 hit “Pump It” around the blistering surf-rock guitar track “Misirlou,” famously recorded in 1962 by what “King of the Surf Guitar”?
Bon Iver’s Justin Vernon wrote and recorded 2007’s For Emma, Forever Ago while holed up for months in an isolated hunting cabin in this US state.
rows.n: Vernon retreated to his father’s remote cabin in Dunn County to recover from mononucleosis.

rows.q: The 2003 Eurodance hit “Dragostea Din Tei”, popularized across early YouTube as the “Numa Numa” song, was performed in this Romance language.
rows.n: The boy band O-Zone originally formed in the Republic of Moldova before striking gold in Romania and beyond.

rows.q: The Libertines were driven by the volatile dynamic between Carl Barat and this co-frontman, whose drug convictions once landed him in Pentonville Prison.
rows.n: Doherty even burgled Barat’s apartment in 2003 while Barat was on tour.

rows.q: Franz Ferdinand hit big in 2004 with ‘Take Me Out’. Their self-titled debut used Constructivist cover art directly inspired by this country’s avant-garde.
rows.n: The band frequently used typography and poster motifs created by Alexander Rodchenko.

rows.q: Karen O famously drenched herself in beer while fronting this New York art-punk trio, whose debut featured the tender ballad ‘Maps’.
rows.n: The acronym title ‘Maps’ stands for ‘My Angels Preparing to Smile’.

rows.q: Floating windmill islands and menacing screens appeared in the video for ‘Feel Good Inc.’, featuring guest vocals from what hip-hop trio?
rows.n: Damon Albarn recruited the trio after learning they were fans of the first Gorillaz record.

rows.q: Jimmy Eat World broke into mainstream emo-pop with Bleed American, an album hastily renamed as self-titled following this real-world tragedy.
rows.n: The album was released in July 2001 and rebranded within weeks of the terror attacks.

rows.q: Reggaeton pioneer Daddy Yankee harbored serious ambitions to play professionally in this sport until an injury derailed his athletic career.
rows.n: He had tried out for the Seattle Mariners before being struck in the hip by an AK-47 stray bullet at age seventeen.

rows.q: At the 2021 Super Bowl, The Weeknd headlined a halftime show where his army of clone dancers all wore what medical item over their faces?
rows.n: The look capped off a year-long album concept satirizing Hollywood plastic surgery culture.

rows.q: The garage rock outfit The Black Keys spent their early days playing DIY blues riffs in the basements of this rust belt tire manufacturing city.
rows.n: Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney attended the same high school in the Ohio city.

rows.q: Facing plagiarism accusations, Olivia Rodrigo retroactively awarded songwriting credits and royalties to Hayley Williams for her 2021 hit “Good 4 U,” which echoed what 2007 Paramore song?
rows.n: Williams and former guitarist Josh Farro received a combined 50 percent share of the publishing royalties.

rows.q: An infamous 2012 internet prank hijacked a Walmart promo contest to exile rapper Pitbull to a remote store in this Alaskan island city. He happily went.
rows.n: Over 70,000 people voted for the location; Pitbull accepted a ceremonial key to the city during his visit.

rows.q: Lupe Fiasco scored a top-ten hit in 2010 with “The Show Goes On,” which heavily interpolates the upbeat guitar riff and vocal melody from what indie band’s 2004 breakthrough “Float On”?
rows.n: Modest Mouse singer Isaac Brock was credited as a co-writer and reportedly approved the sample personally.

rows.q: Rascal Flatts scored a massive 2006 crossover hit by covering “Life Is a Highway,” originally written and recorded in 1991 by this Canadian heartland rocker.
rows.n: Cochrane’s original reached number six on the Billboard Hot 100 before the Pixar remake found a new generation.

rows.q: Before adopting her colorful alias, Kesha Sebert made an uncredited vocal appearance on this hit 2009 rap track by Flo Rida, earning zero royalties.
rows.n: She walked into the studio during recording, and producer Dr. Luke asked her to drop the hook for free.

rows.q: In 2006, Bon Jovi became the first rock group to top Billboard’s Hot Country Songs chart with a duet featuring Jennifer Nettles, lead vocalist of this country duo.
rows.n: “Who Says You Can’t Go Home” earned the cross-genre pairing a Grammy for Best Country Collaboration with Vocals.

rows.q: Kid Rock’s 2008 smash “All Summer Long” mashes up the guitar riff from Lynyrd Skynyrd’s “Sweet Home Alabama” with the piano chords of this 1978 Warren Zevon track.
rows.n: Zevon received posthumous songwriting credit and royalties for the hybrid summer anthem.

rows.q: Avicii’s 2011 EDM anthem “Levels” is built around a soaring vocal loop from the 1962 soul track “Something’s Got a Hold on Me” by what legendary singer?
rows.n: Flo Rida used the exact same Etta James vocal sample later that year for his hit single “Good Feeling.”

rows.q: Driving the yellow ‘Pussy Wagon’ truck in the 2010 ‘Telephone’ video, Lady Gaga and Beyonce paid homage to what Quentin Tarantino film?
rows.n: Quentin Tarantino personally lent the truck to Lady Gaga from his private collection.

rows.q: A record-shattering 2017 crossover single, “Meant to Be” spent 50 weeks atop Hot Country Songs, pairing Florida Georgia Line with this Brooklyn-born pop singer.
rows.n: Rexha co-wrote the track during an impromptu late-night Nashville studio session with Tyler Hubbard.

rows.q: Shaboozey scored a record-breaking crossover hit in 2024 with “A Bar Song (Tipsy),” which directly interpolates a 2004 club anthem by this one-hit rapper.
rows.n: J-Kwon earned co-writing royalties on the song, which topped both country and pop charts simultaneously.

rows.q: M.I.A.’s 2007 smash “Paper Planes” features a prominent guitar riff and melody sampled straight from “Straight to Hell,” a 1982 song by what legendary English punk band?
rows.n: Mick Jones and Joe Strummer were given co-writing credits on the Grammy-nominated hit.

rows.q: Drake’s 2018 chart-topper “Nice for What” features a chopped-and-screwed vocal sample of the hook from “Ex-Factor,” a 1998 track from what singer’s sole solo studio album?
rows.n: The sampled song appeared on The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill, which won Album of the Year at the 1999 Grammys.

rows.q: Swedish electronic pioneer Tim Bergling picked this stage name after a friend told him it represents the deepest level of Buddhist hell.
rows.n: He had to add an extra ‘i’ because his original choice was already claimed on MySpace.

rows.q: Sufjan Stevens launched a cheekily ambitious project in 2003 to make fifty albums for fifty states, but only finished Michigan and this Midwestern neighbour.
rows.n: He later admitted the 50-state pledge was a promotional stunt he never intended to complete.

rows.q: Madonna’s 2012 Super Bowl halftime performance sparked controversy when which guest British-Sri Lankan rapper flashed the camera an unscripted middle finger?
rows.n: The NFL sued M.I.A. for 16 million dollars before reaching a confidential settlement.

rows.q: When Donald Glover wanted a stage name for his rap career, he simply ran his real name through an online name generator for this hip-hop group.
rows.n: The generator handed him Childish Gambino during his sophomore year at NYU.

rows.q: After touring through the 1990s, Lollapalooza reinvented itself in 2005 as a stationary weekend destination in what lakefront Chicago park?
rows.n: Founder Perry Farrell signed an agreement to keep the festival anchored in Chicago through 2032.

rows.q: In 2022, Beyoncé kicked off her Renaissance era with “Break My Soul,” looping the iconic bass synthesizer line from the 1993 house anthem “Show Me Love” by what American singer?
Avicii’s 2013 country-EDM juggernaut “Wake Me Up” features an acoustic guitar hook played by Mike Einziger, the lead guitarist of this alt-rock band.
rows.n: Einziger co-wrote the track alongside Aloe Blacc, who provided the hit’s soulful lead vocals.

rows.q: After dominating early 2000s MTV pop charts, Michelle Branch pivoted to Nashville in 2005 to form this duo, scoring a country number-one hit with “Leave the Pieces.”
rows.n: Branch formed the duo with friend Jessica Harp, earning a Grammy nomination before splitting in 2007.

rows.q: Beyoncé recruited this MacArthur Fellow and Carolina Chocolate Drops multi-instrumentalist to provide the clawhammer banjo for her 2024 chart-topper “Texas Hold ‘Em.”
rows.n: Giddens played both minstrel banjo and viola on the track, showcasing early African American string traditions.

rows.q: Sparking a viral global dance craze during 2020 lockdowns, Master KG’s hit “Jerusalema” features uplifting vocals sung in this South African language.
rows.n: Nomcebo Zikode wrote and sang the lyrics after struggling for years as a gospel backing vocalist.

rows.q: Glastonbury faced heavy pushback in 2008 for booking its first hip-hop headliner, who mocked critics by opening his set with ‘Wonderwall’. Name this rapper.
rows.n: Jay-Z was mocking Oasis guitarist Noel Gallagher, who had publicly complained about a hip-hop headliner.

rows.q: Brad Paisley’s 2013 attempt at a cross-genre racial harmony dialogue, titled “Accidental Racist,” sparked fierce critical mockery for its verse by this hip-hop star.
rows.n: LL Cool J defended his guest verse, rapping lines contrasting his do-rag with Paisley’s Confederate flag t-shirt.

rows.q: The Killers swiped their band name from the bass drum of a fictional group appearing in the video for ‘Crystal’ by this British post-punk outfit.
rows.n: Brandon Flowers spotted the fictitious moniker in New Order’s 2001 music video.

rows.q: Featuring fairy-tale staging and giant animatronic faces, the massive electronic dance festival Tomorrowland is held each summer in what European country?
rows.n: It takes place in the provincial recreational park De Schorre in the town of Boom.

rows.q: Tennessee’s Bonnaroo Music and Arts Festival took its name from an acclaimed 1974 album by what New Orleans piano legend?
rows.n: The album is Desitively Bonnaroo, using New Orleans slang meaning ‘a really good time.’

rows.q: Burna Boy’s 2022 Afrobeats smash “Last Last” leans heavily on a prominent sample of the 2000 hit “He Wasn’t Man Enough” by this R&B singer.
rows.n: Braxton reportedly receives sixty percent of the songwriting royalties from the track.

rows.q: Before his solo career yielded the acclaimed album Southeastern, Jason Isbell spent six formative years playing guitar and writing songs in this southern rock outfit.
rows.n: Isbell joined the group at age 22, penning signature tracks like “Outfit” and “Decoration Day.”

rows.q: Though trained in Seoul as a member of Blackpink, rapper and dancer Lisa was born and raised in this Southeast Asian kingdom.
rows.n: Her 2021 debut “Lalisa” broke the Guinness record for most-viewed YouTube music video by a soloist in 24 hours.

rows.q: Golden Hour, the 2018 album by Kacey Musgraves, was largely written and recorded in a studio located above the horse stables at the Nashville farm of this pop-rocker.
rows.n: Crow lent Musgraves the converted loft space, which helped inspire the album’s breezy acoustic texture.

rows.q: Before releasing art-pop masterworks like St. Vincent, Annie Clark toured as a multi-instrumentalist in this massive, choral Dallas rock collective.
rows.n: She played guitar and sang in their signature robes, and toured with Sufjan Stevens shortly after.

rows.q: Rosalía scored her first global streaming smash in 2019 alongside J Balvin on a track whose Spanish title translates to “With Height”.
rows.n: The song also features Rosalía’s frequent co-writer and producer Pablo Díaz-Reixa, known as El Guincho.

rows.q: Back in 2009, this Motown-inspired girl group became the very first South Korean act to crack the Billboard Hot 100 with their single “Nobody”.
rows.n: To build their US profile, the quintet opened for the Jonas Brothers on a massive North American arena tour.

rows.q: Unlike their Broadway shows, Rodgers and Hammerstein wrote Cinderella for CBS television, giving the title role to this 21-year-old rising British star.
rows.n: Over 100 million people watched the live broadcast, which was staged during her run in My Fair Lady on Broadway.

rows.q: Gilbert and Sullivan subtitled this 1879 swashbuckling comic opera ‘The Slave of Duty’, poking fun at the rigid honor of an apprentice named Frederic.
rows.n: Frederic was bound to pirates because his nursery maid mistook the word ‘pilot’ for ‘pirate.’

rows.q: George Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue famously kicks off with a dramatic, two-and-a-half-octave upward glissando played on this single-reed woodwind.
rows.n: Clarinetist Ross Gorman improvised the wailing smear in rehearsal, and Gershwin kept it.

rows.q: In 1990, the Three Tenors gave their legendary debut concert at the Baths of Caracalla on the eve of this international sporting event’s championship match in Rome.
rows.n: West Germany defeated Argentina 1–0 in the final match the following evening.

rows.q: Unlike a piano, whose hammers strike strings, this Renaissance and baroque keyboard instrument generates sound by mechanically plucking them.
rows.n: Because plucking cannot produce subtle changes in volume, the piano superseded it.

rows.q: Though known as the Waltz King, Johann Strauss II scored a major operatic hit with this champagne-soaked 1874 farce named for a winged mammal.
rows.n: The title translates to ‘The Bat’, referring to a character left passed out drunk in a costume.

rows.q: The first-chair player in the first violin section holds this leadership title, directing the orchestra’s tuning and entering for a solo bow.
rows.n: In British and Commonwealth orchestras, this role is usually called the orchestra leader.

rows.q: Despite a fierce preservation fight led by music patrons, the original Metropolitan Opera House was razed in 1967 after the company relocated to this arts complex.
rows.n: The original 1883 opera house stood at 39th and Broadway and was nicknamed The Yellow Brick Brewery.

rows.q: Gioachino Rossini built up volume so relentlessly in his overtures that critics gave him a nickname featuring this Italian term for getting louder.
rows.n: The gradual, driving build became widely known as the Rossini crescendo.

rows.q: Before she was dubbed the First Lady of Song, a 21-year-old Ella Fitzgerald scored her first smash hit in 1938 with this swing version of a nursery rhyme.
rows.n: Fitzgerald updated the 19th-century children’s rhyming game alongside lyricist Al Feldman.

rows.q: Felix Mendelssohn was inspired to write his ‘Hebrides’ overture after visiting Fingal’s Cave, a sea cave made of basalt columns in this country.
Richard Rodgers partnered with Oscar Hammerstein II only after this brilliant but unreliable lyricist dismissed the script of Oklahoma as unworkable.
rows.n: Hart died of pneumonia only eight months after Oklahoma opened on Broadway, having battled severe alcoholism.

rows.q: Before it hit the stage on roller skates, Andrew Lloyd Webber originally pitched Starlight Express as an animated TV series based on this children’s book franchise.
rows.n: Author Wilbert Awdry refused to hand over the rights because Lloyd Webber wanted full creative control of the songs.

rows.q: Bela Bartok’s pantomime ballet The Miraculous Mandarin was banned for obscenity after its 1926 Cologne premiere by the city’s mayor, this future founding Chancellor of West Germany.
rows.n: Adenauer found the plot of street thugs and prostitution so repulsive that he blocked all further staging in Cologne.

rows.q: Sunday in the Park with George is one of only ten musicals to win this American prize for drama, which it claimed in 1985 despite losing the Tony to La Cage.
rows.n: It was only the sixth musical in history to win the drama Pulitzer, following A Chorus Line in 1976.

rows.q: Also known as kettledrums, these large copper percussion instruments are unique in the standard drum section because they are tuned to specific pitches.
rows.n: Modern players use foot pedals to shift the drumhead tension and pitch during a piece.

rows.q: Thelonious Monk composed the ballad “Pannonica” in tribute to jazz patron Pannonica de Koenigswarter, an heiress born into this wealthy banking dynasty.
rows.n: Charlie Parker died in her suite at the Stanhope Hotel while watching television in 1955.

rows.q: The Sound of Music ends with the von Trapps hiking into Switzerland, but climbing the Alps from their Salzburg home would have taken them directly into this nation.
rows.n: In reality, the family walked to their local train station and rode to Italy with valid transit visas.

rows.q: Choreographer Twyla Tharp collaborated with this Talking Heads frontman on her 1981 dance production The Catherine Wheel, commissioning him to compose its pulsating electronic score.
rows.n: Byrne released the soundtrack as his debut solo studio album later that same year.

rows.q: The eerie four-note motif of this 13th-century Latin hymn for the dead echoes throughout Stephen Sondheim’s score for Sweeney Todd.
rows.n: The same medieval melody opens The Shining and appears prominently in Berlioz’s Symphonie Fantastique.

rows.q: Known as the “Prince of Cool,” this soft-toned trumpeter struggled to rebuild his embouchure after losing his front teeth in a 1968 San Francisco beating.
rows.n: Fitted with dentures, he retrained his embouchure and revived his career in Europe.

rows.q: Originally written with French lyrics by Jacques Prevert, “Autumn Leaves” was given English verses by this Savannah-born lyricist of “Moon River.”
rows.n: Mercer also co-founded Capitol Records and won four Academy Awards for Best Original Song.

rows.q: To suit the tiny vocal range of this Mary Poppins actress, Stephen Sondheim wrote Send in the Clowns in short, breathless phrases.
rows.n: She won the 1973 Tony for Best Actress in a Musical for originating Desiree Armfeldt in A Little Night Music.

rows.q: A classic documentary on the recording of Company captures this raspy-voiced star hitting vocal exhaustion at 4 a.m. while singing The Ladies Who Lunch.
rows.n: Director D. A. Pennebaker captured her breakdown; she returned rested the following afternoon and nailed the track.

rows.q: John Coltrane’s 1961 rendition of “My Favorite Things” brought popularity back to this higher-pitched woodwind, largely sidelined in jazz since Sidney Bechet.
rows.n: Miles Davis gave Coltrane his first soprano sax during a European tour in 1960.

rows.q: In David Sedaris’s hit holiday radio essay The Santaland Diaries, he recounts his humiliating gig as a Macy’s Christmas elf under what festive alias?
rows.n: Sedaris first read the essay on NPR’s Morning Edition in 1992, instantly launching his literary career.

rows.q: When Jesus Christ Superstar was first recorded as a 1970 concept album, this Deep Purple frontman provided the rock vocals for Jesus.
rows.n: Gillan declined to star in the film adaptation because Deep Purple was already booked for a world tour.

rows.q: Combining the Greek word for song with the French word for play, what theatrical genre originally relied on orchestral cues to heighten stage villainy?
rows.n: Jean-Jacques Rousseau helped pioneer the form in 1770 with his musical scene Pygmalion.

rows.q: Known for his opera ‘Prince Igor’, Alexander Borodin spent most of his waking hours working as a professor of this scientific field, not as a composer.
rows.n: He co-discovered the aldol reaction and considered music merely a hobby for his spare time.

rows.q: Dave Brubeck’s 1959 hit “Take Five” was not written by Brubeck, but by this quartet alto saxophonist who joked he wanted to sound like a dry martini.
rows.n: Desmond left all his royalties from “Take Five” to the American Red Cross in his will.

rows.q: Edward Elgar dedicated his ‘Enigma Variations’ to his friends pictured within, labeling variation nine ‘Nimrod’ after a biblical figure known for this pursuit.
rows.n: It was a pun on the surname of his publisher, August Jaeger; ‘Jaeger’ is German for hunter.

rows.q: In Leo Delibes’s lighthearted 1870 ballet Coppelia, the villager Franz risks his engagement by smittenly blowing kisses to the title character, who is actually this type of object.
rows.n: The story comes from E.T.A. Hoffmann’s macabre tale ‘The Sandman,’ heavily scrubbed of its dark horror elements.

rows.q: After originating Norma Desmond in London, this Broadway powerhouse was fired by Andrew Lloyd Webber and replaced by Glenn Close for the New York run.
rows.n: LuPone used her million-dollar settlement to build what she called the Andrew Lloyd Webber Memorial Swimming Pool.

rows.q: In the opening of Sunset Boulevard, Norma Desmond mistakes screenwriter Joe Gillis for an undertaker who has arrived to deliver a tiny coffin for this pet.
rows.n: The dead pet in Billy Wilder’s original film was inspired by real Hollywood burials for exotic studio animals.

rows.q: As an aspiring teenage writer, Stephen Sondheim found a mentor in this neighboring lyricist, who slammed his first musical as terrible.
rows.n: Hammerstein spent the rest of the day critiquing the script, giving Sondheim what he called a masterclass in theater.

rows.q: Michel Fokine improvised a short four-minute solo set to Saint-Saens for Anna Pavlova in 1905, creating this signature piece that she performed thousands of times worldwide.
rows.n: Saint-Saens reportedly told Pavlova after seeing her dance that he had not written the swan to die.

rows.q: This real-life assassin of President James Garfield performs an upbeat cakewalk on his way to the gallows in Sondheim’s Assassins.
rows.n: Guiteau actually wrote a bizarre hymn called I am Going to the Lordy and read it aloud on the scaffold in 1882.

rows.q: Jerome Robbins made his choreographic debut in 1944 with the ballet Fancy Free, about three sailors on leave. Within eight months, he helped expand it into this Broadway musical.
rows.n: Leonard Bernstein composed the score for both the ballet and the musical, which gave the world New York, New York.

rows.q: The Olivier-winning 2007 play A Disappearing Number dramatizes the Cambridge partnership between G.H. Hardy and this self-taught Indian genius, who claimed formulas came to him from a goddess.
rows.n: Hardy famously rated his own mathematical talent at 30, but awarded Ramanujan a score of 100.

rows.q: Charles Mingus wrote the haunting 1959 elegy “Goodbye Pork Pie Hat” as a tribute to this tenor sax pioneer, who had died just two months earlier.
rows.n: Young was famous for his flat-brimmed pork pie hats and for dubbing Billie Holiday “Lady Day.”

rows.q: In 1943, Rodgers and Hammerstein’s hit musical Oklahoma debuted on tour under this optimistic, three-word title.
rows.n: The title was changed after the rousing anthem was written during out-of-town tryouts in Boston.

rows.q: When this legally blind piano virtuoso walked into a club where Fats Waller was playing, Waller stood up and told the crowd, “God is in the house.”
rows.n: Classical greats Sergei Rachmaninoff and Vladimir Horowitz attended his club sets in awe.

rows.q: Facing bitter winter cold in Puccini’s La Bohème, the philosopher Colline sings a poignant farewell aria to this long-worn item before pawning it.
Southern lawmakers tried to ban South Pacific over this controversial song, which argues that racial prejudice is not innate but taught to children.
rows.a: You’ve Got to Be Carefully Taught
rows.n: Rodgers and Hammerstein refused to cut the song, calling it the core moral message of the entire production.

rows.q: Stephen Sondheim brought British-style cryptic crosswords to American readers by constructing them for this city-named magazine throughout the late 1960s.
rows.n: He built the puzzles for the magazine’s first year of publication in 1968 after helping launch it with Clay Felker.

rows.q: Before winning the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature, Toni Morrison earned a Pulitzer for this 1987 novel centered on the ghost of an enslaved woman’s murdered infant.
rows.n: Morrison was the first African American woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

rows.q: The alias Lewis Carroll was born when Charles Dodgson translated his first two names into this ancient tongue, then converted them back.
Reflecting its themes of exile and brotherly envy, John Steinbeck’s East of Eden takes its title from a line in Genesis describing the banishment of this murderer.
rows.n: Steinbeck mirrors the Cain and Abel dynamic across two generations of the Trask family.

rows.q: Spoken from the back of a Madrid taxi, ‘Isn’t it pretty to think so?’ is the cynical closing line of this 1926 Ernest Hemingway novel about the Lost Generation.
rows.n: In Britain, the novel was published under the title Fiesta.

rows.q: Between writing novels, Vladimir Nabokov worked as a research fellow at Harvard, cataloging thousands of specimens of these winged insects.
rows.n: His controversial 1945 theory on the migration of Polyommatus blues was proven correct by DNA in 2011.

rows.q: Octavio Paz, who won the 1990 Nobel Prize, resigned as Mexico’s ambassador to India in 1968 to protest a government massacre of student demonstrators in this capital city.
rows.n: The crackdown occurred in the Tlatelolco district just ten days before the 1968 Summer Olympics opened.

rows.q: Before winning a Pulitzer for poetry, Wallace Stevens spent decades working a nine-to-five as an insurance vice president in this Connecticut capital.
rows.n: He walked to work each morning and reportedly composed verses in his head along the route.

rows.q: ‘It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done’ marks the final heroic thoughts of this cynical English lawyer at the guillotine in A Tale of Two Cities.
rows.n: Carton took the place of Charles Darnay to save the happiness of Lucie Manette.

rows.q: Marjory Stoneman Douglas galvanized South Florida conservation efforts with her landmark 1947 book characterizing what wetland as a “River of Grass”?
rows.n: Her book proved instrumental in rallying support when President Harry Truman dedicated the national park that year.

rows.q: Truman Capote spent months in the tiny agricultural community of Holcomb in this Midwestern state while reporting his groundbreaking true-crime book In Cold Blood.
rows.n: Capote’s childhood friend Harper Lee served as his research assistant and helped charm wary locals.

rows.q: American poet Hart Crane wrote his ambitious 1930 modernist epic The Bridge as an optimistic answer to ‘The Waste Land,’ a bleak poem by this author.
rows.n: Crane rented the exact Brooklyn Heights room where engineer Washington Roebling once watched the bridge’s rise.

rows.q: Vladimir Nabokov chose this moniker for the obsessive, self-justifying European academic who narrates his controversial 1955 novel Lolita.
rows.n: The character claims in the prologue that the name is a pseudonym invented to preserve his privacy during his trial.

rows.q: In the 1920s, future novelist Eric Blair policed colonial subjects in this Asian territory, an ordeal that inspired his essay Shooting an Elephant.
rows.n: His disgust with imperial rule there formed the backbone of his 1934 debut novel Burmese Days.

rows.q: Writing under male aliases sharing their initials, Charlotte Brontë was Currer Bell, Emily was Ellis, and this youngest sister was Acton Bell.
rows.n: Her novel The Tenant of Wildfell Hall is often considered one of the earliest feminist novels.

rows.q: At the start of Gabriel García Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude, Colonel Aureliano Buendía faces a firing squad and remembers discovering this cold substance.
Described as an unappreciated author whose books are sold in adult shops, what recurring sci-fi hack serves as Kurt Vonnegut’s alter ego?
rows.n: Vonnegut based the character on real-life science-fiction novelist Theodore Sturgeon.

rows.q: David Cornwell adopted the alias John le Carré because his employer, this British foreign intelligence service, barred agents from publishing.
rows.n: His cover was later blown in 1964 by the notorious Soviet double agent Kim Philby.

rows.q: Soviet authorities blocked Boris Pasternak from collecting his 1958 Nobel Prize for this epic romance, which had to be smuggled out of the country to be printed in Italy.
rows.n: The CIA actually funded a secret Russian-language print run to distribute at the 1958 Brussels World’s Fair.

rows.q: Paul’s first letter to Corinth speaks of seeing “through a glass, darkly,” inspiring the title of a 1977 drug dystopia by this author.
rows.n: Dick dedicated the novel to friends who suffered brain damage or died from substance abuse.

rows.q: In 2013, an ornate West End ceiling collapsed onto theatergoers during a stage adaptation of this Mark Haddon novel about a mystery-solving autistic boy.
rows.a: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time
rows.n: Falling plaster injured nearly 80 audience members, but no fatalities occurred in the 112-year-old Apollo Theatre.

rows.q: Joseph Heller originally titled Catch-22 as Catch-18, but changed the number to avoid clashing with Mila 18, a novel set in the Jewish ghetto of this capital.
rows.n: Heller considered Catch-11 and Catch-14 before deciding 22 sounded funnier.

rows.q: Taking its title from King David’s biblical grief, what 1936 William Faulkner novel chronicles the rise and ruin of plantation founder Thomas Sutpen?
rows.n: Guinness once cited a 1,288-word sentence in this novel as the longest in literature.

rows.q: Generations pass, but “the sun also ariseth” according to this Old Testament wisdom book that supplied Ernest Hemingway with a title.
rows.n: The passage in chapter one reads: “The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place.”

rows.q: For his bleak title No Country for Old Men, Cormac McCarthy lifted the opening line of this 1928 W. B. Yeats poem on aging and art.
rows.n: The poem opens: “That is no country for old men. The young / In one another’s arms, birds in the trees…”

rows.q: James Joyce’s Ulysses was banned from entering the United States until a landmark 1933 federal court case determined the book was not obscene, but rather this psychological style of writing.
rows.n: Judge John M. Woolsey ruled the book’s effect was not prurient, calling it ‘emetic’ rather than aphrodisiac.

rows.q: A German V-2 rocket descent inspires the opening line, ‘A screaming comes across the sky,’ in this dense 1973 epic by Thomas Pynchon.
J.R.R. Tolkien gave The Hobbit this four-word subtitle, which Bilbo Baggins later adopts as the title for his own completed memoirs.
rows.n: In The Lord of the Rings, Bilbo leaves the completed red manuscript to Frodo.

rows.q: James Joyce concludes Ulysses with an unpunctuated, eight-sentence soliloquy by this character, who ends on the repeated word ‘Yes.’
rows.n: Her monologue forms the eighteenth and final ‘Penelope’ episode of the book.

rows.q: Hester Prynne’s deformed, vengeful husband adopts a physician’s persona in Boston, tormenting Arthur Dimmesdale under this frosty pseudonym.
Kurt Vonnegut drew on his frustrating years in corporate public relations at this Schenectady manufacturing giant when writing Player Piano.
rows.n: His older brother Bernard was a researcher at the same company, pioneering cloud-seeding.

rows.q: The 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to which British philosopher, recognizing his varied humanitarian writings rather than his landmark logic text, Principia Mathematica?
rows.n: His set-theory paradox asks whether the set of all sets that do not contain themselves contains itself.

rows.q: Facing deadly anti-aircraft fire over WWII Italy, Catch-22 protagonist John Yossarian serves in this hazardous crew role in the nose of a B-25 Mitchell.
rows.n: Joseph Heller flew 60 missions in the very same role over Italy and North Africa during World War II.

rows.q: Prolific Victorian novelist Anthony Trollope held a senior role in the British General Post Office, where he introduced this roadside feature.
Gavroche, the heroic street urchin who dies gathering cartridges from dead soldiers in Les Misérables, is the neglected biological son of this crooked couple.
rows.n: Victor Hugo wrote that Gavroche had two younger brothers whom he unknowingly helped feed on the street.

rows.q: Published in Britain a month before its US debut, Herman Melville’s masterpiece was stripped of its epilogue and bore this simple, two-word title.
rows.n: Melville dedicated the book to Nathaniel Hawthorne in token of admiration for his genius.

rows.q: An 1818 sonnet beginning “Lift not the painted veil” gave Somerset Maugham a novel title and was written by this drowned Romantic poet.
rows.n: Shelley drowned in a sudden storm off the coast of Italy in 1822, four years after writing the sonnet.

rows.q: William Sydney Porter began writing under the alias O. Henry while serving three years in an Ohio federal prison for this white-collar crime.
rows.n: He was convicted of siphoning funds while working as a teller at the First National Bank in Austin.

rows.q: Lockwood pieces together the tragic history of Heathcliff and Catherine in Wuthering Heights from the fireside gossip of this longtime family housekeeper.
rows.n: Also known as Ellen, she is one of literature’s ultimate examples of an unreliable, meddling narrator.

rows.q: Chilean Nobel laureate Pablo Neruda chose his pen name to honor Jan Neruda, a nineteenth-century poet from this Central European nation.
rows.n: Jan Neruda was a key figure of the Czech National Revival; Nerudova Street in Prague bears his name.

rows.q: In Dashiell Hammett’s noir classic The Maltese Falcon, the supposedly jewel-encrusted statuette everyone kills for turns out to be a fake made of this base metal.
rows.n: Detective Sam Spade realizes the black enamel is merely concealing a solid hunk of worthless lead.

rows.q: Miss Havisham’s crumbling, cobwebbed mansion in Great Expectations bears this ironic Latin-derived name, meaning “enough.”
rows.n: The name implied that whoever possessed the grand estate could never want for anything more in life.

rows.q: In Kurt Vonnegut’s Slaughterhouse-Five, Billy Pilgrim travels through time and gets abducted by aliens, but works back on Earth in this eye-care profession.
rows.n: Billy practises in the fictional town of Ilium, New York, after marrying his boss’s daughter.

rows.q: Before settling on Pride and Prejudice, Jane Austen shopped her manuscript to publishers under this two-word title, highlighting Elizabeth and Darcy’s hasty judgments.
rows.n: Austen wrote the first draft between 1796 and 1797, when she was just twenty-one.

rows.q: Holden Caulfield cherishes a left-handed baseball mitt belonging to his late brother Allie, which was covered in these written works scribbled in green ink.
rows.n: Allie wrote poems on his glove so he would have something to read while waiting in the outfield.

rows.q: Lewis Carroll presented his hand-lettered 1864 original manuscript to Alice Liddell under the working title Alice’s Adventures Under [what]?
rows.n: Carroll added the Mad Tea-Party and Cheshire Cat only when expanding it for publication.

rows.q: Born Macon Dead III, the protagonist of Toni Morrison’s 1977 novel Song of Solomon goes through life with this dairy-themed nickname because he was nursed too long.
rows.n: A neighborhood gossip spots him nursing past infancy and gives him the moniker that sticks for life.

rows.q: Setting a standard for fictional world-building, William Faulkner set nearly all of his Southern Gothic novels in this imaginary Mississippi county.
rows.n: Faulkner derived the name from two Chickasaw words meaning “split land.”

rows.q: Former high school basketball standout Harry Angstrom navigates suburban angst across four John Updike novels while going by this twitchy animal nickname.
rows.n: Updike won two Pulitzer Prizes for the series: for Rabbit Is Rich and Rabbit at Rest.

rows.q: Aravind Adiga won the 2008 Booker Prize for his debut novel about an ambitious chauffeur named Balram Halwai, titled for this apex predator.
rows.n: Adiga was just 33 when he won, making him one of the youngest winners in the prize’s history.

rows.q: “O my son, my son!” William Faulkner doubled the grief-stricken lament of this biblical king over his slain son to title a 1936 novel.
rows.n: Absalom was killed after getting his long hair entangled in the boughs of an oak tree during battle.

rows.q: A 1706 satire warning that “dunces are all in confederacy” against a genius gave John Kennedy Toole a title and was penned by this Irish author.
rows.n: Swift wrote the line in his collection Thoughts on Various Subjects, Moral and Diverting.

rows.q: Edward FitzGerald’s translation of this Persian astronomer’s rubaiyat supplied Agatha Christie with the title The Moving Finger.
Disillusioned with high society and an unfaithful wife, Pierre Bezukhov seeks spiritual regeneration in War and Peace by joining this secretive fraternity.
rows.n: Pierre attempts to reorganize his estates based on Masonic virtues, only to be swindled by his overseers.

rows.q: The narrator of Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man secretly decorates his underground cellar home with 1,369 of these electrical items, running on stolen power.
rows.n: He lights them with power tapped illegally from Monopolated Light & Power to prove his existence.

rows.q: Veterinarian Alf Wight used the pen name James Herriot for All Creatures Great and Small, borrowing the name from a Scottish star of this sport.
rows.n: Jim Herriot was a goalkeeper playing for Birmingham City when Wight watched him on television.

rows.q: In Agatha Christie’s mystery novels, what six-letter French word for an herbal infusion does Belgian sleuth Hercule Poirot routinely sip to soothe his nerves?
rows.n: Christie noted that Poirot considered English tea to be hot water flavored with brown paint.

rows.q: H.G. Wells never gave a first name to the sinister albino scientist who invents an invisibility formula, known only by this surname.
rows.n: Before terrorizing Sussex, Griffin practiced his invisibility technique on his landlord’s white cat.

rows.q: Dracula washes ashore in England aboard this doomed Russian schooner from Varna, steering into Whitby harbor with its dead captain lashed to the helm.
rows.n: The ship carried fifty boxes of Transylvanian earth, and only a giant black dog was seen escaping the wreck.

rows.q: Dorian Gray cruelly abandons the actress Sibyl Vane after her acting turns wretched during a performance as this tragic Shakespearean heroine.
rows.n: Having fallen in genuine love with Dorian, she suddenly found the pretend passion of Romeo and Juliet hollow.

rows.q: Maya Angelou took the title I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings from “Sympathy,” an 1899 poem composed by this pioneering Black American poet.
rows.n: Angelou used the line for her memoir to honor Dunbar, who died of tuberculosis at age thirty-three.

rows.q: Janie Crawford finds true passion with a charming younger gambler who goes by this sweet, two-word dessert nickname in Their Eyes Were Watching God.
rows.n: His real name is Vergible Woods, but Janie and the Eatonville locals know him almost exclusively as Tea Cake.

rows.q: Readers unravel the mystery of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde largely alongside this austere London lawyer and loyal old friend of Henry Jekyll.
rows.n: Stevenson introduces him as a man of rugged countenance who never smiled, yet was lovable in his loyalty.

rows.q: Long after Moby-Dick was forgotten by the public, Herman Melville earned a steady wage on the Manhattan docks in this federal inspector role.
rows.n: He held the post for nineteen years, writing poetry in the evenings until retiring in 1885.

rows.q: Bram Stoker spent nearly thirty years managing the Lyceum Theatre and assisting this legendary Victorian actor who inspired Count Dracula.
rows.n: Stoker based Dracula’s sweeping, theatrical mannerisms on Irving’s dramatic stage presence.

rows.q: Locked in the Château d’If, Edmond Dantès is tutored in languages, history, and a fortune in buried treasure by this elderly Italian priest and fellow captive.
rows.n: The character was inspired by Abbé José Custódio de Faria, a Goan priest who pioneered scientific hypnotism.

rows.q: In the final, unpunctuated soliloquy of James Joyce’s Ulysses, Molly Bloom vividly recalls her youth and romances on what Mediterranean military outpost?
rows.n: Molly was raised on the Rock as the daughter of an Irish army officer stationed with the Royal Dublin Fusiliers.

rows.q: Against his generals’ advice, Mark Antony wagers everything on a disastrous sea battle against Octavian off this Greek promontory.
rows.n: Cleopatra fled mid-fight with sixty ships, and Antony inexplicably abandoned his fleet to follow her.

rows.q: For a single penny, Globe patrons could stand in the yard exposed to the weather; Shakespeare famously referred to this standing audience as these.
rows.n: Hamlet complains in Act 3 that they are ‘capable of nothing but inexplicable dumb-shows and noise.’

rows.q: Richard III fruitlessly offers his kingdom for a horse at this 1485 battle, the bloody climax of the Wars of the Roses.
rows.n: The defeat brought an end to the Plantagenet dynasty and crowned Henry Tudor as Henry VII.

rows.q: Berowne scolds himself in Love’s Labour’s Lost for becoming a faultfinder in romance, giving English the earliest recorded use of this six-letter noun for a reviewer.
rows.n: The word traces to the ancient Greek kritikos, meaning able to judge or discern.

rows.q: Shakespeare opens a famous history play with this villainous Duke of Gloucester complaining about peacetime: “Now is the winter of our discontent.”
rows.n: He complains he has nothing to do in peacetime because he is “rudely stamped” and lacks love’s majesty.

rows.q: Washington D.C.’s Folger Library holds 82 First Folios, paid for by founder Henry Clay Folger, who made his fortune leading this oil monopoly.
rows.n: His wife Emily helped him track down copies at auction, eventually securing over a third of all survivors.

rows.q: Ironically enough, the famously long-winded royal councillor who hides behind a tapestry is the one who claims that “brevity is the soul of wit.” Name him.
rows.n: He takes nearly thirty lines of rambling preamble just to deliver that sentence to the king and queen.

rows.q: In 1603, Shakespeare’s troupe traded their Lord Chamberlain patron for a royal upgrade, renaming themselves for this newly crowned Scottish monarch.
rows.n: Under James’s royal patent, the troupe was allowed to perform anywhere in the kingdom.

rows.q: Centuries before Sherlock Holmes adopted the line, this English king rallied his soldiers outside Harfleur by shouting “The game’s afoot.”
rows.n: The line comes at the end of his famous “Once more unto the breach, dear friends” speech.

rows.q: She famously excused her youthful fling with Julius Caesar as her “salad days, when I was green in judgment.” Name this ruler.
rows.n: She speaks the line to her attendant Charmian while missing Mark Antony.

rows.q: Shakespeare’s only son died in 1596 at age eleven, leaving a name scholars constantly link to a certain Danish prince. What was the boy’s name?
rows.n: Hamnet and his twin sister Judith were named after Shakespeare’s Stratford neighbors, the Sadlers.

rows.q: Mercutio despises Juliet’s hotheaded cousin Tybalt, constantly mocking him as the “Prince of” these animals after a character in medieval folklore.
rows.n: The nickname refers to Tibert the Cat from the popular folk tales of Reynard the Fox.

rows.q: Hamlet tells Horatio that he can still vividly visualize his deceased father using this four-word phrase, which became standard for mental imagination.
rows.n: Horatio startles him seconds later by confessing he saw the actual ghost the previous midnight.

rows.q: Assembled by actors John Heminges and Henry Condell in 1623, what collected edition preserved eighteen plays that had never before been printed?
rows.n: Durham University’s stolen 1623 copy was recovered in 2008 when a man walked into D.C.’s Folger Shakespeare Library.

rows.q: In the 1995 film Richard III starring Ian McKellen, the title tyrant is reimagined as an alternate-history fascist dictator in this decade.
rows.n: McKellen’s look was inspired in part by Oswald Mosley and Edward VIII’s real-life flirtations with fascism.

rows.q: Moments before dying by his own hand, which tragic military commander begs his listeners to describe him as “one that loved not wisely but too well”?
rows.n: He delivers the final speech after realizing he was tricked into murdering his innocent wife Desdemona.

rows.q: Tricked into believing he jumped from its famous chalk cliffs, the blinded Gloucester collapses on the shore of this English port.
rows.n: The high cliff featured in King Lear has been nicknamed Shakespeare Cliff since the 18th century.

rows.q: Macbeth hires two thugs to murder Banquo and his young son, but the boy escapes into the dark to keep the witches’ prophecy alive. Name this royal ancestor.
rows.n: English lore traced King James I’s royal Stuart lineage straight back to this mythical boy.

rows.q: Carved into Shakespeare’s ledger stone, a rhyming epitaph promises a blessing to those who spare his stones and this penalty to anyone moving his bones.
rows.n: The epitaph warns: ‘Bleste be the man that spares thes stones, / And curst be he that moves my bones.’

rows.q: Before secretly conducting the wedding of Romeo and Juliet, which holy man offers the prophetic warning that “violent delights have violent ends”?
rows.n: He performs the ceremony hoping it will finally turn their families’ rancor into pure love.

rows.q: Disguised as a young male doctor of law named Balthazar, this heiress appeals to Shylock by declaring that “The quality of mercy is not strained.”
rows.n: When her plea fails, she uses the strict letter of the law to prevent him from taking a pound of flesh.

rows.q: Before returning to Denmark to mourn his poisoned father, Hamlet was hitting the books at this real German university.
rows.n: Shakespeare put Hamlet at the same university where Martin Luther launched the Protestant Reformation.
