rows.q: King Duncan unwisely compliments the pleasant air outside Macbeth’s castle in this Scottish city, hours before his murder.
rows.n: The historical Macbeth had a stronghold nearby, but Duncan was likely killed in battle, not in bed.

rows.q: Before falling into debt, William’s father John Shakespeare held civic posts in Stratford and worked in this trade, crafting luxury leather goods.
rows.n: He was also fined in 1552 for leaving an unauthorized dunghill outside his house on Henley Street.

rows.q: Following Mark Antony’s funeral oration in Julius Caesar, a bloodthirsty Roman mob tears apart an innocent poet simply because he shares this name with an assassin.
rows.n: When he cries out that he is a poet and no plotter, the mob shouts to tear him for his bad verses.

rows.q: After a drunken brawl costs him his military rank in Othello, a distraught Cassio laments losing the ‘immortal part’ of himself by shouting what word three times?
rows.n: A manipulative Iago dismisses Cassio’s despair, calling reputation ‘an idle and most false imposition.’

rows.q: During the performance of Hamlet’s mousetrap play, which queen offers the dry critique, “The lady doth protest too much, methinks”?
rows.n: She is responding to Hamlet, who asked her directly how she liked the performance.

rows.q: Othello leaves Venice in Act 1 to command the military garrison defending this eastern Mediterranean island against the Ottoman fleet.
rows.n: A storm wipes out the Turkish fleet before any fighting begins, moving the drama entirely indoors.

rows.q: In The Taming of the Shrew, Petruchio excuses his sun-struck vision with this glittering nine-letter adjective, centuries before it named a handheld rhinestone tool.
rows.n: He uses the coined word to explain why he just mistook an elderly traveler for a fresh young maiden.

rows.q: Facing the First Folio’s title page, a poem advising readers to “look / Not on his Picture, but his Book” was written by this rival playwright.
rows.n: Jonson also contributed the famous eulogy praising Shakespeare as ‘not of an age, but for all time.’

rows.q: Grieving his slaughtered family in Macbeth, Macduff coins this four-word idiom by comparing the ruthless tyrant to a bird of prey diving on its target.
rows.n: The archaic adjective fell comes from Old French and means fierce, cruel, or lethal.

rows.q: Due to Shakespeare’s shaky geography, Valentine travels by sea between Verona and this landlocked northern Italian city.
rows.n: Shakespeare repeatedly treats Milan and Verona as coastal ports connected by navigable waterways.

rows.q: Roman Polanski’s bloody 1971 adaptation of Macbeth was notably financed by this magazine founder, who was looking to branch into prestigious film production.
rows.n: Playboy Productions bankrolled the film after major Hollywood studios balked at Polanski’s grim, violent vision.

rows.q: In the closing lines of Julius Caesar, which victorious leader stands over Brutus’s body and praises him as “the noblest Roman of them all”?
rows.n: He points out that unlike the other conspirators, Brutus acted out of genuine concern for Rome.

rows.q: In A Midsummer Night’s Dream, bellows-mender Francis Flute protests being cast as this tragic lover because he has a beard coming, but Quince insists.
rows.n: The craftsman crew butchered Ovid’s tale of Pyramus and Thisbe as wedding entertainment for Duke Theseus.

rows.q: Who tries to coax Brutus into joining the plot against Caesar by insisting that “The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves”?
Prancing around in yellow stockings, this duped steward recites a forged letter claiming that “Some are born great, some achieve greatness.”
rows.n: The letter was forged by the maid Maria to trick him into making a fool of himself.

rows.q: To punish a sea captain whose wife insulted her, a witch in Macbeth casts a curse that he will suffer this seven-letter verb meaning to shrink or diminish.
rows.n: The witch vows the sailor will dwindle, peak, and pine over eighty-one exhausting weeks at sea.

rows.q: Peter Greenaway’s experimental 1991 Tempest adaptation, Prospero’s Books, cast this legendary British stage actor who had played Prospero four times on stage.
rows.n: Gielgud voiced every single character in the script himself, save for a few lines delivered by Miranda.

rows.q: Leaping into an open grave to out-grieve a rival in Hamlet, the Danish prince uses this four-letter verb for loud, theatrical raving for the first time in English.
rows.n: The word was adapted from the Dutch ranten, which meant to talk foolishly or rave deliriously.

rows.q: Exiled from Verona after killing Tybalt in a street brawl, Romeo hides out in this neighboring northern Italian city.
rows.n: Romeo buys his lethal poison from a desperate apothecary there before rushing back to Juliet.

rows.q: An exchange of bitter insults during the siege of Troy in Troilus and Cressida gifted breakup letters with this two-word expression of relief upon someone leaving.
rows.n: The full line in Act 2 is simply: A good riddance.

rows.q: Borrowed from a comic servant archetype in Italian commedia dell’arte, this four-letter word for wildly goofy behavior debuted in Love’s Labour’s Lost.
rows.n: The stock character Zanni was an acrobatic, foolish servant, named after a dialect form of Giovanni.

rows.q: In Forbidden Planet, the sci-fi reframing of The Tempest, what is the name of the advanced, extinct alien race whose technology fuels Morbius’s id monster?
rows.n: The film marked the screen debut of Robby the Robot, who effectively stood in for the spirit Ariel.

rows.q: Two plays co-written by Shakespeare and John Fletcher were left out of the First Folio: the lost Cardenio, and this tale of two captive Theban cousins.
rows.n: The play is based on Chaucer’s ‘The Knight’s Tale’ and was not published until 1634.

rows.q: Twelfth Night begins with which lovesick nobleman demanding more melodies to cure his romantic heartache, pleading, “If music be the food of love, play on”?
rows.n: Despite his flowery opening obsession with Olivia, he ends up marrying Viola.

rows.q: Buried chest-deep in dirt and left to starve at the end of Titus Andronicus, this unrepentant villain only regrets that he hadn’t committed ten thousand more crimes.
rows.n: His remorseless relish in evil made him the direct dramatic ancestor of Richard III and Iago.

rows.q: Diagon Alley gets its name from a pun on “diagonally,” while the sinister, dark-arts shopping street next door puns on this word.
rows.n: Knockturn Alley is home to Borgin and Burkes, the sinister pawn shop where Tom Riddle once worked.

rows.q: Throughout his miserable day of cavity checks and lost sneakers, Judith Viorst’s Alexander repeatedly threatens to move to this distant nation.
rows.n: Viorst named Alexander and his brothers after her own three sons, who also had bad days.

rows.q: Lloyd Alexander drew heavily on the Mabinogion, setting his Newbery-winning Prydain fantasy cycle in a legendary version of this Celtic UK nation where he trained during the 1940s.
rows.n: Alexander fell in love with Welsh castles and folklore while stationed near Rhyl during the war.

rows.q: Long before creating his pigeon and Elephant & Piggie series, Mo Willems won six Emmy Awards writing and animating for this beloved PBS program.
rows.n: Willems also voiced several animated shorts on the show during his tenure from 1993 to 2002.

rows.q: Said to have been carved by Death from a riverbank branch, what coveted magical artifact in Harry Potter possesses a core made from the hair of a Thestral?
rows.n: It is the only known wand with a Thestral hair core, a substance that can only be harnessed by those who grasp death.

rows.q: In Ludwig Bemelmans’ first Madeline book, the fearless Parisian schoolgirl becomes the envy of her peers after having this organ removed.
Hansel and Gretel famously drop bread crumbs, but during their first abandonment in the woods, Hansel left a trail using shiny white these.
rows.n: The moon shone brightly on the white flint pebbles, showing the children the way home.

rows.q: Controversially in The Last Battle, this elder Pevensie sister is barred from Narnia after trading magical adventures for nylons and lipstick.
rows.n: Her exclusion prompted authors like J.K. Rowling and Neil Gaiman to publicly criticize the theological choice.

rows.q: Gryffindor’s resident ghost, Sir Nicholas, was brought to life on the silver screen by this founding member of Monty Python.
rows.n: Cleese appeared in the first two films before being dropped from subsequent installments.

rows.q: Mordicai Gerstein’s 2004 Caldecott winner depicts the illegal 1974 high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers performed by which French tightrope artist?
rows.n: As punishment, the court ordered Petit to perform a free high-wire show for children in Central Park.

rows.q: Adapting an Ian Fleming book for the 1968 cinema version, Roald Dahl invented this terrifying, cage-wielding villain not found in the original novel.
rows.n: The role in Chitty Chitty Bang Bang was played by Australian ballet dancer Robert Helpmann.

rows.q: Publisher Bennett Cerf placed a 50-dollar wager that Dr. Seuss could not complete an entire readable book using only this many distinct words.
rows.n: Seuss won the bet with Green Eggs and Ham, though Cerf allegedly never paid up the cash.

rows.q: In Peter, Paul and Mary’s 1963 folk ballad “Puff, the Magic Dragon,” the title beast frolics in the autumn mist of what fictional seaside land?
rows.n: The song peaked at number two in 1963, kept off the top spot by Little Peggy March’s I Will Follow Him.

rows.q: William Goldman set the bulk of The Princess Bride in this fictional European monarchy ruled by Prince Humperdinck, which shares its name with an old gold coin.
rows.n: Its sworn rival kingdom is Guilder, named after the historic Dutch currency.

rows.q: Alice starts her adventures underground by chasing a rabbit, but when she steps through the looking-glass, the landscape she traverses is organized like this board game.
Charlie’s sweet adventures were inspired by Dahl’s days at Repton School, where students were mailed secret test batches from what chocolate maker?
rows.n: Dahl recalled rating twelve experimental bars each term on an official feedback score sheet.

rows.q: Bluebeard tests his young bride’s obedience with a key to a forbidden room, which betrays her curiosity because it is stained with indelible what?
rows.n: The key was enchanted, so scrubbing and scouring could not remove the stain.

rows.q: On Asteroid B-612, the Little Prince must constantly weed out the fast-growing saplings of this gigantic African tree before they rip his home apart.
rows.n: Antoine de Saint-Exupery used the invasive trees as a parable for the rise of fascism.

rows.q: Ed Young’s 1990 Caldecott winner Lon Po Po is a Chinese retelling of which classic European fairy tale, featuring three young sisters outwitting a disguised predator?
rows.n: The title translates roughly to Granny Wolf, who poses as the girls’ grandmother while their mother visits relatives.

rows.q: Mark Twain modeled Tom Sawyer’s hometown of St. Petersburg on this real Mississippi River boyhood home of his, which now hosts an annual National Tom Sawyer Days festival.
rows.n: The real cave where Twain and his friends played became the inspiration for McDougal’s Cave.

rows.q: A brightly colored alphabet races to the top of this tropical tree in a 1989 rhyming classic by Bill Martin Jr. and John Archambault.
rows.n: Lois Ehlert created the vibrant collages from paper she hand-painted with acrylics.

rows.q: Bilbo Baggins begins his unexpected journey in Bag End, an underground smial built beneath the Hill on the northern edge of this peaceful Shire village.
rows.n: Peter Jackson reconstructed the movie set as a permanent tourist attraction in Matamata, New Zealand.

rows.q: Narrated by Death, this bestselling 2005 novel by Markus Zusak centers on Liesel Meminger, a young girl growing up in Nazi Germany who steals banned books.
rows.n: Zusak was inspired by stories of World War II and the Holocaust told by his German and Austrian parents.

rows.q: Claudia and Jamie Kincaid escape boring suburban chores by hiding out and bathing in the fountain of this sprawling Fifth Avenue museum in New York.
rows.a: Metropolitan Museum of Art (or The Met)
rows.n: E.L. Konigsburg was inspired after her own children complained about walking during a family picnic.

rows.q: Neil Gaiman set The Graveyard Book in an overgrown Victorian burial ground inspired by this North London cemetery, where Karl Marx and George Eliot are buried.
Brokenhearted when this “Swedish Nightingale” turned down his marriage proposal, Hans Christian Andersen channeled his grief into writing “The Nightingale.”
rows.n: Nicknamed the Swedish Nightingale, she later toured America under showman P.T. Barnum.

rows.q: Arthur Ransome’s Swallows and Amazons series sends four children sailing across a lake pieced together from Windermere and Coniston Water in this English national park.
rows.n: Ransome based the Walker children on the grandchildren of the historian W.G. Collingwood.

rows.q: After his infant son was hurt in a 1960 carriage crash, Dahl helped develop a medical shunt to drain excess fluid caused by what brain condition?
rows.n: The Wade-Dahl-Till valve successfully treated thousands of pediatric patients worldwide.

rows.q: Farmer Brown faces a barnyard labor strike in Click, Clack, Moo when his cows refuse to produce milk until he provides them with these cozy items.
rows.n: The cows drafted their demands on an old Underwood typewriter found in the barn.

rows.q: Meg and Charles Wallace are stunned when Mrs Whatsit reveals she used to be one of these celestial objects before falling in Madeleine L’Engle’s A Wrinkle in Time.
rows.n: She sacrificed her form to push back the cosmic darkness, taking the guise of an old woman dressed in ragged sheets.

rows.q: Warwick Davis played Charms master Filius Flitwick on screen, but he also portrayed this treacherous Gringotts goblin teller.
rows.n: Verne Troyer played Griphook’s physical body in the first film, while Davis provided his voice.

rows.q: Johanna Spyri’s 1881 novel tears Heidi away from her idyllic Swiss Alps and packs her off to work as a companion to an invalid girl in this German financial hub.
rows.n: The city air makes Heidi so homesick that she begins sleepwalking, prompting the doctor to send her home.

rows.q: Lois Lowry’s protagonist Jonas first perceives color when he spots a flash of red on which piece of fruit while playing catch in The Giver?
rows.n: Red is the first color to break through the Sameness, followed by Fiona’s red hair and the sled in Jonas’s memories.

rows.q: Buried in Buckinghamshire, Roald Dahl was laid to rest with snooker cues, vintage burgundy, and this motorized cutting tool, just in case he woke up.
rows.n: He was buried at the Church of St Peter and St Paul in Great Missenden in 1990.

rows.q: Claudia and Jamie Kincaid hide in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in a 1968 Newbery classic, investigating an angel statue carved by which Italian Renaissance master?
rows.n: Mrs. Frankweiler possessed the secret pencil sketch proving Michelangelo was indeed the sculptor.

rows.q: Banned in Franco’s Spain as pacifist propaganda, Munro Leaf’s 1936 classic tells of a bull who prefers sniffing flowers beneath this kind of oak tree.
rows.n: Munro Leaf wrote the text in under an hour on a rainy Sunday to give his friend work to sketch.

rows.q: Harry Potter’s childhood torment at Number 4 Privet Drive takes place in Little Whinging, a fictional commuter town J.K. Rowling placed in this wealthy county south of London.
rows.n: Rowling chose Surrey because she wanted an aggressively mundane suburban backdrop to contrast with magic.

rows.q: Long before the poisoned apple, Snow White’s wicked stepmother nearly killed the princess using a poisoned one of these everyday grooming tools.
rows.n: The dwarfs returned home from the mines just in time to pull the comb from her hair.

rows.q: Look closely at the bedroom in Margaret Wise Brown’s Goodnight Moon, and you will spot a painting and open copy of this other 1942 classic of hers.
rows.n: Clement Hurd’s illustration depicts the mother rabbit fishing for her runaway child.

rows.q: Lilliput reduced Gulliver to a giant among six-inch citizens, but Jonathan Swift reversed the joke in his next voyage by marooning him in this land of towering behemoths.
rows.n: Swift described Brobdingnag as a vast peninsula jutting off the northwest coast of North America.

rows.q: Hans Christian Andersen’s original tragic ending sees the Little Mermaid dissolve into sea foam to become a spirit of this classical element.
rows.n: She must spend 300 years performing good deeds on Earth to earn an immortal human soul.

rows.q: Geisel reserved his Dr. Seuss pen name for books he illustrated. For stories drawn by others, he used what pen name, his own surname spelled backward?
Tucked inside his garden writing hut, Roald Dahl wrote exclusively on yellow legal pads using this specific brand of yellow No. 2 pencil.
rows.n: He began every writing session with six freshly sharpened pencils arranged on his desk.

rows.q: Before it was charmed to evaluate and sort first-year students, Hogwarts’ Sorting Hat originally sat on the head of this house founder.
rows.n: Gryffindor also left behind the silver, ruby-encrusted goblin sword that Harry pulls from the hat.

rows.q: Dr. Seuss’s lone live-action feature film, The 5,000 Fingers of Dr. T., centered on a tyrannical teacher forcing 500 boys to play what instrument?
rows.n: The massive set featured a continuous, curved keyboard that spanned several sound stages.

rows.q: Norton Juster’s The Phantom Tollbooth sees Milo drive his toy car past the Sea of Knowledge to visit this word-obsessed capital ruled by King Azaz the Unabridged.
rows.n: Its rival city is Digitopolis, ruled by the King’s estranged brother, the Mathemagician.

rows.q: The phrase “fairy tale” traces to Madame d’Aulnoy, a 17th-century French author whose gatherings in this type of reception room launched the genre.
rows.n: Her 1697 book Les Contes des Fées popularized the phrase contes de fées.

rows.q: Dr. Seuss struck it rich in 1928 by penning a long-running ad campaign for Flit, an insecticide manufactured by this oil titan.
rows.n: His contract with Standard Oil barred him from most other commercial art, pushing him to books.

rows.q: Perrault’s “Sleeping Beauty” doesn’t end with a wedding: the prince’s mother is revealed to be this mythical man-eating creature who targets her grandkids.
rows.n: The mother-in-law’s cannibalistic scheme collapses when she jumps into a vat of vipers.

rows.q: After an enchanted flounder makes his greedy wife a king, an emperor, and the pope, a fisherman returns empty-handed when she demands to become this.
rows.n: The flounder revokes all her wishes, leaving the couple back in their filthy vinegar jug.

rows.q: Paddington Bear settles into 32 Windsor Gardens, but he makes daily morning trips to drink cocoa and chat with antique dealer Mr. Gruber on this real Notting Hill street.
rows.n: The film adaptations retained the setting, turning Mr. Gruber’s shop into a neighborhood staple.

rows.q: Before his editor suggested something cuter, Eric Carle’s famished hero was this specific page-munching insect pest.
rows.n: Editor Ann Beneduce suggested a caterpillar instead, prompting Carle to shout ‘Butterfly!’

rows.q: Eleanor Roosevelt invited Roald Dahl to the White House after falling in love with this 1943 debut book of his, written for a planned Disney film.
rows.n: Dahl stayed as a weekend houseguest with the Roosevelts at Hyde Park and the White House.

rows.q: Flying in the desperate April 1941 Battle of Athens, Dahl piloted which legendary British monoplane fighter alongside RAF squadron leader Pat Pattle?
rows.n: Dahl’s outnumbered squadron flew against hundreds of German bombers over the port of Piraeus.

rows.q: Reforged from the broken shards of Narsil, Aragorn’s sword is renamed Anduril, which translates to the “Flame of the” what?
rows.n: Elven smiths reforge the blade in Rivendell before Aragorn rides to summon the Army of the Dead.

rows.q: Brian Selznick’s 2008 Caldecott winner follows a Parisian orphan who repairs an automaton created by which pioneering filmmaker behind A Trip to the Moon?
rows.n: Spanning 533 pages, it remains by far the longest book to ever win the picture-book-focused Caldecott Medal.

rows.q: In Andersen’s gruesome tale “The Red Shoes,” cursed Karen is unable to stop dancing, leading her to beg this town official to sever her feet with an axe.
rows.n: Even after her feet were severed, the red shoes danced away into the forest with them.

rows.q: King Caspian’s majestic flagship in The Voyage of the Dawn Treader is carved from stern to gilded bowsprit to resemble this mythical monster.
rows.n: The ship’s prow is shaped like a dragon’s head, with its wings forming the vessel’s waist.

rows.q: Decades before Walt Disney moved the story to North America, Felix Salten’s original 1923 novel was set in a forest in this Alpine country.
rows.n: Salten was an Austrian writer; his original deer was a European roe deer, not a white-tailed deer.

rows.q: Dispatched to Washington as a British spy during WWII, Roald Dahl famously grumbled to handlers about having to seduce this conservative congresswoman.
rows.n: Dahl begged MI6 boss William Stephenson to take him off the assignment due to her fierce stamina.

rows.q: Prior to his wartime RAF service, young Roald Dahl lived in colonial East Africa working as an overseas salesman for this petroleum giant.
rows.n: He was stationed in Mombasa and Dar es Salaam, dealing with supply routes and safari snakes.

rows.q: In Louis Sachar’s Newbery-winning Holes, the Yelnats family curse began in this European country, where great-great-grandfather Elya broke his promise to Madame Zeroni.
rows.n: Madame Zeroni wanted to drink from the mountaintop stream, but Elya sailed to America before fulfilling his promise.

rows.q: On Christmas Eve in 1956, BBC cameraman Michael Bond bought a lonely teddy bear left on a shelf at this London department store, inspiring Paddington.
rows.n: He named the bear after the nearby rail station because he lived within walking distance.

rows.q: Fleeing Paris ahead of Nazi troops in 1940, Margret and H.A. Rey escaped on this mode of transit with the manuscript of Curious George in tow.
rows.n: Hans Rey assembled two makeshift bikes out of spare parts just hours before the city fell.

rows.q: According to a popular translation myth, Charles Perrault misheard the French word for this rodent’s fur, “vair,” as glass when outfitting Cinderella.
rows.n: Vair was a precious gray-and-white squirrel fur widely used for lining aristocratic cloaks.

rows.q: Awarded to the winner of the Super Bowl since 1967, the Vince Lombardi Trophy is handcrafted every year by which famed luxury jewelry company?
rows.n: Vice president Oscar Riedener sketched the initial design on a cocktail napkin during a 1966 lunch with Pete Rozelle.

rows.q: Major League Baseball’s annual designated hitter trophy was renamed in 2004 for Edgar Martínez, a seven-time All-Star who spent his entire 18-year career playing for this franchise.
rows.n: Martínez was so dominant that MLB permanently stamped his name on the award the year he retired.

rows.q: A lifelong fan of the franchise, Aaron Rodgers sat in the green room for over four hours in 2005 after this hometown team passed on him to draft Alex Smith at number one.
rows.n: Rodgers famously quipped on draft day that he wouldn’t be as disappointed as the 49ers would be for passing.

rows.q: Spending his entire 22-season career with the same franchise, Hall of Famer Stan ‘The Man’ Musial won three World Series titles with this National League team.
rows.n: Musial finished his career with exactly 1,815 hits at home and 1,815 hits on the road.

rows.q: Drafted first overall in 1986 by this NFL team, Bo Jackson refused to sign after owner Hugh Culverhouse cost him his college baseball eligibility. Name the franchise.
rows.n: Jackson played for the Kansas City Royals instead before the Raiders took a late-round flyer on him.

rows.q: In 1963, Lamar Hunt relocated his AFL champion Texans to Missouri, picking this civic-themed moniker to honor Kansas City mayor H. Roe Bartle.
rows.n: Mayor Bartle had earned the nickname ‘Chief’ as a longtime Boy Scouts executive.

rows.q: Shoeless Joe Jackson earned his legendary moniker after playing part of a 1908 minor-league game in stocking feet because his new spikes had given him these.
rows.n: Jackson only played barefoot in that single game, but a heckler’s taunt stuck to him for the rest of his career.

rows.q: Linebacker Chuck Howley picked off two passes in Super Bowl V, making this losing squad the only defeated team to claim Super Bowl MVP honors.
rows.n: Howley refused to accept the MVP trophy after Dallas lost 16-13 to the Baltimore Colts.

rows.q: Florida and Georgia play their annual neutral-site football grudge match in this sprawling city on the banks of the St. Johns River.
rows.n: The matchup was long dubbed the World’s Largest Outdoor Cocktail Party until schools asked broadcasters to drop it.

rows.q: On February 29, 1980, this 51-year-old hockey icon scored his 800th NHL goal while playing alongside his two sons for the Hartford Whalers.
White Sox slugger Frank Thomas was given this bruising, two-word nickname by broadcaster Ken Harrelson because he routinely punished opposing pitchers.
rows.n: Harrelson claimed he coined it in 1992 after seeing Thomas launch massive batting-practice shots into the upper deck.

rows.q: Alabama and Auburn’s heated football rivalry earned its Iron Bowl moniker because it was played for decades in this heavy-industry hub city.
rows.n: Birmingham’s Legion Field hosted every Iron Bowl between 1948 and 1988 before Auburn finally got home games.

rows.q: In 1989, this first-year Dallas Cowboys head coach pulled off the blockbuster Herschel Walker trade with Minnesota, stockpiling picks that built a 1990s dynasty.
rows.n: Dallas used those picks to draft cornerstone stars like Emmitt Smith, Russell Maryland, and Darren Woodson.

rows.q: The annual showdown between the Washington Huskies and Washington State Cougars awards a trophy named for this signature state fruit.
rows.n: Washington produces more than half of the fresh apples grown in the entire United States.

rows.q: Before settling into the Superdome in 1975, New Orleans’s Sugar Bowl was played on the campus of this private Crescent City university.
rows.n: Tulane Stadium was also the site of three early Super Bowls before being demolished in 1980.

rows.q: Long before moving to an NFL dome in Glendale, the Fiesta Bowl spent its first 35 years in Tempe on the campus of this university.
The winner of NASCAR’s Daytona 500 hoists a trophy named for GM design chief Harley J. Earl, the styling pioneer who created this iconic fiberglass American sports car in 1953.
rows.n: The trophy is topped with a silver miniature of Earl’s futuristic 1953 Firebird I concept car.

rows.q: This surname belongs to both the Mariners designated hitter who hit “The Double” in the 1995 ALDS and the Red Sox ace who won the 1999 pitching Triple Crown.
rows.n: Edgar and Pedro are both in the Baseball Hall of Fame, inducted in 2019 and 2015 respectively.

rows.q: In 1970, Pirates pitcher Dock Ellis threw an improbable no-hitter against San Diego while admitting he was entirely under the influence of this psychedelic drug.
rows.n: Ellis mistakenly thought Pittsburgh had an off-day and dropped acid before realizing he had to pitch game one.

rows.q: Golf’s amateur clash between the U.S. and Britain awards the Walker Cup, founded by donor George Herbert Walker, the maternal grandfather of which future U.S. president?
rows.n: Walker’s daughter Dorothy married Prescott Bush, making 41 the namesake’s direct grandson.

rows.q: Conspiracy theorists claimed the NBA froze an envelope in 1985 to ensure the Knicks landed the top pick and drafted this Georgetown superstar center.
rows.n: The 1985 draft was the NBA’s very first lottery, instituted to combat blatant regular-season tanking.

rows.q: Boston tanked the 1996-97 season hoping to land the top lottery pick, but lost out to San Antonio, who drafted this legendary Wake Forest center first overall.
rows.n: Duncan teamed up with David Robinson to deliver San Antonio its first NBA championship two years later.

rows.q: Long before decamping for the desert of Arizona, the NFL’s oldest continuously operating franchise began play on the South Side of what Midwestern city?
rows.n: They were founded in 1898 as the Morgan Athletic Club before becoming the Chicago Cardinals.

rows.q: Strictly outlawed in professional baseball until the National League permitted it in 1884, this pitching delivery shares its name with a looping boxing punch.
In 1935, Philadelphia Athletics manager Connie Mack built a 33-foot ‘spite wall’ in right field to stop residents on 20th Street from watching games from these perches.
rows.n: Nearby homeowners had erected bleachers on their roofs and sold cheap tickets, undercutting Mack during the Depression.

rows.q: Dallas hosts the Red River Rivalry between Texas and Oklahoma right in the middle of this massive October exposition.
rows.n: The Cotton Bowl stands in Fair Park, meaning fans can grab a Fletcher’s Corny Dog right outside the gate.

rows.q: Iowa and Minnesota play for Floyd of Rosedale, a hefty bronze trophy sculpted in the likeness of this barnyard livestock animal.
rows.n: Minnesota’s governor won a live prize pig in a 1935 bet with Iowa’s governor, inspiring the trophy.

rows.q: Now simply known as the Cardinal, Stanford changed its athletic team name in 1972 after dropping this Native American mascot.
rows.n: The Stanford Tree, beloved by fans and reviled by rivals, is merely the marching band’s unofficial mascot.

rows.q: In 1980, Red Auerbach dealt the top pick to Golden State for Robert Parish and the third pick, using that third selection on this future Hall of Fame forward from Minnesota.
rows.n: The Warriors drafted Joe Barry Carroll first overall, whom fans soon mocked as ‘Joe Barely Cares.’

rows.q: Decades after donating the silver bowl that became the Davis Cup, Harvard tennis star Dwight F. Davis served in Calvin Coolidge’s cabinet in this military-minded secretary position.
rows.n: Davis also served as Governor-General of the Philippines from 1929 to 1932.

rows.q: The rough-and-tumble 1934 St. Louis Cardinals were nicknamed this ‘Gang’ after a reporter remarked their dirty uniforms made them look like gas-plant workers.
rows.n: Led by brothers Dizzy and Paul Dean, the gritty squad won 95 games and beat Detroit in a wild seven-game World Series.

rows.q: St. Louis Browns owner Bill Veeck famously sent three-foot-seven Eddie Gaedel to bat in 1951, sporting this fractional number on his jersey.
rows.n: Gaedel walked on four straight pitches; the American League president officially voided his contract the next day.

rows.q: What Canadian fitness model and WWE Hall of Famer won a then-record seven Women’s Championships between 2000 and 2006?
rows.n: Born Patricia Stratigeas, she headlined Monday Night Raw alongside rival Lita in 2004.

rows.q: June 15, 1977 is mourned by Mets fans as the Midnight Massacre, the night front-office brass traded away this beloved three-time Cy Young winner to the Reds.
rows.n: Seaver threw his only career no-hitter a year later while wearing a Cincinnati uniform.

rows.q: Before the Cubs moved in, Wrigley Field was built for the Chicago Whales of this short-lived third major league, which folded after the 1915 season.
rows.n: The Federal League’s antitrust lawsuit eventually led to MLB’s long-standing Supreme Court antitrust exemption.

rows.q: After Eric Lindros refused to wear a Quebec Nordiques sweater in 1991, he was dealt to Philly in a package that included this future Swedish Hall of Famer.
rows.n: Forsberg went on to win two Stanley Cups and the 2003 Hart Trophy with the relocated franchise in Colorado.

rows.q: Sandwiched between LeBron James at number one and Carmelo Anthony at three in the 2003 NBA draft, the Detroit Pistons used the second pick on this Serbian big man.
rows.n: Milicic played just 4.7 minutes per game his rookie year, earning the bench nickname ‘The Human Victory Cigar.’

rows.q: Nicknamed “The King” by Old Trafford faithful, this flamboyant French forward sparked Manchester United to four Premier League titles in five seasons.
rows.n: His United career was famously paused for eight months after he kung-fu kicked a Crystal Palace fan in 1995.

rows.q: The Ryder Cup was founded by British merchant Samuel Ryder, who built a fortune selling small packets of these garden items to English suburbanites for a single penny.
rows.n: Ryder took up golf at age 50 on doctor’s orders to get fresh air and soon funded the match.

rows.q: Following consecutive European Cup titles, Béla Guttmann was denied a pay raise in 1962 and cursed this Portuguese club to never win another continental final.
rows.n: They have lost all eight European finals they have played in since Guttmann cast his hex.

rows.q: The Denver Nuggets take their name from Colorado’s 19th-century mining rush, but their fuzzy costumed mascot Rocky is a mountain creature of what specific kind?
rows.n: Rocky the Mountain Lion was inducted into the Mascot Hall of Fame in 2008.

rows.q: Known today as the Jets, New York’s AFL franchise shared the Polo Grounds for their first three seasons under which colossal mythological moniker?
rows.n: Sonny Werblin bought the bankrupt team in 1963 and renamed them the Jets to reflect modern air travel.

rows.q: Detouring through small-town Ohio before heading to Detroit in 1934, the Lions spent four seasons playing under what Greek-warrior nickname?
The Baltimore Orioles share a name with Maryland’s state bird, which was originally christened in the 1700s because its orange and black matched the heraldry of which founding family?
rows.n: Specifically Cecil Calvert, Lord Baltimore, whose heraldic colors still form Maryland’s state flag.

rows.q: Dodger Stadium opened in 1962 in this ravine, following a contentious decade-long battle in which the city evicted a largely Mexican-American neighborhood.
rows.n: The land was originally taken under eminent domain for public housing before the city traded it to Walter O’Malley.

rows.q: Boston’s NFL franchise debuted in 1932 sharing a nickname and a ballpark with which local Major League Baseball team?
rows.n: Owner George Preston Marshall renamed them the Boston Redskins in 1933 when they moved to Fenway Park.

rows.q: In 1968, Harvard scored 16 points in the final 42 seconds against Yale, inspiring a legendary student paper headline: ‘Harvard Beats Yale,’ this tie score.
rows.n: The Harvard Crimson’s famous banner headline is celebrated in a feature-length documentary.

rows.q: When the 1994 MLB strike wiped out the season, Cleveland settled the ‘player to be named later’ terms of a trade for this 3,000-hit slugger by paying for Minnesota’s dinner.
rows.n: Executives from the two clubs met over dinner and Cleveland general manager John Hart picked up the check.

rows.q: During their miraculous 1951 pennant comeback, the New York Giants stole opposing catchers’ signs from the center-field clubhouse using this optical device.
rows.n: Coach Herman Franks relayed signals from the clubhouse to the bullpen using an electric buzzer wired to the wall.

rows.q: Pitching’s top prize honors Cy Young, but ‘Cy’ was a nickname inspired by his cyclone fastball. What was his actual, birth-certificate first name?
rows.n: Born Denton True Young in Ohio, he won 511 games, an MLB record that will likely stand forever.

rows.q: The NBA regular-season title trophy honors Maurice Podoloff, who ran the league from its 1946 birth while simultaneously serving as president of a league in this other pro sport.
rows.n: Podoloff led the American Hockey League from 1940 to 1952, balancing both sports from the same desk.

rows.q: College football’s oldest traveling prize, Michigan and Minnesota’s Little Brown Jug was originally bought for 30 cents to store this fluid.
rows.n: Michigan coach Fielding Yost feared Minnesota locals might tamper with his team’s water supply.

rows.q: Before it was rebranded for Houston’s domed stadium in 1966, the synthetic turf developed by Monsanto was sold under what chemical-sounding trade name?
rows.n: It was first installed at a Rhode Island prep school field house in 1964 before revolutionizing baseball fields.

rows.q: Clad in Western hats to honor Calgary’s cowboy culture, the 1988 Winter mascots Hidy and Howdy were a brother-and-sister duo of these arctic predators.
rows.n: They were the first Olympic mascots to be designed as a duo rather than a single character.

rows.q: At the 1976 German Grand Prix, Arturo Merzario famously pulled this rival from a blazing cockpit before safety crews arrived.
rows.n: Lauda gave Merzario a gold Rolex in gratitude, returning to race just six weeks later at Monza.

rows.q: Named for a breed of miniature domestic chicken, this boxing weight class sits directly between flyweight and featherweight.
rows.n: The name traces to the Indonesian port town of Bantam, from which the small fowl were originally exported.

rows.q: Sled dog drivers are known as mushers because English-speaking frontiersmen misheard this French command meaning “walk!” or “march!”
rows.n: Real modern dog sledders rarely say “mush”—they shout “hike!” or “let’s go!” instead.

rows.q: Long before headlining UFC pay-per-views, Ronda Rousey took home bronze in Beijing in 2008, making her the first American woman to medal in this Olympic event.
rows.n: Her mother, AnnMaria De Mars, became the first American to win a Judo World Championship back in 1984.

rows.q: At the 1908 London Games, shooters fired wax bullets at frock-coated mannequins in an event inspired by this old form of honor combat.
rows.n: Competitors wore heavy protective coats and face masks with glass visors.

rows.q: Ancient Greek competitors spent hours training in this venue, which takes its name from the Greek word for “naked.”
rows.n: Greek athletes oiled their bodies before workouts and scraped off the sweat and sand afterward with a strigil.

rows.q: Mocked by comedians for its self-contradictory name, this aquatic discipline awarded Olympic medals from 1984 to 1992.
rows.n: The swimmer synchronized her movements to the music, not to a partner.

rows.q: The first athlete disqualified for doping at an Olympic Games was Swedish pentathlete Hans-Gunnar Liljenwall in 1968, after testing positive for this beverage ingredient.
rows.n: Liljenwall drank two beers before the pistol shooting round to steady his nerves.

rows.q: Before golf and tennis adopted it for sweeping the four majors, this phrase described winning all thirteen tricks in a hand of contract bridge.
rows.n: It was borrowed into sports writing in 1930 when Bobby Jones won all four major golf titles in one year.

rows.q: Before becoming an Olympic event, modern keirin track cycling originated in this Asian country primarily as a legal pari-mutuel gambling sport.
rows.n: Developed in post-WWII Japan in 1948, keirin races still draw massive betting handle alongside boat and motorcycle racing.

rows.q: Cycling commentators use this French word for the main pack of riders. To a tailor or knitter, it literally means a little ball of thread.
rows.n: The word also gave us “platoon,” as both describe a tightly bundled group.

rows.q: Debuting at the Tokyo 2020 Summer Olympics with park and street disciplines, what action sport saw 13-year-old Momiji Nishiya win an inaugural gold?
rows.n: Nishiya was one of the youngest individual gold medalists in Olympic history, winning the women’s street event.

rows.q: Instead of red, early British Grand Prix cars were painted green after a 1903 race held in Ireland honored what national emblem?
rows.n: Racing on public roads was illegal in Britain, so Ireland hosted the Gordon Bennett Cup, giving birth to British Racing Green.

rows.q: Winning gold in Rome in 1960, Ethiopian marathoner Abebe Bikila became East Africa’s first Olympic champion, famously completing the course without this standard equipment.
Famously saddled with billions in stadium debt that took until 2006 to pay off, which Canadian city hosted the 1976 Summer Olympics?
rows.n: It took 30 years to pay off the debt on the Olympic Stadium, nicknamed the ‘Big Owe.’

rows.q: In 1900, Paris held the only Olympic tournament for this mallet-and-hoop lawn game, making it one of the first events open to female competitors.
rows.n: The event was sparsely attended; only one spectator reportedly bought a ticket.

rows.q: Sydney 2000 avoided koalas and kangaroos for its mascots, opting instead for native animals including Syd the platypus, Millie the echidna, and Olly, this noisy kingfisher.
rows.n: Olly was named after the word Olympics, while Syd stood for Sydney and Millie for the millennium.

rows.q: Modern boxing rules bear the name of the 9th Marquess of Queensberry, whose outrage over his son’s romance with this playwright led to a famous libel trial.
rows.n: Queensberry left a calling card at Wilde’s club accusing him of posing as a somdomite (sic), sparking the feud.

rows.q: The two arched handles on a gymnastics horse are called pommels, taking their name from the French word for this round fruit.
rows.n: Saddle-makers originally used the word because the front knob resembled an apple.

rows.q: Following the fatal 1982 bout between Ray Mancini and Duk-koo Kim, professional boxing authorities trimmed championship matches from fifteen rounds to this new limit.
rows.n: Studies showed brain trauma spiked late in bouts when fighters were severely dehydrated, prompting the shift.

rows.q: Sixteen years before the first Winter Olympics took place in Chamonix, this chilly sport made its debut at the 1908 London Summer Games, held on indoor ice.
rows.n: Madge Syers won the first women’s gold; she had competed against men six years earlier.

rows.q: The iconic rainbow jersey awarded to cycling world champions incorporates five bands matching the exact colors of what international symbol?
rows.n: The Union Cycliste Internationale introduced the five-color bands in 1927, borrowing the Olympic palette directly.

rows.q: In the peloton, the lantern rouge is the unofficial title claimed by the rider who finishes in what specific position?
rows.n: Named after the red lantern hung on the caboose of a train, riders once intentionally slowed down to win the publicity it brought.

rows.q: Set to return to the Olympics in 2028, this bat-and-ball sport was previously played only once, in 1900, when Great Britain defeated France.
rows.n: Most players on the French team were actually British expats living in Paris.

rows.q: At the 1970 World Cup, British referee Ken Aston introduced yellow and red cards, an innovation he conceived while waiting at one of these London street fixtures.
rows.n: Aston realized a universal color code would bridge language barriers after a chaotic 1966 match.

rows.q: This sliding sport got its name from the early technique where crews rocked violently back and forth inside the sled to build up momentum.
In the world of professional sumo, this grand champion rank is the only one from which a wrestler can never be demoted, though a severe slump demands his retirement.
rows.n: Wrestlers at this apex rank wear a massive braided white hemp rope called a shimenawa during ring-entering rituals.

rows.q: In 1982, the ‘Disgrace of Gijón’ saw West Germany and Austria kick the ball aimlessly for eighty minutes to preserve a 1-0 result that eliminated which North African team?
rows.n: Algeria had shocked West Germany 2-1 earlier; the scandal forced FIFA to schedule final group games simultaneously.

rows.q: The 1908 London Games remain the only Olympics to stage motorized contests, awarding three medals in this water sport.
Australia’s strict quarantine laws on foreign horses forced the 1956 Melbourne Olympics to stage all equestrian events five months early in this European capital.
The Maglia Rosa worn by the leader of the Giro d’Italia is pink because of the newsprint color of this sponsoring sports daily.
rows.n: The newspaper created the race in 1909 to boost its circulation, printing on pale pink paper since 1899.

rows.q: At the 2018 PyeongChang Games, this Japanese superstar became the first men’s singles figure skater to win consecutive Olympic titles since 1952.
rows.n: After every performance, his dedicated fans would shower the ice with hundreds of Winnie-the-Pooh plushies.

rows.q: Invented in the 1930s by Swedish coach Gosta Holmer, this continuous training method translates literally into English as “speed play.”
rows.n: Holmer developed it after Sweden was repeatedly trounced by Finnish running legend Paavo Nurmi.

rows.q: Before moving to Goodison Park in 1892, Everton played their home matches at this ground, leaving over a rent dispute that prompted the landlord to form Liverpool FC.
rows.n: John Houlding owned the land at Anfield and created Liverpool to play in the newly empty stadium.

rows.q: Olympic rowers and wrestlers who lose early can still chase bronze through this round, named from a French verb meaning “to fish out again.”
rows.n: The term was originally used for candidates who barely failed an exam and got a second evaluation.

rows.q: In 1994, Oleg Salenko set a single-game men’s World Cup record by scoring five goals in a 6-1 blowout against Cameroon while representing which national team?
rows.n: Salenko shared the 1994 Golden Boot with Hristo Stoichkov despite Russia exiting in the group stage.

rows.q: Borrowed from a Hindi word for a wheel or circle, this seven-and-a-half-minute period is polo’s equivalent of a quarter.
rows.n: The root word is “chakra,” which shares an ancient Indo-European root with the English word “wheel.”

rows.q: Decades before NBA players caught lobs at the rim, French circus acrobats cried this exclamation right before a leap.
rows.n: It entered English pop culture via the caveman comic strip Alley Oop before finding a home in basketball.

rows.q: Only one person has won world championships on both two wheels and four. Name this British driver who took titles in 500cc bikes and Formula One.
rows.n: Surtees won four 500cc motorcycle world titles before taking the 1964 Formula One championship with Ferrari.

rows.q: Atlético Madrid earned their domestic nickname ‘Los Colchoneros’ because their red-and-white striped shirts originally mirrored the traditional fabric pattern used on what bedroom items?
rows.n: At the turn of the century, cheap mattress ticking in Spain was universally sold in red-and-white stripes.

rows.q: At the 2012 London Olympics, this 17-year-old high schooler won four gold medals for the U.S. in swimming, sweeping both the 100-meter and 200-meter backstroke events.
rows.n: She declined over $100,000 in endorsement money prior to London so she could swim for her high school.

rows.q: What British steeplechase includes notorious obstacles named Becher’s Brook, The Chair, and the Canal Turn?
rows.n: Run at Aintree near Liverpool, horses face four miles and two and a half furlongs over thirty spruce fences.

rows.q: Before home games at Goodison Park, an ‘Everton Mint Lady’ tosses sweets to the crowd, honoring a local confectionery shop that gave Everton which sugary club nickname?
rows.n: Mother Noblett’s Toffee Shop originally patented the black-and-white striped Everton Mint.

rows.q: Chicago originally won the bid for the 1904 Summer Games, but organizers relocated them to St. Louis to coincide with this massive world’s fair.
rows.n: The games were stretched over four and a half months and overshadowed by the fair’s exhibits.

rows.q: When the 12th Earl of Derby and Sir Charles Bunbury founded a classic horse race in 1780, they determined its name by doing this.
rows.n: Bunbury got a consolation prize: his horse, Diomed, won the inaugural race.

rows.q: Freestyle skiers choreographed spins and flips to music on snow in this theatrical discipline, an Olympic demonstration sport in 1988 and 1992.
rows.n: Officially named acroski, it died out after moguls and aerials gained full medal status.

rows.q: Dan Gurney started the victory tradition of spraying champagne at Le Mans in 1967, drenching team owner Carroll Shelby and this CEO of Ford.
rows.n: Gurney spontaneously shook the magnum of Moët after winning the 24 Hours of Le Mans in a Ford GT40.

rows.q: Which English club plays at Bramall Lane and takes their sharp, steel-themed nickname ‘The Blades’ from their city’s historic cutlery trade?
rows.n: Sheffield was renowned worldwide for centuries as England’s hub of steel production and cutlery.

rows.q: The last-place finisher in the Tour de France earns this French moniker, named for the red signal light once hung on the caboose of a train.
rows.n: In early Tours, riders fought to finish last because it brought lucrative post-race exhibition appearance fees.

rows.q: Juventus wears their famous black-and-white stripes thanks to an English player who arranged in 1903 to ship replacement kits from this Nottingham club, the world’s oldest league side.
rows.n: Notts County was founded in 1862, one year before the English Football Association was formed.

rows.q: Every spring, Paris-Roubaix finishes on an outdoor concrete velodrome where the champion receives a trophy consisting of what utilitarian object?
Boca Juniors fans are called ‘Xeneizes’ in honor of the Italian immigrants who founded the club in 1905, who hailed overwhelmingly from which major Mediterranean port city?
rows.n: ‘Xeneize’ is the Ligurian dialect word for Genoese; Genoa’s historic harbor is the Porto Antico.

rows.q: Famous for wrecking real-world friendships, the 1954 strategic board game Diplomacy was reportedly the favorite pastime of which realpolitik-practicing U.S. Secretary of State?
rows.n: Kissinger reportedly played ongoing correspondence games with diplomats while directing American foreign policy.

rows.q: Danish polymath Piet Hein invented a 3D packing puzzle of seven polycubes in 1933, naming it after the tranquilizing state-sponsored narcotic in what dystopian Aldous Huxley novel?
rows.n: The puzzle is the Soma cube; Hein conceived it while attending a quantum mechanics lecture by Heisenberg.

rows.q: Before rescuing Princess Peach, Mario’s objective in 1981’s Donkey Kong was saving this damsel in distress from a rooftop in New York City.
rows.n: Originally known simply as ‘Lady’ in Japan, she was later named after a Nintendo employee’s wife.

rows.q: The drawing screen of an Etch A Sketch gets its silver-gray coating from static electricity and an extremely fine powder of this lightweight metallic element.
rows.n: Two knobs control a stylus that scrapes lines through the powder on the inside of the glass.

rows.q: Behind the 25-card grid of Vlaada Chvatil’s Codenames sit field agents, innocent bystanders, and this single black card that triggers instant defeat.
rows.n: Tapping the Assassin immediately hands victory to the opposing team, regardless of the remaining score.

rows.q: Walt Disney envisioned EPCOT not as a theme park, but as a functioning futuristic city. In the acronym EPCOT, what does the letter C stand for?
rows.n: The full acronym stands for Experimental Prototype Community of Tomorrow.

rows.q: Flipping through a British phone book to find an English-sounding replacement for ‘Laura Cruz,’ Core Design settled on what adventurer surname?
rows.n: The developers found the name while looking for an address near their offices in Derby, England.

rows.q: Publishing giant Simon & Schuster launched in 1924 with just one title: a crossword compilation that came packaged with what attached writing utensil to help readers solve it?
rows.n: It became a runaway smash, selling over 100,000 copies in its first year and putting the firm on the map.

rows.q: A 1984 copyright lawsuit against Trivial Pursuit proved the game lifted questions from author Fred L. Worth because it copied his fake trap fact that this TV detective’s first name is Philip.
rows.n: The rumpled detective never had an official first name, though his badge once flashed ‘Frank.’

rows.q: P.T. Barnum drew crowds in 1842 with the Feejee Mermaid, which was actually the mummified torso of this mammal sewn onto a fish tail.
rows.n: Most surviving specimens were originally crafted by Japanese fishermen as religious charms.

rows.q: To avoid a lawsuit from a real-life heavyweight champ, Capcom USA swapped character names, giving the boxer this Tolkienesque moniker.
rows.n: In the Japanese version, the boxer is M. Bison, the claw fighter is Balrog, and the dictator is Vega.

rows.q: Marketed in retro comic books with illustrations of smiling aquatic humanoids with crowns, ‘Sea-Monkeys’ are actually a cryptobiotic variety of this tiny crustacean.
rows.n: Creator Harold von Braunhut also held the patent for X-Ray Goggles.

rows.q: Congressional hearings over graphic fatalities in 1992’s Mortal Kombat prompted the U.S. video game industry to form this self-regulatory board.
rows.n: Senators Joe Lieberman and Herb Kohl threatened government regulation if publishers did not label their content.

rows.q: In the 1981 arcade shooter Galaga, players can double their firepower by intentionally letting an alien boss capture their ship with this beam.
rows.n: Destroying the boss on a subsequent pass releases your trapped fighter to fly alongside your current ship.

rows.q: If a numismatist hoards currency, a devotee of phillumeny collects these small, combustible advertising items often picked up in hotel lobbies.
To keep grids challenging, standard American newspaper crossword guidelines mandate that every answer in the puzzle must have a length of at least how many letters?
rows.n: Two-letter words are barred because they leave too few intersecting options to create varied wordplay.

rows.q: When the original three-booklet boxed set of Dungeons & Dragons was published in 1974, it featured only three character classes: Magic-User, Fighting-Man, and this divine healer.
rows.n: The Thief class was not added until the Greyhawk supplement arrived a year later.

rows.q: Richard Tait and Whit Alexander created the party game Cranium in 1998, famously refusing traditional toy stores and instead launching sales inside which coffee chain?
rows.n: Cranium became the first board game sold in Starbucks, moving over 100,000 copies in its first holiday season.

rows.q: Banned by informal house rules in GoldenEye 007 multiplayer, this short Bond villain henchman was virtually impossible to hit with auto-aim.
Disney veteran Don Bluth provided full-motion cartoon animation for the 1983 arcade hit Dragon’s Lair, stored on what optical disc format?
rows.n: Arcade cabinets were notorious for breaking down because players forced the laser pickup to skip constantly.

rows.q: The medieval tile-laying game Carcassonne popularized the iconic wooden human-shaped playing pieces that gamer Alison Hansel dubbed with this portmanteau of “my people.”
rows.n: The term was coined in an online forum in 2000 and officially added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2015.

rows.q: Schoolteacher Eleanor Abbott invented the board game Candy Land in 1948 to entertain quarantined children while she herself was recovering from this epidemic viral disease.
rows.n: Because players didn’t need to read, children paralyzed in iron lungs could still play.

rows.q: An attic hidden inside Disneyland’s snowy Matterhorn mountain famously houses a miniature half-court for playing this sport.
Sony developed the original 1994 PlayStation as a standalone console only after a planned CD-ROM partnership bitterly collapsed with which rival?
rows.n: Nintendo publicly announced a partnership with Philips the morning after Sony unveiled their joint console project.

rows.q: id Software popularized 1993’s Doom by giving away its entire nine-level first episode through this try-before-you-buy distribution model.
rows.n: Players were encouraged to copy episode one freely, then call id Software to purchase episodes two and three.

rows.q: Universal Studios’ classic Jaws ride featured a 3-ton animatronic Great White shark nicknamed this, after Steven Spielberg’s lawyer.
rows.n: The friendly great white shark in Pixar’s Finding Nemo was named Bruce as an homage.

rows.q: Packed inside Sega’s 1999 Dreamcast was this modular hardware device, making it the first home console ready for online play out of the box.
rows.n: Players could browse the early web using Planetweb or play Phantasy Star Online over a standard telephone line.

rows.q: Millions of NES console bundles shipped with this two-tone plastic light gun peripheral, recolored neon orange in 1989 to satisfy toy laws.
rows.n: The gun functioned via an optical sensor detecting rapid black-and-white flashes drawn on a CRT screen.

rows.q: Twister was facing cancellation in 1966 until sales skyrocketed overnight after Johnny Carson played the game on The Tonight Show with this glamorous Hungarian-American actress.
rows.n: Milton Bradley was initially accused of selling ‘sex in a box’ before the segment aired.

rows.q: During the Vietnam War, U.S. soldiers frequently had metal Slinky toys shipped overseas to sling into high tree branches, using them as makeshift versions of this device.
rows.n: The coiled steel significantly boosted the range of portable field radios.

rows.q: Elizabeth Magie patented The Landlord’s Game in 1904 to illustrate the progressive economic theories of which American thinker, famous for advocating a single tax on land?
rows.n: Magie designed two rule sets: a cooperative mode where all created wealth, and a monopolist mode to crush opponents.

rows.q: Built in 1884 by British winter vacationers, the terrifying Cresta Run natural ice skeleton track operates in what posh Swiss Alpine resort?
rows.n: Riders on the Cresta Run still slide headfirst on traditional toboggans, reaching speeds over eighty miles per hour.

rows.q: At the dartboard, throwers must stay behind this toe line, whose name is traditionally pronounced to rhyme with ‘hockey.’
rows.n: Though rumored to come from ‘S. Hockey & Sons’ beer crates, Oxford traces it to an old word for a notch or groove.

rows.q: Widely used in novelty baseball cards and 3D postcards, what type of printing uses curved plastic ridges to produce shifting images?
rows.n: The grooved plastic sheet refracts light differently depending on the angle from which you view it.

rows.q: Standard English Scrabble assigns point values from 1 to 10, but only one consonant tile carries a face value of exactly five. Which letter is it?
rows.n: Q and Z are worth 10 points, J and X are worth eight, while F, H, V, W, and Y are all worth four.

rows.q: Before Ideal Toy Corporation rebranded it for export in 1980, Erno Rubik’s colorful 3D puzzle was sold in Hungary under what straightforward, two-word name?
rows.n: Ideal wanted a trademarkable name that sounded mysterious, ultimately naming it after the inventor.

rows.q: Longtime puzzle editor Will Shortz graduated from Indiana University in 1974 with an individualized major in this field, making him the only person known to hold a college degree in it.
rows.n: Shortz also earned a law degree from the University of Virginia, but skipped the bar to create puzzles.

rows.q: Before licensing the concept to Bluebird Toys in 1989, Chris Wiggs built the very first Polly Pocket playset for his daughter inside an empty container of this cosmetic item.
rows.n: He carved tiny wooden furniture and a small doll to fit inside the hinged shell.

rows.q: In speedcubing, what theological two-word name is given to the minimum number of moves needed to solve a Rubik’s Cube from any starting position, proven in 2010 to be exactly 20?
rows.n: Researchers used Google supercomputers to test all 43 quintillion starting configurations to prove it.

rows.q: To determine the starting letter for each round, players in the fast-paced category game Scattergories roll an oversized die with how many sides?
rows.n: The letters Q, U, V, X, Y, and Z are omitted from the 20-sided die so players are spared impossible rounds.

rows.q: Chess players dread this German term for a predicament where any legal move on the board weakens your position, but passing your turn is illegal.
rows.n: It translates literally as ‘move compulsion,’ first appearing in German chess literature in the 19th century.

rows.q: The world-conquest board game Risk was invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, a French filmmaker best remembered for this Oscar-winning 1956 short film about a loyal object.
rows.a: The Red Balloon (accept Le ballon rouge)
rows.n: His original French board game was titled La Conquête du Monde (The Conquest of the World).

rows.q: Knitters who have to unravel several rows to fix an error call the process by this amphibian-sounding verb, because you ‘rip it, rip it.’
rows.n: The pun on ‘ribbit’ has been standard crafting slang since at least the mid-20th century.

rows.q: Sega’s internal mascot contest featured an early sketch of Dr. Robotnik in pajamas, visually inspired by this mustachioed U.S. president.
rows.n: Designer Naoto Ohshima blended Roosevelt’s face with an egg shape to craft Sonic’s iconic nemesis.

rows.q: Borrowing its name from a Latin word meaning ‘by things,’ what term describes a crossword gimmick where solvers must cram multiple letters, a word, or a symbol into a single grid square?
rows.n: The Latin phrase is ‘non verbis sed rebus’—meaning ‘not by words, but by things.’

rows.q: Sherlock Holmes decodes a substitution cipher in a 1903 short story where mysterious messages scrawled on walls are drawn entirely as these human figures.
rows.n: In ‘The Adventure of the Dancing Men,’ little stick figures holding flags represent the ends of words.

rows.q: Scotland Yard pits a team of detectives against a concealed fugitive criminal who moves across London under what lettered codename?
rows.n: Mister X wears a visor cap during play so the detectives cannot read where his eyes wander on the board.

rows.q: Rare book collectors use this rust-colored animal term for the faint, reddish-brown stains that develop on aged paper over centuries.
rows.n: The blotches are typically triggered by fungal reactions with iron impurities in vintage rag paper.

rows.q: When French mathematician Édouard Lucas published the Tower of Hanoi puzzle in 1883, he invented a legend claiming that the universe would end when priests moved 64 disks in this Asian country.
rows.n: Lucas attributed the puzzle to the Temple of Kashi Vishwanath in the sacred city of Varanasi.

rows.q: Ephraim Hertzano invented Rummikub in the 1940s to circumvent a government ban on playing cards enacted by the Communist authorities of which Eastern European nation?
rows.n: Hertzano hand-carved his earliest tile sets out of salvaged plastic in his backyard workshop.

rows.q: Cirque du Soleil was co-founded in Quebec by this former fire-eater and stilt-walker, who later spent 35 million dollars to visit space.
rows.n: He spent twelve days aboard the International Space Station in 2009.

rows.q: Before Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson published Dungeons & Dragons in 1974, Gygax co-authored this 1971 medieval miniature wargame that first introduced fantasy combat rules.
rows.n: Chainmail featured a 14-page fantasy supplement detailing rules for wizards, giants, and breath weapons.

rows.q: The ubiquitous ‘HO scale’ in model railroading got its two-letter moniker because its 1:87 proportions make it exactly this relative size.
rows.n: O scale was already popular, so European manufacturers marketed the smaller trains as ‘Half-O’ in the 1930s.

rows.q: Vinyl collectors inspect this smooth, music-free inner ring next to the record label to find secret etched catalog codes and mastering engineer signatures.
rows.n: Legendary engineer George Peckham famously etched jokes and his signature ‘Porky Prime Cut’ in that space.

rows.q: Harland Sanders cut his chicken’s cooking time from thirty minutes to nine by modifying one of the first commercial models of this kitchen appliance to fry with steam.
rows.n: He retrofitted commercial cookers with pressure valves, despite friends warning him the machines might explode.

rows.q: Years before buying the team in 1992, Little Caesars founder Mike Ilitch played professional minor-league baseball for this American League franchise.
rows.n: A knee injury ended his playing career in 1955; he and his wife Marian founded Little Caesars four years later.

rows.q: French tarragon has the Latin species name dracunculus, meaning “little” what, after a medieval belief that the serpent-like root cured venomous bites?
rows.n: The common English name tarragon also derives via Arabic tarkhun from the Greek word for dragon, drakon.

rows.q: Pickled in vinegar or brine to garnish lox and chicken piccata, culinary capers are not seeds or fruits, but which unopened reproductive part of the bush?
rows.n: If left unharvested, the buds blossom into delicate white flowers that later form larger caperberries.

rows.q: The Jerusalem artichoke is neither an artichoke nor from the Middle East, but rather the edible tuber of this tall, yellow-flowered plant.
rows.n: ‘Jerusalem’ is an English corruption of girasole, the Italian word for sunflower.

rows.q: Neither sweet nor a baked good, culinary sweetbreads are organ meats taken from either the pancreas or this immune gland in the chest.
rows.n: Sweetbreads from calves and lambs are prized by chefs for their mild flavor and tender, velvety texture.

rows.q: Factory machines in 1928 failed to roll chocolate-coated caramel into spheres, inspiring this candy’s self-deprecating name.
rows.n: The manufacturer embraced the defect, concluding that naming them duds was cheaper than retooling the machines.

rows.q: Before inventing his peanut butter cups in his basement in 1928, H.B. Reese worked as a dairy farmer for this rival chocolate titan.
rows.n: Reese used Hershey’s chocolate to coat his cups, a partnership that ended when Hershey bought the Reese company in 1963.

rows.q: Before opening the first Wendy’s, Dave Thomas made his fortune turning around four struggling Columbus franchises of this rival fast-food brand.
rows.n: He sold his 45 percent stake back to Harland Sanders for over a million dollars, using the proceeds to start Wendy’s.

rows.q: Alfredo di Lelio’s rich pasta took off after Mary Pickford and this swashbuckling star of The Mark of Zorro ate it on their 1920 Roman honeymoon.
rows.n: The Hollywood couple showed their gratitude by presenting Alfredo with an engraved solid gold fork and spoon.

rows.q: Created in 1982 by an Italian miller looking to rival the French baguette, this airy, flour-dusted loaf was named after the Italian word for ‘slipper.’
rows.n: Arnaldo Cavallari patented the recipe as ciabatta polesana to protect Italian bakers from foreign bread.

rows.q: Antoine’s in New Orleans created Oysters Rockefeller in 1889 as a domestic stand-in for this baked French appetizer, which was facing a shipping shortage.
rows.n: Jules Alciatore named the dish for John D. Rockefeller because the herb-butter sauce was incomparably rich.

rows.q: To dispel rumors that his nickel frankfurters were made from low-grade meat, Nathan Handwerker paid men to eat at his Coney Island stand dressed as these professionals.
rows.n: He gave them free hot dogs to stand outside in white medical coats and stethoscopes to reassure skeptical patrons.

rows.q: Southern blue-collar workers spent decades making a mid-morning ritual of pairing a marshmallow MoonPie with this budget-friendly soda brand.
rows.n: The combo was celebrated in country music because a five-cent pie and a ten-ounce bottle offered maximum calories.

rows.q: Traditionally crimped along its curved edge so miners could hold it with dirty hands, this savory turnover holds protected status in England.
rows.n: Miners believed leaving the dirty crust behind also appeased the knockers, mischievous mine spirits.

rows.q: While its name promises game meat, the British tavern staple Welsh rabbit consists of a savory melted cheese sauce poured over this food.
rows.n: 18th-century English diners used ‘Welsh’ as a derisive term for cheap substitutes, like cheese for game.

rows.q: Legend says gluttonous clergymen choked on the twisted pasta known as strozzapreti, meaning stranglers of what holy men?
rows.n: The name reflects historical anti-clerical sentiment in Romagna, where priests collected taxes in food.

rows.q: Essential to Worcestershire sauce and pad thai for fruity sourness, which sticky pod takes its name from Arabic for “Indian date”?
rows.n: From the Arabic tamr hindi; despite the name, the tamarind tree is indigenous to tropical Africa.

rows.q: To determine whose name got top billing when they merged their ice cream parlors in 1953, Burt Baskin and Irv Robbins relied on this classic contest of chance.
rows.n: Baskin won the flip, putting his name first; the famous 31-flavor concept was devised soon after by an ad agency.

rows.q: The upscale tenderloin cut known as Chateaubriand was created by a private chef for a French diplomat who helped pioneer this emotive literary movement.
rows.n: Author Francois-Rene de Chateaubriand is considered a founding father of French Romantic literature.

rows.q: Debuting from the Fox-Cross Candy Company in 1925, this vanilla nougat candy bar took its rhythmically catchy name from a trendy dance craze.
rows.n: The bar is often frozen before eating so consumers can crack it into bite-sized shards with a quick tap.

rows.q: Legend says the French upside-down pastry Tarte Tatin was created by accident when an innkeeper overcooked this fruit in butter and sugar.
rows.n: Stéphanie Tatin slapped pastry over the pan to salvage burning caramelized apples at her Loire Valley hotel.

rows.q: For decades, Thurl Ravenscroft gave a booming voice to Tony the Tiger, but holiday listeners know his deep bass best from this Dr. Seuss song.
rows.a: You’re a Mean One, Mr. Grinch
rows.n: Because he was uncredited on the 1966 TV special, Dr. Seuss took out a full-page trade ad to give Ravenscroft credit.

rows.q: The 1893 debut recipe for the Waldorf salad called for only apples, celery, and mayonnaise; this crunchy ingredient now considered essential was added later.
rows.n: Oscar Tschirky, the maitre d’ who concocted it, omitted nuts entirely in his 1896 cookbook The Cook Book.

rows.q: Pink peppercorns are not true pepper. People with an allergy to which curved, kidney-shaped tree nut are warned against eating them?
rows.n: Both belong to the family Anacardiaceae, which also includes mangos, sumac, and poison ivy.

rows.q: Opening their first drive-in in 1948, Harry and Esther Snyder sped up In-N-Out’s service by introducing an ordering system centered on this two-way audio device.
rows.n: Harry Snyder built the electronic speaker box in his garage, eliminating the need for carhops to walk up to cars.

rows.q: Prized for a high melting point that lets you fry or grill it without turning into a puddle, halloumi cheese originated on which island?
rows.n: Traditional Cypriot halloumi is made from sheep and goat milk, often layered with fresh mint.

rows.q: In Greek mythology, Daphne escaped Apollo by transforming into which evergreen culinary tree, whose leaves now season soups, stocks, and stews?
rows.n: Apollo wore a crown of its leaves in grief, establishing the laurel wreath as the ancient symbol of triumph.

rows.q: The spongy flatbread known as injera serves as both plate and utensil in Ethiopian dining. What tiny ancient grain makes up the flour?
rows.n: Teff is one of the smallest grains on Earth; about 150 grains weigh as much as a single wheat kernel.

rows.q: Legend says Chicken Marengo was cooked on the battlefield using tomatoes, mushrooms, and crayfish after French forces beat the Austrians in this modern country.
rows.n: Marengo is located in Piedmont, northwestern Italy; the June 1800 battle secured Napoleon’s political power.

rows.q: A Minnesota clinician accidentally invented this breakfast cereal in 1921 when a batch of wheat bran gruel spilled onto a hot stove.
rows.n: Originally marketed as Washburn’s Gold Medal Whole Wheat Flakes, the crunchy accident was rebranded in 1925.

rows.q: Harvested from wild acacia trees across the Sahel, what hardened natural tree sap serves as an emulsifier in gummy candies, royal icing, and sodas?
rows.n: Sudan produces the vast majority of the world’s supply, largely from Acacia senegal trees.

rows.q: Most cheap ground “cinnamon” sold in North American groceries is not true Ceylon cinnamon, but which coarser, pungent bark from a related Chinese tree?
rows.n: Cassia has higher levels of coumarin, a blood-thinning compound that led European regulators to limit its daily intake.

rows.q: During the freezing 1950 Battle of Chosin Reservoir, trapped U.S. Marines were saved when supply drops accidentally parachuted in this candy.
rows.n: The radio operator used ‘Tootsie Rolls’ as a code word for 60mm mortar shells, but the base depot took it literally.

rows.q: Billed as “the eighth wonder of the world” at the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair, what breakfast staple was produced by botanist Alexander Anderson firing heated grain out of iron cannons?
rows.n: Anderson sold the explosive manufacturing process to Quaker Oats, who marketed it as “food shot from guns.”

rows.q: General Tso’s chicken was invented in Taiwan by a chef who named it for a 19th-century military hero from this spicy, garlic-loving Chinese province.
rows.n: Chef Peng Chang-kuei was born in Hunan, but the sweet batter-fried version was popularized in New York City.

rows.q: Providing Szechuan pepper with its tingling numbing buzz, the prickly ash shrub does not produce true peppercorns, but belongs to which fragrant fruit family?
rows.n: The tingling sensation comes from hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, which excites light-touch mechanical receptors on the tongue.

rows.q: Real wasabi is notoriously fussy to prep: sushi chefs traditionally grate the rhizome on an oroshiki paddle surfaced with the rough skin of which predator?
Harmon Dobson gave early Whataburger locations towering A-frame roofs with bright orange stripes so they could be spotted easily by people in this profession.
rows.n: Dobson was an avid private aviator and wanted his roadside stands to catch the attention of planes flying overhead.

rows.q: Cheddar cheese is naturally pale, but English and American dairies have long dyed it bright orange using the seed pulp of which tropical American shrub?
rows.n: The coloring agent was initially used to trick consumers into thinking cheese came from high-carotene summer milk.

rows.q: Before shutting down in 1948 to pioneer their 15-cent burger assembly line, the McDonald brothers ran a drive-in specializing in this slow-cooked style of meat.
rows.n: McDonald’s Bar-B-Q had a 25-item carhop menu before the brothers realized burgers accounted for 80 percent of sales.

rows.q: It looks almost identical to grains of white rice, but the Italian word orzo literally translates to what other cereal grain?
rows.n: In Italy, this rice-shaped pasta is often marketed as risoni, which translates to large rice.

rows.q: Delmonico’s created a rich cream-and-sherry seafood dish for sea captain Ben Wenberg, but after a brawl with the owner, it was renamed with this slight anagram.
Ask for Smarties in Canada and you will receive candy-coated chocolate; the tart tablet candies sold as Smarties in the U.S. are called this.
rows.n: The candy was renamed Rockets in Canada to avoid a trademark battle with the British chocolate confection.

rows.q: Until Mars changed its branding in 1990 to match the US market, the candy bar known globally as Snickers was sold in the UK under what name?
rows.n: Mars briefly revived the retro packaging for a limited edition in the UK in 2019.

rows.q: Cap’n Crunch wears a blue naval jacket sporting only three gold stripes on each sleeve, which officially gives him this lower naval rank.
rows.n: In 2013, the U.S. Navy officially joked on Twitter that Cap’n Crunch was an unauthorized imposter.

rows.q: Troy Smith rebranded his drive-in as Sonic in 1959, ditching this original, dapper headwear name after discovering it was already trademarked.
rows.n: Smith discovered the name Top Hat was already trademarked, rebranding as Sonic in 1959 to match his speaker system.

rows.q: Chinese five-spice relies on star anise, which faced global shortages in the 2000s when its shikimic acid was hoarded to make which antiviral flu drug?
rows.n: Swiss drugmaker Roche required massive harvests of Chinese star anise during the 2005 avian flu epidemic.

rows.q: Eight months into running the pizzeria that became Domino’s, James Monaghan traded his 50 percent share to his brother Tom in exchange for this vehicle.
rows.n: James needed a dependable ride to deliver mail; Tom’s remaining half eventually made him a multi-billionaire.

rows.q: Commercial pancake syrups often mimic maple flavor using sotolon, an aromatic compound extracted not from trees, but from the seeds of which curry spice?
rows.n: A mysterious maple aroma that baffled New York City residents in 2005 was traced to a fenugreek-processing factory in NJ.

rows.q: Contrary to an urban legend about roast beef, the initials in Arby’s actually stand for founders Leroy and Forrest, known collectively by what two-word phrase?
rows.n: They originally wanted to name the chain Big Tex, but an Akron business already held the rights.

rows.q: When 17-year-old Fred DeLuca needed money to launch what became Subway, he got a $1,000 loan from Peter Buck, a family friend whose day job was in this branch of science.
rows.n: Dr. Buck held a PhD in physics and spent decades working on nuclear power plants for General Electric.

rows.q: Invented in 1927 by Harry Baker, what light, airy cake gets its fluffy texture by folding whipped egg whites into an oil-based batter rather than butter?
rows.n: Baker guarded his secret recipe for twenty years before selling it to General Mills in 1947.

rows.q: Auguste Escoffier created Peach Melba at the Savoy Hotel in honor of soprano Nellie Melba, presenting it under an ice swan inspired by this Wagner opera.
rows.n: In Lohengrin, the mysterious hero arrives in a boat drawn by a swan; Escoffier was an avid opera buff.

rows.q: Two decades before launching Chick-fil-A in 1967, founder S. Truett Cathy perfected his fried chicken recipe at a diner named for what mythical creature?
rows.n: The Dwarf Grill in Hapeville, Georgia had only ten counter stools and four tables, inspiring the diminutive name.

rows.q: According to French legend, a distracted shepherd accidentally invented Roquefort cheese when he left his lunch in a cave while pursuing one of these.
rows.n: Months later, the cave mold Penicillium roqueforti had turned his forgotten sheep’s curds into blue cheese.

rows.q: Though green cardamom is native to India’s Malabar Coast, which Central American nation produces over half of the world’s commercial supply today?
rows.n: German plantation owner Oscar Majus Kloeffer introduced the spice to the cloud forests of Alta Verapaz in 1914.
