rows.q: Bourbon vanilla is named for the former royal name of which Indian Ocean island, where enslaved 12-year-old Edmond Albius invented hand-pollination in 1841?
rows.n: Albius’s bamboo-stick pollination method transformed vanilla from a rare Mexican vine into a global commercial crop.

rows.q: Alfredo sauce famously coats this flat, thick noodle whose Italian name translates directly into English as little what?
rows.n: Restaurateur Alfredo di Lelio invented the dish in 1908 to coax his wife into eating after childbirth.

rows.q: Formulated in Caltanissetta in 1868 from a recipe gifted by Capuchin monks, the rich amaro Averna is the signature bitter herbal liqueur of what large Mediterranean island?
rows.n: Salvatore Averna’s son Paolo later turned the cloistered monastic recipe into an internationally known digestif.

rows.q: Traditionally prescribed for a classic Manhattan cocktail, this spicy whiskey must be distilled from a mash of at least 51 percent of its namesake grain.
rows.n: Bourbon became the common substitute when Pennsylvania and Maryland rye distilleries shut down in Prohibition.

rows.q: Equal parts gin, maraschino, and lime juice, the revived Prohibition-era Last Word owes its vivid green color and herbal bite to this monastic liqueur.
rows.n: Only two Carthusian monks at a time know the complete recipe of 130 botanical ingredients.

rows.q: Named on labels throughout the American South, what two-word whiskey brewing method recycles spent mash from an earlier run to control acidity?
rows.n: Chemist and physician James C. Crow refined the technique in Kentucky during the 1830s.

rows.q: In 18th-century London, what adjective meaning strong or robust originally denoted a fortified version of porter before becoming a dark style of its own?
rows.n: The term originally applied to any strong beer, including pale ales, before attaching firmly to dark roasts.

rows.q: British sailors tested navy strength gin by dousing it onto this shipboard supply, knowing that at 57 percent ABV it would still ignite if soaked.
rows.n: If the spirit was watered down below 114 proof, the gunpowder would fail to spark.

rows.q: Until a synthetic dye took over in 2006, Campari’s unmistakable crimson hue came from carmine, a natural coloring harvested by crushing thousands of these tiny scaly insects.
rows.n: Cochineal bugs feed on prickly pear cacti, mostly farmed for dye in Peru and the Canary Islands.

rows.q: Observing Dutch soldiers swigging genever before charging into combat during the Thirty Years’ War, English troops coined what two-word idiom?
Mix a Dark ‘n Stormy with any dark rum other than this Bermuda-based brand and you risk a trademark infringement lawsuit from their legal team.
In 19th-century San Francisco, brewers who fermented lager yeast at warm temperatures without refrigeration created what trademarked style of ‘beer’?
rows.n: Anchor Brewing trademarked the term in 1981, forcing rivals to label their versions California Common.

rows.q: Ngiam Tong Boon concocted the Singapore Sling at this colonial-era luxury hotel, giving it a pink hue so women could drink alcohol in public discreetly.
rows.n: Guests drinking Slings at the Long Bar are still encouraged to throw their peanut shells on the floor.

rows.q: Regardless of the country where it is distilled, any bottle bearing the label “single malt” must be made using 100 percent of which cereal grain?
rows.n: The word “single” in the name refers to a single distillery, not a single barrel or harvest.

rows.q: Adding hops during or after fermentation rather than in the boil lets craft brewers extract aromatic oils without added bitterness, a process known as what?
rows.n: The term originated in British cask brewing, where dried hop cones were tossed straight into the cask.

rows.q: A proper 1944 Trader Vic’s Mai Tai gets its rich sweetness from orgeat, a syrup traditionally flavored with orange flower water and this ground nut.
rows.n: Tahitian guest Carrie Guild allegedly named the drink after exclaiming ‘Maita’i roa ae,’ or ‘out of this world.’

rows.q: Though it tastes strongly of marzipan, traditional amaretto gets its flavor not from almonds, but from the kernels inside the pits of this orange orchard stone fruit.
rows.n: The pits contain benzaldehyde, which gives both apricots and bitter almonds their shared marzipan aroma.

rows.q: Street vendors across Mexico ferment the discarded rinds of this spiky tropical fruit with piloncillo and cinnamon to make the fizzy brew tepache.
rows.n: Naturally present yeasts on the pineapple peel kickstart fermentation within just two to three days.

rows.q: The French aperitif Kir combines white wine with crème de cassis. It was popularized by Félix Kir, a priest and Resistance hero who served as mayor of this mustard-loving city.
rows.n: Kir originally used the local Aligoté white wine, which was notoriously acidic before the cassis sweetened it.

rows.q: First appearing in print in the 1930s, what term originally referred to festive non-alcoholic party drinks meant to resemble highballs or martinis?
rows.n: The Merriam-Webster dictionary traces the earliest known printed usage back to an issue of The Coco-Tree in 1936.

rows.q: Tujague’s in New Orleans claims the 1918 creation of this bright green dessert cocktail, named after an insect its minty hue supposedly resembles.
rows.n: Philip Guichet originally concocted the crème de menthe and cacao drink for a New York cocktail contest.

rows.q: Packaged in a glass bottle shaped like a monk with folded hands and a rope belt, Frangelico gets its rich, buttery sweetness from this specific woodland nut.
rows.n: The liqueur is made in Piedmont, a region renowned for its prized Tonda Gentile hazelnuts.

rows.q: When the Irish Free State adopted Brian Boru’s harp for its coat of arms in 1922, it had to turn the instrument right because what brewery had trademarked the left-facing one?
rows.n: Guinness registered the emblem in 1876, giving it legal priority over the government.

rows.q: Luxardo Maraschino liqueur is distilled from sour cherries in Padua today, but the distillery was founded in 1821 in Zadar, a historic port city in what modern Adriatic country?
rows.n: The Luxardo family fled Zadar for Italy after World War II when their original distillery was destroyed.

rows.q: What reverent two-word phrase do distillers use for the percentage of liquor lost to natural evaporation while aging in porous wooden barrels?
rows.n: The liquid that permanently soaks into the wood pores of the barrel is called the devil’s cut.

rows.q: Many white rums are aged in oak for years, then stripped of their amber hue prior to bottling by filtering through what porous black substance?
rows.n: Facundo Bacardi developed charcoal filtration in 19th-century Cuba to produce a lighter spirit.

rows.q: Scotch distillers routinely recycle casks, but American law strictly mandates that bourbon must mature in charred oak containers that are brand what?
rows.n: Those once-used bourbon barrels are shipped to Scotland and the Caribbean for aging other spirits.

rows.q: Produced in Benevento, an Italian town long branded in folklore as a gathering place for sorceresses, the herbal yellow liqueur Strega translates into English as what person?
rows.n: Its bright yellow hue comes from saffron, one of about 70 botanical ingredients in the secretive recipe.

rows.q: When James Bond invents the Vesper in Casino Royale, he calls for gin, vodka, and half a measure of this aromatized aperitif wine, later reformulated.
rows.n: Modern cocktail historians suggest using Cocchi Americano to replicate the original quinine-heavy kick.

rows.q: Designed to guarantee purity against fake or adulterated liquor, the 1897 Bottled-in-Bond Act required whiskey to be bottled at what exact proof?
rows.n: It also requires the whiskey to age for at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse.

rows.q: Winemakers crafting Sauternes or Tokaji welcome Botrytis cinerea, a beneficial grey fungus better known by this aristocratic two-word moniker.
rows.n: The fungus shrivels grapes, evaporating water while concentrating natural sugars and acids without souring them.

rows.q: For decades, bars served the pre-Prohibition Aviation cocktail without its sky-blue tint because this floral liqueur was missing from American shelves.
rows.n: The Austrian brand Rothman & Winter helped revive the ingredient for U.S. bars in 2007.

rows.q: In 1883, research director Emil Hansen isolated the first pure culture of lager yeast at the laboratory of this flagship Danish brewery.
rows.n: Rather than patenting pure lager yeast, Carlsberg shared samples freely with rival brewers worldwide.

rows.q: Geneticists surprised winemakers in 1996 by proving Cabernet Sauvignon is the natural hybrid child of Sauvignon Blanc and this other red parent grape.
rows.n: The spontaneous cross likely occurred in a southwestern French vineyard sometime in the 17th century.

rows.q: To legally qualify as Tennessee whiskey, unaged spirit must undergo the Lincoln County Process by dripping through charcoal made from what tree?
rows.n: Benjamin Prichard’s is the only Tennessee whiskey exempt from this rule by grandfather clause.

rows.q: Bottles of Chianti Classico carry the symbol of this farm animal, tracing back to a medieval border race with rival Siena won by an early wake-up.
rows.n: Legend says Florence starved their black rooster so it crowed early, giving their horseman a huge head start.

rows.q: Celebrated for its dark, heavy profile and distilled along a namesake river, Demerara rum is legally tied to what South American nation?
rows.n: Demerara Distillers operates the last remaining original wooden pot stills on earth.

rows.q: Named for the excommunicated guerrilla general whose volunteers conquered Sicily, this classic Italian cocktail combines Campari with fresh orange juice.
rows.n: The crimson Campari represents Garibaldi’s famous Redshirts, while the orange juice represents Sicily.

rows.q: Hailing from Philadelphia’s Bellevue-Stratford hotel, the Clover Club cocktail gets its rosy blush and tart flavor not from grenadine, but this berry.
rows.n: The drink took its name from a regular gathering of Philadelphia lawyers, writers, and bankers.

rows.q: Derived from a southern German mispronunciation of the town of Einbeck, what rich malty lager translates literally to ‘billy goat’ and often shows one on its label?
rows.n: Variations include Doppelbock, Maibock, and Eisbock, all keeping the goat iconography alive.

rows.q: Brewed in early spring and cellared over summer before German brewing laws took effect, what calendar-named style is the traditional beer of Oktoberfest?
rows.n: Bavarian laws in 1553 forbade brewing between April and September to prevent summer spoilage.

rows.q: Ancient Greeks coated clay amphorae with Aleppo pine resin to preserve wine, inspiring what pungent, resinous white wine style still made today?
rows.n: Retsina holds traditional appellation status in Greece and is typically made from Savatiano and Roditis grapes.

rows.q: Duke Philip the Bold banned this grape in 1395 as vile and disloyal to Pinot Noir, banishing it south to the region of Beaujolais.
rows.n: Philip wanted lower-yielding Pinot Noir to dominate Burgundy, but Gamay found its ideal granite soil in Beaujolais.

rows.q: Syrup and sherbet share an Arabic root with this colonial fruit-and-vinegar cordial, often added to soda or rum.
rows.n: Before modern refrigeration, vinegar kept fresh summer fruit acidity preserved through winter.

rows.q: Harry Craddock popularized a famous hangover cure combining gin, Cointreau, and Lillet Blanc in 1930 under the name ‘Corpse’ what ‘#2’?
rows.n: Craddock famously warned in The Savoy Cocktail Book that four taken in swift succession would un-revive the corpse.

rows.q: Prized for its complex semi-oxidized leaves, the name of this traditional Chinese tea translates literally into English as “black dragon.”
rows.n: Legend holds a tea harvester fled when a harmless black snake slithered onto his sun-drying leaves.

rows.q: Reviving an ancient Italian category of fragrant rosolio liqueurs, Italicus is flavored with chamomile, gentian, and the essential oil of this Calabrian citrus fruit.
rows.n: Bergamot is also the distinctive citrus oil used to flavor Earl Grey tea.

rows.q: Alfonso Bialetti based his iconic octagonal Moka pot on an early domestic appliance that pumped boiling soapy water up a tube to clean these.
rows.n: Watching his wife operate a laundry boiler inspired the rising-steam design for brewing espresso.

rows.q: Bavarian brewing lore says an apprentice left barrels out in freezing weather, accidentally discovering this potent style by skimming off the frozen water.
rows.n: Because alcohol freezes at a lower temperature than water, removing the ice concentrates both ABV and flavor.

rows.q: While most vintage sours lean on gin or rum, the 1922 bullfighting-inspired Blood and Sand uniquely takes this smoky, malted spirit as its base.
rows.n: Named after the silent film with Rudolph Valentino, it balances cherry liqueur, sweet vermouth, and orange.

rows.q: American producers cannot legally print the word “straight” on a bottle of bourbon or rye unless the spirit has aged in oak for at least how long?
rows.n: If straight whiskey is aged for less than four years, the label must state its exact age.

rows.q: Established in 2007 to certify beer sommeliers, this four-tiered hospitality program takes its name from an Italian word for a knowledgeable tour guide.
rows.n: The Italian term ultimately honors the loquacious Roman orator Marcus Tullius Cicero.

rows.q: Munich’s Spaten brewery introduced this crisp, golden lager in 1894 to rival Czech pilsners, naming it from the German word for ‘light’ or ‘bright.’
rows.n: Traditional Munich drinkers initially resisted the pale newcomer, preferring their dark Dunkels.

rows.q: Combining dessert and a caffeine hit, the Italian name of this espresso-poured-over-gelato treat translates literally into English as what?
rows.n: Vanilla or fiordilatte gelato is traditional, hot espresso melting it into a creamy swirl.

rows.q: Before yeast is pitched to kick off fermentation, the warm, sugary liquid drained from the grain mash is known by what four-letter brewing term?
In 1954, the mayor of this famed Rhône wine village drummed up press by passing a local ordinance banning flying saucers from its vineyards.
rows.n: The quirky law is still on the books and specifies extraterrestrial crafts will be impounded immediately.

rows.q: It strengthens the glass and gives a server a thumb-rest: what is the four-letter term for the concave dimple at the bottom of a wine bottle?
rows.n: In traditional glassblowing, the punt mark was left where the pontil rod broke off from the cooling glass.

rows.q: By legal statute, any spirit labeled as Irish whiskey must be aged in wooden casks on the island of Ireland for a minimum of how many years?
rows.n: Scotch whisky operates under an identical three-year legal minimum for cask aging.

rows.q: In the final stave of A Christmas Carol, a reformed Scrooge promises to help Bob Cratchit over a bowl of this hot, port-and-roasted-orange punch.
rows.n: Victorian punches were named for church ranks, with the Smoking Bishop outranking the simpler Smoking Beadle.

rows.q: A favorite of Pablo Picasso, who featured its bottle in a 1912 collage, the French aperitif Suze gets its earthy bite and bright yellow color from the roots of this alpine flower.
rows.n: The yellow gentian plant takes up to ten years to mature before its taproots can be harvested.

rows.q: Royal Navy sailors dubbed their diluted rum “grog” after the foul-weather grogram coat favored by this vice admiral who ordered the mix in 1740.
rows.n: Vernon added citrus juice to fight scurvy, accidentally inventing one of the first naval cocktails.

rows.q: For a one-penny admission, Londoners could buy a dish of brew and read the papers at 17th-century coffeehouses, earning them this collegiate nickname.
rows.n: Both Lloyd’s of London and the London Stock Exchange began as informal discussions in these coffeehouses.

rows.q: French for on the dregs, this label phrase indicates a wine like Muscadet or Champagne was aged in prolonged contact with dead yeast sediment.
rows.n: Yeast autolysis imparts a rounder, creamier texture and complex aromas of fresh brioche and toast.

rows.q: Essential in tropical tiki cocktails, the Jamaican liqueur historically known as pimento dram is flavored not by fiery peppers, but by the dried berries of this tree spice.
rows.n: Spanish explorers confused the dried berries with peppercorns, which led to the name pimienta.

rows.q: Afternoon tea became an aristocratic British ritual in the 1840s thanks to Anna Maria Russell, who held this ducal title and needed a late snack.
rows.n: Dinner was creeping past eight in the evening, leaving an unbearable gap after the midday meal.

rows.q: In 1996, the French government granted its prestigious Appellation d’Origine Contrôlée to sugarcane juice rum produced on what Caribbean island?
rows.n: It remains the only rum anywhere in the world to hold an official French AOC designation.

rows.q: Abraham Perold created South Africa’s signature Pinotage grape in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with this variety, then known locally as Hermitage.
rows.n: Perold planted four experimental seeds in his garden and forgot them until a cleanup crew nearly dug them up.

rows.q: Holding exactly nine imperial gallons—or a quarter of a standard UK barrel—what is the traditional wooden or stainless steel cask used for British real ale?
rows.n: Its name derives from the Middle Dutch ‘vierdekijn’, meaning ‘little fourth’.

rows.q: Winter comfort aside, the word “toddy” originally entered English from Hindi to describe a fermented alcoholic drink drawn from the sap of this tree.
rows.n: British colonists adapted the term for warm mixtures of hot water, spirits, sugar, and spices.

rows.q: Most coffee cherries contain two flat-faced seeds, but about five percent develop a single, rounded bean known by this garden-vegetable name.
rows.n: Roasters sort them out to roast alone, as their spherical shape rolls and heats more evenly in the drum.

rows.q: Holding nine liters, or the equivalent of a full 12-bottle case, this oversized Champagne bottle format takes its name from an ancient Assyrian king.
rows.n: Five Assyrian kings bore the name Shalmaneser; Salmanazar V laid siege to Samaria in the 8th century BCE.

rows.q: Despite its name, British sloe gin is actually a liqueur made by infusing astringent sloe berries, which grow wild on this thorny, white-flowered hedgerow shrub.
rows.n: Sloe berries are practically unpalatable raw due to their intense astringency until after the first autumn frost.

rows.q: Frustrated by bitter grounds and messy brass sieves in 1908, German housewife Melitta Bentz invented the paper coffee filter using this page torn from her son’s notebook.
rows.n: She punctured holes into a brass pot with a nail and set the absorbent sheet inside.

rows.q: In the early 1900s, Savoy head bartender Ada Coleman spiced up sweet vermouth and gin to create the Hanky Panky by adding a dash of this bitter Italian amaro.
Nazi Germany’s feared Gestapo got its name from an abbreviation of Geheime Staatspolizei, created in 1933 by this future Luftwaffe commander.
rows.n: Göring founded the Prussian political police unit before handing control to Heinrich Himmler in 1934.

rows.q: You don’t need to be in the middle of a storm to feel nausea, but the condition takes its name from the Greek word for this mode of transit.
rows.n: From nausia, meaning seasickness, directly derived from naus, the Greek word for ship.

rows.q: Ancient Greek skywatchers noticed five celestial bodies shifting against the background of fixed stars, naming them planets after this type of traveler.
rows.n: The Greek phrase asteres planetai literally translated to ‘wandering stars.’

rows.q: Gladiators clashed in an arena, a venue named not for combat but for this gritty substance spread across the floor to absorb blood.
rows.n: Harena was the Latin word for sand, which effectively soaked up spilled blood and sweat in Roman venues.

rows.q: Elizabethan doctors blamed a fit of melancholy on an excess of black what, one of the four humors of classical medicine?
rows.n: Melas means ‘black’ and chole means ‘bile.’ The other three humors were blood, phlegm, and yellow bile.

rows.q: In the 1840s, British frontier soldiers in the Punjab dyed their white tunics with river mud, adopting this color named after the Urdu for “dust.”
rows.n: From Persian “khak,” meaning dust or earth. Sir Harry Lumsden introduced the color for camouflage.

rows.q: Before it became a byword for chaotic noise, bedlam was the slang name Londoners used for the Hospital of St. Mary of this biblical town.
rows.n: Founded in 1247 as a priory, it later became infamous as Bethlem Royal psychiatric hospital.

rows.q: Revellers cut loose at carnival right before the solemn fast of Lent, fitting since its Latin roots translate to bidding farewell to what food?
rows.n: Likely from carne vale, ‘farewell to meat,’ since meat was forbidden during the 40 days of Lenten fasting.

rows.q: The digital icon term “emoji” sounds like “emoticon,” but its Japanese coiner combined the character for “letter” with the character for what?
rows.n: “E” means picture and “moji” means character. The English resemblance to “emotion” is pure chance.

rows.q: Old Norse sagas described warriors fighting in an uncontrollable frenzy as “berserk,” a compound word meaning a man wearing the pelt of what beast?
rows.n: From “ber” (bear) and “serkr” (shirt). Warriors devoted to Odin were believed to channel animal fury.

rows.q: City transit took a leap in 1820s France with horse-drawn carriages named after this Latin dative plural word meaning for all, which we clip into a short vehicle name.
rows.n: A carriage stand in Nantes was near a hatter named Omnes, who advertised with the pun Omnes Omnibus.

rows.q: Sixteenth-century Europeans named the tulip for its visual resemblance to “tülbent,” a Turkish term for what article of clothing?
rows.n: Ottoman subjects tucked flowers into their turbans, leading European travelers to confuse the two.

rows.q: Following a bitter 1903 party vote in London, Lenin named his hardline faction the Bolsheviks after the Russian word for what political outcome?
rows.n: “Bolshinstvo” means majority. Julius Martov’s rival faction took the name Mensheviks, meaning minority.

rows.q: Linguists split the word helicopter not into heli and copter, but helico and pter, the latter being Greek for which body part?
rows.n: Helico- means spiral and pteron means wing, the same root found in pterodactyl.

rows.q: Invented as a wipe-clean coating for fabric, this clear food wrap took its name from cellulose and a Greek root meaning to appear.
rows.n: Brandenberger was originally trying to make a stain-resistant coating for tablecloths.

rows.q: Gordon Gould coined the word laser in his 1957 notebook by swapping the first letter of this 1953 device that amplified microwaves instead of light.
rows.n: Charles Townes built the first maser at Columbia University, winning the 1964 Nobel Prize in Physics.

rows.q: If you are ostracized, you are cast out, but someone who is cantered rides on horseback at an easy pace named for pilgrims riding to this English cathedral city.
rows.n: It is an abbreviation of ‘the Canterbury gallop,’ the comfortable pace of Chaucerian travelers.

rows.q: In medieval Arabic medicine, the mathematical term “algebra” was far from abstract: “al-jabr” referred to the surgical reset of broken what?
rows.n: The root meaning is “reunion of broken parts.” Al-Khwarizmi later applied it to balance equations.

rows.q: Walt Disney conceived EPCOT as a functioning company town rather than a theme park, giving it an acronym ending with this future time period.
rows.n: EPCOT stands for Experimental Prototype Community of Tomorrow.

rows.q: English inventor Frederick Walton gave this smooth floor covering a name derived from the Latin for flax oil, losing the mark in 1878.
rows.n: The name combines the Latin linum, meaning flax, and oleum, meaning oil.

rows.q: Long before it featured tomatoes, the ancestor of ketchup was an East Asian trade condiment brewed from the fermented entrails of what animal?
rows.n: Hokkien merchants called it “kê-tsiap.” British sailors later made versions with walnuts and mushrooms.

rows.q: To the citizens of classical Athens, calling someone a hypokrites was no insult, but the everyday title for someone working this stage job.
rows.n: It originally meant ‘one who answers,’ referring to the stage actor conversing with the Greek chorus.

rows.q: First found in the 14th-century poem Piers Plowman as the name of a demon, what compound word evolved to mean a scruffy, ragged street child?
rows.n: In the late 1980s, the word was shortened to ragga to name a digital subgenre of dancehall reggae.

rows.q: Patented in 1937, this large metal trash bin owes its generic name to the Dempster brothers, who mechanically hoisted them onto trucks.
Developed in the 1950s for soap opera actors who forgot lines, this scrolling screen device soon lost its trademark to common usage.
rows.n: Actor Fred Barton Jr. co-invented it using half a motorized butcher-paper roll.

rows.q: Centuries before corporate marketing adopted it, a Scottish Highland clan charging into battle screamed their “slogan,” Gaelic for what two-word phrase?
rows.n: From “sluagh-ghairm,” where “sluagh” means army or host and “gairm” means shout or cry.

rows.q: A German firm took this vacuum-flask brand name from the Greek word for warm, losing its exclusive U.S. trademark in a landmark 1962 case.
rows.n: The vacuum flask itself was invented by James Dewar, who never patented it.

rows.q: A spa owes its name to a Belgian resort town famous for its mineral springs, located in the forested hills of which region of Belgium?
rows.n: English travelers in the 16th and 17th centuries popularized the town name as a generic term.

rows.q: Austrian inventor Eduard Haas III coined the name PEZ by plucking three letters from the German word for this original breath-freshening mint flavor.
rows.n: Haas took the first, middle, and last letters of Pfefferminz. The dispenser was designed to look like a lighter.

rows.q: American soldiers in the 1899 Philippine-American War coined “boondocks” from “bundok,” the Tagalog word for what terrain feature?
rows.n: The term evolved in marine slang to mean remote wilderness, and later any rural backwater.

rows.q: Along with Strelka, meaning ‘Little Arrow,’ the dog Belka safely orbited Earth in 1960. Belka’s name comes from the Russian word for this bushy-tailed rodent.
rows.n: Belka means squirrel; her co-pilot Strelka’s name translates to Little Arrow.

rows.q: Derived from Latin for ‘little bracelet,’ what seven-letter term refers to the metal band crimped around a pencil to hold the eraser firmly in place?
rows.n: The same collar binds paintbrush bristles to their handles and caps the ends of wooden walking canes.

rows.q: The wide, flowing necktie called an ascot shares its name with a famous racecourse in Berkshire, England, founded by which British monarch in 1711?
rows.n: The neckwear was standard morning dress at the prestigious Royal Ascot meeting.

rows.q: Canadian geologist Abraham Gesner patented this common lamp oil in 1854, coining its brand name from the Greek word for wax.
Latin for ‘little moon,’ what is the anatomical name for the pale, crescent-shaped area visible at the base of your fingernail?
rows.n: It is the only visible portion of the nail matrix, the deep tissue that generates new nail cells.

rows.q: Watch one perch on a fence and the name makes sense: squirrel comes from two ancient Greek words that describe a shadow cast by its own what?
rows.n: From skiouros, combining skia (‘shadow’) and oura (‘tail’)—literally ‘shadow-tailed.’

rows.q: Connecting the nasal septum to the upper lip, what vertical groove takes its anatomical name from the Greek word for a love potion?
rows.n: In embryology, it forms where the nasomedial and maxillary processes fuse during the sixth week of gestation.

rows.q: A copper-nickel coin or small fare in German-speaking lands was called a groschen, but the coin and currency known as the dollar trace back to Joachimsthal, a valley in which modern nation?
rows.n: Thalers were minted from rich silver mines in Joachimsthal, now the Czech town of Jachymov.

rows.q: A classic taxicab pairs a fare meter with an abbreviation for this two-wheeled, horse-drawn French carriage that supplied the back half.
rows.n: The carriage name comes from the French cabrioler, meaning to leap, because the light vehicle bounced on roads.

rows.q: The sturdy twill trousers known as dungarees got their name from Dungri, a dockside district in this bustling Indian port city.
rows.n: Also historically known as Bombay, the district exported coarse blue calico cloth to England.

rows.q: Traditional English marmalade is made with Seville oranges, but the spread got its name from “marmelo,” the Portuguese word for what knobby fruit?
rows.n: The original Portuguese “marmelada” was a solid fruit paste made exclusively of quinces and honey.

rows.q: Today we apply toxic to nasty chemicals and bad relationships, but the ancient Greek toxikon specifically referred to poison smeared on what weapon?
rows.n: The Greek phrase toxikon pharmakon literally translated to ‘poison for archery.’

rows.q: A curated collection of poetry or literature is an anthology, built from Greek roots that literally describe a gathering of what natural beauties?
rows.n: Anthos means flower and logia means collection; early anthologies were framed as bouquets of verse.

rows.q: Coined in 1933 by Choudhry Rahmat Ali, the acronym Pakstan was built from five Muslim homelands: Punjab, Afghania, Kashmir, Sindh, and this southern region.
rows.n: The letter I was inserted later to ease English pronunciation, while pak also means pure in Urdu.

rows.q: The earthy aroma that rises from dry ground after rainfall is largely driven by what organic compound, whose name translates from Greek as ‘earth smell’?
rows.n: Human sensory receptors can detect geosmin at minuscule levels, down to about five parts per trillion.

rows.q: In architecture, it is the space between two arches. In evolutionary biology, what eight-letter word denotes a phenotypic trait that is merely a byproduct?
rows.n: Biologists Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin borrowed the architectural term in a famous 1979 critique.

rows.q: Colonial administrators in Madras relished mulligatawny soup, a fiery dish whose Tamil name literally translates to two words: pepper and what?
rows.n: From “milagu-tannir” (pepper water). British army cooks added chicken, mutton, and cream to thicken it.

rows.q: GlaxoSmithKline and Colgate once went to federal court over trademark rights to this whimsical six-letter word, the industry term for a dollop of toothpaste.
rows.n: The word also describes the tiny pre-production plastic pellets that spill into waterways worldwide.

rows.q: If you call an awkward friend a “klutz,” you’re using a Yiddish insult that literally compares them to an unshaped block of what material?
rows.n: Borrowed from Middle High German “klotz,” meaning a heavy, unhewn wooden log or wedge.

rows.q: In ancient Athens, sycophant referred to an informer who exposed contraband, borrowing its name from the Greek for which sweet Mediterranean fruit?
rows.n: The roots are sykon (fig) and phainein (to show), though scholars still debate why figs needed showing.

rows.q: An arrogant snob might look down their nose at you, fitting since supercilious derives from the Latin word for which facial feature?
rows.n: Supercilium literally translates to ‘above the eyelid’ and was associated with haughty expressions.

rows.q: The cheap, gaudy ornaments we call tawdry got their name via a slurred pronunciation of the lace neckbands sold at the fair of this saint in Ely, England.
rows.n: St. Audrey was said to have repented wearing lavish necklaces in youth before dying of a neck tumor.

rows.q: Mayonnaise is widely believed to have been named in honor of the 1756 French capture of Port Mahon, a deep harbor on which Spanish Balearic island?
rows.n: The Duke de Richelieu’s chef reportedly whipped up the sauce when cream ran short.

rows.q: The Mexican salamander axolotl takes its name from Aztec mythology, fusing the Nahuatl word for “water” with the name of which domestic animal?
rows.n: Named for Xolotl, a dog-headed god of fire who disguised himself as a water creature to avoid death.

rows.q: Peace treaties that restore borders to their exact pre-conflict state invoke the full Latin phrase “_____ ante bellum.” What two-word phrase fills the blank to mean the existing state of affairs?
rows.n: The War of 1812 ended under this principle with the Treaty of Ghent, with neither side losing territory.

rows.q: Outside of Great Britain, the largest thriving community of native Welsh speakers is found in the Chubut Province of this South American nation.
rows.n: Welsh immigrants founded Y Wladfa in Patagonia in 1865 specifically to protect their language.

rows.q: Stanley Morison supervised the creation of this workhorse serif typeface in 1931 after publicly criticizing the London daily newspaper that commissioned it.
rows.n: The Times of London used it for over 40 years before commissioning newer custom variants.

rows.q: Known for three centuries as “the indecipherable cipher,” the polyalphabetic Vigenère cipher was secretly cracked in 1854 by this British pioneer of programmable computing engines.
rows.n: Babbage never published his method; the breakthrough was independently published nine years later by Friedrich Kasiski.

rows.q: In Through the Looking-Glass, Humpty Dumpty explains blended words like ‘slithy’ by comparing them to this two-compartment piece of leather luggage.
rows.n: Lewis Carroll used the metaphor to show how ‘lithe’ and ‘slimy’ packed neatly into one term.

rows.q: Playwright John Dryden popularized this two-word term for a risqué pun in 1673, cementing a grammatical quirk that native French speakers call double entente.
rows.n: “Entendre” in modern French is an infinitive verb meaning “to hear,” not a noun meaning “meaning.”

rows.q: Alfred Vail calibrated Morse code using letter frequency, assigning the single dot to E. He assigned its counterpart, a single dash, to which most common consonant in English?
rows.n: Vail estimated frequencies by visiting a local printing office and counting letters in the compositor’s type bins.

rows.q: Pilots say “Roger” to confirm receipt because in the 1940s military phonetic alphabet, Roger was the designation for this letter of the alphabet.
rows.n: R stood for “received”; NATO adopted the modern replacement word “Romeo” in 1956.

rows.q: When fisherman Ned Maddrell died in 1974, he was mourned as the last fluent native speaker of the Gaelic tongue belonging to this Irish Sea territory.
rows.n: Language activists recorded Maddrell extensively, and bilingual immersion schools now teach the tongue.

rows.q: American slang uses “bread” for cash, but Londoners got there first through Cockney rhyming slang, pairing bread with this sweet pantry staple.
rows.n: “Bread and honey” rhymed with money; over time, the rhyming tail was dropped, leaving only “bread.”

rows.q: When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 before international rivals could intervene, commentators routinely described the takeover with this French phrase, meaning an “accomplished fact.”
rows.n: It entered English during the 1850s, popularized by British coverage of French imperial politics.

rows.q: Paralyzed by locked-in syndrome, author Jean-Dominique Bauby blinked to dictate his memoir The Diving Bell and the Butterfly using a French alphabet ordered by this specific metric.
Laura Branigan’s 1982 smash “Gloria” was an English adaptation of a hit originally written and recorded three years earlier in what Romance language?
rows.n: Umberto Tozzi’s original Italian version was a massive hit across Europe before Branigan’s English cover.

rows.q: Theaters keep a single bare bulb illuminated on an empty stage overnight, a safety tradition named in stage jargon after this kind of apparition.
rows.n: Superstition holds that the light appeases theater ghosts by letting them see to perform after hours.

rows.q: Fittingly self-descriptive, the name of this contradictory figure of speech is built from two ancient Greek roots meaning ‘sharp’ and ‘dull.’
rows.n: The ‘oxy’ root also appears in oxygen, while ‘moros’ gave English the word moron.

rows.q: Words like chocolate, coyote, and avocado entered English by way of Spanish from this indigenous language, once the dominant tongue of the Aztec Empire.
rows.n: Over 1.5 million people in central Mexico still speak varieties of Nahuatl today.

rows.q: Home to over 800 languages, Papua New Guinea uses this English-based creole as a national lingua franca. Its name translates to ‘talk pidgin.’
rows.n: Despite the name, it is technically a full-fledged creole with standardized grammar and vocabulary.

rows.q: Featuring characters made of intersecting lines and dots, the geometric pigpen cipher is alternately named for this secretive fraternal organization whose lodges used it for records.
rows.n: The cipher maps letters into the compartments of a tic-tac-toe grid and an X shape, with and without interior dots.

rows.q: Torts classes use the “but-for” test to establish causation, naming it after this three-word Latin phrase meaning an absolute prerequisite.
rows.n: The phrase translates literally as “without which, not” and was originally coined in medieval philosophy.

rows.q: British broadcast journalists regularly send reporters onto the street to conduct “vox pop” interviews with passersby, a slang abbreviation of what full two-word Latin phrase?
rows.n: It forms the first half of the famous Latin maxim “Vox populi, vox Dei,” meaning the voice of the people is God’s.

rows.q: Before Michael Ventris cracked Linear B, classicist Alice Kober analyzed its inflections on 180,000 homemade flashcards stored in empty cartons of these tobacco products.
rows.n: Paper shortages during WWII forced Kober to cut index cards from spare church circulars.

rows.q: Before it infected office memos everywhere, this reviled typeface was created by Vincent Connare for the dialogue bubbles of a cartoon dog named Rover.
rows.n: Rover was a cartoon assistant in Microsoft Bob, a software interface meant for novices.

rows.q: Sylvia Plath’s The Bell Jar and Jack Kerouac’s On the Road are famous examples of this three-word French genre term, which translates literally as a “novel with a key.”
rows.n: The genre dates to 17th-century French writer Madeleine de Scudéry, who wrote historical romances mocking nobles.

rows.q: The fatal flaw that allowed Allied cryptanalysts at Bletchley Park to systematically eliminate rotor settings was that an Enigma machine could never encode a letter as this.
rows.n: Because the reflector bounced current back through the scrambler wheels, no circuit could loop back to its own key.

rows.q: Roman schoolteachers smoothed out beeswax tablets with the flat end of a stylus to wipe them clean, inspiring what Latin phrase for a blank slate or an uninfluenced mind?
rows.n: John Locke cemented the term in modern philosophy in 1689 to argue that humans are born without innate ideas.

rows.q: Alongside English, Malay, and Mandarin Chinese, Singapore recognizes this Dravidian tongue of southern India and Sri Lanka as an official language.
rows.n: Singapore has four official languages, but Malay alone is designated as the symbolic national language.

rows.q: Paraded in front of North Vietnamese television cameras in 1966, captured U.S. Navy pilot Jeremiah Denton blinked his eyes in Morse code to secretly spell out what single word?
rows.n: Denton’s broadcast provided the U.S. military with the first hard confirmation that American POWs were being mistreated.

rows.q: Paraguay is the only South American country where a majority of the population speaks an indigenous language, this official tongue shared with Spanish.
rows.n: Over 80% of Paraguayans speak it, including the vast majority of people without indigenous heritage.

rows.q: Ancient medical theory held that cold blood produced an unflappable temperament. That belief gave us what hyphenated French loanword for remarkable composure under extreme pressure?
rows.n: It translates literally as “cold blood,” though in English “in cold blood” took on a much more sinister meaning.

rows.q: Australians use the mild insult “drongo” to brand an incompetent fool, named for an unlucky 1920s animal of this kind that ran 37 races and won zero.
rows.n: Drongo was actually quite fast, finishing second in several top races, but never crossed the line first.

rows.q: French hunters originally used this two-word term to warn each other of dangerous wild boars. Today, English speakers use it to describe a persistent irritant or dreaded personal nemesis.
rows.n: The phrase translates literally to “black beast” and began appearing regularly in English letters around 1830.

rows.q: Exiled from Spain in 1492, Sephardic Jewish communities across the Mediterranean kept their medieval Romance tongue alive under this common name.
rows.n: It incorporates elements of Hebrew, Turkish, and Greek, and was historically written in Hebrew letters.

rows.q: Traditional printing guidelines dictate that when an asterisk marks the first footnote on a page, this weapon-shaped symbol denotes the second.
rows.n: Also called an obelus, it is followed by the double dagger if a third footnote is needed.

rows.q: Spoken on a sunny Mediterranean archipelago, Maltese holds the distinction of being the European Union’s only official language from this Afroasiatic family.
rows.n: Derived from Siculo-Arabic, it is also the only Semitic tongue written entirely in the Latin alphabet.

rows.q: John F. Kennedy’s line ‘ask not what your country can do for you’ is a classic example of this rhetorical device, named after the crisscrossing Greek letter chi.
The Rosetta Stone bears three scripts: Greek at the bottom, hieroglyphs up top, and this cursive script in the middle, derived from the Greek word for ‘popular.’
rows.n: Demotic served as everyday business writing in Egypt for over a thousand years.

rows.q: Around 1795, this American statesman invented a portable “wheel cipher” of 36 wooden disks rotating on an axle, a system reinvented by the U.S. Army over a century later.
rows.n: Designated the M-94, the Army used the cylinder cipher widely from 1922 through the early years of World War II.

rows.q: Mary, Queen of Scots was executed in 1587 after her ciphered letters detailing an assassination plot were intercepted and broken by the spy network of this ruthless Elizabethan spymaster.
rows.n: Walsingham’s cryptanalyst forged an encrypted postscript asking the conspirators for the names of their accomplices.

rows.q: Long before desktop publishing, the vertical space between lines of printed type earned this heavy name from the metal strips used to separate rows.
rows.n: Typesetters slid thin physical strips of lead between cast metal lines to adjust line height.

rows.q: Cupid once bribed the Roman god of silence with a flower to keep Venus’s affairs secret, giving English what two-word Latin phrase for covert activities?
rows.n: Plaster roses were frequently carved into dining room ceilings to remind guests that dinner chatter was secret.

rows.q: Singer Miriam Makeba brought global fame to ‘The Click Song,’ performed in this South African language that was also Nelson Mandela’s mother tongue.
rows.n: The song’s actual title is ‘Qongqothwane,’ which refers to a knock-beetle that brings good fortune.

rows.q: French artist Paul Gavarni popularized this two-word term with an 1840s cartoon series about blunt children. Today, it describes an unruly genius who shocks their creative industry.
rows.n: Fashion designers like Jean Paul Gaultier and Alexander McQueen were famously branded with the moniker.

rows.q: Decades before Navajo code talkers served in the Pacific, the U.S. Army pioneered indigenous battlefield ciphers in WWI using soldiers from this Oklahoma-based tribe.
rows.n: Nineteen Choctaw telephone operators helped American forces break German lines during the 1918 Meuse-Argonne offensive.

rows.q: On the rugged island of La Gomera in this Spanish archipelago, residents communicate across deep ravines using a whistled dialect of Spanish.
rows.n: Silbo Gomero converts vowels and consonants into whistling pitches, audible across two miles.

rows.q: Resembling a backwards capital P with two vertical stems, this proofreading mark gets its unusual English name from a corruption of the word ‘paragraph.’
rows.n: Medieval scribes used it to save costly parchment by starting new thoughts without a line break.

rows.q: In 2004, the International Telecommunication Union introduced its first new Morse code character in decades: a mashup of the letters A and C used to represent this internet symbol.
rows.n: Transmitted without a pause as “.--.-.”, the hybrid character is unofficially dubbed the “commat.”

rows.q: Though Madagascar sits off the coast of East Africa, its national language belongs not to an African family, but to this oceanic family that includes Tagalog.
rows.n: Seafarers from Borneo crossed the Indian Ocean and settled the island around 1,500 years ago.

rows.q: The illustrated 15th-century Voynich manuscript, written in an undeciphered script, takes its name from Wilfrid Voynich, who bought it in 1912 while working in which trade?
rows.n: He acquired it from a cash-strapped Jesuit college near Rome.

rows.q: Carved along stone edges in early medieval Ireland, the letters of the Ogham alphabet are traditionally named after different species of what kind of plant?
rows.n: Each letter is composed of one to five notches cut across a central stem line.

rows.q: The mysterious, undeciphered Rongorongo tablets of Easter Island are carved in reverse boustrophedon, requiring the reader to do what to the tablet at the end of each line?
rows.n: The next line is carved upside down relative to the previous one.

rows.q: In 80 BC, Cicero defended a murder suspect by asking what two-word Latin question, still asked by modern detectives seeking a financial motive?
rows.n: Attributed originally to Roman consul Lucius Cassius, it translates literally to “to whose benefit?”

rows.q: In a 1954 Harper’s essay, Sylvia Wright coined this term for misheard song lyrics after misinterpreting a Scottish ballad about the Earl of Moray.
rows.n: The ballad said they ‘laid him on the green,’ which Wright heard as ‘Lady Mondegreen.’

rows.q: Better known for collecting fairy tales, this German philologist coined the linguistic term ‘umlaut’ in 1819 to describe a vowel shift.
rows.n: His brother Wilhelm was also a scholar, but Jacob handled the bulk of the linguistic theory.

rows.q: Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s 1775 comedy The Rivals introduced Mrs. Malaprop, who gave her name to verbal blunders after describing an alligator as this literary device.
rows.n: She famously called the beast ‘an allegory on the banks of the Nile.’

rows.q: If you visit Aruba, Bonaire, or Curaçao, you will hear Dutch alongside this Spanish- and Portuguese-based creole that holds co-official status.
rows.n: Its name derives from papear, an old colloquial Portuguese and Spanish word meaning to chat.

rows.q: Sequoyah signed his engravings with a maker’s mark years before inventing the Cherokee syllabary while working as a craftsman in this metal trade.
rows.n: He was fascinated by the ‘talking leaves’ of white settlers and wanted the Cherokee to have their own.

rows.q: Derived from ancient Greek for the path taken by a certain draft animal while plowing, this term describes text that alternates direction every line.
rows.n: The name comes from ‘bous,’ meaning ox, and ‘strephein,’ meaning to turn.

rows.q: Anglo-Saxon and Old Norse poetry relied heavily on this type of compound metaphor, which swapped out simple nouns for poetic phrases like ‘whale-road.’
rows.n: Other classic kennings include ‘sky-candle’ for the sun and ‘slaughter-dew’ for blood.

rows.q: Attached to the letter C in French and Portuguese, the cedilla accent mark takes its name from a diminutive Spanish word for this letter of the alphabet.
rows.n: The hook originally developed from a miniature handwritten ‘z’ positioned under the c.

rows.q: Wyndham Lewis founded the aggressive British avant-garde group Vorticism, but its swirling name was coined by this expatriate American poet of The Cantos.
rows.n: Pound called the vortex ‘the point of maximum energy’ in the movement’s brash journal, BLAST.

rows.q: Before carving Mount Rushmore, Gutzon Borglum was hired in 1915 to carve Confederate leaders into the side of this Georgia quartz monadnock.
rows.n: Borglum was fired over furious design squabbles, and his initial carving was blasted away.

rows.q: In February 1994, thieves stole the National Gallery of Norway’s version of Edvard Munch’s The Scream on the very same day this international sporting event opened nearby.
rows.n: Held in Lillehammer, Norway, the Games drew police attention away from the gallery. It was recovered months later.

rows.q: Co-founded by Billy Childish in 1999 to oppose conceptual art, Stuckism took its name from an insult hurled at him by this Turner Prize nominee, famous for exhibiting her unmade bed.
rows.n: Emin reportedly yelled at Childish: ‘Your paintings are stuck, your poetry is stuck, you are stuck.’

rows.q: Though famous for painting his mother in grey and black, this American sued critic John Ruskin for libel after Ruskin accused him of flinging a pot of paint in the public’s face.
rows.n: Whistler won the 1878 trial, but the jury awarded him contemptuous damages of just one farthing.

rows.q: In 1735, William Hogarth followed up A Harlot’s Progress with this moralizing eight-canvas series charting the downfall of the spendthrift Tom Rakewell.
rows.n: Hogarth delayed selling engravings of the series until Parliament passed a law protecting artist copyright.

rows.q: Barbara Hepworth’s towering bronze Single Form stands outside the UN Secretariat building as a memorial to this Secretary-General, killed in a 1961 plane crash.
rows.n: Hammarskjold was an ardent collector and friend who had discussed a UN commission with her.

rows.q: Following the unsolved 1990 heist of thirteen masterpieces from Boston’s Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, visitors today still see these objects hanging in their place.
rows.n: The museum keeps the blank frames on the walls per Isabella’s will and in the hope the stolen art will return.

rows.q: Salvador Dalí claimed his surreal melting timepieces in The Persistence of Memory were not inspired by Einstein’s physics, but by a portion of this French cheese melting in the sun.
rows.n: The painting has been in the permanent collection of New York’s Museum of Modern Art since 1934.

rows.q: Long before his 2008 HOPE poster, street artist Shepard Fairey sparked a viral sticker campaign featuring the stylized face of which 7-foot-4 French professional wrestler?
rows.n: The sticker was paired with the text OBEY and began as an inside joke while Fairey was in art school.

rows.q: John Singer Sargent caused a stir at the 1884 Paris Salon with Madame X, prompting him to repaint the canvas after critics took offense at this specific piece of her gown falling down.
rows.n: The scandal hurt Sargent’s portrait commissions in Paris so badly that he soon relocated to London.

rows.q: Painted from his asylum window in Saint-Rémy, Vincent van Gogh’s The Starry Night features this towering, flame-shaped tree in the foreground, long associated with cemeteries.
rows.n: Van Gogh painted the view before sunrise, inventing the idealized Dutch-style village tucked below the hills.

rows.q: When Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc named Der Blaue Reiter, Marc supplied horses, while Kandinsky brought a love of blue and this dragon-slaying patron saint of Moscow.
rows.n: Kandinsky featured Saint George on horseback on the cover of the 1912 Blaue Reiter Almanac.

rows.q: In 1863, after the Paris Salon rejected more than half the submitted works, this French emperor appeased the furious artists by establishing the Salon des Refusés.
rows.n: Over a thousand artists exhibited, drawing huge crowds eager to mock the avant-garde works of Manet and Whistler.

rows.q: To capture the sickly pallor of dying sailors for The Raft of the Medusa, Théodore Géricault kept severed human limbs in his studio, borrowed from this type of facility.
rows.n: Géricault also interviewed survivors and had a carpenter build a scale replica of the raft in his studio.

rows.q: Leonardo da Vinci’s deteriorating mural of The Last Supper was not painted for a Roman pontiff, but for the Duke of this northern Italian city on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie.
rows.n: Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan, paid for the commission and chose the Dominican convent as his family mausoleum.

rows.q: Long before Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel, rival sculptor Pietro Torrigiano permanently remodeled his face with a punch that broke this specific feature.
rows.n: Torrigiano fled Florence soon after to escape Lorenzo de’ Medici’s wrath for the assault.

rows.q: Picasso dictated that Guernica could not hang in Spain until democracy was restored. Since 1992, it has resided in Madrid at a national museum named for which Spanish queen?
rows.n: Picasso deposited it at MoMA in 1939; it finally crossed the Atlantic to Spain in 1981.

rows.q: Born Doménikos Theotokópoulos in Crete, this master of the Spanish Renaissance painted dramatic, elongated figures, including The Burial of the Count of Orgaz.
rows.n: He signed his canvases in Greek letters with his full birth name, adding ‘Kres’ (Cretan).

rows.q: French artist Victorine Meurent caused back-to-back scandals for Édouard Manet, modeling as the reclining nude in Olympia and the naked picnicker in this earlier 1863 work.
rows.n: Meurent was an accomplished painter in her own right, later accepted into the prestigious Salon herself.

rows.q: At a 1936 London exhibition, Salvador Dalí nearly suffocated when the helmet jammed on this heavy maritime outfit he wore to give a lecture.
rows.n: The audience applauded his desperate flailing, assuming his suffocation was part of the act.

rows.q: Hanging in London’s National Gallery, J.M.W. Turner’s The Fighting Temeraire depicts an aging warship being towed for scrap after earning renown in this decisive 1805 naval clash.
The Art Nouveau movement took its name from an 1895 Paris gallery opened by Siegfried Bing, an art dealer who made his fortune importing decorative goods from this Asian nation.
Folklore claims Daniel Chester French modeled Abraham Lincoln’s hands at the Lincoln Memorial to secretly form his initials in this visual communication system.
rows.n: French had previously sculpted Gallaudet University’s founder tutoring a deaf student.

rows.q: In 2016, Cloud Gate sculptor Anish Kapoor sparked outrage across the art world by purchasing exclusive artistic rights to this super-black, light-swallowing material.
rows.n: Artist Stuart Semple retaliated with ‘Pinkest Pink,’ legally barring Kapoor from buying it.

rows.q: In the 1920s, avant-garde provocateur Marcel Duchamp largely gave up making art so he could compete internationally for France in this board game.
rows.n: His obsession annoyed his first wife so much that she allegedly glued all his pieces to the board.

rows.q: New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani threatened to cut funding to the Brooklyn Museum in 1999 because Chris Ofili’s The Holy Virgin Mary incorporated dung from this giant animal.
rows.n: Ofili used clumps of resin-coated elephant dung both on the canvas itself and as supportive feet beneath the frame.

rows.q: In 1897, Gustav Klimt and his allies broke away from Vienna’s conservative art establishment, adopting this name that literally means the formal withdrawal from an organization.
rows.n: Their exhibition building bore the motto: ‘To every age its art, to every art its freedom.’

rows.q: Damien Hirst shocked the art establishment in 1991 with a dead tiger shark floating in formaldehyde, giving it the title The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone doing what?
rows.n: The original 14-foot shark decayed due to inadequate preservation and had to be replaced by a fresh catch in 2006.

rows.q: Virtually unknown in her lifetime, photographer Vivian Maier shot over 150,000 candid street photos while working for four decades in Chicago and New York in this day job.
rows.n: Her massive archive was discovered in 2007 when an unpaid storage locker was auctioned off in Chicago.

rows.q: Seeking to create art out of absence, Robert Rauschenberg spent a month in 1953 erasing a dense drawing given to him by this Dutch-American Abstract Expressionist.
rows.n: De Kooning intentionally gave Rauschenberg a dense drawing in charcoal and grease pencil that would be hard to erase.

rows.q: Legend holds that the founders of Dada found their name in 1916 by randomly sliding a paper knife into a dictionary, landing on a French nursery word for this child’s toy.
rows.n: While Tristan Tzara claimed the dictionary story, Hugo Ball’s diary says he and Richard Huelsenbeck found it.

rows.q: The label Cubism took off in 1908 after Henri Matisse mocked an L’Estaque landscape by this French co-founder of the style as being made of ‘little cubes.’
rows.n: Braque and Picasso worked so closely in those early Cubist years that they sometimes joked they were married.

rows.q: Eugène Delacroix’s bare-breasted allegorical figure in Liberty Leading the People does not commemorate the 1789 Revolution, but an 1830 uprising that occurred in this month.
rows.n: The July Revolution, or Three Glorious Days, replaced King Charles X with King Louis Philippe I.

rows.q: Amédée Ozenfant and Charles-Édouard Jeanneret coined Purism in 1918 to reform Cubism. Jeanneret is better known today for his pioneering modernist architecture under which pseudonym?
rows.n: Their 1918 manifesto was titled Après le cubisme (After Cubism).

rows.q: The glowing diner in Edward Hopper’s 1942 classic Nighthawks features an exterior ad for Phillies, a five-cent brand of this product.
rows.n: Hopper and his wife Jo both posed as models for the three customers and the soda jerk behind the counter.

rows.q: Édouard Manet caused an uproar at the 1865 Paris Salon with Olympia, not just for the nude woman’s defiant stare, but for this startled black animal perched at her feet.
rows.n: The black cat was seen as a symbol of sexual promiscuity, replacing the traditional loyal dog in Renaissance nudes.

rows.q: British tabloids erupted in outrage in 1976 when the Tate Gallery spent public funds to purchase Carl Andre’s Equivalent VIII, a sculpture made solely of 120 of these construction items.
rows.n: One outraged visitor vandalized the sculpture with blue food dye; the Tate safely cleaned all 120 bricks.

rows.q: Mannerism derives from the Italian word maniera, popularized as a marker of artistic style by this 16th-century Tuscan author of Lives of the Artists.
rows.n: Vasari used maniera to praise Michelangelo’s grace and virtuosity before it came to imply artificiality.

rows.q: Following 1923 cataract surgery that removed the lens of his right eye, Claude Monet was briefly able to perceive this invisible form of radiation.
rows.n: Human lenses naturally block ultraviolet light; without one, Monet saw water lilies in blue-violet.

rows.q: When Kazimir Malevich first displayed his stark Black Square in 1915, he hung it across a top corner of the room, the spot where Russian Orthodox homes traditionally placed this item.
rows.n: Malevich intended his Suprematist square to replace traditional religious imagery with pure artistic feeling.

rows.q: Known for his crisp black-and-white landscapes of Yosemite, Ansel Adams originally trained for over a decade to pursue a professional career playing this musical instrument.
rows.n: Adams credited the discipline of piano scales for his meticulous, methodical approach to darkroom work.

rows.q: Among the picnickers in Georges Seurat’s pointillist canvas A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, a woman on the right holds a leash attached not to a dog, but to this exotic pet.
rows.n: In French slang of the 1880s, a pet monkey was a discreet symbol for a kept woman or prostitute.

rows.q: The weathered wooden farmhouse seen in the distance of Andrew Wyeth’s 1948 canvas Christina’s World still stands as a National Historic Landmark in this coastal New England state.
rows.n: The real Christina Olson suffered from a hereditary muscular disorder and crawled across her family’s fields.

rows.q: Marcel Duchamp threw the 1917 New York art world into chaos when he submitted an ordinary porcelain urinal to an exhibition, cheekily signing it with this alias.
rows.n: The name mocked J.L. Mott Iron Works, the plumbing fixture company where Duchamp bought the ready-made urinal.

rows.q: A lucrative 1958 commission asked Mark Rothko to paint murals for this swank Manhattan restaurant, where he hoped to ruin the appetite of every diner.
rows.n: After dining there himself and hating the pretension, he returned the cash advance and kept the art.

rows.q: In 1960, Jean Tinguely unveiled Homage to New York in the MoMA sculpture garden, designed to perform this chaotic final act until firefighters stepped in.
rows.n: The 23-foot machine caught fire on cue from an onboard chemical smoke bomb.

rows.q: Pioneer photojournalist Henri Cartier-Bresson almost exclusively used a standard 50mm lens mounted on a compact rangefinder camera made by this German manufacturer.
rows.n: Cartier-Bresson often wrapped the camera’s shiny chrome parts in black tape to stay inconspicuous in public.

rows.q: Stanley Kubrick based the eerie hallway appearance of the Grady sisters in The Shining on a 1967 portrait of identical twins taken in New Jersey by this photographer.
rows.n: The photo, Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey, depicts seven-year-old sisters Cathleen and Colleen Wade.

rows.q: Banksy directed the 2010 street art documentary Exit Through the Gift Shop, which follows Thierry Guetta, an eccentric cameraman who adopts this artistic alter ego.
rows.n: Critics still debate whether Guetta is a genuine pop-artist convert or an elaborate hoax engineered by Banksy.

rows.q: Despite Hieronymus Bosch being Netherlandish, his bizarre triptych The Garden of Earthly Delights hangs in Madrid’s Prado because this austere 16th-century Spanish monarch bought it.
rows.n: The deeply religious Philip kept Bosch’s surreal moralizing triptychs in his private apartments at El Escorial.

rows.q: In Emanuel Leutze’s Washington Crossing the Delaware, the young soldier holding the American flag beside Washington is meant to depict this future U.S. president.
rows.n: The historical Monroe was an 18-year-old lieutenant in the crossing, though wounded at Trenton the next day.

rows.q: Painted on the Berlin Wall in 1990, Dmitri Vrubel’s famous street mural depicts Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev sharing a fraternal kiss on the lips with this East German head of state.
rows.n: The mural was based on a real photograph taken in 1979 during the 30th anniversary of East Germany.

rows.q: Protesting the arrest of Emmeline Pankhurst in 1914, suffragette Mary Richardson slashed Velázquez’s Rokeby Venus at London’s National Gallery using this bladed kitchen tool.
rows.n: Richardson earned the nickname Slasher Mary and served a prison sentence for six strikes to the canvas.

rows.q: F.T. Marinetti launched Futurism in 1909 by publishing his provocative manifesto on the front page of this prominent Parisian daily newspaper.
Roy Lichtenstein’s pop style relied on hand-painted grids of tiny colored circles, mimicking an industrial printing method named for this 19th-century American illustrator.
rows.n: Day invented the cheap color printing process in 1879 to shade backgrounds in newspapers and comic books.

rows.q: An anti-Vietnam protest at this Ivy League school was kicked off in 1969 when Claes Oldenburg planted a 24-foot tube of lipstick mounted on tank treads in a plaza.
rows.n: The lipstick tip was originally an inflatable vinyl balloon that demonstrators had to pump up.

rows.q: The dinner jacket earned its common American nickname after wealthy young clubmen debuted tailless formal jackets at an 1886 autumn ball in this New York enclave.
rows.n: James Brown Potter copied the tailless style from the Prince of Wales at Sandringham before bringing it stateside.

rows.q: While denim is a corruption of the French town name Nîmes, the word jeans traces back to the French pronunciation of this Italian seaport.
rows.n: Genoese sailors used the sturdy fustian fabric to protect their goods and make heavy-duty work pants.

rows.q: Famous for its double ring of medieval ramparts and 52 watchtowers, this restored hilltop citadel in southern France gave its name to an award-winning tile-placement board game.
rows.n: Players place cardboard tiles to build out roads, monasteries, and fortified walled cities just like the real place.

rows.q: World Trade Center architect Minoru Yamasaki framed the Twin Towers with narrow 18-inch windows largely because he personally struggled with this phobia.
rows.n: The tight column spacing meant occupants could never look straight down, creating a psychological sense of safety.

rows.q: The fedora hat takes its name from an 1882 stage play written by Victorien Sardou for this legendary French actress, who wore the soft felt hat as Princess Fédora.
rows.n: Bernhardt frequently adopted menswear and cross-dressed on stage, turning the hat into a feminist symbol.

rows.q: Sported worldwide by The Beatles in the 1960s, this mandarin-collared jacket was named after this first prime minister of India.
rows.n: Nehru actually wore the longer traditional achkan; Western designers shortened it into a hip-length jacket.

rows.q: Aeronautical engineer Corradino D’Ascanio designed an affordable scooter for Piaggio in 1946. Its narrow waist and buzzing engine earned it a name meaning what insect?
rows.n: Enrico Piaggio reportedly exclaimed ‘Sembra una vespa!’ (‘It looks like a wasp!’) upon seeing the prototype.

rows.q: Prague Castle was the backdrop for a famous 1618 incident that ignited the Thirty Years’ War, in which angry Protestant nobles threw two Catholic regents out of this.
rows.n: The victims survived a 70-foot drop; Catholics credited angels, while Protestants credited a dung heap.

rows.q: Stacking by the millions on patios worldwide, the ubiquitous white plastic chair known as the Monobloc is mass-produced using what process that squirts molten resin into a die?
rows.n: A complete chair can be popped out of the polished steel mold in roughly seventy seconds.

rows.q: Aiming for broken-in comfort in 1956, Charles Eames designed his iconic lounge chair to evoke the warm, receptive look of a well-used mitt from this sport.
rows.n: Eames specifically cited the worn leather of a first baseman’s mitt as his visual goal for the chair.

rows.q: A devastating fire in 1992 that destroyed over a hundred rooms at Windsor Castle prompted Queen Elizabeth II to describe that year with this Latin phrase.
rows.n: The phrase translates to ‘horrible year’; 1992 also saw separations for three of her four children.

rows.q: German critics mocked Dieter Rams’s 1956 Braun SK4 phonograph for its stark pale box and clear acrylic lid, nicknaming it after the glass casket of what fairy-tale heroine?
rows.n: The ‘Schneewittchensarg’ nickname stuck, though the radio became a defining touchstone of modern design.

rows.q: Alvar Aalto’s 1932 Paimio Armchair curved laminated birch at a reclined angle designed to open the chest and ease breathing for patients fighting what bacterial lung disease?
rows.n: Aalto designed the Paimio sanatorium’s building, lighting, sinks, and furniture as an all-encompassing healing space.

rows.q: Paying homage to De Stijl art in 1965, Yves Saint Laurent designed six blocky, primary-colored wool jersey shift dresses named after this Dutch painter.
rows.n: Saint Laurent hid all the dress seams inside the thick black grid lines to match the paintings.

rows.q: In 1993, Miuccia Prada launched a rebellious, youth-focused secondary fashion line, naming the brand after this personal childhood nickname.
Cologne Cathedral was built over more than six centuries largely to house a gilded reliquary holding the supposed bones of these three gift-bearing biblical visitors.
rows.n: Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa seized the relics from Milan and presented them to Cologne in 1164.

rows.q: Towering above the prayer halls of Islamic architecture, minarets take their name from the Arabic word manarah, which originally denoted what seaside navigational guide?
rows.n: Early towers may have displayed signal fires; the root nar means fire in Arabic.

rows.q: Built as a royal gift honoring a major victory in the War of the Spanish Succession, Blenheim Palace is famously the 1874 birthplace of this British prime minister.
rows.n: Blenheim is the only non-royal, non-episcopal country house in England to hold the title of ‘palace.’

rows.q: Christian Louboutin got the idea for his signature red shoe soles when he snatched a bottle of this cosmetic product from an assistant to paint a prototype.
rows.n: Louboutin felt a prototype lacked energy until he coated the black sole in Chanel red nail polish.

rows.q: NASA’s blue circular insignia is nicknamed the meatball. What creeping creature provides the nickname for the minimalist, red-ribbon wordmark introduced in 1975?
rows.n: Designed by Danne & Blackburn, the worm was officially retired in 1992 but revived in 2020 for select missions.

rows.q: Uncle Sam’s stern, pointing pose on James Montgomery Flagg’s 1917 recruitment poster was directly adapted from a British wartime ad featuring which field marshal?
rows.n: The original British poster urged volunteers with the slogan ‘Lord Kitchener Wants You.’

rows.q: The central hall of a Western church is the nave, taking its name from the Latin word for this vessel because early wooden roofs mirrored an upturned hull.
Surrealist fashion pioneer Elsa Schiaparelli collaborated with Salvador Dalí in 1937 to create an organza evening gown printed with this large red crustacean.
rows.n: Dalí initially wanted to smear real mayonnaise across the finished dress, but Schiaparelli refused.

rows.q: The iconic tongue logo for the Rolling Stones, designed by John Pasche in 1970, was inspired by Mick Jagger’s mouth and the protruding tongue of which Hindu goddess?
Coco Chanel popularized the striped knit shirt known as the marinière after observing the uniforms worn by fishermen in this coastal French region.
rows.n: An 1858 French naval decree required official sailors’ knit shirts to have exactly 21 white stripes.

rows.q: Matthew Carter designed the sans-serif font Verdana and the serif Georgia in the 1990s, optimizing them to look legible on pixelated screens for which tech giant?
The individual molded spindles supporting a staircase handrail are called balusters, named from an Italian word for the blossoming calyx of this ruby-seeded fruit.
rows.n: A row of balusters joined by a top rail forms a balustrade, popularized during the Renaissance.

rows.q: Classical columns carved as draped women are caryatids. Their male equivalents, often seen straining under entablatures, take their name from this Greek Titan doomed to hold up the sky.
rows.n: The earliest known architectural Atlantes stood at the Greek Temple of Olympian Zeus in Agrigento, Sicily.

rows.q: A distinctive red triangle registered by this English brewery in 1876 holds the historic distinction of being the United Kingdom’s very first registered trademark.
rows.n: A Bass employee camped outside the registrar’s office on New Year’s Eve 1875 to secure Trademark No. 1.

rows.q: Completed on February 29, 2012, this 2,080-foot lattice tower in the Sumida district overtook Tokyo Tower as Japan’s tallest structure.
rows.n: Its height of 634 meters is a pun on Musashi, an ancient name for the region surrounding Tokyo.

rows.q: Before outfitting the Sex Pistols, Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren rebranded their London boutique with this scandalous three-letter name.
rows.n: The shop sold rubber fetishwear and ripped graphic tees, creating the signature look of the Sex Pistols.

rows.q: Strict architectural purists insist that a carved stone monster on a Gothic building isn’t a gargoyle unless it diverts rainwater. Without a drainage spout, it’s properly called this.
rows.n: The name comes from Italian grottesche, referring to Roman wall paintings rediscovered in underground ruins.

rows.q: The 1957 Treaty of Rome was signed inside the Palazzo dei Conservatori atop this smallest and most sacred of Rome’s seven historic hills.
rows.n: Michelangelo designed the trapezoidal piazza and the palace facades atop the hill for Pope Paul III.

rows.q: Recognized as the father of haute couture, 19th-century Parisian designer Charles Frederick Worth was the first to stitch these signature items into garments.
rows.n: Worth transformed dressmaking from anonymous tailoring into recognized personal artistry.

rows.q: Before all 10,344 of its glass panes were replaced in the 1970s, Boston’s windy John Hancock Tower was mockingly dubbed the ‘Palace’ of this cheap building material.
rows.n: Engineers used thousands of plywood sheets to cover empty window frames while testing why panes were falling out.

rows.q: Aristocratic 18th-century English estates used sunken turf ditches to keep livestock off the lawn without spoiling panoramic views. Strolling guests were surprised by this chuckling name for them.
rows.n: Horace Walpole wrote that the ditch was so called because visitors cried out in surprise upon finding it.

rows.q: Famous for seismic resistance, the doors and windows of classic Inca stone architecture at Machu Picchu typically taper into this four-sided shape.
rows.n: The inward-sloping trapezoidal shape helped Inca stone structures withstand major earthquakes.

rows.q: Perched atop Cap Diamant overlooking the Saint Lawrence River, this turreted Canadian Pacific luxury hotel dominates the skyline of Old Quebec.
rows.n: Guinness World Records considers it the most photographed hotel in the world.

rows.q: Decorative Art Deco metal features on the 31st floor of the Chrysler Building were modeled after winged versions of this functional automobile component.
rows.n: Higher up on the 61st floor, the corners sprout gargoyle-like American bald eagles made of Nirosta steel.

rows.q: Defying gravity without vertical posts beneath, the overhanging concrete terraces of Frank Lloyd Wright’s Fallingwater rely on this structural beam supported at only one end.
rows.n: Wright fought with his engineers, who secretly added extra steel rebar because they doubted the cantilevers.

rows.q: Architect Bertrand Goldberg gave Chicago’s twin Marina City residential towers scalloped concrete balconies, earning the high-rises this agricultural nickname.
rows.n: The bottom nineteen stories of each tower are exposed spiral parking decks overlooking the Chicago River.

rows.q: Due to its continuous, loop-shaped structural legs, Rem Koolhaas’s Beijing CCTV headquarters is widely known to local residents by this cheeky sartorial nickname.
rows.n: Koolhaas deliberately designed the building as a closed loop to defy the traditional vertical skyscraper race.

rows.q: Dining at an Italian seaside restaurant, Philippe Starck was inspired to sketch his alien-looking Juicy Salif citrus squeezer after squeezing lemon onto this tentacled seafood.
rows.n: The original grease-stained paper placemat containing his rapid squid doodles is preserved at the Alessi Museum.

rows.q: Paramount Pictures founder W.W. Hodkinson first doodled the studio’s star-ringed mountain logo on a napkin, modeling it on Ben Lomond peak in which home state of his?
rows.n: The original logo featured 24 stars, one for each movie star under contract with Paramount at the time.

rows.q: Before his Walkie-Talkie tower melted a car in London, architect Rafael Viñoly’s curved facade at this Las Vegas hotel created a similar ‘death ray’ over its pool.
rows.n: Poolside guests reported scorched plastic cups and singed hair before sun-blocking film was installed.

rows.q: Credited with defining London’s Swinging Sixties, designer Mary Quant adopted this cheerful flower as her official brand logo, stamping it on tights and cosmetics.
rows.n: Quant picked the black-and-white daisy because she found it cheerful, modern, and unpretentious.

rows.q: Sailing past the island of the hypnotic Sirens, Jason’s crew survived because this legendary musician drowned them out on his lyre.
rows.n: Only one Argonaut jumped ship: Butes heard the song and leaped into the sea, but Aphrodite saved him.

rows.q: Fleeing death when the Aztec gods agreed to sacrifice themselves to set the sun in motion, the trickster god Xolotl transformed into several plants and beasts, ending as this aquatic salamander.
rows.n: Its Nahuatl name translates to ‘water dog,’ nodding to Xolotl’s canine appearance.

rows.q: A five-letter word for mass dread derives from Pan, the nature god who aided Athens at this 490 BC battle by terrorizing the Persians.
rows.n: The Athenians were so grateful for Pan’s battlefield assist that they dedicated an annual sacrifice to him.

rows.q: Hebe served as the cupbearer on Mount Olympus before Heracles married her. Romans honored this divine personification of youth under what Latin name shared with a Turin soccer club?
rows.n: Young Roman men offered a coin at her shrine upon donning adult clothing.

rows.q: German pharmacist Friedrich Sertürner coined the name “morphine” in honor of Morpheus, the Greek god associated with this nightly realm.
rows.n: Morpheus got his name from the Greek word for shape, because he gave shape to the people in human dreams.

rows.q: Heracles couldn’t reach the man-eating Stymphalian birds, so he flushed them into bow range with bronze rattles crafted by this god.
rows.n: The bronze clappers, called krotala, made enough racket to scare the birds out of the dense marsh.

rows.q: When Heracles found that cutting off a head of the Lernaean Hydra only caused two more to grow, his nephew Iolaus helped defeat it by doing this to each stump.
rows.n: Eurystheus argued the labor did not count toward the original ten because Heracles accepted help.

rows.q: To clean King Augeas’s filthy cattle yards in a single day for his fifth labor, Heracles bypassed shovels by diverting two of these geographic features.
rows.n: He diverted the Alpheus and Peneus rivers, flushing out decades of manure in a single afternoon.

rows.q: When Odysseus set sail for Troy, he entrusted his household and son Telemachus to this loyal advisor, giving English a word for a trusted guide.
rows.n: The goddess Athena frequently disguised herself as Mentor when giving advice to young Telemachus.

rows.q: During his journey back to Ithaca, Odysseus had to drag weeping sailors back to his ships after they consumed this plant, which induced euphoric forgetfulness.
