rows.n: Eating the sweet plant caused the men to lose all memory of home and all desire to leave the island.

rows.q: In Tartarus, the father of Pelops was punished with receding water and fruit just out of reach, giving English this verb meaning to torment by teasing.
rows.n: His crime was stealing ambrosia from Olympus and serving his own boiled son to the gods at a banquet.

rows.q: Taiwanese computer giant Asus shortened its name from this mythological winged stallion in order to place higher alphabetically in phone books.
rows.n: Asus revived the full winged horse in 2019 as a mascot for its Republic of Gamers hardware brand.

rows.q: When a devastating plague hit Rome in 293 BC, the Senate imported the Greek healing god Asclepius from Epidaurus in the physical guise of this sacred crawling creature.
rows.n: The snake reportedly slithered off the ship and chose Tiber Island for its new sanctuary.

rows.q: The Greek fleet was stranded at Aulis until Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter, appeasing Artemis after he bragged of outhunting her by killing this animal.
rows.n: Euripides wrote that Artemis spared Iphigenia at the altar, substituting a deer at the very last moment.

rows.q: Hermes guided souls and protected thieves, but his Roman equivalent Mercury got his name directly from the Latin word “merx,” honoring his patronage of this specific domain.
rows.n: The same Latin root gave English words like “merchant,” “market,” and “mercenary.”

rows.q: Footwear giant Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, whose famous headless sculpture stands atop a grand staircase in this museum.
rows.n: The Winged Victory of Samothrace was discovered on a Greek island in 1863 before moving to Paris.

rows.q: Flying home with Medusa’s severed head, Perseus made a detour to Ethiopia to slay a sea beast and rescue this princess, who was chained to a rock.
rows.n: The beast was sent by Poseidon after Queen Cassiopeia boasted she was fairer than the Nereids.

rows.q: The phrase “hermetic seal” derives from the Greek god Hermes, honoring his legendary association with this esoteric proto-science of transmutation.
rows.n: The term references Hermes Trismegistus, a syncretic figure credited with inventing a magical airtight glass seal.

rows.q: Odysseus’s old nurse recognizes him by a thigh scar, sustained in his youth on Mount Parnassus while hunting this ferocious beast with his grandfather.
rows.n: The hunt took place during a visit to his trickster grandfather, Autolycus.

rows.q: In Apuleius’s tale “The Golden Ass,” the Roman love god Cupid falls for this mortal princess, whose name translates from Greek as “soul” and who is often depicted with butterfly wings.
rows.n: Venus subjected her to grueling trials, including sorting a mountain of grains before nightfall.

rows.q: In his quest to gain cosmic wisdom and drink from the Well of Mimir, Odin sacrificed this sensory organ, leaving it at the bottom of the water.
rows.n: Odin also hung from the branches of Yggdrasil for nine nights to learn the secrets of the runes.

rows.q: In an effort to delay her father’s pursuit of the Argo, the sorceress Medea murdered this male relative of hers and scattered his severed limbs into the sea.
rows.n: King Aeetes had to halt his warships to recover the body parts of his son Absyrtus for burial.

rows.q: Emergency sirens take their name from Homer’s mythical temptresses, whose dangerous songs Odysseus shielded his crew from using this substance.
rows.n: Odysseus wanted to hear their song himself, so he had his crew lash him tightly to the ship’s mast.

rows.q: After warning that the wooden horse was a trap, the Trojan priest Laocoon and his two young sons were dragged to their deaths by two giant what?
rows.n: The Trojans misread the attack as Athena’s punishment for striking the wooden horse with his spear.

rows.q: When his pen snapped while feverishly taking down the monumental epic Mahabharata, the elephant-headed scribe god Ganesha snapped off this part of his own body to keep writing.
rows.n: The sage Vyasa demanded Ganesha write without pausing, so Ganesha made do with ivory.

rows.q: Japanese folklore depicts the shapeshifting raccoon dog known as the tanuki drumming on its belly and possessing comically oversized, elastic versions of these organs.
rows.n: Tanuki used their elastic scrotums as fishing nets, raincoats, or makeshift parachutes.

rows.q: Juno Moneta watched over Rome’s state finances from the Capitoline Hill. Her surname gave the English language both “mint” and this common word.
rows.n: Her epithet Moneta comes from the Latin verb “monere,” meaning to warn or advise.

rows.q: The word “clue” originally meant a ball of thread, referring to the spool given to Theseus by this Cretan princess to escape the Labyrinth.
rows.n: Theseus abandoned Ariadne on Naxos on the journey home, where she was discovered and married by Dionysus.

rows.q: According to the Prose Edda, Thor successfully crushes the Midgard Serpent at Ragnarok, only to stagger this many steps before dying.
rows.n: The number nine recurs frequently in Norse myth, including Odin hanging for nine nights on Yggdrasil.

rows.q: Dionysus roamed the earth with his rotund tutor Silenus, the god of drunkenness who was perpetually too intoxicated to walk and therefore rode on the back of this beast of burden.
rows.n: When King Midas returned an intoxicated Silenus to Dionysus, the god rewarded Midas with the golden touch.

rows.q: In Greek myth, the Three Fates determined the span of mortal lives. Clotho spun the thread, Lachesis measured it, and this eldest sister snipped it with her shears.
rows.n: Her name translates to ‘inflexible’ or ‘unchangeable,’ referencing the finality of her cut.

rows.q: While Greeks loathed Ares as a bloodthirsty brute, Romans honored his counterpart Mars with a dual portfolio, venerating him as a guardian of war and this peaceful livelihood.
rows.n: The Roman month of March, dedicated to Mars, was the season to plant crops as well as begin military campaigns.

rows.q: Aeolus tied all adverse gales into an ox-hide bag to give Odysseus calm seas, leaving only this gentle western wind free to blow his fleet home.
rows.n: His crew opened the bag within sight of Ithaca’s shores, mistakenly assuming it was stuffed with treasure.

rows.q: Persuading the giant wolf Fenrir that the binding chain was harmless required this Norse god of war to bravely pledge his right hand in the beast’s maw.
rows.n: When Fenrir realized the enchanted ribbon Gleipnir could not be broken, he bit Tyr’s hand off.

rows.q: To dispatch the fire-breathing Chimera, Bellerophon tipped his spear with this soft metal, suffocating the beast with its own heat.
rows.n: The monster’s fiery breath melted the lead block, searing its throat and suffocating it.

rows.q: Driven to suicide by madness and shame, Ajax the Great impaled himself on a sword he had received as a gift of honor from this top Trojan champion.
rows.n: Hector had received Ajax’s purple belt in return, which Achilles later used to drag Hector’s body.

rows.q: According to Inuit tradition, walruses, seals, and whales were born when the sea goddess Sedna had these body parts sliced off by her father as she desperately clung to his skin kayak.
rows.n: Because she has no hands, Sedna relies on human shamans to comb lice out of her hair.

rows.q: On his quest along the road to Athens, Theseus eliminated this sadistic innkeeper who forced travelers to fit his iron bed by stretching or amputating them.
rows.n: His punishment gave English the term “procrustean,” describing ruthless enforcement of conformity.

rows.q: In Greek myth, this giant bronze automaton created by Hephaestus guarded Crete until Medea drained his life-giving ichor through a bolt in his ankle.
Greek nymphs fled the woodland god Pan and his rustic pipe tunes. His Roman counterpart, celebrated with purification rituals during the Lupercalia, went by this name.
rows.n: Farmers believed Faunus caused nightmare hallucinations and spoke through forest echoes.

rows.q: The Judgement of Paris began when Eris hurled an apple marked ‘to the fairest’ into the wedding reception of Peleus and this sea nymph.
rows.n: The couple would become the parents of Achilles, whom Thetis famously tried to make immortal.

rows.q: To lure the sun goddess Amaterasu out of the cave where she hid in grief, the Shinto gods threw a noisy party and baited her vanity by hanging this shiny object on a sacred tree.
rows.n: Drawn out to look at her reflection, she was pulled free and light returned to the world.

rows.q: When sprouted dragon teeth became an army of Spartoi warriors, Jason tricked them into slaying each other by hurling this ordinary object.
rows.n: Cadmus used the exact same rock trick when founding Thebes to thin out the dragon-tooth soldiers.

rows.q: The young Irish warrior Setanta earned the name Cu Chulainn after he accidentally killed the ferocious guard hound belonging to this royal blacksmith.
rows.n: To make amends, the boy offered to guard Culann’s estate himself until a new hound could be raised.

rows.q: Charged with slaying the hundred-eyed giant Argus, Hermes put every watchful eye to sleep by playing this reed instrument.
rows.n: After Hermes slew the slumbering giant, Hera placed Argus’s hundred eyes onto the peacock’s feathers.

rows.q: Indigenous Algonquian traditions state that a cannibalistic Wendigo can only be permanently slain by melting this frozen organ.
rows.n: Because the Wendigo is an embodiment of winter starvation, its icy core must be melted by blazing fire.

rows.q: Ares had a savage companion goddess of war named Enyo. Her Roman counterpart was this martial deity, whose name provides the Latin root for the English word “bellicose.”
rows.n: Roman generals were forbidden from bringing armies into the city, so they met the Senate in her temple outside.

rows.q: Marooned on Lemnos for a decade due to a foul-smelling snakebite, this Greek archer had to be retrieved because he held the bow of Heracles.
rows.n: Sophocles wrote a surviving tragedy named after him about Odysseus coming back to fetch him.

rows.q: Russian folklore holds that Koschei the Deathless can only be killed by snapping this small sewing tool hidden inside a nested egg.
rows.n: The egg is inside a duck, which is inside a hare, inside an iron chest buried beneath an oak tree.

rows.q: The gilded herald sounding a trumpet atop the spires of most Latter-day Saint temples depicts which angel, who reportedly revealed the gold plates to Joseph Smith?
rows.n: Mormon tradition holds that Moroni was an ancient American prophet who buried the records around 421 CE.

rows.q: Before reaching the numbered trumps of the Major Arcana, standard decks begin with this wanderer strolling toward a precipice, carrying the number zero.
In 1951, mountaineer Eric Shipton took a famous photo of an enormous ‘Yeti’ footprint while surveying a route up this mountain.
rows.n: Shipton placed his ice axe next to the 13-inch footprint for scale, igniting global interest.

rows.q: In the Gospel of Luke, this wealthy chief tax collector was so short he had to climb a sycamore tree just to see Jesus walk by.
rows.n: After hosting Jesus for dinner, he pledged to give half his wealth to the poor.

rows.q: Sagittarius the archer points his drawn bow straight into the night sky at Antares, a red supergiant nicknamed the heart of this neighboring constellation.
rows.n: The name Antares means ‘rival of Mars,’ due to its striking reddish hue in the summer sky.

rows.q: According to medieval folklore, fairies would secretly kidnap sleeping human infants from their cradles and replace them with sickly, impish substitutes known by what name?
rows.n: Parents were warned not to leave an infant unbaptized or unattended lest a swap occur.

rows.q: Saint Sebastian, a Roman guard martyred under Diocletian, is commonly depicted tied to a post and shot full of these weapons.
rows.n: He survived the arrow wounds, only to be clubbed to death shortly after confronting the emperor.

rows.q: Billabongs and creeks across Australia are said to conceal this amphibious monster, famous in Aboriginal mythology for its nocturnal bellow.
rows.n: Early European colonists in Australia took the stories seriously and mounted search parties.

rows.q: In German weather folklore, immigrants to Pennsylvania originally watched for the shadow of this spiny mammal on Candlemas before drafting the groundhog as a substitute.
rows.n: The German proverb held that if the hedgehog saw his shadow on Candlemas, winter would last six more weeks.

rows.q: In tarot’s Minor Arcana, the four suits are Cups, Swords, Pentacles, and this fiery suit that directly corresponds to the Clubs in an ordinary deck of playing cards.
rows.n: Depending on the deck translation, the suit is also called Rods, Batons, or Staves.

rows.q: In West African and Caribbean storytelling, all the world’s wisdom and folktales were purchased from the sky god by what trickster, often depicted as an eight-legged weaver?
rows.n: He bought the stories by capturing a leopard, hornets, and a python for the sky god Nyame.

rows.q: Astrologers occasionally debate adding a thirteenth zodiac sign between Scorpio and Sagittarius, named for Ophiuchus, who is depicted wrestling with this creature.
rows.n: The name Ophiuchus translates from Greek as ‘serpent-bearer,’ representing the healer Asclepius.

rows.q: Believed extinct for decades, the Arakan forest turtle shares its order with Kurma, the world-supporting second avatar of what major Hindu preserver god?
rows.n: In the churning of the ocean myth, Kurma’s shell served as the pivot foundation for Mount Mandara.

rows.q: Superstitious actors dread the “Scottish play” curse, reinforced in 1947 when an actor playing Macbeth was fatally stabbed in an onstage duel by this Thane of Fife.
rows.n: Harold Norman had reportedly mocked the superstition before the performance; he died from the wound weeks later.

rows.q: In 1560, the foiled Conspiracy of Amboise was organized by members of this French Protestant group seeking to wrest power from the Catholic House of Guise.
rows.n: Hundreds of conspirators were hanged from the ramparts of the Chateau d’Amboise after the plot leaked.

rows.q: Of the twelve classical signs of the Western zodiac, eleven are represented by humans, beasts, or chimeras. Name the only sign symbolized by an inanimate object.
rows.n: Represented by the scales, it was historically viewed by the Greeks as the claws of Scorpius.

rows.q: Urban legend traces Friday the 13th’s unlucky status to October 1307, when France’s King Philip IV arrested scores of knights belonging to this crusading order.
rows.n: Philip accused the Templars of heresy and devil worship, largely to seize their considerable wealth.

rows.q: According to the Great Race myth, cats despise this fellow animal because it tricked them into oversleeping, permanently costing the cat a place in the Chinese zodiac.
rows.n: The rat also rode across the river on the ox’s back before jumping off at the finish to place first.

rows.q: King Herod famously ordered the beheading of John the Baptist after being charmed by the dance of this stepdaughter.
rows.n: Though famous in art and Oscar Wilde’s play, the New Testament never actually names her.

rows.q: Boxing Day falls on December 26, the liturgical feast day of this Biblical deacon who is celebrated in carol as “Good King Wenceslas” looked out and revered as the first Christian martyr.
rows.n: He was stoned to death outside Jerusalem around 34 AD after giving a fiery speech to the Sanhedrin.

rows.q: In classical astrological depictions, the sign Capricorn isn’t just an ordinary goat, but a mythical hybrid sporting the tail and hindquarters of this creature.
rows.n: The sea-goat depiction dates back to Enki, the ancient Sumerian god of water and wisdom.

rows.q: Mortal men in Celtic folklore can force these seal-people to stay on land by stealing and hiding their shed animal skin.
rows.n: If the selkie ever manages to find their hidden pelt, they immediately return to the sea.

rows.q: Jesus performed his very first miracle by turning water into wine at a wedding feast in this Galilean village.
rows.n: At his mother Mary’s prompting, Jesus produced six stone jars filled with fine wine.

rows.q: Starving winter travelers in Algonquian lore risk transforming into this insatiable monster after resorting to cannibalism.
rows.n: Psychiatry coined the term ‘Wendigo psychosis’ for a rare delusion of craving human flesh.

rows.q: A card of sacrifice rather than execution, Major Arcana number XII depicts a haloed figure suspended upside down by only one of this body part.
rows.n: The posture references ‘shame paintings’ in Renaissance Italy, used to publicly humiliate traitors.

rows.q: In Job, God describes this mighty grass-eating beast whose tail moves like a cedar, traditionally viewed in Jewish folklore as ruler of the land.
rows.n: Talmudic lore held that at the end of time, Behemoth and Leviathan would slay one another in a great duel.

rows.q: Jacob worked seven years to marry Rachel, only to wake up the morning after the wedding and find out his uncle had swapped in her older sister, named what?
rows.n: Jacob was allowed to marry Rachel a week later, but had to agree to another seven years of hard labor.

rows.q: Legend says this cryptid of the New Jersey Pine Barrens was born in 1735 as the cursed thirteenth child of a woman named Mother Leeds.
rows.n: In 1909, a wave of sightings caused widespread panic and temporarily closed local schools.

rows.q: Written in 1487 by inquisitor Heinrich Kramer, this notorious Latin treatise on the persecution of witches translates to ‘The Hammer of Witches.’
rows.n: It became a bestseller across Europe despite being formally condemned by the Catholic Church.

rows.q: Slavic and Baltic folklore claims that at the exact midnight stroke of Midsummer’s Eve, this seedless, non-flowering woodland plant magically bursts into a glowing red blossom.
rows.n: Finding the mythical fern flower was said to grant prosperity, animal speech, and the power to find treasure.

rows.q: Commissioned by Pope Damasus I, Saint Jerome spent decades translating the Hebrew and Greek scriptures into Latin, creating this edition.
rows.n: The name comes from versio vulgata, meaning the version in common circulation.

rows.q: Mother Teresa was born in 1910 in the city of Skopje, then part of the Ottoman Empire but today the capital of which Balkan nation?
rows.n: Born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu to Kosovar Albanian parents, she left Skopje at age 18 to join the Sisters of Loreto.

rows.q: Terrified before a battle against the Philistines, King Saul disguised himself to consult a necromancer known as the Witch of this village.
rows.n: George Lucas took the name of the Ewok-inhabited moon in Return of the Jedi from this biblical town.

rows.q: Purim’s triangular hamantaschen are often said to represent the villain Haman’s hat or ears, but the pastry’s Yiddish name originally meant “pockets” filled with these seeds.
rows.n: It originated from the German pastry “Mohntaschen,” combining “Mohn” (poppy seed) and “Taschen” (pockets).

rows.q: To disarm this Japanese water imp, bow deeply so water spills from the cup on its head, or toss it a cucumber to appease it.
rows.n: Cucumber sushi rolls are called kappa maki in Japanese restaurants after this creature.

rows.q: Courtly love latched onto Saint Valentine in 1382, when this English poet wrote in “The Parliament of Fowls” that every bird chooses its mate on Valentine’s Day.
rows.n: The poem was composed in honor of the engagement of King Richard II to Anne of Bohemia.

rows.q: Paul the Apostle earned his living practicing this humble trade, which he shared with his Corinthian friends Aquila and Priscilla.
rows.n: Today the term tentmaking is still used in ministry for pastors who work second jobs.

rows.q: According to Christian tradition, the apostle Thomas traveled farthest to preach the Gospel, ending his life in this Asian country.
rows.n: The Saint Thomas Christians in Kerala trace their origins directly to his arrival in 52 AD.

rows.q: Methuselah is celebrated in Genesis for outliving every other ancestor before the Flood. Give his famously recorded age within five years.
rows.n: His father Enoch lived 365 years before God took him, making him one of the few who never died.

rows.q: A sealed jar unearthed by Egyptian farmers near Nag Hammadi in 1945 preserved thirteen ancient papyrus codices written by what early, heresy-branded mystical sect?
rows.n: The find preserved lost non-canonical texts, including the complete Gospel of Thomas.

rows.q: According to Christian tradition, the three Magi brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Derived from tree resin, myrrh was traditionally utilized in the ancient Near East for this somber purpose.
rows.n: In theological symbolism, myrrh foreshadowed Jesus’s mortality and bodily preparation for the tomb.

rows.q: In traditional Western astrology, Gemini the twins and Virgo the maiden both fall under the patronage and rule of this swift planetary deity.
The Book of Revelation was penned by John while living in exile on this small Greek island in the Aegean Sea.
rows.n: Visitors can still see the Cave of the Apocalypse, where he supposedly had his visions.

rows.q: Munich’s first Oktoberfest in 1810 was a royal wedding celebration that did not feature beer tents at all, but rather reached its grand finale with this athletic spectacle on an open meadow.
rows.n: The meadow was named Theresienwiese in honor of the bride, Princess Therese; the race was won by a coachman.

rows.q: Medieval bestiaries claimed that what arctic bird was not hatched from eggs, but spontaneously grew from driftwood submerged in seawater?
rows.n: Because it was thought not to reproduce by normal flesh, medieval clergy allowed it to be eaten during Lent.

rows.q: Child sacrifices to Moloch once took place in the Valley of Hinnom, a grim reputation that turned its Hebrew name into this synonym for hell.
Set on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, the philosophical dialogue of the Bhagavad Gita forms part of book six of which massive ancient Sanskrit epic?
rows.n: At around 200,000 verse lines, it is roughly ten times the length of the Iliad and Odyssey combined.

rows.q: A fiery pair of brothers, the apostles James and John were nicknamed by Jesus as Sons of this weather phenomenon.
rows.n: In Aramaic, the nickname Jesus gave them was Boanerges.

rows.q: The wealthy Queen of Sheba visited Solomon with gifts of gold and spices; modern historians place her Sabaean kingdom mostly in this Arabian nation.
rows.n: Ancient Saba grew wealthy controlling the frankincense and myrrh caravan trade routes.

rows.q: Scurrying up and down the world tree Yggdrasil to ferry insults between an eagle at the top and a serpent below, the gossiping creature Ratatoskr is what kind of animal?
rows.n: Ratatoskr translates roughly to “drill-tooth” or “bore-tooth” in Old Norse.

rows.q: In the King James Genesis account, God divides the primordial waters above from the waters below on the second day by creating what vaulted expanse of sky?
rows.n: The Hebrew word “raqia” implies a solid dome beaten out like metal, holding back the cosmic deep.

rows.q: Warding off malicious envy across Greece and Turkey, the blue-and-white glass talisman designed like an eyeball is known by this five-letter name.
rows.n: Its full Turkish name is ‘nazar boncugu,’ which translates literally to ‘evil eye bead.’

rows.q: To take on the Midianites, Gideon whittled his massive army down to just this many men, selecting only those who lapped water like dogs.
rows.n: They routed the enemy by blowing trumpets and smashing clay jars to expose burning torches at night.

rows.q: Old-school sailors tattooed these two barnyard animals—one on each foot—as lucky charms against drowning, since neither could swim and gods would take pity.
rows.n: In shipwrecks, crated pigs and roosters often survived because their lightweight wooden coops floated.

rows.q: Monks of the Svetambara tradition in Jainism wear white robes, but those in the Digambara sect wear nothing at all, a name that translates literally to “clad in” what?
rows.n: Digambara monks consider complete renunciation of worldly goods, including clothes, vital to liberation.

rows.q: Times Square’s New Year’s Eve ball drop evolved from 19th-century harbor time balls, which dropped at fixed times so navigators on nearby ships could calibrate this clock.
Catalan tradition sees children feed a wooden log wearing a red beret throughout December, then beat it on Christmas Eve so it will defecate sweets under what name?
rows.n: The name translates to “Christmas log” or “pooping log,” accompanied by a traditional rhyming song.

rows.q: Lunar New Year’s tradition of hanging red paper and setting off firecrackers arose to terrify this legendary beast, who emerged each spring to devour villagers.
rows.n: Passing the new year is called “guo nian” in Chinese, which literally means “surviving the Nian.”

rows.q: The second chimpanzee in space, who completed two orbits in 1961 to clear the way for John Glenn, shared his name with this grandson of Adam and Eve.
rows.n: In the Book of Genesis, Enos was the son of Seth and father of Kenan.

rows.q: While singing in his church choir, 3M employee Art Fry realized Spencer Silver’s weak adhesive could make temporary bookmarks for this specific book.
rows.n: Fry was frustrated that loose paper bookmarks kept slipping out of his hymnal during church services.

rows.q: Thirty-three interactive public information terminals at the 1982 Knoxville World’s Fair gave the public their first hands-on experience with what display input technology?
rows.n: Developed by Elographics, the transparent resistive sensor overlay was mounted over ordinary CRT television monitors.

rows.q: Dramatized in the film Flash of Genius, inventor Robert Kearns sued this Detroit automaker for stealing his patented intermittent windshield wipers, winning millions.
rows.n: His grueling patent fight with Detroit automakers was dramatized in the 2008 film Flash of Genius.

rows.q: Concorde pilots lowered the supersonic airliner’s distinctive droop nose during takeoff and landing for this basic practical reason.
rows.n: The airliner’s steep landing angle meant the raised nose completely blocked the runway from view.

rows.q: In 1852, physicist George Gabriel Stokes coined the term fluorescence after noticing a vibrant glow under ultraviolet light in specimens of this halide mineral.
rows.n: A rare purple-banded ornamental variety found only in Derbyshire, England, is called Blue John.

rows.q: Robert Kearns sued major automakers over his patented intermittent windshield wiper, which he modeled on the motion of this facial feature.
rows.n: Kearns spent decades in court defending his design, a battle dramatized in the film Flash of Genius.

rows.q: Introduced in Sweden in 1952, what two-wheeled vehicle was legally defined by having an engine displacement under 50 cc and pedals for auxiliary propulsion?
rows.n: The word was coined by Swedish journalist Harald Nielsen, combining motor and pedaler.

rows.q: Hans Geiger developed the radiation counter at Manchester under the supervision of this New Zealand-born father of nuclear physics.
rows.n: Walther Muller later improved the sensor tube in 1928, making it the Geiger-Muller counter.

rows.q: Seymour Cray gave his 1976 Cray-1 supercomputer the curved silhouette of which capital letter, both to shorten internal wiring and add bench seating?
rows.n: Keeping the wiring under four feet allowed signals to travel fast enough to break processing records.

rows.q: An exhausting rowboat trip to deliver melting portions of this cold dessert to his fiancée inspired Ole Evinrude to invent the outboard motor.
rows.n: The dessert had turned into soup by the time he arrived, motivating him to motorize small rowboats.

rows.q: Tim Berners-Lee coded the first web browser at CERN in 1990 on an advanced workstation built by which short-lived computer company founded by Steve Jobs?
rows.n: Jobs started NeXT after leaving Apple in 1985; Apple bought it in 1997, turning its OS into macOS.

rows.q: Painter Samuel Morse was in Washington making a portrait of this French hero of the American Revolution when his wife died back home.
rows.n: Word arrived by horse after his wife was already buried, prompting him to pursue instant messaging.

rows.q: Annoyed by smudgy fountain pens, journalist Laszlo Biro filed his first ballpoint pen patent in 1938 while living in this capital city.
rows.n: Biro later fled to Argentina, where ballpoint pens are still known as ‘biromes.’

rows.q: Nolan Bushnell lifted the brand name Atari for his video game venture from a polite warning call, analogous to “check” in chess, used in this ancient Asian board game.
rows.n: In Go, calling “atari” warns your opponent that one or more of their stones is about to be surrounded and captured.

rows.q: Stephanie Kwolek was attempting to develop lightweight tire fibers when she accidentally synthesized Kevlar in 1965 at this Delaware chemical company.
rows.n: Kevlar proved five times stronger than steel by weight and was quickly adapted for military body armor.

rows.q: Lake Mead was formed behind Hoover Dam, but this sprawling reservoir on the Utah-Arizona border formed behind Glen Canyon Dam.
rows.n: Named for John Wesley Powell, the one-armed Civil War vet who first mapped the canyon by boat.

rows.q: James Murray Spangler invented the portable electric vacuum cleaner while trying to ease his asthma while working as this in a store.
rows.n: Spangler sold his patent to his cousin’s husband, William Hoover, a leather-goods maker.

rows.q: Swiss engineer George de Mestral came up with Velcro after examining burrs on his dog. The brand name blends crochet, meaning hook, with this plush French fabric.
rows.n: De Mestral took ten years to perfect the nylon hooks and loops before receiving his patent in 1955.

rows.q: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin watched balloons take flight while serving as an official military observer during this 1860s war.
GPS navigation pioneer Garmin was founded in Kansas in 1989, lifting its portmanteau name from the first names of co-founders Min Kao and this engineer.
rows.n: The pair initially named their startup ProNav, but rebranded to Garmin after a rival firm claimed infringement.

rows.q: Built to outshine Paris’s Eiffel Tower, the original Ferris wheel debuted in 1893 at the World’s Columbian Exposition in this city.
rows.n: It could carry over 2,000 passengers at once across 36 wooden cars.

rows.q: In 1939, Hewlett-Packard made its first big sale from a Palo Alto garage, supplying Walt Disney with eight audio oscillators to test surround sound for this film.
rows.n: Disney used the gear to develop Fantasound, an early precursor to modern cinematic surround sound.

rows.q: In 1943, naval engineer Richard James accidentally created the Slinky after knocking a tension spring off a shelf while designing stabilizers for these vessels.
rows.n: James watched the fallen spring step end over end across a stack of books and onto the floor.

rows.q: The Oresund Bridge famously carries cars and trains between Copenhagen, Denmark, and this coastal Swedish city.
rows.n: The crossing transitions halfway into an underwater tunnel so it won’t block planes using Copenhagen Airport.

rows.q: Boston dentist William Morton tried to privatize anesthesia under the trade name Letheon, concealing that his miracle gas was simply this volatile, sweet-smelling liquid.
rows.n: Morton’s attempt to corner the market on painless surgery led to lifelong legal battles with former partners.

rows.q: John Roebling tested his pioneering wire cable design on an 1866 Ohio River suspension bridge linking Covington, Kentucky, with this major city.
rows.n: With a 1,057-foot span, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world until Roebling surpassed it in Brooklyn.

rows.q: While building Cambridge’s EDSAC in 1949, Maurice Wilkes realized with sudden dread that a large part of his future life would be spent doing this to code.
rows.n: He wrote in his memoirs that the cold realization hit him as he was walking up the laboratory stairs.

rows.q: In 1838, computing pioneer Charles Babbage took a detour into rail safety by inventing this wedge-shaped metal grill for locomotive fronts.
rows.n: Babbage called it a pilot, designed to deflect livestock and debris without derailing the train.

rows.q: Engineers redesigned Japan’s bullet train nose to eliminate sonic booms upon exiting tunnels, modeling its shape on the beak of this bird.
rows.n: The kingfisher dives cleanly from air into water with almost no splash, inspiring the train’s design.

rows.q: Instead of calculating artillery tables, ENIAC’s first live test run in late 1945 evaluated the feasibility of what weapon designed at Los Alamos?
rows.n: Edward Teller traveled to Philadelphia to pore over the million punch cards generated by the run.

rows.q: The Pont du Gard in southern France is a towering Roman aqueduct that once carried spring water into this ancient city, whose name lives on in denim fabric.
rows.n: Denim gets its name from serge de Nimes, a sturdy twill fabric made in the city.

rows.q: When Rudolf Diesel demonstrated his revolutionary new engine at the 1900 Paris Exposition, he ran it not on petroleum, but oil from this legume.
rows.n: Diesel believed his engine would empower farmers by letting them produce their own homegrown fuel.

rows.q: The punched cards used in Joseph Marie Jacquard’s 1804 automated loom directly inspired Charles Babbage’s designs for this mechanical computer.
rows.n: Ada Lovelace noted that the engine ‘weaves algebraic patterns just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers.’

rows.q: A dropped glass flask coated with dried cellulose led Édouard Bénédictus to invent safety glass, which was quickly adapted in World War I for eyepieces in this gear.
rows.n: Car companies adopted safety glass widely after Henry Ford put it in Model A windshields in 1927.

rows.q: Chemist John Walker refused to patent his 1826 friction match because it was too useful, allowing rival Samuel Jones to copy it under this devilish brand name.
rows.n: Walker believed his friction match was too beneficial to patent, leaving others to profit off the idea.

rows.q: Teenaged Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline calculator in the 1640s to help his father with his exhausting day job as one of these officials.
rows.n: His father was appointed by Cardinal Richelieu as the king’s commissioner of taxes in Rouen.

rows.q: The Firth of Forth rail bridge in Scotland is a massive, soot-red landmark famous for utilizing this structural truss design featuring projecting arms.
rows.n: Engineers demonstrated the design using human models sitting on chairs holding wooden poles.

rows.q: Modern aircraft wings generate lift via a fluid dynamics principle published in the 1738 treatise Hydrodynamica by which member of a legendary Swiss mathematical dynasty?
rows.n: He devised the St. Petersburg paradox, showing that people will only pay a small sum to enter an infinite-payoff game.

rows.q: After an active radar magnetron melted a chocolate peanut bar in his pocket, Percy Spencer patented the microwave oven for this Massachusetts defense contractor.
rows.n: The first commercial microwave Spencer built in 1947 was nearly six feet tall and weighed 750 pounds.

rows.q: Larry Page and Sergey Brin originally nicknamed their Stanford search engine this anatomical compound word because it crawled web backlinks.
rows.n: BackRub’s web crawler ran on Stanford’s private servers until it hogged too much bandwidth in 1996.

rows.q: Originally founded in 1940s Hawaii to supply coin-op games to military bases, Sega derived its brand name from an abbreviation of which two words?
rows.n: The company moved to Tokyo in the 1950s and officially shortened its name to Sega Enterprises in 1965.

rows.q: Gates and Allen didn’t start Microsoft in Seattle or the Bay Area, but in this southwestern city, setting up shop near early microcomputer manufacturer MITS.
rows.n: Microsoft was headquartered in Albuquerque from 1975 to 1979 before relocating home to Washington state.

rows.q: The black box flight recorder was invented in 1953 by David Warren after investigating deadly crashes of this de Havilland commercial jet.
rows.n: Square passenger windows created stress points that caused early Comets to break up mid-flight.

rows.q: To build the Brooklyn Bridge’s massive stone towers, workers dug out river mud inside pressurized wooden boxes called these, suffering mysterious crippling cramps upon returning to the surface.
rows.n: The illness, then called caisson disease, is what divers now know as the bends or decompression sickness.

rows.q: Alan Turing proposed his famous test for machine thinking in a 1950 paper titled Computing Machinery and this quality.
rows.n: Turing originally framed the challenge as the ‘Imitation Game,’ which titled a 2014 biopic.

rows.q: John Harrison’s breakthrough marine chronometer H4, which solved the maritime longitude problem in 1761, was an oversized version of this item.
rows.n: Harrison replaced pendulum mechanisms with a balance spring that remained accurate on turbulent seas.

rows.q: Invented in 1948 by Ralph Teetor, automotive cruise control was made even more remarkable by this sensory condition Teetor had lived with since youth.
rows.n: Irritated by his lawyer’s jerky driving habits, Teetor used his refined sense of touch to build the prototype.

rows.q: Blackboard sketches drawn by a 14-year-old Utah farm boy helped this independent inventor defeat RCA in a grueling patent battle over electronic television.
rows.n: Farnsworth conceived the idea of scanning an image line by line while plowing a potato field in parallel rows.

rows.q: Invented in the 1890s at a British military arsenal near Calcutta, this expanding soft-point bullet was outlawed for international warfare in 1899.
rows.n: The 1899 Hague Declaration specifically prohibited bullets that expand or flatten easily in the human body.

rows.q: When mutineers seized HMS Bounty in 1789, they took the K2, an ultra-precise navigation timepiece built by Larcum Kendall based on the marine chronometer designed by what English horologist?
rows.n: Harrison’s H4 chronometer solved the longitude problem; the Bounty’s stolen K2 copy is now in a Greenwich museum.

rows.q: Hatmakers Thomas and William Bowler created their stiff-crowned bowler hat in 1849 specifically to protect the heads of men in this estate job.
rows.n: The design kept low-hanging branches from knocking hats off while riding horseback.

rows.q: Master Chief’s AI companion Cortana gets her name from Curtana, a legendary blunt blade that forms part of the coronation regalia of which European monarchy?
rows.n: Curtana is also known as the Sword of Mercy, traditionally carried before the British sovereign.

rows.q: In The Legend of Zelda series, the sacred Triforce is composed of three golden triangles representing three essential virtues: Courage, Wisdom, and this attribute claimed by Ganon.
rows.n: Courage belongs to Link and Wisdom to Princess Zelda, maintaining balance across the realm of Hyrule.

rows.q: Jeff Bezos initially registered Amazon under the magical name Cadabra, but abandoned it when his lawyer misheard the moniker as this grim word.
rows.n: Bezos also registered Relentless.com in 1994, which still redirects straight to the Amazon homepage.

rows.q: Months before hosting home videos and skate tricks, YouTube was launched on Valentine’s Day 2005 with the slogan ‘Tune in, Hook up’ as this type of site.
rows.n: Co-founder Jawed Karim admitted not a single user uploaded a dating video, so they opened it to all clips.

rows.q: The uncanny 1990s Dancing Baby animation hit mainstream television as a recurring biological-clock hallucination for this Fox title lawyer.
rows.n: Calista Flockhart played the neurotic Boston attorney across five seasons.

rows.q: In 1996’s Super Mario 64, executing three properly timed running hops in rapid sequence sends Mario into a high somersault via what maneuver?
rows.n: Mario shouts ‘Yahoo!’ when executing the leap, which allows him to clear otherwise impassable gaps.

rows.q: In a cruel twist of startup fate, the founder of this pioneering 1990s dating site lost his girlfriend to a man she met on his own platform.
rows.n: Gary Kremen launched Match.com in 1995, requiring all company employees to create active personal profiles.

rows.q: After single-handedly wiping out his World of Warcraft guild in a legendary 2005 video, Leeroy Jenkins famously consoled himself by announcing he at least had this food.
rows.n: His guildmates later admitted the entire chaotic raid had been staged for fun.

rows.q: Software tools like Dolphin and MAME rely on what computing process, allowing modern hardware to mimic the architecture of retro consoles and arcade cabinets?
rows.n: Emulation differs from simulation by recreating a target system’s exact internal hardware behavior.

rows.q: Originally pitched as a bodyguard adventure, the first Assassin’s Creed was developed as a spin-off to which acrobatic Ubisoft series?
rows.n: The working title was “Prince of Persia: Assassins,” with Altaïr protecting an AI prince.

rows.q: Decades before the web, visionary Ted Nelson coined the term ‘hypertext’ and began designing a utopian network named after what Coleridge pleasure-dome?
rows.n: Nelson founded Project Xanadu in 1960; its first official software release didn’t arrive until 2014.

rows.q: Grateful Dead lyricist John Perry Barlow co-founded the Electronic Frontier Foundation and in 1996 issued a defiant ‘Declaration of the Independence of’ what realm?
rows.n: Barlow typed out the famous anti-regulation manifesto while attending the World Economic Forum in Davos.

rows.q: Mario’s fire-breathing arch-nemesis Koopa was named after gukbap, a hearty beef-and-rice soup from which country’s cuisine?
rows.n: Miyamoto loved visiting Korean barbecue restaurants in Japan and picked names from their menus.

rows.q: While planning the crossover Kingdom Hearts, Square executives wanted Mickey Mouse as the lead, while Disney pushed for this ill-tempered sailor to take the starring role.
rows.n: Director Tetsuya Nomura rejected both suggestions and designed the human hero Sora instead.

rows.q: Garrett Camp conceived the rideshare giant Uber after getting stuck paying an $800 private chauffeur bill to get home on this specific holiday evening.
rows.n: Camp and Travis Kalanick launched UberCab in San Francisco in 2010 to split the cost of black-car rides.

rows.q: Decades before it became a standard Linux archive format, the .tar file format was created in 1979 to write files sequentially to magnetic spools of this medium.
rows.n: “Tar” stands for Tape Archive, built for Unix tape-backup drives.

rows.q: In 1989, Nintendo filed a federal lawsuit against this video rental giant, claiming that photocopying game instruction manuals for rental customers was copyright infringement.
rows.n: The dispute was settled out of court, with Blockbuster agreeing not to photocopy Nintendo’s copyrighted manuals.

rows.q: Before modern chatbots, Joseph Weizenbaum created the conversational program ELIZA at MIT in the 1960s, naming it after a heroine from what George Bernard Shaw play?
rows.n: Like Eliza Doolittle learning upper-class diction, the computer was taught to simulate human speech.

rows.q: Now valued in the billions, this blocky multiplayer gaming platform launched in beta in 2004 under the clunkier name DynaBlocks.
rows.n: Co-founders David Baszucki and Erik Cassel created the final name by mashing ‘robots’ and ‘blocks’ together.

rows.q: The term “rickroll” took off in 2007 when 4chan users posting fake links to the first trailer for this 2008 Rockstar Games crime epic sent viewers to Rick Astley instead.
John Carmack titled the groundbreaking shooter Doom after a scene in which 1986 pool-hall movie, where Tom Cruise is asked what is in his cue case?
rows.n: Carmack loved Cruise’s cocky delivery of the word and felt it fit the game’s disruptive tech.

rows.q: MIT named its beginner visual language after a hip-hop DJ technique of manipulating vinyl records back and forth on a turntable. What is the language?
rows.n: Just like DJs mix different music clips, Scratch lets users snap code blocks together.

rows.q: The thundering phrase “Fus Ro Dah”—an Unrelenting Force shout that blasted enemies off cliffs—spawned countless remix videos from this 2011 Bethesda RPG.
rows.n: In the game’s dragon language, the words translate to Force, Balance, and Push.

rows.q: Before the web eclipsed it, the dominant internet information protocol was Gopher, created in 1991 and named after the rodent mascot of what Big Ten school?
rows.n: Gopher was displaced after the university announced it would charge licensing fees for commercial use.

rows.q: Nintendo created Jumpman and Donkey Kong only after failing to secure a license to make an arcade game starring this spinach-fueled cartoon sailor.
rows.n: Shigeru Miyamoto substituted Jumpman for Popeye, Pauline for Olive Oyl, and Donkey Kong for Bluto.

rows.q: A clumsy military funeral prompt in 2014’s Advanced Warfare inspired the meme “Press F to pay respects” in this blockbuster shooter franchise.
rows.n: PC players literally had to press the F key to touch a fallen soldier’s casket.

rows.q: At the 1991 Consumer Electronics Show, Nintendo stunned the industry by abandoning its CD-ROM deal with Sony to announce a partnership with this Dutch electronics titan instead.
rows.n: The ill-fated alliance yielded the Philips CD-i and four notoriously terrible Nintendo-licensed spin-off games.

rows.q: In what 2001 browser MMORPG developed by Jagex do players explore the realm of Gielinor, train skills like woodcutting, and trade on the Grand Exchange?
rows.n: The game once held the Guinness World Record for the most updated MMORPG in history.

rows.q: Nintendo legend Gunpei Yokoi got the idea for the Game & Watch handheld line after watching an office worker kill time on a bullet train by fidgeting with one of these desk devices.
rows.n: Yokoi pitched the idea to Nintendo CEO Hiroshi Yamauchi during a car ride, leading to the 1980 launch of Ball.

rows.q: Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger launched Wikipedia in 2001 primarily as a speedy draft-feeder for this earlier, strictly peer-reviewed encyclopedia.
rows.n: Nupedia had a strict seven-stage approval process and approved fewer than 25 articles before shutting down.

rows.q: Borland code-named its Pascal visual programming environment Delphi because it was built to connect smoothly to a database system made by which tech giant?
rows.n: Chief developer Danny Thorpe quipped, “If you want to talk to the Oracle, go to Delphi.”

rows.q: Mosaic, the graphical browser that brought the web to the masses in 1993, was developed at NCSA on the campus of what Big Ten university?
rows.n: Co-creator Marc Andreessen soon left the school to found Netscape with venture capitalist Jim Clark.

rows.q: “All your base are belong to us” became one of the web’s first viral catchphrases thanks to the botched English translation of this 1989 arcade shooter.
rows.n: The bad translation only appeared in the 1991 European Sega Mega Drive port.

rows.q: Scorpion’s terrifying battle cry “Get over here!” in the original Mortal Kombat games was voiced by this co-creator of the franchise.
rows.n: Boon holds a Guinness World Record for the longest-serving video game voice actor for that single line.

rows.q: At the inaugural E3 in 1995, after Sega announced the Saturn was launching immediately for $399, Sony’s Steve Race delivered a famous one-sentence keynote consisting only of this price.
rows.n: Race walked up to the podium, said “$299,” and immediately walked off, stealing all momentum from Sega’s launch.

rows.q: In 1993, id Software packed all the graphics and levels for Doom into archive files with this three-letter extension, short for “Where’s All the Data?”
rows.n: John Carmack designed the WAD format so fans could easily modify and build levels.

rows.q: Internet celebrity Grumpy Cat got her signature scowl from feline dwarfism, but she had this culinary real name inspired by a condiment.
Nobuo Uematsu assembled the haunting choir lyrics for Sephiroth’s theme, “One-Winged Angel,” by pulling Latin verses from this medieval poetry collection.
rows.n: Carl Orff famously set the same collection to music in 1936, including “O Fortuna.”

rows.q: Developed in 1990 by Alan Emtage, the world’s first internet search engine, Archie, was built while he was a student and sysadmin at what Montreal university?
rows.n: Archie didn’t index web pages; it indexed downloadable files hosted across anonymous FTP sites.

rows.q: Before Sonic replaced it in 1991, the Sega Genesis launched in North America bundled with this arcade beat-‘em-up about a centurion resurrected by Zeus.
rows.n: The game’s scratchy digitized voice line “Rise from your grave!” became an early showcase for Genesis audio.

rows.q: Computer scientist Steve Wilhite created the ubiquitous GIF format in 1987 while working for what pioneering online service provider based in Ohio?
rows.n: Wilhite famously asserted before his death that the acronym is pronounced with a soft ‘g,’ like Jif.

rows.q: The Super Nintendo outclassed the Genesis in audio thanks to its SPC700 sound chip, secretly engineered by Ken Kutaragi while on the payroll of this future rival.
rows.n: Sony executives were furious when they discovered Kutaragi moonlighting, but CEO Norio Ohga let him finish the chip.

rows.q: The web’s first clickable banner ad appeared on HotWired in 1994. What telecom giant paid for it, cheekily asking, ‘Have you ever clicked your mouse right here? You will’?
rows.n: An astonishing 44% of people who saw the primitive banner ad actually clicked through.

rows.q: Stewart Butterfield is a master of the pivot: he built Slack out of a failed video game, but previously created this photo-sharing hub out of another one.
rows.n: Butterfield was building an MMORPG called Game Neverending before spinning off its photo-saving feature.

rows.q: In 1992, Sega orchestrated the first synchronized global video game launch for Sonic’s sequel, coining this rhyming weekday pun in its multimillion-dollar ad blitz.
rows.n: Before Sonic 2sday on November 24, 1992, video games were shipped irregularly to retailers without strict street dates.

rows.q: Valve’s crowbar-wielding protagonist Gordon Freeman inherited his surname from which visionary physicist, famed for his hypothetical star-encasing megastructures?
Alexis Ohanian doodled Reddit’s alien mascot Snoo during college classes, deriving the creature’s name from a quick slur of this three-word question.
rows.n: Ohanian sketched Snoo in his notebook at UVA; the site was originally envisioned as the front page of what’s new.

rows.q: The snarky closing anthems “Still Alive” and “Want You Gone” from Valve’s Portal games were both penned by which internet-famous comedy folk musician?
rows.n: Coulton was hired after Valve game designers attended one of his concerts in Seattle.

rows.q: Packet switching, the bedrock of ARPANET, was independently conceived in the 1960s by Donald Davies and Paul Baran, who worked at what Santa Monica think tank?
rows.n: Baran was tasked with designing a telecommunications network capable of surviving a nuclear strike.

rows.q: Before a blue hedgehog took over in 1991, Sega’s unofficial company mascot was this big-eared kid who had to win games of rock-paper-scissors to beat bosses.
rows.n: His built-in Master System adventure, Alex Kidd in Miracle World, was Sega’s primary weapon against Mario in the 80s.

rows.q: Ron Gilbert created the adventure game scripting engine SCUMM for a 1987 Lucasfilm title, giving it an acronym that ended with the name of this creepy house.
rows.n: SCUMM stood for “Script Creation Utility for Maniac Mansion.”

rows.q: NES players had to shoot arrows to kill the bunny-like Pols Voice, but in Japan, players screamed at them using this feature built directly into Controller 2 of the Famicom.
rows.n: The microphone was cut from the Western NES controller, making the Japanese instruction manual’s advice useless.

rows.q: Marketer Gary Thuerk earned infamy in 1978 by sending the first ARPANET spam email, pitching a line of mainframe computers built by what Massachusetts company?
rows.n: The blast generated millions in sales of DEC-20 systems, even as the defense department scolded him.

rows.q: During the 1993 congressional hearings on violent video games, Sega was grilled over Mortal Kombat and this full-motion video game about a teenage sleepover besieged by vampires.
rows.n: Nintendo VP Howard Lincoln smugly claimed the game would never appear on a Nintendo system. It arrived on Switch in 2018.

rows.q: Trademark battles forced Mozilla to abandon the browser name Phoenix, after which they briefly adopted this second fiery avian moniker before settling on Firefox.
rows.n: An open-source database project already named Firebird complained loudly, forcing Mozilla to rebrand again.

rows.q: Andy Rubin didn’t build Android for phones: he and his co-founders originally designed the mobile OS to run inside these handheld devices.
rows.n: Rubin pivoted to mobile phones in 2004 after realizing the stand-alone digital camera market was shrinking.

rows.q: Kevin Systrom didn’t set out to build a photo platform: Instagram began life as a check-in app named for his favorite style of American whiskey.
rows.n: Systrom spelled it Burbn, but stripped out all the check-in tools once he noticed users loved the photo filters.

rows.q: Despite being classified as an “Electric Mouse” in the Pokedex, designer Atsuko Nishida revealed Pikachu’s look and cheek pouches were actually based on this rodent.
Blizzard Entertainment was founded in 1991 under this six-syllable name, which cleverly paired a chemical element with a biological nerve junction.
rows.n: Founders Michael Morhaime and Allen Adham briefly tried Chaos Studios before settling on Blizzard in 1994.

rows.q: In March 1985, the very first commercial .com domain name was registered to what Massachusetts computer firm, famous for building specialized Lisp machines?
rows.n: Symbolics.com was registered years before the web existed, remaining active under the original firm until 2009.

rows.q: Introduced in 1961 to replace the pound, South Africa’s currency, the rand, takes its name from a geological ridge famous for deposits of this metal.
rows.n: The Witwatersrand ridge near Johannesburg was the site of the 1886 gold rush that transformed the region.

rows.q: Panama does not print paper money, but mints coins called balboas, named for the first European explorer to reach this body of water.
rows.n: Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama in 1513, claiming the ocean and its shores for Spain.

rows.q: In 1988, this southern hemisphere country became the first to issue polymer plastic banknotes, commemorating its bicentenary with a ten-dollar bill.
rows.n: Developed by the CSIRO and the central bank, the polymer technology has since been exported to dozens of nations.

rows.q: Sales of this popular 1970s appetite-suppressant candy plummeted by 50% in the mid-1980s because its brand name was an exact homophone of a terrifying public health crisis.
rows.n: The manufacturer tried rebranding the product as Diet Ayds before giving up completely.

rows.q: Henry Ford’s prefabricated Amazonian company town fell into ruin after fungal blights devastated his plantation of what industrial resource?
rows.n: Monoculture planting invited South American leaf blight, destroying Ford’s attempt to dodge British rubber cartels.

rows.q: Before he led the free world, this future U.S. president appeared in print ads in the 1940s and 50s touting the crisp comfort of Chesterfield cigarettes.
rows.n: He sent cartons of Chesterfields to friends as Christmas gifts with his personal endorsement on the sleeve.

rows.q: Designed to evoke both Europe and the cradle of civilization, the official symbol for the euro currency is based on this Greek letter.
rows.n: Officially designed by a team under Arthur Eisenmenger, the two parallel lines represent monetary stability.

rows.q: Designer Rob Janoff added a bite to the side of the Apple logo to give it scale, so customers wouldn’t mistake the fruit for this smaller, pitted one.
rows.n: Janoff confirmed the bite also prevented it from looking like a tomato.

rows.q: That twin-tailed, crowned sea creature on the green Starbucks logo is not a generic mermaid, but this mythical beast known for luring sailors to ruin.
rows.n: The original 1971 brown logo was based on a 16th-century Norse woodcut and featured bare breasts.

rows.q: The original Waldorf-Astoria Hotel was demolished in 1929 to clear land for what iconic Art Deco skyscraper that opened two years later?
rows.n: The new Waldorf Astoria reopened in 1931 on Park Avenue, where it became the world’s tallest hotel.

rows.q: Sony’s founders combined the Latin word for sound with this 1950s American slang term for a sharp young man, chosen because they saw themselves as energetic, modern upstarts.
rows.n: Akio Morita dropped the second “n” because in romanized Japanese, “son-ny” sounded like a phrase for losing money.

rows.q: Constantly rejected for having “good taste” instead of tasting good, this beret-wearing spokes-fish spent decades pitching StarKist tuna.
Flying over the Florida Straits to deliver airmail in 1927, Pan American Airways made its first scheduled international flight from Key West to which Caribbean capital?
rows.n: The flight covered 90 miles in an amphibious monoplane to meet a U.S. postal contract deadline.

rows.q: Miss Chiquita debuted in 1944 wearing a towering fruit hat inspired by the extravagant stage costumes of this “Brazilian Bombshell” performer.
rows.n: Miss Chiquita was initially animated as an upright banana before becoming a human woman in 1987.

rows.q: Japanese optical firm Canon debuted its first camera in 1934 as the “Kwanon,” naming the device after a multi-armed bodhisattva of mercy revered in this world religion.
rows.n: The original camera logo showed Kwanon surrounded by flames with a thousand hands holding various treasures.

rows.q: While most EU members have adopted the euro, Poland still uses this historic national currency, whose name literally translates to ‘golden.’
rows.n: Introduced under King Sigismund I in the 16th century, it was originally pegged to 30 Prussian groschen.

rows.q: Formed in 1925 by the merger of Holt and C.L. Best, this machinery manufacturer trademarked its brand name after an onlooker said its tractors crawled.
rows.n: The company officially adopted its iconic ‘Hi-Way Yellow’ color scheme on its equipment in 1931.

rows.q: The carmaker Subaru borrows its name from the Japanese term for this celestial cluster, which is why its metallic grille badge features six prominent stars.
rows.n: While Western astronomy traditionally counts seven sisters, classical Japanese tradition sees only six with the eye.

rows.q: Netflix shed nearly a million subscribers in 2011 after CEO Reed Hastings announced a disastrous plan to spin off its DVD-by-mail service under this short-lived moniker.
rows.n: Facing customer outrage, Hastings scrapped the split just 23 days after announcing it.

rows.q: Pasadena grocer Joe Coulombe sold his chain Trader Joe’s in 1979 to German billionaire Theo Albrecht, the co-founder of which low-cost supermarket giant?
rows.n: Aldi split into North and South in 1961 over a dispute between brothers about whether to sell cigarettes.

rows.q: Replacing the peso in the 1890s, the national currencies of both Costa Rica and El Salvador were named in honor of this Italian-born explorer.
rows.n: El Salvador replaced its colón with the U.S. dollar in 2001, but Costa Rica still uses the currency.

rows.q: Founded in New York in 1905, what kosher deli brand famously advertised its all-beef hot dogs with the slogan “We answer to a higher authority”?
rows.n: Conagra acquired the brand in 1993 but kept the strict Orthodox rabbinical certification.

rows.q: Japanese electronics maker Sharp took its corporate name from an invention by founder Tokuji Hayakawa: a 1915 mechanical version of this everyday writing implement.
rows.n: Hayakawa called his product the “Ever-Ready Sharp Pencil”; the company pivoted to radios after an earthquake.

rows.q: Southwest Airlines co-founders Herb Kelleher and Rollin King famously sketched their initial triangle route on a napkin, linking Dallas, Houston, and which other Texas city?
rows.n: Legal challenges from rival carriers kept Southwest grounded for four years before its first flight in 1971.

rows.q: The lavish Savoy Hotel in London was built in 1889 by Richard D’Oyly Carte, funding the project with his profits producing the comic operas of which Victorian duo?
rows.n: He built the hotel right next to the Savoy Theatre, where their works like The Mikado premiered.

rows.q: Founded in 1764 with the permission of King Louis XV, this luxury French crystal manufacturer takes its name from the commune in Grand Est where its kilns still operate.
rows.n: During the 1855 Paris Exposition, the company amazed crowds with a pair of 17-foot crystal candelabras.

rows.q: American slang for a five-dollar bill, a ‘fin,’ does not come from fish, but from the word for five in this Germanic language.
rows.n: The Yiddish word finf evolved into underworld slang in Germany and Britain before jumping across the Atlantic.

rows.q: Delta Air Lines took flight in the 1920s as Huff Daland Dusters, a crop-dusting outfit formed to protect Southern cotton crops from what notorious beetle?
rows.n: Cotton farmers were desperate; the beetle crossed the Rio Grande in the 1890s and devastated yields.

rows.q: Formed in 1982 and acquired by Mastercard in 1988, what interbank network connects ATMs worldwide under a logo of two overlapping blue circles?
rows.n: It was founded by a bank consortium that included Mellon Bank, NBD, and First Interstate Bancorp.

rows.q: On The Big Bang Theory, Dr. Bernadette Rostenkowski out-earns her aerospace engineer husband Howard by landing a lucrative research job in what corporate industry?
rows.n: Her company, the fictional Zangen Enterprises, frequently tested questionable weight-loss drugs.

rows.q: Following the deadly 1996 Everglades crash of Flight 592, disgraced discount carrier ValuJet salvaged its business by acquiring and adopting the name of which airline?
rows.n: The combined company operated under the AirTran name until Southwest acquired it in 2011.

rows.q: British computing pioneer Sir Clive Sinclair lost his personal fortune in 1985 on this notorious, pedal-assisted electric trike that critics mocked as a low-riding death trap.
rows.n: Drivers sat just inches off the tarmac, making them virtually invisible to truck and bus drivers.

rows.q: Coca-Cola launched this deliberately bland clear cola in 1992 as a “kamikaze” product, designed to confuse consumers and kill off Crystal Pepsi in its cradle.
rows.n: Coke’s marketing chief Sergio Zyman intentionally designed it to fail and take Pepsi’s drink down with it.

rows.q: Swedish automaker Volvo registered its trademark in 1915 for a new line of ball bearings. In Latin, what two-word first-person declaration does the brand name literally translate to?
rows.n: Volvo was originally created as a subsidiary of the major Swedish ball-bearing manufacturer SKF.

rows.q: Long before finding success with the iPad, Apple partnered with Japanese toymaker Bandai in 1996 to release this commercial disaster of a multimedia home game console.
rows.n: Priced at an exorbitant $600, it sold fewer than 50,000 units before Steve Jobs pulled the plug.

rows.q: Hoping to distance its holding company from tobacco lawsuits and smoking stigmas in 2003, Philip Morris Companies rebranded under this name, derived from the Latin for “high.”
rows.n: Branding firm Landor Associates coined the name from the Latin word “altus.”

rows.q: Carl Sagan’s team begged to include ‘Here Comes the Sun’ on the Golden Record, but this British record label behind the Beatles refused to clear the rights.
rows.n: All four Beatles gave their blessing to send the track into deep space, but EMI demanded an exorbitant royalty fee.

rows.q: Graphic designer Irina Blok modeled the little green robot logo for Google’s Android operating system on the universal pictograms found on doors to these rooms.
rows.n: Blok made the design open-source, allowing users to modify and customize the little green mascot.

rows.q: Months before its parent firm Arthur Andersen collapsed in the Enron scandal, its spun-off IT consulting arm rebranded on New Year’s Day 2001 to this portmanteau.
rows.n: A Danish employee suggested the name, blending “accent” and “future.”

rows.q: Station agent Richard Sears launched his mail-order empire in 1886 by buying and reselling a shipment of what unwanted items delivered to his depot by mistake?
rows.n: He teamed up with watchmaker Alvah Roebuck the following year, expanding from timepieces into catalog retail.

rows.q: Before a 1981 tornado hit its flagship store and sparked a cut-rate sale, Best Buy operated as an audio retailer named for which classic 1965 musical movie?
rows.n: The tornado sale brought in so much cash that founder Richard Schulze retooled the business model.

rows.q: Toy company Mattel got its moniker as a portmanteau of its founders: Harold “Matt” Matson and this inventor who supplied the back half of the name.
rows.n: Handler’s wife Ruth co-founded the firm and famously created Barbie, naming the doll after their daughter.

rows.q: Introduced in 1911 as a breakthrough water-in-oil cosmetic cream, Nivea derived its brand name from a Latin adjective describing the pure color of this winter weather feature.
rows.n: The Latin word “niveus” means snow-white, describing the unblemished look of the whipped emulsion.

rows.q: Decades before its mocked pastel pens “for Her,” Bic lost millions in 1989 attempting to sell disposable, lighter-sized spray bottles of this luxury cosmetic product.
rows.n: Shoppers found the idea of drugstore bargain perfume unappealing, and Bic dropped it within two years.

rows.q: The Republic of Molossia, a micronation based in the Nevada desert, pegs the value of its official currency to pre-made tubes of chocolate chip cookie dough made by this brand.
rows.n: Molossia also claims an ongoing, bloodless state of war against East Germany, dating back to 1983.

rows.q: The Oscar-nominated stop-motion studio behind Coraline and ParaNorman was named after space dog Laika by its owner, a co-founder of this sportswear giant.
rows.n: Nike co-founder Phil Knight bought Will Vinton Studios in 2002 and rebranded it as Laika in 2005.

rows.q: Folgers famously claimed ‘The best part of wakin’ up is Folgers in your cup.’ In their notorious 2009 holiday ad, Peter returns home from volunteering in this continent.
rows.n: The ad developed a bizarre internet cult following due to perceived romantic tension between the siblings.

rows.q: Wheaties dubbed itself the “Breakfast of Champions” in the 1930s, placing this New York Yankees first baseman on the box as its very first athlete.
rows.n: Gehrig appeared on the back of the box in 1934; athletes didn’t make the front until 1958.

rows.q: Before Alexander Hamilton took over the ten-dollar bill, the Roman numeral X printed on the back earned it this nickname, after a log-sawing frame.
rows.n: The term originated in the 1850s, while a twenty-dollar bill was occasionally called a double sawbuck.

rows.q: Prior to adopting its iconic brass bell in 1903, the New York Stock Exchange struck this metallic percussion instrument to signal the close of trade.
rows.n: A Chinese gong was struck until the ringing bell proved louder and more durable for the expanding trading floor.

rows.q: Introduced by the CBOE in 1993, this three-letter volatility index is widely known on trading desks as Wall Street’s ‘fear gauge.’
rows.n: It tracks options on the S&P 500 index to measure market expectations of 30-day forward volatility.

rows.q: Fashion watchmaker Fossil was named by founders Tom and Kosta Kartsotis as an affectionate, ribbing family nickname for what specific relative of theirs?
rows.n: The brothers started the Dallas-based accessories giant in 1984 under the name Overseas Products International.

rows.q: First opened in Massachusetts in 1963, the pharmacy chain CVS originally stood for these three words promising bargain retail therapy.
rows.n: The chain operated purely as a discount health and beauty store for several years before adding pharmacies.

rows.q: Codenamed “Project Pink” and marketed aggressively to social-media-obsessed teens, this mobile phone lasted just 48 days before Microsoft pulled the plug in 2010.
rows.n: Verizon returned almost all of its stock after selling fewer than 10,000 units.

rows.q: Barred from using his own surname for a new car firm, August Horch created the Audi brand by translating his last name into Latin, which is an imperative command meaning what in English?
rows.n: The four interlocking rings on Audi’s logo represent the 1932 merger of Audi, DKW, Horch, and Wanderer.

rows.q: Many European stock exchanges use the word ‘Bourse,’ which traces back to a 13th-century inn run by the Van der Beurse family in this Belgian city.
rows.n: The family’s coat of arms featured three leather purses, creating an enduring pun for financial exchange.

rows.q: In 1975, musician Brian Eno and artist Peter Schmidt published what deck of cards bearing cryptic prompts meant to help creatives resolve lateral dilemmas?
rows.n: David Bowie relied heavily on the card prompts while recording his Berlin Trilogy albums.

rows.q: After creating the Game Boy and producing Metroid, which legendary Nintendo engineer saw his stellar career derailed by the red-tinted 1995 flop of the Virtual Boy?
rows.n: Yokoi left Nintendo the following year and tragically died in a car accident in 1997.

rows.q: British writer Guy Beringer coined this mealtime term in an 1895 essay arguing that hungover Sunday revelers deserved a cheerful late-morning alternative to heavy roasts.
rows.n: His essay ‘Brunch: A Plea’ was published in Hunter’s Weekly and called for lighter midday socializing.

rows.q: In 1905, public health physician Harold Antoine des Voeux coined this four-letter term to describe the deadly soot-laden haze that frequently blanketed London.
rows.n: Des Voeux later founded Britain’s National Smoke Abatement Society to push for cleaner air.

rows.q: Designed by Arthur Heineman, the world’s first establishment bearing this accommodation label opened in San Luis Obispo in 1925 to serve auto travelers on Route 101.
rows.n: Heineman’s Milestone Mo-Tel charged motorists $1.25 per night for a bungalow with an attached garage.

rows.q: In 2004, Guardian journalist Ben Hammersley needed a snappy name for amateur audio shows distributed via RSS feeds, coining what widespread term?
rows.n: Hammersley invented the word while scrambling to hit a word count deadline for an article about internet radio.

rows.q: In a 1965 speech to Parliament, British shadow chancellor Iain Macleod coined this economic term to describe the toxic mix of sluggish output and soaring prices.
rows.n: Macleod told MPs that Britain faced not just stagnation or inflation individually, but both at once.

rows.q: In 1989, Australian breeder Wally Conron deliberately created this hybrid canine for a blind woman in Hawaii whose husband had severe dog allergies.
rows.n: Conron later stated in interviews that creating the designer breed was his life’s biggest regret.

rows.q: In a 1947 memo at Bell Labs, statistician John Tukey condensed Claude Shannon’s concept of a single unit of digital data into what three-letter word?
rows.n: Shannon formally credited Tukey for the term in his groundbreaking 1948 paper on mathematical communication.

rows.q: The BBC first used what six-letter industry shorthand in 1953 to classify its scripted, laugh-tracked comedy format exemplified by Pinwright’s Progress?
rows.n: Pinwright’s Progress, about an eccentric shopkeeper, aired ten live episodes between 1946 and 1947.

rows.q: At the Oscars on February 29, 1940, Hattie McDaniel won for Gone with the Wind, despite being barred from its premiere in this Georgia city.
rows.n: Producer David O. Selznick tried to secure her entry, but MGM advised her not to attend due to Jim Crow laws.

rows.q: Modern warfare’s longest siege of a capital city ended on February 29, 1996, in this host city of the 1984 Winter Olympics.
rows.n: The siege lasted 1,425 days, almost a year longer than the World War II siege of Leningrad.

rows.q: On February 29, 1692, the first warrants of the Salem witch trials were issued for Sarah Good, Sarah Osborne, and this enslaved woman.
rows.n: Tituba confessed to witchcraft under interrogation, naming several other townspeople to avoid execution.

rows.q: Born on Leap Day in 1860, Herman Hollerith built an electromechanical tabulator for the 1890 census, creating a firm that became what giant?
rows.n: Hollerith’s firm merged with three others in 1911 to create CTR, which took the name IBM in 1924.

rows.q: Born on Leap Day in 1976, this Queens rapper topped the Billboard Hot 100 with Jennifer Lopez on ‘I’m Real’ and Ashanti on ‘Always on Time.’
rows.n: Born Jeffrey Atkins, he scored five top-ten hits on the Billboard charts between 2001 and 2002.

rows.q: Born on February 29, 1792, this Italian composer retired at age 37, having written The Barber of Seville and 38 other operas.
rows.n: He spent much of his long retirement in Paris hosting musical salons and developing gourmet recipes.

rows.q: On February 29, 1960, Hugh Hefner opened the first members-only Playboy Club, complete with Bunny waitresses, in this magazine hometown.
rows.n: Members received a special metal key to enter; within a decade, clubs operated in over twenty cities worldwide.

rows.q: On February 29, 1504, Christopher Columbus bluffed local chiefs with a lunar eclipse while his damaged fleet was stranded on this island.
rows.n: Columbus and his crew remained marooned there for over a year before a rescue caravel arrived from Hispaniola.

rows.q: Back to the Future’s Dr. Emmett Brown conceived the flux capacitor after hitting his head on a bathroom sink while hanging what household object?
rows.n: Doc Brown drew his first sketch of the flux capacitor on November 5, 1955.

rows.q: Peter Sellers played three roles in Dr. Strangelove, but an injury prevented him from playing a fourth: the B-52 pilot who rides a bomb down, recast with what cowboy actor?
rows.n: Director Stanley Kubrick kept Pickens in the dark about the film being a satire.

rows.q: In The Da Vinci Code, symbology professor Dr. Robert Langdon searches for the Holy Grail inside Rosslyn Chapel, a 15th-century site located just south of what capital city?
rows.n: Rosslyn Chapel saw an estimated 70 percent jump in visitors after the book’s release.

rows.q: Armed with an MIT physics doctorate, Dr. Gordon Freeman triggers an alien invasion during an experiment gone wrong at what fictional New Mexico research facility?
rows.n: The rival Aperture Science facility in the Portal games was built to compete with it.

rows.q: On Friends, paleontologist Dr. Ross Geller spirals when a coworker steals his Thanksgiving leftover sandwich, which famously featured what gravy-soaked layer of bread?
rows.n: Monica Geller’s secret recipe was an extra slice of sourdough drenched in hot gravy.

rows.q: In Christopher Marlowe’s Elizabethan tragedy, scholar Doctor Faustus surrenders his soul to Lucifer in exchange for twenty-four years of service from what demon?
rows.n: Marlowe’s Faustus earned his doctorate in divinity at the University of Wittenberg.

rows.q: In Carl Sagan’s Contact, radio astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway detects humanity’s first alien transmission originating from what bright star in the constellation Lyra?
rows.n: Vega was the first star other than the Sun ever to be photographed, back in 1850.

rows.q: In Jurassic Park, paleontologist Dr. Alan Grant unearths a juvenile velociraptor skeleton at a badlands dig site in what western U.S. state?
rows.n: The fictional Snakewater dig was based on Montana’s fossil-rich Hell Creek Formation.

rows.q: In The Matrix Reloaded, Morpheus delivers a rousing speech in a cavernous temple to rally the underground citizens of what last human city?
rows.n: The filmmakers staged the hedonistic cave dance sequence using hundreds of extras in an Alameda aircraft hangar.

rows.q: The culinary and cultural term “Cajun” evolved as an 18th-century anglicized corruption of what French colonial region in the Maritimes?
rows.n: After Britain expelled French-speaking Acadians during the Great Upheaval, many migrated to southwestern Louisiana.

rows.q: In 1998, GMC launched what flagship luxury trim line on its Yukon SUV, borrowing a peak name that federal maps would not restore until 2015?
rows.n: Alaska had officially recognized Denali since 1975, but Ohio politicians blocked the federal shift to honor McKinley.

rows.q: Before the Titanic foundered in 1912, what nearly identical lead ship of her White Star Line class had entered passenger service a year earlier?
rows.n: Olympic carried thousands of troops during World War I and was the only ship of the trio to survive into retirement.

rows.q: Featuring “With or Without You” and “One Tree Hill”, what 1987 U2 studio album was originally developed under the working title “The Two Americas”?
rows.n: Band photographer Anton Corbijn suggested the Mojave desert shoot and introduced them to the twisted yucca trees.

rows.q: Before moving east to attend Georgetown and Yale, future president Bill Clinton spent his teenage years in what Arkansas resort community?
rows.n: Clinton was born in Hope, Arkansas, but his mother relocated the family to Hot Springs when he was seven.

rows.q: Loosely inspired by the 1958 Starkweather murders, what 1973 Terrence Malick debut film stars Martin Sheen and Sissy Spacek on the run?
rows.n: Malick financed a large portion of the modest production using his own savings and loans from personal friends.

rows.q: Throughout Better Call Saul, Kim Wexler battles career burnout while representing what expanding regional bank as its outside legal counsel?
rows.n: Its conservative CEO, Kevin Wachtell, routinely frustrated Kim by ignoring her sensible regulatory advice.

rows.q: Frederic Chopin’s heart was preserved in cognac and smuggled back to this capital city, where it remains entombed in Holy Cross Church.
Boasting vibrant blue-and-crimson facial ridges, this largest of all monkey species was long classified alongside baboons until given its own genus.
rows.n: Their colorful rears are just as vibrant as their faces, helping troops stay together in dense rainforests.

rows.q: Largely ghostwritten by speechwriter Ted Sorensen, this 1956 volume profiling eight principled U.S. senators won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography.
rows.n: John F. Kennedy remains the only U.S. president to win a Pulitzer Prize for biography.

rows.q: Originally composed by Thomas Arne for the 1740 masque Alfred, this rousing patriotic anthem is the traditional climax of the Last Night of the Proms.
