rows.n: The original lyric is actually a command—Britannia, rule the waves—rather than the common misquote rules.

rows.q: Observed by Samuel Pepys in London in 1662, this traditional seaside puppet show features a cackling, hooked-nosed rogue who repeatedly bickers with his wife.
rows.n: The character of Punch descends directly from Pulcinella, the unruly clown of Italian commedia dell’arte.

rows.q: In Valve’s 1998 shooter Half-Life, silent physicist Gordon Freeman begins his escape from the Black Mesa research facility armed with this signature melee weapon.
rows.n: Valve’s corporate headquarters in Washington features a bronze replica of the crowbar displayed in its lobby.

rows.q: Floated with a dash of vanilla-anise Galliano liqueur, this classic two-ingredient cocktail of vodka and orange juice becomes a Harvey Wallbanger.
rows.n: Legend claims American petroleum workers in the Persian Gulf secretly mixed the drink using tools from their kits.

rows.q: Radical environmentalists George Hayduke and Doc Sarvis sabotage desert billboards and bulldozers across the Southwest in this 1975 Edward Abbey novel.
rows.n: Abbey’s satirical book directly inspired the founding of the militant activist network Earth First! in 1980.

rows.q: Dominated by the jagged volcanic peak of Mount Otemanu, this luxury island retreat lies about 160 miles northwest of Tahiti.
rows.n: Its traditional Tahitian name is Pora Pora, meaning ‘first born’; early European visitors transcribed it with a B.

rows.q: Jacques Offenbach’s high-spirited ‘Infernal Galop’ from Orpheus in the Underworld became the signature tune for this high-kicking cabaret dance.
rows.n: In the 1830s, the dance was considered scandalous because women wore split-crotch pantaloons beneath their skirts.

rows.q: Founded around 1916 at Zurich’s Cabaret Voltaire by Hugo Ball and Tristan Tzara, this avant-garde movement championed nonsense and anti-art.
rows.n: Marcel Duchamp channeled the movement by submitting a store-bought urinal titled Fountain to a 1917 exhibition.

rows.q: Overlooking the Hudson River in Ossining, New York, this maximum-security prison popularized the American criminal idiom ‘up the river.’
rows.n: In 1953, convicted Soviet spies Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed in its electric chair.

rows.q: Christiaan Eijkman won a Nobel Prize after showing that chickens fed polished white rice developed this nerve-damaging thiamine deficiency.
rows.n: Eijkman initially suspected a bacterial toxin before his colleague Gerrit Grijns realized rice bran held a vital nutrient.

rows.q: Endemic to Madagascar, this solitary nocturnal lemur uses a bizarrely thin, elongated middle finger to tap tree bark and fish out grubs.
rows.n: Local Malagasy folklore often views the creature as an omen of bad luck, leading people to kill them on sight.

rows.q: In the late 1920s, entrepreneur Donald Duncan bought out the California manufacturing business of Pedro Flores to mass-produce this classic toy.
rows.n: Flores, an immigrant from the Philippines, is credited with adding the looped string that lets the toy sleep.

rows.q: Known for exceptionally sweet, low-sulfur onions grown in its rich volcanic soil, this southeastern Washington city shares a name with its county.
rows.n: Its name translates roughly to ‘many waters’ or ‘place of many waters’ in the native Sahaptin language.

rows.q: Chinese stargazers recorded a brilliant supernova in 1054 whose remnant, Messier 1, is better known by what crustacean name?
rows.n: It was named in the 1840s by the Earl of Rosse, whose sketch of it resembled a crab.

rows.q: In old English common-law ejectment lawsuits, John Doe was the fictional plaintiff, while what rhyming name was assigned to the defendant?
rows.n: Both names were invented so real parties could test land titles without technical hassles.

rows.q: In a season six Friends episode, what word does Ross insist is a martial arts concept of total awareness, which Phoebe and Rachel mock?
rows.n: The actual martial-arts term for relaxed awareness that Ross was mangling is zanshin.

rows.q: Invented by Aki Maita and released by Bandai in 1996, what egg-shaped keychain device challenged owners to virtually raise a digital creature?
rows.n: Its name blends tamago, the Japanese word for egg, with the English word watch.

rows.q: Before adapting her own 1976 gothic debut into a 1994 film, what author initially decried the casting of Tom Cruise as the vampire Lestat?
rows.n: After watching the completed film, she bought full-page trade ads to apologize to Cruise.

rows.q: In 1935, a California postman named Rudolph patented a popular, pebbly-skinned variety of what subtropical fruit?
rows.n: The Hass variety now accounts for about 95 percent of all avocados sold in the United States.

rows.q: Medieval pilgrims walking the Camino de Santiago across northern Spain traditionally collected and wore the shell of what marine mollusk?
rows.n: The shell’s grooves symbolize various routes converging on the apostle St. James’s shrine.

rows.q: While coaching the Patriots in 1994, two-time Super Bowl champion Bill Parcells was saddled by his players with what piscine nickname?
rows.n: He reportedly earned it after sarcastically asking a player if he thought he was Charlie the Tuna.

rows.q: Earning ten Emmy nominations and four wins, who spent eleven seasons playing cynical cocktail waitress Carla Tortelli on Cheers?
Seeking sixpence paperbacks that cost no more than a pack of cigarettes, Allen Lane founded what British publishing house in 1935?
rows.n: Lane chose the mascot after sending an office junior to Regent’s Park Zoo to sketch the bird in various poses.

rows.q: Carved by Polynesian settlers between the 13th and 16th centuries, what monolithic volcanic-stone statues dominate Easter Island?
Back-to-back Stanley Cup champions in both the early 1990s and late 2010s, what NHL franchise plays its home games at PPG Paints Arena?
rows.n: The team’s original home, the Civic Arena, was dubbed “The Igloo,” which inspired the cold-climate nickname.

rows.q: In Greek myth, which Titaness and wife of Cronus saved her infant son Zeus from being devoured by tricking his father with a stone?
rows.n: The stone Cronus swallowed instead was called the Omphalos and was later placed at Delphi as a sacred relic.

rows.q: Acquired by Disney for 350 million dollars in 2007, what multiplayer virtual world let players waddle across an icy island?
rows.n: At its peak, the game boasted over 200 million user accounts before Disney officially shuttered it in 2017.

rows.q: Parodying his own stammer, Lewis Carroll cast himself as what creature who oversees the nonsensical Caucus-Race in Wonderland?
rows.n: Carroll’s real name was Charles Dodgson; when stuttering, he often introduced himself as “Do-do-Dodgson.”

rows.q: Featuring a raucous boarding-school food fight in its music video, what fruit-titled track was the third single from Harry Styles’ 2017 debut?
rows.n: Despite its title, the song’s lyrics never actually mention the fruit, focusing instead on a wild romance.

rows.q: In 1598, after a lease dispute, the Lord Chamberlain’s Men dismantled The Theatre timber by timber and hauled the lumber across the Thames to erect this playhouse.
rows.n: The original Globe was later destroyed by fire in 1613 during a performance of Henry VIII.

rows.q: Following the storming and intentional demolition of the Bastille in 1789, the Marquis de Lafayette sent the fortress’s principal iron key to this U.S. president.
rows.n: The cast-iron key remains on display at Washington’s Mount Vernon estate.

rows.q: Stripped of asbestos and dismantled between 2006 and 2008, the modernist Palast der Republik in Berlin once housed the parliament of this former communist state.
rows.n: The site is now occupied by the rebuilt Humboldt Forum, modeled on the Prussian royal palace.

rows.q: When its 47-story Manhattan tower was demolished in 1968, the Singer Building had spent six decades advertising Isaac Singer’s global empire of these appliances.
rows.n: At 612 feet, it was the tallest building ever peacefully demolished until 270 Park Avenue in 2021.

rows.q: Demolished in 1964, Manhattan’s Polo Grounds served as the inaugural home for the New York Mets before the team moved to this newly opened venue in Queens.
rows.n: The Mets played two seasons at the Polo Grounds after the baseball Giants moved to San Francisco.

rows.q: Demolished in 2002 and replaced by luxury flats, Manchester’s famed Haçienda nightclub was largely bankrolled by the royalties of this “Blue Monday” synth-pop band.
rows.n: The club was run by Factory Records and famously lost money despite packed dance floors.

rows.q: In Charles Dickens’s Oliver Twist, the villainous Fagin spends his final night awaiting the gallows inside this grim London prison, which was demolished in 1902.
rows.n: The site is now home to the Old Bailey, which incorporated some of Newgate’s original masonry.

rows.q: Architectural historian Charles Jencks declared Modernism dead when the first high-rise block of the Pruitt-Igoe housing complex was dynamited in 1972 in this city.
rows.n: Architect Minoru Yamasaki had designed the complex only twenty years earlier.

rows.q: In 1858, a German mathematician co-discovered what non-orientable surface with only one side and one boundary, formed by giving a paper strip a half-twist?
rows.n: German mathematician Johann Benedict Listing independently discovered the surface a few months earlier.

rows.q: In 1947, designer Juli Lynne Charlot popularized what flared felt garment for teenage girls, originally featuring dachshunds before switching canine breeds?
rows.n: Charlot designed it with no sewing skills, cutting a circle out of felt to eliminate the need for seams.

rows.q: In a Brothers Grimm tale, what diminutive villain stamps his right foot so deep into the earth that he tears himself in two when his name is guessed?
rows.n: In the original 1812 edition, he did not tear himself in half, but flew out the window on a cooking ladle.

rows.q: Identified as vitamin B2, what yellow micronutrient is added to fortified flour and gives an electric neon glow to urine after taking multivitamins?
rows.n: Its name combines ribose sugar with “flavus,” the Latin word for yellow.

rows.q: Created by Cincinnati franchise owner Lou Groen in 1962 to feed Catholic customers during Lent, what was the first new item added to McDonald’s menu?
rows.n: Groen’s fish sandwich soundly beat Ray Kroc’s rival idea, the Hula Burger, which featured grilled pineapple.

rows.q: Known for its vibrant arts scene and historic rough edges, what central San Francisco neighborhood shares its name with a bygone red-light district of Manhattan?
rows.n: The Manhattan nickname arose in the 1870s when a police captain called it the choice precinct for bribes.

rows.q: What producer won Album of the Year Grammys for the O Brother, Where Art Thou? soundtrack and Robert Plant and Alison Krauss’s Raising Sand?
rows.n: Born Joseph Henry Burnett, he toured as a guitarist in Bob Dylan’s Rolling Thunder Revue in the mid-1970s.

rows.q: C. Auguste Dupin solves the blackmail of an unnamed royal woman by finding an incriminating document hidden in plain sight in what 1844 Edgar Allan Poe story?
rows.n: It is the third and final detective story featuring Dupin, following The Murders in the Rue Morgue and Marie Rogêt.

rows.q: Packaged in a dark apothecary bottle and famously served with a slice of cucumber rather than lime, what Scottish spirit bills itself as a “most unusual gin”?
rows.n: Hendrick’s uses two distinct stills: a Carter-Head still and an antique Bennet pot still dating back to 1860.

rows.q: Introduced in 1914 to promote an anti-caking agent that prevented clumping in damp weather, what brand’s mascot is an umbrella-toting girl in a yellow dress?
rows.n: The slogan “When It Rains It Pours” was adapted from the traditional proverb “It never rains but it pours.”

rows.q: Diego Rivera’s 1933 mural Man at the Crossroads was famously covered up and destroyed after the artist refused to scrub Vladimir Lenin’s face from what Midtown Manhattan complex?
rows.n: Rivera later recreated the fresco in Mexico City, adding John D. Rockefeller Jr. drinking martinis under a microscope.

rows.q: Cinema’s quintessential “final girl” for her turns as Laurie Strode in Halloween, what actress took home her first Academy Award in 2023 for Everything Everywhere All at Once?
rows.n: Her Oscar win came 62 years after her mother, Janet Leigh, was nominated for Psycho in the same supporting category.

rows.q: Borrowing their moniker from a passage in C.S. Lewis’s Mere Christianity, what Texas alternative pop band climbed to number two on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1999 with “Kiss Me”?
rows.n: The band formed in New Braunfels, Texas, when guitarist Matt Slocum met lead vocalist Leigh Nash in church.

rows.q: In 1968, ABC hired what razor-witted author of Myra Breckinridge to debate conservative William F. Buckley Jr. on live television, prompting an infamous screaming match?
rows.n: Buckley threatened to punch Vidal in the face after Vidal called him a “crypto-Nazi” on air.

rows.q: After nine seasons defending the innocent as Perry Mason, what Canadian-born actor spent eight more in a wheelchair as San Francisco police consultant Robert T. Ironside?
rows.n: Burr won two Emmys playing Mason and was nominated six more times for his work on Ironside.

rows.q: Founded in 1804 as a British penal colony at Sullivan’s Cove, what state capital sits at the base of Mount Wellington on the estuary of the River Derwent?
rows.n: It is Australia’s second-oldest capital city, surpassed in age only by Sydney.

rows.q: Entering the NHL in 1970 alongside Vancouver, Buffalo picked this team name from a fan contest, honoring a curved weapon meant to be sharp on both offense and defense.
rows.n: Seymour Knox chose the name because a sabre is known to be sharp on both offense and defense.

rows.q: Aram Khachaturian originally dashed off this frantic, whirling final-act piece in just one day for his 1942 ballet Gayane, later lamenting that it eclipsed his serious work.
rows.n: Its whirling rhythm was inspired by an Armenian war dance where soldiers displayed their blade skills.

rows.q: Sound designer Ben Burtt created the distinctive hum of this sci-fi weapon by blending the idle buzz of a film projector with interference from an old television set.
rows.n: Burtt won a Special Achievement Academy Award in 1978 for creating the soundscape of Star Wars.

rows.q: Derived from the practice of backing a gem with metal to enhance its shine, this four-letter term denotes a character whose traits contrast with and highlight the protagonist’s.
rows.n: The jeweler’s trick is also why Hamlet compares himself to a foil when addressing Laertes.

rows.q: Tracing to maritime customs of discharging guns to signal peaceful intent, this specific artillery honor is reserved for sitting presidents and visiting foreign heads of state.
rows.n: The U.S. initially fired one shot per state, officially standardizing on 21 in 1875.

rows.q: In season six of The Office, Dunder Mifflin is acquired by this Florida printer company, whose CEO Jo Bennett is played by Kathy Bates.
rows.n: Christian Slater appeared in an orientation video explaining the company’s confusing pronunciation.

rows.q: Borrowed into English in the 18th century from an Italian word for “response,” this seven-letter noun describes a quick, stinging verbal retort delivered in a battle of wits.
rows.n: It derives from the Italian “risposta,” which simply means an answer or reply.

rows.q: While a turtle’s domed dorsal shell is known as the carapace, this eight-letter anatomical term refers to the flatter ventral shell that protects its belly.
rows.n: In most species, males have slightly concave plastrons to facilitate mating.

rows.q: Before-and-after: Queen Elsa’s chilly, Oscar-winning Disney anthem merges with Lindsey Buckingham’s bitter 1977 breakup hit for Fleetwood Mac.
rows.a: Let It Go Your Own Way
rows.n: Buckingham wrote the song as a pointed message to Stevie Nicks, who hated singing the lyric “packing up, shacking up.”

rows.q: Before-and-after: Paul McCartney’s explosive 1973 007 theme for Roger Moore collides with Madonna’s electroclash Bond track from 2002.
rows.a: Live and Let Die Another Day
rows.n: McCartney’s track was the first Bond theme nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

rows.q: Before-and-after: Gene Kelly’s puddle-splashing 1952 musical title track blends with the 2020 dance-pop duet by Lady Gaga and Ariana Grande.
rows.a: Singin’ in the Rain on Me
rows.n: Kelly filmed his iconic lamppost dance while suffering from a 103-degree fever.

rows.q: Before-and-after: The Rembrandts’ clapping-heavy Friends theme song crashes into the Kinks’ distorted 1964 proto-punk breakthrough.
rows.a: I’ll Be There for You Really Got Me
rows.n: Dave Davies created the signature guitar fuzz by slicing his amplifier speaker cone with a razor blade.

rows.q: Before-and-after: The Bee Gees’ strutting Saturday Night Fever disco smash unites with Simple Minds’ soaring 1985 synth-rock hit.
rows.n: The drum track on Stayin’ Alive is a looped two-bar excerpt from Night Fever after their drummer left mid-session.

rows.q: Before-and-after: Elton John’s 1972 ballad about an isolated astronaut joins R.E.M.’s 1992 tribute to comedian Andy Kaufman.
rows.n: Bernie Taupin said he was inspired to write Rocket Man after spotting a shooting star while driving to his parents’ house.

rows.q: Before-and-after: Gladys Knight’s 1973 soul journey away from L.A. merges with Ray Charles’ 1960 ode adopted as an official state song.
rows.a: Midnight Train to Georgia on My Mind
rows.n: Gladys Knight’s hit was originally written by Jim Weatherly as Midnight Plane to Houston.

rows.q: Before-and-after: Johnny Cash’s mariachi-tinged 1963 country chart-topper links up with James Taylor’s introspective 1970 folk ballad.
rows.n: Ring of Fire was co-written by June Carter about falling in love with Cash while he was still married.

rows.q: Launched in 2010 by Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger, this photo-sharing app gained 25,000 users on its first day and was snapped up by Facebook 18 months later.
rows.n: The very first photo posted to the platform was a picture of a stray dog near a taco stand in Mexico.

rows.q: Drafted eleventh overall in 2011, this ferocious Houston Texans defensive end won NFL Defensive Player of the Year three times in a four-year span.
rows.n: Only Lawrence Taylor and Aaron Donald have also won the award three times.

rows.q: Often served over turkey or chicken, this complex Mexican sauce from Puebla blends dried chilies and spices with a hint of bitter chocolate.
rows.n: Legend says 17th-century Dominican nuns invented it in a panic for an archbishop’s visit.

rows.q: Founded in 1959, this Chicago sketch comedy troupe took its self-deprecating name from A.J. Liebling’s New Yorker articles mocking the city.
rows.n: Its alumni include Bill Murray, Catherine O’Hara, John Belushi, and Tina Fey.

rows.q: Billed as Mr. Showmanship, pianist Liberace made this ornate, multi-armed candleholder a glittering personal trademark on his grand pianos.
German inventor Wilhelm Bruhn designed this mechanical distance-tracking fare computer in 1891, giving hailed public cars their modern short name.
rows.n: Taxi was clipped from taximeter, while cab came from the horse-drawn cabriolet.

rows.q: A bronze statue outside Emirates Stadium immortalizes this French striker, who scored 175 Premier League goals for Arsenal and won the 1998 World Cup.
rows.n: He was the attacking centerpiece of Arsenal’s 2003-04 undefeated Invincibles.

rows.q: Known for a roof structure that traps crowd noise, this home venue of the Seattle Seahawks and Sounders set a Guinness noise record of 137.6 decibels.
rows.n: It was originally called Seahawks Stadium, then Qwest Field and CenturyLink Field.

rows.q: Fresh off Casablanca and Gaslight, this Swedish actress played an excommunicated French martyr in an eponymous 1948 technicolor historical epic.
rows.n: Bergman also played Joan on Broadway in Maxwell Anderson’s Joan of Lorraine, which won her a 1947 Tony Award.

rows.q: Gloriana, the allegorical ruler of Fairyland in Edmund Spenser’s epic 1590 poem The Faerie Queene, was written to flatter this excommunicated English monarch.
rows.n: Pope Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570, declaring her subjects released from any allegiance to her.

rows.q: Before his 1497 excommunication, fiery friar Girolamo Savonarola led Florence’s Bonfire of the Vanities, where this painter of The Birth of Venus allegedly burned works.
rows.n: A devastated Botticelli became a follower of the friar and largely abandoned classical, mythological scenes.

rows.q: Excommunicated after fatally stabbing a rival in a church, this warrior crowned himself king of Scots and won national independence at Bannockburn in 1314.
rows.n: The Pope finally lifted Robert’s excommunication in 1328, only one year before the king’s death.

rows.q: Jonathan Pryce portrayed the excommunicated Argentine leader Juan Perón opposite Madonna in this 1996 musical drama directed by Alan Parker.
rows.n: Pope Pius XII excommunicated Perón in 1955 after he expelled two Catholic bishops who opposed his regime.

rows.q: Long before astronomers confirmed exoplanets, this Italian Dominican friar was executed for heresy in 1600 after insisting stars were distant suns circled by planets.
rows.n: A 22-kilometer-wide crater on the far side of the Moon was named in his honor in 1970.

rows.q: Created by Napoleon’s chef after an 1800 victory in Piedmont, this classic sautéed chicken dish features tomatoes, mushrooms, garlic, and traditionally crayfish.
rows.n: Pius VII excommunicated Napoleon in 1809; Napoleon retaliated by having the pontiff kidnapped and held prisoner.

rows.q: Excommunicated by John XXIII in 1962, Fidel Castro gave a four-hour courtroom defense in 1953 that concluded with this four-word vow about history.
rows.n: The line ended Castro’s trial speech after he led the failed July 26 assault on the Moncada Barracks.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the tennis icon behind the Battle of the Sexes scales the Empire State Building as cinema’s original giant ape.
rows.n: She defeated Bobby Riggs in 1973; the original ape scaled the tower in 1933.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the ABBA-soundtracked smash musical laces up cleats as the legendary two-time World Cup-winning US soccer forward.
rows.n: She scored 158 international goals and won gold in Atlanta and Athens.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Tom Hanks leads a WWII squad through Normandy to rescue a 12-time Olympic medalist American swimmer.
In this before-and-after, the fiery four-time Warriors champion forward becomes the Jim Crow-era motorist guide that won 2018’s Best Picture.
rows.n: Victor Hugo Green first published his guide for Black travelers in 1936.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Cameron Diaz stars in a cringe 1998 comedy alongside the first American woman to win Olympic all-around gymnastics gold.
rows.a: There’s Something About Mary Lou Retton
rows.n: Retton scored perfect 10s on floor and vault in Los Angeles to capture gold.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, MLB’s 511-game-winning pitcher puts on the Ritz in Mel Brooks’s 1974 parody of Mary Shelley’s gothic monster.
rows.n: Young pitched the first perfect game in American League history in 1904.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the five-time Wizards All-Star point guard is left behind to clean a deserted Earth as Pixar’s trash-compacting robot.
rows.n: The robot’s name stands for Waste Allocation Load Lifter: Earth-Class.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Boston’s “Larry Legend” wears a blindfold alongside Sandra Bullock to survive a 2018 post-apocalyptic thriller.
rows.n: Over 45 million Netflix accounts watched the thriller in its first week.

rows.q: Months after taking office in 1979, which British prime minister stood in Parliament and publicly exposed royal art curator Anthony Blunt as a Soviet spy?
rows.n: Blunt had secretly confessed in 1964 in exchange for immunity, but Thatcher decided the public deserved the truth.

rows.q: David Greenglass, a machinist whose testimony condemned his sister Ethel Rosenberg, stole atomic secrets while stationed at which secret New Mexico lab?
rows.n: Decades later, Greenglass admitted he had lied on the stand about Ethel’s role to protect his own wife.

rows.q: In John le Carré’s classic Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, the treacherous MI6 mole code-named Gerald was modeled after which real Cambridge Five double agent?
rows.n: Philby was le Carré’s former colleague at MI6 before defecting to the Soviet Union in 1963.

rows.q: Steven Spielberg’s 2015 thriller Bridge of Spies starred which actor as James B. Donovan, the lawyer who negotiated the release of captured U-2 pilot Gary Powers?
rows.n: Mark Rylance won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his portrayal of Soviet spy Rudolf Abel.

rows.q: The FX Cold War drama The Americans, about two deep-cover KGB sleeper agents in suburban Virginia, was created by Joe Weisberg, a former officer in which agency?
rows.n: Because of his background, Weisberg had to submit every script to the CIA’s Publications Review Board before filming.

rows.q: Francis Gary Powers was flying a U-2 spy plane developed by the legendary Skunk Works division of which aerospace company when he was shot down in 1960?
rows.n: Led by Kelly Johnson, Skunk Works built the first U-2 in just eight months to monitor Soviet military installations.

rows.q: Cold War spy exchanges, including the swap of Francis Gary Powers for Rudolf Abel, took place on the Glienicke Bridge connecting Berlin to which German city?
rows.n: Because it sat on the border between West Berlin and East Germany, it earned the nickname Bridge of Spies.

rows.q: In one of its most infamous Cold War assassination attempts, the CIA tried to slip a lethal botulinum capsule into which frozen dairy treat ordered by Fidel Castro?
rows.n: The waiter tasked with delivering it accidentally broke the frozen capsule while trying to unstick it from a freezer.

rows.q: Article 275 of the Treaty of Versailles forced Germany to respect French appellations, stripping its winemakers of the right to use this sparkling name.
rows.n: German producers subsequently popularized the term Sekt for their domestic sparkling wines.

rows.q: Phased out by the 1987 Montreal Protocol, chlorofluorocarbons damage the ozone layer when ultraviolet light frees atoms of which halogen element?
rows.n: A single chlorine atom can break down over 100,000 ozone molecules before being removed from the stratosphere.

rows.q: Serving as the Bolshevik Commissar for Foreign Affairs, which future exile led the Soviet delegation at the 1918 Treaty of Brest-Litovsk talks?
rows.n: Trotsky walked away with a policy of ‘neither war nor peace’, prompting the Central Powers to resume invading.

rows.q: Signed in 1840, the Treaty of Waitangi is considered the founding document of New Zealand, formalizing ties between the British Crown and what people?
rows.n: Discrepancies between the English and Maori texts over the concept of ‘sovereignty’ led to decades of conflict.

rows.q: The 1985 agreement abolishing internal European border checks was signed aboard a riverboat in Schengen, a winemaking village in what tiny nation?
rows.n: Schengen was chosen because it sits beside the tripoint where Luxembourg, France, and Germany meet.

rows.q: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas, which carved up the globe between Spain and Portugal, was prompted by papal bulls issued by this infamous Borgia pope.
rows.n: His 1493 bull Inter caetera drew a meridian that Tordesillas later shifted 270 leagues further west.

rows.q: The British delegation refused to pose for a painting of the 1783 Treaty of Paris, leaving an iconic canvas unfinished by which American-born artist?
rows.n: West was the official history painter to King George III, which made his British sitters’ boycott rather awkward.

rows.q: Mediated by Theodore Roosevelt, the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth was negotiated at a naval shipyard that, despite the treaty’s name, is in this U.S. state.
rows.n: The Portsmouth Naval Shipyard sits in Kittery, Maine, across the harbor from Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

rows.q: Rob Reiner named his production company Castle Rock, fittingly directing this 1990 psychological thriller where James Caan is held captive by his number one fan.
rows.n: It is the only film adaptation of a Stephen King novel to win an Academy Award in an acting category.

rows.q: Frigg extracted oaths from fire, water, and beasts never to harm her son Baldr, but skipped this modest parasitic evergreen that Loki later turned into a dart.
rows.n: Because it grew on an oak rather than in the earth, Frigg deemed mistletoe too young to pose any threat.

rows.q: The northern border of this state’s Bootheel marks the 36°30’ parallel, drawn in an 1820 compromise as the northern limit for slavery in western territories.
rows.n: Wealthy planter John Hardeman Walker lobbied aggressively to keep his bootheel farmland inside the state.

rows.q: In 2002, this hip-hop pioneer scored a Billboard smash by running her own lyrics backward in the chorus of Work It, after already breaking ground with The Rain.
rows.n: The reversed line is literally the previous lyric played backwards: I put my thing down, flip it and reverse it.

rows.q: Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota serves as the primary source for this 2,300-mile river that French explorer La Salle claimed for France in 1682.
rows.n: It takes approximately 90 days for a drop of water to travel from Lake Itasca to the Gulf of Mexico.

rows.q: Blamed by Vincent van Gogh for blowing over his easels in Arles, this fierce northwesterly wind regularly chills the Rhône valley and the Gulf of Lion.
rows.n: It frequently exceeds speeds of 50 knots, blowing away cloud cover to create intensely clear skies.

rows.q: In 1770, a 14-year-old Mozart attended Wednesday Tenebrae services at the Sistine Chapel and wrote down this jealously guarded Gregorio Allegri choral work entirely from memory.
rows.n: Pope Clement XIV was so impressed by young Mozart’s musical piracy that he awarded him the Golden Spur.

rows.q: Driven by Cold War dread, programmer Dave Theurer gave players a trackball and three base batteries to defend six California cities in this 1980 Atari arcade hit.
rows.n: Theurer suffered recurring nightmares during development that his hometown was being wiped out by nukes.

rows.q: Before publishing Dianetics in 1950, which future church founder supported himself by writing pulp sci-fi and westerns for magazines like Astounding Stories?
rows.n: His 1950 book Dianetics: The Modern Science of Mental Health sold millions and launched the Scientology movement.

rows.q: Jimmy Chamberlin played drums and James Iha played guitar alongside frontman Billy Corgan in which 1990s alternative rock band?
rows.n: Despite the name, Corgan claimed that ‘Smashing’ in the band name was an adjective, not an active verb.

rows.q: Founded by Mel and Patricia Ziegler in 1978 as a safari-themed travel clothing company, what retailer was bought by Gap five years later?
rows.n: Early stores were famous for theatrical decor, featuring actual army surplus jeeps and safari bush planes.

rows.q: Camille Saint-Saëns barred all public performances of this playful 14-movement suite during his life, fearing for his serious reputation.
rows.n: He exempted only ‘The Swan’, worried that pieces depicting braying donkeys and fossilized tunes would ruin him.

rows.q: Named after the Greek god who carried Psyche to Cupid’s palace, what six-letter word traditionally refers to a mild westerly breeze?
rows.n: The Romans called him Favonius, and his name later inspired train lines and the Lincoln-Zephyr automobile.

rows.q: Featuring a Great Seal designed by a woman and famous for its rare star garnets, Idaho is officially known by what two-word moniker?
rows.n: Nearly every known type of gemstone has been found in Idaho, earning it the Gem State nickname in 1890.

rows.q: Deriving her name from the Greek verb meaning ‘to conceal,’ which sea nymph detained Odysseus on the remote island of Ogygia for seven years?
rows.n: Hermes eventually ordered her to release him so Odysseus could return home to Penelope in Ithaca.

rows.q: Used to conceal wood grain flaws on 1950s Fender Stratocasters and Gibson Les Pauls, what two-tone guitar finish fades from gold to a dark rim?
rows.n: Makers sprayed darker lacquer around the perimeter to hide three-piece mismatched wood bodies.

rows.q: Tossing stones into the subterranean Qumran caves in late 1946, young Bedouin goatherds accidentally uncovered what ancient hoard of biblical manuscripts?
rows.n: Over 25,000 fragments representing more than 900 manuscripts were ultimately recovered across eleven caves.

rows.q: In 1898, teenager Jim White began exploring Carlsbad Caverns after mistaking a massive funnel of bats for a smoke plume in what future U.S. state?
rows.n: White explored the caverns with a homemade wire ladder; New Mexico did not achieve statehood until 1912.

rows.q: Excavations inside Liang Bua cave on an Indonesian island revealed a species of three-foot-tall archaic humans playfully nicknamed after what fantasy race?
rows.n: Officially cataloged as Homo floresiensis, the specimens lived on Flores alongside giant rats and dwarf elephants.

rows.q: Discovered in a walled-up chamber of China’s Mogao Caves in 1900, the 868 AD woodblock-printed Diamond Sutra is a sacred text of what world religion?
rows.n: Daoist monk Wang Yuanlu stumbled upon the hidden Library Cave, which preserved tens of thousands of manuscripts.

rows.q: Facing a British naval blockade during the War of 1812, the US military mined saltpetre from Kentucky’s Mammoth Cave to produce what essential explosive?
rows.n: Workers leached calcium nitrate from guano-rich cave soil using large wooden vats that remain inside the cave today.

rows.q: Granted rare access by the French culture ministry, Werner Herzog used 3D cameras inside Chauvet Cave to shoot what 2010 documentary?
rows.n: Herzog and his tiny crew were restricted to a narrow metal walkway and used battery-powered, non-heating lights.

rows.q: In 1976, programmer Will Crowther mapped Kentucky’s Mammoth Cave system to create what pioneering interactive text adventure, originally named ADVENT?
rows.n: Crowther’s game popularized the magic word “xyzzy” and helped spawn the entire interactive fiction genre.

rows.q: In 1879, eight-year-old Maria Sanz de Sautuola looked up inside Spain’s Altamira Cave and spotted vibrant prehistoric paintings of what large, horned mammal?
rows.n: European archaeologists initially dismissed the polychrome charcoal and ochre paintings as a modern hoax.

rows.q: Before West Virginia’s Silver Bridge tragically collapsed in 1967, locals blamed eerie sightings of this red-eyed winged cryptid said to haunt the town.
rows.n: John Keel’s 1975 book The Mothman Prophecies popularized the link between the creature and the bridge disaster.

rows.q: Christopher Walken’s villain Max Zorin falls to his death from the top of the Golden Gate Bridge in this 1985 James Bond film.
rows.n: It was Roger Moore’s seventh and final turn as 007, released when he was 57 years old.

rows.q: Nicknamed ‘Galloping Gertie’ before collapsing in a 1940 windstorm, the original Tacoma Narrows Bridge crossed a tidal strait of this large Pacific inlet.
rows.n: The dramatic twisting collapse was captured on 16mm Kodachrome film by local camera-shop owner Barney Elliott.

rows.q: On April Fools’ Day in 1979, the Oxford University Dangerous Sports Club staged the modern debut of this extreme sport off Bristol’s Clifton Bridge.
rows.n: The four jumpers were arrested shortly after climbing back up, but the stunt inspired a worldwide commercial craze.

rows.q: In 1995, the unfinished Akashi Kaikyo suspension bridge had its towers shifted nearly three feet apart by a magnitude 6.9 earthquake near this port city.
rows.n: Despite the epicenter sitting right in the Akashi Strait, the bridge suffered no major structural damage.

rows.q: Flanked by New York’s mayor, this sideburned U.S. president led the ceremonial first public walk across the Brooklyn Bridge on opening day in 1883.
rows.n: Arthur had become president less than two years earlier following James A. Garfield’s assassination.

rows.q: Vancouver’s Lions Gate suspension bridge was privately funded in the 1930s by this Irish brewing dynasty to open access to their suburban real estate.
rows.n: The family bought 4,000 acres of West Vancouver for $18.75 an acre before selling the bridge to the province in 1955.

rows.q: Lisbon’s red suspension bridge was renamed in 1974 to celebrate this floral-named military coup that overthrew Portugal’s Estado Novo dictatorship.
rows.n: The landmark was originally named the Salazar Bridge after former Portuguese prime minister Antonio de Oliveira Salazar.

rows.q: From the Greek for “little star,” this typographical symbol was used by Aristarchus of Samothrace to mark duplicate or suspect lines in Homer.
rows.n: Aristarchus also used the obelus, a horizontal line, to mark lines he believed were bogus.

rows.q: In June 1905, a mutiny over maggot-infested meat erupted aboard this Black Sea vessel of the Imperial Russian Navy, later immortalized on film.
rows.n: The mutineers sailed the ship to Constanta, Romania, where they surrendered it to local authorities.

rows.q: Agatha Christie’s murder mystery set at Monkswell Manor opened in London in 1952 and remains the world’s longest-running play under this rodent title.
rows.n: Christie gave the play’s royalties to her grandson Mathew Prichard as a ninth-birthday present.

rows.q: Burton Cummings and Randy Bachman scored a 1970 US number-one hit with “American Woman” as members of this Winnipeg rock group.
rows.n: The band adopted the moniker after their label released a promo record credited to “Guess Who?” to build mystery.

rows.q: Captain James Cook introduced this word into English in 1777 after observing Polynesian customs in Tonga that prohibited touching consecrated objects.
rows.n: In Tonga, Cook transcribed the indigenous concept as “tapu,” noting it carried strict religious sanctions.

rows.q: Introduced in 1932 by the Hollywood Candy Company, this peanut-encrusted candy bar surrounds a core of salted caramel fudge without a speck of chocolate.
rows.n: The creators reportedly named it PayDay because they settled on the recipe on the company’s wage distribution day.

rows.q: Created by Bill Wright, this long-running BBC quiz show tests competitors under a single spotlight in a black leather chair for two intense minutes.
rows.n: Wright based the interrogation-style format on his experiences being questioned by the Gestapo in WWII.

rows.q: Barbara Stanwyck earned an Oscar nomination as a bedridden invalid who accidentally overhears a contract killing on a crossed wire in this 1948 thriller.
rows.n: The film was expanded from Lucille Fletcher’s hit 1943 radio play, which starred Agnes Moorehead.

rows.q: In the only significant federal appeals court case interpreting the Third Amendment, 1982’s Engblom v. Carey, striking prison guards sued after their dorm rooms were given to this military force.
rows.n: The Second Circuit ruled that National Guard members qualify as ‘soldiers’ under the Third Amendment.

rows.q: French demographer Alfred Sauvy coined the geopolitical term ‘Third World’ in 1952, deliberately echoing this pre-revolutionary social class that encompassed the common people.
rows.n: The First Estate was the Catholic clergy and the Second was the nobility; the Third was everyone else.

rows.q: Following the 1453 fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans, Eastern Orthodox theologians and tsars famously proclaimed this city to be the ‘Third Rome.’
rows.n: The concept was popularized in 1510 letters written by the Russian monk Philotheus of Pskov.

rows.q: In baseball, third base earned this scorching two-word nickname in the 1880s due to the ferocious velocity of balls batted straight down the foul line.
rows.n: Sportswriter and future Cincinnati Reds president Ren Mulford Jr. is credited with coining the moniker.

rows.q: Formulated in part by chemist Walther Nernst, the Third Law of Thermodynamics dictates that the entropy of a pure crystalline substance drops to zero at this theoretical temperature.
rows.n: Absolute zero is mathematically defined as minus 273.15 degrees Celsius or minus 459.67 Fahrenheit.

rows.q: The small pink fold resting in the inner corner of the human eye, the plica semilunaris, is a harmless vestige of this protective membrane seen sweeping sideways across a cat’s eye.
rows.n: Unlike humans, birds, reptiles, and many mammals use it actively to lubricate and protect the cornea.

rows.q: During the Third Crusade, Richard the Lionheart conquered this Mediterranean island from a rogue Byzantine ruler, using it as a supply base before selling it to the Knights Templar.
rows.n: Richard married Berengaria of Navarre in Limassol on Cyprus that same month.

rows.q: In the 1949 film noir The Third Man, Orson Welles delivers his famous monologue on cuckoo clocks and the Renaissance while riding this amusement attraction in Vienna’s Prater park.
rows.n: Welles famously ad-libbed the cuckoo clock comparison, which was not in Graham Greene’s original script.

rows.q: Yul Brynner’s Siamese monarch tutors an Olympic figure skater embroiled in a 1994 baton attack in what royal before-and-after?
rows.n: Allison Janney won Best Supporting Actress as Tonya’s mother; Brynner took Best Actor for playing King Mongkut.

rows.q: Prince shreds a Minneapolis guitar solo before looking after an autistic savant brother in what musical before-and-after?
rows.n: Prince won Best Original Song Score in 1985, while Dustin Hoffman won his second Best Actor Oscar for Rain Man in 1989.

rows.q: The Bard cures his Elizabethan writer’s block while romancing an ailing Radcliffe hockey fan in what tragic before-and-after?
rows.n: Shakespeare in Love won seven Oscars in 1999; Francis Lai won Best Original Score for Love Story’s tear-jerker theme.

rows.q: An alcoholic musician mentors an aspiring singer who becomes a paralyzed Vietnam veteran in what patriotic before-and-after?
rows.a: A Star Is Born on the Fourth of July
rows.n: Oliver Stone won Best Director for Fourth of July; versions of A Star Is Born won Oscars in 1937, 1976, and 2018.

rows.q: A suburban dad obsessed with rose petals dines with an enchanted French castle’s furry lord in what before-and-after?
rows.n: Beauty and the Beast was the first animated Best Picture nominee; American Beauty took Best Picture eight years later.

rows.q: A novice Austrian nun flees over the Alps only to con an Iowa town with seventy-six trombones in what before-and-after?
rows.n: Both films began as smash Broadway stage musicals and won Oscars for their adapted film scores in the 1960s.

rows.q: A Staten Island secretary climbing the Wall Street corporate ladder is committed to a 1960s mental ward in what before-and-after?
rows.n: Carly Simon won an Oscar for Working Girl’s Let the River Run; Angelina Jolie won Best Supporting Actress in 2000.

rows.q: A hitman with a pneumatic cattle gun hunts stolen cartel cash alongside alien-policing agents in what before-and-after?
rows.a: No Country for Old Men in Black
rows.n: Javier Bardem won Best Supporting Actor as Anton Chigurh; Rick Baker took his fifth Oscar for MIB’s makeup effects.

rows.q: General Mills rolled out a trio of finger snacks in 1965, but while Whistles and Daisys fizzled out, this cone-shaped corn snack became a staple of school lunches.
rows.n: General Mills spent millions developing the machinery to fry the corn dough into hollow cones.

rows.q: Edgar Wright and Simon Pegg tied together Shaun of the Dead, Hot Fuzz, and The World’s End as an unofficial trilogy named after this brand of ice cream cone.
rows.n: Each film features a different flavor: strawberry for gore, blue original for police, and mint for aliens.

rows.q: Boasting a tall, slender bowl engineered to retain carbonation and channel bubbles upward, this stemmed glassware eclipsed the wide-mouthed coupe in the late 20th century.
rows.n: Despite popular myth, historical records disprove that the rival coupe was molded from Marie Antoinette’s breast.

rows.q: First conquered in 1865 in an expedition where four men plunged to their deaths during the descent, this jagged pyramid on the Swiss-Italian border is one of the deadliest peaks in the Alps.
rows.n: The four climbers who perished broke their rope after slipping on an ice slope near the summit.

rows.q: A voiceless trumpeter swan named Louis learns to read, write, and play music to win the heart of a swan named Serena in this 1970 children’s novel by E.B. White.
rows.n: It was the third and final children’s book written by White, following Stuart Little and Charlotte’s Web.

rows.q: King Alfred the Great of Wessex began uniting England under the shared identity of this Germanic cultural group, whose rule over the island ended abruptly at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
rows.n: The term was coined by continental writers to distinguish English Saxons from continental Old Saxons.

rows.q: Australian chemist David Warren developed this dual cockpit audio and data-logging system in the 1950s. Despite its popular monochromatic nickname, international law requires it painted orange.
rows.n: Warren’s father had died in an unexplained 1934 plane crash, inspiring his life’s work on the device.

rows.q: Hatched from an egg spat out by his dying villainous father, this green-skinned warrior begins as Goku’s mortal enemy before becoming young Gohan’s surrogate father in Dragon Ball Z.
rows.n: Series creator Akira Toriyama frequently stated that Piccolo was his personal favorite character.

rows.q: In the Book of Genesis, God promises Abraham and his descendants this ancient territory, famously described as flowing with milk and honey.
rows.n: Abraham journeyed there from Ur, but Moses died on Mount Nebo before he could enter.

rows.q: Seized by Edward I in 1296 and placed inside Westminster’s coronation chair, this sacred red sandstone block was finally returned to Scotland in 1996.
rows.n: It temporarily returned to London in 2023 for the coronation of King Charles III.

rows.q: Rousseau penned the famous line years earlier, but anti-royalist rumors falsely claimed Marie Antoinette told starving peasants to eat this pastry.
rows.n: The phrase qu’ils mangent de la brioche appeared in Rousseau’s Confessions when Marie was just nine.

rows.q: While watching an NFL game at the White House in 2002, George W. Bush briefly lost consciousness and bruised his cheek after choking on what snack?
rows.n: He fainted due to a temporary drop in heart rate, startling his two pet dogs, Barney and Spot.

rows.q: Trained by Tom Smith and ridden by Red Pollard, this Depression-era champion racehorse famously upset Triple Crown winner War Admiral in 1938.
rows.n: He was named 1938 American Horse of the Year despite War Admiral’s Triple Crown pedigree.

rows.q: In 2022’s Everything Everywhere All at Once, the nihilistic villain Jobu Tupaki concentrates all her cosmic despair onto what baked breakfast item?
rows.n: Directors the Daniels said the bagel joke was inspired by a depressed feeling that nothing matters.

rows.q: Danny and his band of vagrant paisano friends drink two-gallon jugs of wine in Monterey in what 1935 novel, John Steinbeck’s first commercial hit?
rows.n: Steinbeck structured the novel as a loose parody of the legends of King Arthur and his knights.

rows.q: Oiled from head to toe and wearing a traditional ta’ovala skirt, this taekwondo athlete went viral as the shirtless flag-bearer for Tonga at Rio 2016.
rows.n: He returned to the Olympics two years later in Pyeongchang as a cross-country skier.

rows.q: Its genus name Ophiophagus means snake-eater in Greek, reflecting what venomous Asian serpent’s habit of preying on other snakes?
rows.n: It is the world’s longest venomous snake, capable of growing over 18 feet in length.

rows.q: After surviving dozens of assassination attempts and smoking 150 cigarettes a day, this self-proclaimed monarch fled Albania when Italy invaded in 1939.
rows.n: He remains the only modern European monarch to have personally fired back at his would-be assassins.

rows.q: Before earning an Oscar nomination for Chicago, Dana Owens scored a 1989 feminist hip-hop anthem with ‘Ladies First’ under what royal stage name?
rows.n: ‘Latifah’ means delicate and kind in Arabic, a nickname given to her by her cousin when she was eight.

rows.q: Named in 1683 to honor the Portuguese wife of Charles II, Catherine of Braganza, this is geographically the largest of New York City’s five boroughs.
rows.n: Brooklyn, established at the same time, was named Kings County in honor of her husband, Charles II.

rows.q: Adapting the first book of T.H. White’s The Once and Future King, Disney’s 1963 animated feature about young King Arthur was released under what title?
rows.n: It was the final Disney animated feature released during Walt Disney’s lifetime before his death in 1966.

rows.q: First won in 1851 by a New York syndicate sailing around the Isle of Wight, the oldest trophy in international sport is known by what naval name?
rows.n: The trophy was held by the New York Yacht Club for 132 years until Australia II broke the streak in 1983.

rows.q: Originally marketed in 1907 as the Health Kup to combat train germs, this disposable paper vessel was rebranded in 1919 after a New York doll company.
rows.n: Inventor Lawrence Luellen originally teamed with Hugh Moore to sell both the cups and water-vending machines.

rows.q: Team Cherry’s acclaimed 2017 indie Metroidvania tasks an insectoid wanderer with exploring the ruined subterranean kingdom of Hallownest. Name the game.
rows.n: Fans have spent years awaiting its sequel, Silksong, starring the needle-wielding warrior Hornet.

rows.q: Guided by his Scottish farm manager James Anderson, which founding father operated one of America’s largest whiskey distilleries in 1799?
rows.n: He produced nearly 11,000 gallons of rye whiskey in 1799, the year he died.

rows.q: Designed as a Sony mascot to rival Mario, this marsupial protagonist was originally codenamed ‘Willy the Wombat’ by Naughty Dog.
rows.n: Co-creator Andy Gavin chose a bandicoot after flipping through a field guide to Tasmanian mammals.

rows.q: Run at a grueling mile and a half, this Long Island race nicknamed ‘The Test of the Champion’ forms the final leg of the Triple Crown.
rows.n: Secretariat set the dirt world record here in 1973, winning by an astonishing 31 lengths.

rows.q: In the tale of the three Peverell brothers, which magical heirloom was requested from Death by the youngest brother, Ignotus?
rows.n: Ignotus passed it to his son, and it eventually descended through the Potter family to Harry.

rows.q: Drawing from 17th-century Spanish swashbuckling plays, what three-word idiom traditionally describes espionage and undercover intrigue?
rows.n: It translates the Spanish ‘comedia de capa y espada’, describing plots full of duelists in disguise.

rows.q: Powered by a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine, what distinctive elliptical-winged interceptor did R.J. Mitchell design to defend British skies?
rows.n: Mitchell tragically died of cancer in 1937, never seeing his fighter turn the tide in the war.

rows.q: Centering on bond trader Sherman McCoy’s downfall in the Bronx, what 1987 satirical bestseller coined the phrase ‘Master of the Universe’?
rows.n: Tom Wolfe spent months riding with Bronx homicide cops before publishing the novel in serial form.

rows.q: Ferdinand Magellan was killed in 1521 on the island of Mactan, located in what modern-day Southeast Asian archipelago of over 7,000 islands?
rows.n: Mactan’s chieftain, Lapulapu, is widely celebrated today as the country’s first national hero.

rows.q: In 2005, thirty-three years after the break-in, Vanity Fair revealed that this former FBI associate director was the secret Watergate source Deep Throat.
rows.n: Felt passed his tips to Bob Woodward during late-night meetings in an underground parking garage in Rosslyn, Virginia.

rows.q: Cartoonist Thomas Nast popularized the Tammany tiger symbol while relentlessly lampooning what corrupt New York City political boss in Harper’s Weekly?
rows.n: Tweed once complained, ‘My constituents can’t read, but they can’t help seeing them damn pictures.’

rows.q: After finding a severed human ear in a field, college student Jeffrey Beaumont is pulled into a dark criminal underworld in what 1986 David Lynch film?
rows.n: Dennis Hopper’s chilling turn as the nitrous-oxide-huffing Frank Booth helped revive his acting career.

rows.q: Under the alias Dread Pirate Roberts, Ross Ulbricht launched what darknet marketplace, which the FBI seized in 2013 alongside millions in Bitcoin?
rows.n: Ulbricht is serving two consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole at a federal prison in Arizona.

rows.q: Cary Grant plays a drama critic who discovers his two maiden aunts have been poisoning lonely bachelors with spiked wine in what 1944 Frank Capra comedy?
rows.n: Boris Karloff originated the role of Jonathan on Broadway, but producers refused to release him to appear in the film.

rows.q: Before sweeping 40 states in the 1912 presidential election, Woodrow Wilson served just two years in elected office as the governor of which U.S. state?
rows.n: Wilson spent eight years as president of Princeton University before party bosses tapped him for the governorship.

rows.q: While mainland herds died out around 10,000 years ago, an isolated relict population of this shaggy, tusked mammal survived on Wrangel Island until 2000 BC.
rows.n: The final Wrangel Island mammoths outlived the construction of Egypt’s Great Pyramid of Giza.

rows.q: Fronted by Brett Anderson, this glamorous alternative rock band won the 1993 Mercury Prize for their self-titled debut, kick-starting the Britpop era.
rows.n: In the United States, trademark conflicts with a Maryland lounge singer forced the band to tour as The London Suede.

rows.q: In May 1932, five years to the day after Lindbergh’s flight, which aviator landed a red Lockheed Vega in a Northern Ireland pasture?
rows.n: Her 15-hour flight from Newfoundland made her the first woman and second person to fly the Atlantic solo.

rows.q: In 2012, which Hollywood director piloted his lime-green Deepsea Challenger submersible nearly 36,000 feet down into the Mariana Trench?
rows.n: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh made the only previous descent to Challenger Deep in 1960.

rows.q: Which American chemist followed his 1954 Nobel Prize for chemical bonding with an unshared 1962 Nobel Peace Prize for his anti-nuclear activism?
rows.n: Marie Curie was the only other individual to win Nobel Prizes in two different categories.

rows.q: Don Budge did it first as an amateur in 1938. Which Australian “Rocket” won all four tennis Grand Slam singles titles in a calendar year in 1962?
rows.n: Laver repeated the calendar Grand Slam in 1969, becoming the only player to do it twice.

rows.q: During the Gemini 4 mission in 1965, which astronaut floated outside his spacecraft for twenty minutes with a handheld gas propulsion gun?
rows.n: His spacewalk came three months after Alexei Leonov performed the world’s first outside Voskhod 2.

rows.q: In July 1947, eleven weeks after Jackie Robinson’s debut, which Hall of Fame outfielder integrated the American League with the Cleveland Indians?
rows.n: Robinson and Doby both won World Series titles within their first decade in the majors.

rows.q: Nicknamed the “First Lady of American Theatre”, which actress completed her EGOT in 1977 with a Grammy for Best Spoken Word Album?
rows.n: Composer Richard Rodgers was the first person to achieve the milestone, finishing his sweep in 1962.

rows.q: Aiming for India in 1500, which Portuguese navigator swung so far west into the Atlantic that he made landfall in modern-day Brazil?
rows.n: He was retracing Vasco da Gama’s route south, but his westward detour claimed South America for Lisbon.

rows.q: Element 100 was discovered in the radioactive debris of the 1952 Ivy Mike thermonuclear detonation and named in honor of which Manhattan Project physicist?
rows.n: While discussing extraterrestrial life at Los Alamos in 1950, he formulated his paradox by asking, “Where is everybody?”

rows.q: Sharing the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac, which Austrian scientist fled Graz following the 1938 Anschluss, having earlier devised a fundamental wave equation?
rows.n: In 1935, he introduced his famous feline thought experiment to illustrate the absurdity of quantum superposition.

rows.q: While attempting to build a perpetual motion machine in the 1650s, which French polymath accidentally invented the mechanical spinning wheel used in modern roulette?
rows.n: In his Pensées, he framed belief in God as an optimal wager based on infinite reward versus finite loss.

rows.q: In materials science, the ratio comparing how much a stretched rubber band thins to how much it lengthens is named for which French mathematician, whose surname translates to “fish”?
rows.n: He introduced the Poisson distribution in 1837 to model the probability of rare, independent events over time.

rows.q: Born in a Surrey village that gave him his surname, which 14th-century Franciscan friar fled papal custody in Avignon after defending apostolic poverty against Pope John XXII?
rows.n: His philosophical principle that simpler explanations should be preferred over complex ones is called Occam’s razor.

rows.q: During an 1861 Royal Institution lecture, which Scottish physicist unveiled the world’s first durable color photograph, made by combining three filtered images of a tartan ribbon?
rows.n: His 1867 demon thought experiment challenged the second law of thermodynamics by sorting fast and slow molecules.

rows.q: Presenting his multivolume Celestial Mechanics to Napoleon, which French astronomer famously brushed off the absence of a divine creator by declaring, “I had no need of that hypothesis”?
rows.n: His deterministic “demon” thought experiment posited that knowing every atom’s position allows calculating the future.

rows.q: On Edinburgh’s Royal Mile, a bronze statue of which Scottish Enlightenment philosopher has a gleaming, polished big toe because students rub it for good luck before their exams?
rows.n: His “guillotine” or razor is the principle that an “ought” cannot be logically derived from an “is.”

rows.q: Stretching over 1,400 miles off Queensland, this vast marine system was first charted by Europeans after Captain James Cook ran HMS Endeavour aground on it in 1770.
rows.n: Cook had to throw ballast and cannons overboard to float his damaged ship free from the coral.

rows.q: Floating in German Gluhwein and studded into orange peels, this pungent spice consists of the dried, unopened flower buds of an Indonesian evergreen tree.
rows.n: Its English name comes from the Latin clavus, meaning nail, due to the shape of the dried bud.

rows.q: Built around a harmonica hook from Lee Oskar’s 1978 song ‘San Francisco Bay,’ this 2013 dance-pop hit paired rapper Pitbull with vocalist Kesha.
rows.n: It was Kesha’s last Billboard Hot 100 number-one hit before her multi-year legal battle with Dr. Luke.

rows.q: While popular myth claims this South American snake suffocates prey, it actually kills by circulatory arrest. Its binomial and common names are identical.
rows.n: It is one of the few animal species whose scientific genus and species match its everyday English name.

rows.q: Wearing matching jumpsuits and numbered masks, this nine-member metal band from Des Moines exploded onto the heavy rock scene with their 1999 self-titled album.
rows.n: Their dedicated global fanbase is famously referred to by the band as ‘Maggots.’

rows.q: Ending with the tragic aria ‘Con onor muore,’ this 1904 Puccini opera follows the young geisha Cio-Cio-San after she is abandoned by a U.S. naval officer.
rows.n: Puccini revised the score multiple times after its Milan premiere was notoriously jeered by the audience.

rows.q: Smashed with a silver hammer upon a pope’s death to prevent forgery, this papal signet ring depicting Saint Peter hauling in a net is known by what maritime title?
rows.n: Today the ring is merely defaced by scratching a cross across the seal rather than smashed into pieces.

rows.q: Scored by judges walking out on the ice with tape measures, this foundational, two-lobed tracing was a mandatory Olympic test until eliminated in 1990.
rows.n: Compulsory geometric tracings originally accounted for 60 percent of a figure skater’s overall score.

rows.q: Starring Chris Hemsworth as black-market mercenary Tyler Rake, what 2020 Netflix thriller follows a lethal rescue mission through Dhaka?
rows.n: The film was adapted from the graphic novel Ciudad, co-written by Avengers director Joe Russo.

rows.q: After wrapping The Office, Ricky Gervais created this BBC comedy following Andy Millman, an aspiring actor who can only land background roles.
rows.n: The show featured major celebrities, from David Bowie to Kate Winslet, playing twisted versions of themselves.

rows.q: To earn this highest commercial grade, olive oil must be extracted purely mechanically with no chemical treatment and have free acidity below 0.8%.
rows.n: Any sensory defects detected by a certified tasting panel will disqualify an oil from this classification.

rows.q: Counterintuitively, a bottle of Champagne or Prosecco bearing this two-word classification tastes slightly sweeter than one labeled Brut.
rows.n: Extra Dry sparkling wine holds 12 to 17 grams of residual sugar per liter, while Brut must stay under 12 grams.

rows.q: In 2020, Major League Baseball adopted the controversial ghost runner rule, placing a runner on second base to start every frame of this phase.
rows.n: Originally introduced during the pandemic to save pitching arms, the rule became permanent in 2023.

rows.q: Sparked by a murder in Taiwan, massive 2019 Hong Kong protests targeted a proposed bill permitting suspects to face what legal process in China?
rows.n: Chief Executive Carrie Lam formally shelved the legislation in September 2019 after months of clashes.

rows.q: In NASA jargon, a spacewalk is officially an EVA. What adjective does the E represent, denoting work performed outside the spacecraft?
rows.n: Alexei Leonov performed the world’s first spacewalk in 1965, floating outside the Voskhod 2 capsule for 12 minutes.

rows.q: Packaged in slim envelopes of 15 sticks, what brand introduced in 1984 became the Wrigley company’s first sugar-free gum?
rows.n: Wrigley sweetened the 1984 release with NutraSweet, introducing peppermint and spearmint flavors first.

rows.q: French is widely nicknamed the “language of” which satirical playwright, who collapsed on stage in 1673 while starring in his own comedy The Imaginary Invalid?
rows.n: Despite hemorrhaging from tuberculosis, he finished the show; he died at home a few hours later.

rows.q: In 2024, Ian McKellen tumbled off a London stage during a battle scene while playing this portly, sack-swilling knight in an adaptation of Henry IV.
rows.n: McKellen credited his padded fat suit with saving him from more severe injuries after he fell into the front row.

rows.q: After 602 people died in a 1903 fire during the musical Mr. Bluebeard at Chicago’s Iroquois Theatre, venues worldwide made this push-operated door hardware mandatory.
rows.n: Trapped patrons had piled against locked, inward-opening doors, prompting sweeping building code reforms.

rows.q: Plagued by concussions and broken bones, Broadway’s Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark saw stunt doubles repeatedly injured while aerial-dueling this glider-riding archenemy.
rows.n: Aerialist Christopher Tierney suffered a fractured skull and cracked vertebrae after a 30-foot plunge in 2010.

rows.q: During her penultimate Broadway performance in 2005, Idina Menzel cracked a rib falling through a trapdoor while playing this green-skinned protagonist.
rows.a: Elphaba (or Wicked Witch of the West)
rows.n: Unable to perform the next day in full costume, Menzel walked out in a red tracksuit for the finale to a huge ovation.

rows.q: In 1984, comedian Tommy Cooper collapsed fatally during a West End variety show broadcast live on TV, while wearing this trademark red Middle Eastern hat.
rows.n: The audience and orchestra roared with laughter, assuming his sudden collapse was a deliberate comedic stunt.

rows.q: Andrew Lloyd Webber’s 1984 West End hit Starlight Express became a nightmare for underwriters because the entire cast performed while strapped into these.
rows.n: Cast members endured hundreds of fractures, concussions, and sprains over the musical’s high-speed London run.

rows.q: In 1613, London’s original Globe Theatre burned to the ground during a performance of this royal history play when a theatrical cannon ignited the thatch roof.
rows.n: Amazingly, all patrons escaped unharmed, including a man whose burning pants were doused with bottled ale.

rows.q: Canada’s most famous modern stamp error is a 1959 invert commemorating the opening of this joint U.S.-Canadian channel connecting the Atlantic to the lakes.
rows.n: Queen Elizabeth II and Dwight D. Eisenhower officially opened the seaway together aboard the royal yacht Britannia.

rows.q: In 1962, the U.S. Post Office intentionally printed 40 million invert errors honoring what Swedish UN Secretary-General to keep speculators from profiting?
rows.n: Hammarskjöld had died in a plane crash the previous year while en route to cease-fire negotiations in the Congo.

rows.q: In 1968, China withdrew its “The Whole Country is Red” stamp within half a day after an editor noticed the printer had left this island territory white.
rows.n: Designer Wang Weisheng was questioned by authorities, but escaped prison because the mistake was deemed an accident.

rows.q: Canada modified its 1954 banknote series after citizens complained that the highlights in Queen Elizabeth’s hair resembled the face of this wicked entity.
rows.n: Engraver George Gundersen had simply copied photographic highlights from an official portrait by Yousuf Karsh.

rows.q: In 2018, Australia printed millions of fifty-dollar bills with a microscopic typo that dropped an “i” from what 14-letter word for accountability?
rows.n: The typo appeared in Edith Cowan’s maiden speech; the Reserve Bank left all 46 million misprinted notes in circulation.

rows.q: One of the world’s first inverted stamp errors occurred in 1855 in Western Australia, when the border was misprinted upside down around this aquatic bird.
rows.n: Philatelists long called it the Inverted Swan, though modern analysis proved the frame was inverted, not the bird.

rows.q: A 1932 Philippine stamp labeled “Pagsanjan Falls” became a famous error after the engraver accidentally depicted Vernal Fall in this California park.
rows.n: An engraver at the Bureau of Engraving and Printing confused two unlabeled waterfall photographs in his file.

rows.q: Philately’s most celebrated misprint, 1918’s Inverted Jenny, accidentally flipped an image of the JN-4 biplane built by what rival of the Wright brothers?
rows.n: William T. Robey bought the sole sheet of 100 inverted stamps for $24; one sold in 2023 for over two million dollars.

rows.q: In Sergei Prokofiev’s Peter and the Wolf, what deep, double-reed woodwind instrument represents the grumbling voice of the Grandfather?
rows.n: Prokofiev scored the other animals as flute for the bird, oboe for the duck, and clarinet for the cat.

rows.q: Katharine Lee Bates was moved to write the lyrics to “America the Beautiful” after taking in the vista from the summit of what Colorado mountain?
rows.n: Explorer Zebulon Pike led an 1806 expedition to map the area, but he never actually managed to reach its summit.

rows.q: Born Ernest Evans, this singer took his stage name as a pun on Fats Domino before sparking an international dance craze in 1960.
rows.n: American Bandstand host Dick Clark’s wife, Barbara, came up with the playful moniker.

rows.q: He collected his first competitive Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay in 2019 for BlacKkKlansman, decades after Do the Right Thing was snubbed.
rows.n: His only previous Oscar was an honorary award presented in 2015 for his lifetime contributions to cinema.

rows.q: Carved to spit rainwater away from masonry walls, these grotesque stone figures take their name from an Old French word for “throat.”
rows.n: If a carved roof monster does not actually serve as a water spout, architecture rules designate it a grotesque.

rows.q: Bound to a stake and shot with arrows for his Christian faith under Diocletian, what third-century Roman martyr became a favorite of Renaissance art?
rows.n: Miraculously surviving the execution, he was nursed back to health by Irene of Rome before being beaten to death.

rows.q: Laurel and Hardy, Harold Lloyd, and the Our Gang children were all launched to comedy stardom by what pioneering movie producer?
rows.n: His studio was nicknamed “The Laugh Factory to the World” and competed head-to-head with Mack Sennett.

rows.q: Nicknamed by Oakland A’s owner Charlie Finley, what Hall of Fame pitcher tossed a perfect game in 1968 and won five World Series rings?
rows.n: Finley fabricated a story that young Jim had run away and returned with a pair of catfish to give him a hook.

rows.q: Raphael’s marble sarcophagus rests inside which ancient Roman landmark, having requested burial beneath the open sky of its famous central oculus?
rows.n: Raphael was buried in 1520 beside his fiancee Maria Bibbiena, though he famously delayed marrying her for years.

rows.q: Facing poverty at his death in 1637, playwright Ben Jonson was buried standing completely upright to fit into a tiny two-foot-square plot in which London landmark?
rows.n: His gravestone was carved with the famous typo ‘O Rare Ben Johnson,’ accidentally adding an extra ‘h’ to his name.

rows.q: Over one million people attended the 1897 dedication of North America’s largest mausoleum, situated in Manhattan’s Riverside Park. By what two-word common name is it known?
rows.n: Julia Dent Grant was laid to rest beside him in 1902 in a matching sarcophagus of Wisconsin red granite.

rows.q: English acquired a generic word for any grand above-ground sepulcher from which Wonder of the Ancient World, erected in the 4th century BC in what is now Bodrum, Turkey?
rows.n: Crusader knights later dismantled much of its stone to fortify the Castle of Saint Peter against the Ottomans.

rows.q: Known to ancient Egyptians as ‘The Place of Truth,’ which barren gorge on the west bank of the Nile opposite Luxor served as the principal burial site for pharaohs for 500 years?
rows.n: Designated KV62, Tutankhamun’s tomb was famously discovered there nearly intact by Howard Carter in 1922.

rows.q: In the late 18th century, bones from the dangerously overflowing Holy Innocents’ cemetery were moved into former limestone quarries, creating what eerie subterranean municipal ossuary?
rows.n: The bones of six to seven million people were transferred entirely at night, accompanied by chanting priests.

rows.q: In the tragic climax of Puccini’s Tosca, the title singer leaps to her death from the battlements of which Roman landmark, named for an archangel and built as Emperor Hadrian’s tomb?
rows.n: A fortified elevated corridor, the Passetto di Borgo, linked the castle to the Vatican so popes could escape sieges.

rows.q: Designed on a gridiron layout honoring Saint Lawrence’s martyrdom, which austere 16th-century monastery and palace near Madrid houses the subterranean Royal Pantheon of Spanish monarchs?
rows.n: Before entering the Royal Pantheon, royal corpses decay for roughly 25 years in a private lead-lined drying room.

rows.q: Lead singer Bruce Dickinson, a licensed commercial pilot, occasionally flew his bandmates and tour gear on a customized jet dubbed Ed Force One. Name this group.
Joseph Goebbels used the metaphor in a 1945 magazine article, but Winston Churchill made what four-syllable term famous a year later in a speech in Fulton, Missouri?
rows.n: Churchill’s 1946 address at Westminster College was formally titled “The Sinews of Peace.”

rows.q: Bearing distinctive hourglass-shaped crossbands, what venomous North American pit viper is responsible for more snakebites each year than any other in the United States?
rows.n: Their venom contains a protein called contortrostatin that halts the growth of certain cancer cells.

rows.q: Charles Dickens gave this title protagonist his own inverted initials, sending him to suffer under Mr. Murdstone and work at a grim London bottling warehouse.
rows.n: Dickens considered it his “favourite child” among his novels, drawing deeply on his own childhood.

rows.q: Songwriter Monroe Rosenfeld coined what nickname for a block of Manhattan’s West 28th Street, likening the din of cheap pianos to banging kitchen cookware?
rows.n: Sheet-music publishers set up shop there to be near the theaters on Broadway.

rows.q: Rescued from a French battlefield in 1918 by an American soldier, what German Shepherd went on to star in nearly thirty silent films for Warner Bros.?
rows.n: Studio legend holds that he won the popular vote for Best Actor at the very first Academy Awards.

rows.q: Folklorists John and Alan Lomax made the first field recordings of this twelve-string guitarist at Angola Prison in 1933, recording classics like “Goodnight, Irene.”
Years before winning an Oscar for Reversal of Fortune, this British actor earned a 1984 Tony Award for his Broadway debut in Tom Stoppard’s play The Real Thing.
rows.n: He played opposite Glenn Close, who also won a Tony for her performance in the production.

rows.q: Mark Twain quipped that this pale cruciferous vegetable is ‘cabbage with a college education.’ Name this Brassica cultivar, whose Romanesco variety grows in fractals.
rows.n: Romanesco cauliflower florets approximate the Fibonacci sequence in their branching spirals.

rows.q: Folk artist Bruce Langhorne inspired a 1965 Bob Dylan title track with a giant Turkish frame drum, which Dylan downsized to what jingling handheld instrument?
rows.n: Langhorne’s drum had small bells attached to the rim, which sparked the jingle-jangle lyric.

rows.q: In 1847, Austrian botanist Stephan Endlicher named what giant coniferous tree genus, widely thought to honor the Cherokee polymath who created his tribe’s syllabary?
rows.n: The spelling shifted slightly from the Cherokee leader’s usual transliteration, Sequoyah.

rows.q: Adopted in 1983, the national flag of what southeastern African nation is famously the only one in the world to feature a modern assault rifle, a bayoneted AK-47?
rows.n: The rifle symbolizes defense and vigilance, crossed with a hoe representing the nation’s agriculture.

rows.q: Zendaya became the youngest two-time Lead Actress drama winner in Emmy history for playing troubled teenager Rue Bennett on what HBO drama series?
rows.n: The series was adapted from an Israeli miniseries of the same name created by Ron Leshem and Daphna Levin.

rows.q: In his 1667 epic Paradise Lost, John Milton coined what chaotic noun—literally meaning ‘all demons’ in Greek—as the name of the high capital of Hell?
rows.n: Milton formed the compound from the Greek roots pan, meaning ‘all’, and daimonion, meaning ‘evil spirit’.

rows.q: Eight years after breaking off her engagement to naval officer Frederick Wentworth, Anne Elliot reunites with him in what final completed novel by Jane Austen?
rows.n: Austen died in July 1817; the novel was published posthumously by her brother that December.

rows.q: Nicknamed the ‘Ceylon magnet’ by Dutch traders because heating it creates an electrostatic charge, what boron silicate gemstone comes in a pink-and-green ‘watermelon’ variety?
rows.n: Heating tourmaline crystals polarizes them electrically, a property known in physics as pyroelectricity.

rows.q: When a 22-foot vat burst at London’s Horse Shoe Brewery in 1814, the city was flooded by 300,000 gallons of what dark ale, traditionally favored by river and street haulers?
rows.n: The tidal wave destroyed two tenement homes and claimed eight lives, but the brewery was cleared of negligence.

rows.q: When 5,000 barrels of burning whiskey flooded Dublin’s streets in 1875, none of the 13 casualties died from burns or smoke. Instead, they all succumbed to what condition?
rows.n: Bystanders drank the flaming river straight from the gutter using their boots and caps until they dropped unconscious.

rows.q: In 2018, firefighters in Werl, Germany used shovels, blowtorches, and hot water to clear a municipal street after a factory storage tank spilled a ton of what sweet?
rows.n: A DreiMeister factory tank leaked liquid milk chocolate, which quickly hardened upon hitting the chilly asphalt.

rows.q: In 2023, two ruptured distillery vats sent 2.2 million liters of red wine cascading through the streets of São Lourenço do Bairro in what European country?
rows.n: The deluge was enough to fill an Olympic swimming pool, prompting officials to divert it to prevent river pollution.

rows.q: In 1986, runoff from a pesticide warehouse fire in Switzerland turned which major river red, wiping out half a million fish as it flowed north toward the North Sea?
rows.n: The Sandoz disaster decimated the river’s eel population and led to strict European industrial safety regulations.

rows.q: In 1979, the largest radioactive spill in U.S. history breached a tailings dam at Church Rock, sending 1,100 tons of uranium mill waste onto the land of which tribe?
rows.n: The accident released more radiation into the local river than Three Mile Island released into the air months earlier.

rows.q: A 2.3-million-gallon wave of molasses tore through Boston in 1919 after a poorly built tank burst in which historic neighborhood, home to Paul Revere’s house?
rows.n: The massive blast killed 21 people and injured 150, traveling through the crowded streets at an estimated 35 mph.

rows.q: A 2017 warehouse roof collapse flooded the town of Lebedyan, Russia with 28 million liters of fruit juice. The facility was owned by which American soft-drink titan?
rows.n: Vast torrents of tomato, apple, and orange juice flowed directly into the Don River, turning the waters bright pink.

rows.q: ‘You and me, baby, ain’t nothin’ but mammals’ is the hook of ‘The Bad Touch,’ a 1999 alt-rock radio staple by which comedic Pennsylvania band?
rows.n: Despite their novelty appeal at home, the single topped the pop charts in Germany, Italy, and Australia.

rows.q: Originally referring to colorful shawls made of native karakul wool, which six-letter word is standard in the U.S. for a crocheted throw blanket?
rows.n: The term became widespread in English in the 1870s thanks to Victorian home-crafting publications.

rows.q: Derived from an Egyptian compound meaning ‘great house,’ which title originally referred to the royal palace before designating the monarch himself?
rows.n: It was not commonly applied to the ruler directly until the New Kingdom reign of Thutmose III.

rows.q: Consisting of gin or vodka mixed with grapefruit juice over ice, which tart highball was popularized by the Post House transit terminal restaurants?
