rows.n: Adding a rim of coarse salt to the glass transforms the cocktail into a Salty Dog.

rows.q: Equipped with an owl-like facial disc to detect prey by sound, what slender raptor known for skimming marshes shares its name with a British jump jet?
rows.n: Unlike most raptors, males of the marsh-hunting species regularly mate with up to five females.

rows.q: In Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone, Hagrid illegally hatches a dragon egg in his hut, producing Norbert, a member of what Scandinavian breed?
rows.n: In the final book, Charlie Weasley reveals that Norbert is female and has been renamed Norberta.

rows.q: Fronted by brothers Pat and Lolly Vegas, which Native American funk-rock band reached number five on the Billboard Hot 100 with ‘Come and Get Your Love’?
rows.n: Their name is a Cajun slang term for a person of mixed racial heritage, nodding to their Yaqui roots.

rows.q: In the 1998 PlayStation classic Metal Gear Solid, Solid Snake infiltrates an Alaskan base to neutralize a rogue uprising led by this elite unit.
rows.n: The rogue unit’s official insignia features a snarling canine gripping a combat knife between its jaws.

rows.q: Owen Wilson, Adrien Brody, and Jason Schwartzman play estranged brothers traveling across India by train in this 2007 Wes Anderson comedy-drama.
rows.n: The movie was preceded by the prologue short Hotel Chevalier, starring Jason Schwartzman and Natalie Portman.

rows.q: In 1972, the island nation led by Sirimavo Bandaranaike adopted a republican constitution that replaced what British colonial name with Sri Lanka?
rows.n: The Ceylon Tea Board still retains the colonial name on its official lion logo trademark.

rows.q: In the formal Japanese ritual of chanoyu, practitioners use a bamboo whisk called a chasen to froth what vivid green powdered substance?
rows.n: The leaves used for matcha are shade-grown for several weeks before harvest to boost chlorophyll levels.

rows.q: Endemic to the Cederberg mountains of South Africa, the broom-like shrub Aspalathus linearis is better known by what Afrikaans name meaning ‘red bush’?
rows.n: Its leaves undergo oxidation to produce its rich amber color, though green unoxidized rooibos is also made.

rows.q: After losing his blue jacket in Mr. McGregor’s garden, Beatrix Potter’s Peter Rabbit is put to bed by his mother and dosed with what calming infusion?
rows.n: Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail, who were good little bunnies, had bread, milk, and blackberries for supper.

rows.q: On the Cosby Show spin-off A Different World, what actress spent six seasons portraying the snooty, pampered Southern belle Whitley Gilbert?
rows.n: Guy also wrote a 2005 biography of Afeni Shakur, the Black Panther activist and mother of Tupac Shakur.

rows.q: In the Dragon Ball franchise, what shape-shifting pig travels with Goku and Bulma, and notoriously wished for a pair of comfortable underwear?
rows.n: He made the wish to prevent Emperor Pilaf from taking over the world.

rows.q: A 130-foot monument in Newcastle upon Tyne honors this Whig Prime Minister, who oversaw the 1832 Reform Act and the abolition of slavery in the British Empire.
rows.n: The monument was partially funded by public subscription to thank him for his political reforms.

rows.q: In 1984, Bruce Springsteen’s “Dancing in the Dark” video featured an unknown Courteney Cox, who soon landed a recurring role as Alex P. Keaton’s girlfriend on this sitcom.
rows.n: Springsteen’s track spent four weeks stuck at number two behind Prince’s When Doves Cry.

rows.q: Cyndi Lauper cast what Hawaiian-shirted pro wrestler, famous for rubber bands in his beard, as her scolding father in the video for “Girls Just Want to Have Fun”?
rows.n: Albano later voiced Mario in The Super Mario Bros. Super Show!

rows.q: Carly Simon’s Bond theme “Nobody Does It Better” plays over the credits of The Spy Who Loved Me, right after 007 skis off a cliff with a parachute bearing what design?
rows.n: The song spent three weeks at number two in 1977, held off by Debby Boone’s You Light Up My Life.

rows.q: Madonna’s pink-gowned music video for “Material Girl” was a frame-by-frame homage to Marilyn Monroe singing about diamonds in what 1953 musical comedy?
rows.n: Material Girl was blocked from number one on the Hot 100 by REO Speedwagon’s Can’t Fight This Feeling.

rows.q: Five days after releasing “Like a Rolling Stone,” Bob Dylan outraged traditionalists by playing it with an electric band at what Rhode Island summer festival?
rows.n: Dylan’s single peaked at number two, held out of the top spot by The Beatles’ Help!

rows.q: In 2021, rap duo Tag Team parodied their 1993 anthem “Whoomp! (There It Is)” as an ice-cream-scooping celebration in an ad campaign for what insurer?
rows.n: Whoomp! (There It Is) spent seven weeks at number two in 1993, stuck behind UB40 and Mariah Carey.

rows.q: Mike Myers fought producer Lorne Michaels to use Queen’s “Bohemian Rhapsody” in Wayne’s World, threatening to walk if forced to use this rival rock band.
rows.n: The film catapulted Bohemian Rhapsody to number two on the Hot 100, sixteen years after its initial release.

rows.q: John Fogerty wrote CCR’s apocalyptic “Bad Moon Rising” after watching a film adaptation of what Stephen Vincent Benét short story about a Faustian trial?
rows.n: CCR holds the Billboard record for most number-two hits without a number-one: five in total.

rows.q: Widely cited as evidence of natural selection, this insect dramatically shifted from pale speckled to dark coloring as coal soot coated English trees.
rows.n: The phenomenon, known as industrial melanism, reversed when clean air laws reduced soot in the mid-20th century.

rows.q: Though purists balked when it debuted for 2003, this mid-size luxury SUV was the very first four-door vehicle ever mass-produced by Porsche.
rows.n: It became Porsche’s best-selling model and generated the profits that kept the 911 sports car in production.

rows.q: In soccer, cleanly kicking or slipping the ball between the spread legs of an oncoming defender is referred to by this slang term.
rows.n: The term may originate from 19th-century slang where “nutmegged” meant being tricked, as with wooden nutmegs.

rows.q: In a mind-bending 2006 anime film by Satoshi Kon, a psychologist enters patients’ subconscious dreams using this titular alter-ego code name.
Neil Young kicks off his 1969 album Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere with this hard-rocking track, famous for a solo played on a single repeating note.
rows.n: Young claimed he wrote the song while bedridden with a 103-degree fever at his home in Topanga Canyon.

rows.q: Claiming descent from the last Incan emperor, this Peruvian singer wowed mid-century audiences with a vocal range spanning nearly five octaves.
rows.n: A persistent 1950s urban legend falsely claimed she was just a Brooklyn housewife named Amy Camus spelled backwards.

rows.q: Appointed to finish her late husband’s term in 1931, this Arkansas politician became the first woman ever elected to the United States Senate.
rows.n: Louisiana Senator Huey Long staged a weeklong, whirlwind campaign tour across Arkansas to help secure her victory.

rows.q: Extending across southwestern Cambodia into eastern Thailand, the densely forested Kravanh range is known in English by this fragrant name.
rows.n: The remote range served as one of the final strongholds of the Khmer Rouge until the late 1990s.

rows.q: Before stepping onto the lunar surface in 1969, this Apollo 11 astronaut earned an MIT doctorate in astronautics, earning the moniker ‘Dr. Rendezvous’.
rows.n: He legally changed his first name to Buzz in 1988, adopting the childhood nickname his sister gave him.

rows.q: Derived from an Italian word for ‘middle’, this low-ceilinged intermediate floor often cantilevers over a theater lobby or opera house seating.
rows.n: In traditional Italian architecture, a mezzanino was a low story between two principal floors of a palace.

rows.q: Known as fior di latte when made with cow’s milk, this soft southern Italian cheese traditionally relies on the milk of water buffaloes.
rows.n: The name comes from the Neapolitan verb mozzare, which refers to cutting the curd pieces by hand.

rows.q: Federico Fellini coined this plural term for intrusive press photographers, taking it from a character’s surname in his 1960 drama La Dolce Vita.
rows.n: Fellini chose the name Paparazzo because it sounded to him like an annoying, buzzing mosquito.

rows.q: Placed above orchestral string passages, this Italian instruction tells violinists and cellists to pluck the strings rather than use their bows.
rows.n: Claudio Monteverdi is widely credited with the first orchestral use of pizzicato in his 1624 dramatic piece.

rows.q: Classified scientifically as Ursus arctos horribilis, this large North American brown bear is identified by a prominent muscular hump between its shoulders.
rows.n: The shoulder hump is packed with muscle that helps the bear dig up roots, burrowing animals, and winter dens.

rows.q: Traditionally calling out from the balcony of a minaret, this Islamic official chants the adhan five times a day to summon the community to prayer.
rows.n: The very first muezzin was Bilal ibn Rabah, a formerly enslaved Ethiopian and trusted companion of Muhammad.

rows.q: Invented at an 1880s New Orleans saloon, this citrusy cocktail made with gin, cream, and orange flower water was famously shaken for over ten minutes.
rows.n: During Mardi Gras in 1915, owner Henry Ramos hired a chain of thirty shaker boys just to handle the cocktail rush.

rows.q: Birmingham, England’s Gravelly Hill Interchange, famed for its complex tangle of slip roads on the M6, was dubbed this by a journalist in 1965.
rows.n: It spans over 30 acres, sits on 559 concrete columns, and carries traffic across six different levels.

rows.q: Software engineers use this tangled term for source code with convoluted control flow, especially caused by the overuse of GOTO statements.
rows.n: The structured programming movement in the late 1960s was popularized largely to eliminate it.

rows.q: When tracking hurricanes, meteorologists display conflicting computer forecast lines together on a single map, a visual tool with this tangled name.
rows.n: The individual lines show differing projections from agencies like the American GFS and European ECMWF.

rows.q: When British troops mocked colonists in Yankee Doodle, they sneered that sticking a feather in a cap was an attempt to look like this kind of dandy.
rows.n: The real macaronis were wealthy young Englishmen who adopted extravagant Italian fashions after the Grand Tour.

rows.q: Bred by Russian nobility to course quarry across open steppes, this aristocratic sight hound was officially known in the West as the Russian Wolfhound.
rows.n: Tsars frequently presented them as diplomatic gifts to foreign monarchs, including Queen Victoria.

rows.q: Voiced by animator Lou Romano, this clumsy, redheaded garbage boy acts as the kitchen puppet of the culinary-minded rat Remy in Ratatouille.
rows.n: He turns out to be the biological son and rightful heir of the late chef Auguste Gusteau.

rows.q: Bearing bright yellow crest feathers that reminded British sailors of flamboyant 18th-century dandies, this is the most populous crested seabird.
rows.n: Its name shares roots with the line about a feathered cap in the patriotic tune Yankee Doodle.

rows.q: This Direct Cinema pioneer filmed Bob Dylan’s 1965 British tour in Dont Look Back and captured David Bowie’s final Ziggy Stardust concert on 16mm.
rows.n: He received an honorary Academy Award for lifetime achievement in documentary filmmaking in 2013.

rows.q: The only unsolved skyjacking in commercial aviation history took place in 1971, when an extortionist calling himself Dan Cooper parachuted from a Boeing 727 into the skies of this U.S. state.
rows.n: Despite an FBI investigation lasting 45 years, neither Cooper nor his body has ever been found.

rows.q: Prompted by a staggering wave of over 130 air hijackings between 1968 and 1972, the FAA mandated in 1973 that every U.S. passenger pass through this electromagnetic screening device.
rows.n: The mandate, paired with bag inspections, caused domestic hijackings to plummet to nearly zero.

rows.q: During the 1972 hijacking of Southern Airways Flight 49, gunmen threatened to crash the plane into a nuclear reactor at this state’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory if their demands were not met.
rows.n: The terrifying 30-hour standoff directly spurred the U.S. government to introduce mandatory airport screening.

rows.q: In September 1970, Palestinian militants hijacked four Western airliners and forced three to land at an airstrip in this Middle Eastern kingdom, triggering a civil war known as Black September.
rows.n: After evacuating passengers, the hijackers blew up all three multi-million-dollar jets on the desert floor.

rows.q: Menahem Golan’s 1986 action film The Delta Force, starring Chuck Norris and Lee Marvin, was a thinly veiled recreation of the real-world hijacking of this airline’s Flight 847 to Beirut.
rows.n: Norris’s character leads a rescue team after hijackers segregate passengers with Jewish-sounding names.

rows.q: On Thanksgiving Eve in 1971, D.B. Cooper commandeered Flight 305, a Boeing 727 operated by this Minnesota-based airline, which merged into Delta in 2008.
rows.n: Cooper demanded $200,000 in cash and four parachutes before jumping over southwestern Washington.

rows.q: Garnet Ace Bailey, an executive and two-time Stanley Cup winner who was killed aboard hijacked United Flight 175 on 9/11, is honored by the lion mascot of this California NHL team.
rows.n: Bailey was traveling with fellow Kings scout Mark Bavis to Los Angeles for training camp.

rows.q: When an Eastern Air Lines flight was hijacked to Cuba in 1969, passengers began laughing and applauding because they recognized this creator and host of Candid Camera sitting among them.
rows.n: Funt tried in vain to persuade his fellow travelers that the gunman was not part of an elaborate prank.

rows.q: Sitting on the Mersey Estuary, which English port city was designated a European Capital of Culture in 2008 alongside Stavanger?
rows.n: The city generated more number-one pop hits per capita than any other city in the world.

rows.q: Venetian printer Aldus Manutius popularized this punctuation mark in 1494 to separate independent clauses without a full stop.
rows.n: Manutius also introduced italic type to save page space and fit more words in pocket editions.

rows.q: In fencing, what primary offensive attack involves kicking the front foot forward while pushing explosively off the back leg?
rows.n: The movement was developed by 16th-century Italian rapier masters and remains fencing fundamental.

rows.q: Essential to Louisiana red beans and rice, which legume contains high levels of the toxin phytohaemagglutinin when undercooked?
rows.n: Just four or five undercooked beans can trigger severe nausea and gastrointestinal distress.

rows.q: Which 1968 musical adaptation directed by Carol Reed was the last film carrying a G rating to win the Oscar for Best Picture?
rows.n: Reed was the uncle of actor Oliver Reed, who played the sinister villain Bill Sikes in the film.

rows.q: Originally recorded with a reggae groove titled ‘Once I Had a Love,’ what 1979 disco-infused track was Blondie’s first US number one?
rows.n: Debbie Harry and Chris Stein wrote the song in 1974, jokingly referring to it as their disco song.

rows.q: Bearing the Spanish surname of Christopher Columbus, what currency unit has been officially used by Costa Rica since 1896?
rows.n: El Salvador also used the colón until officially adopting the United States dollar in 2001.

rows.q: In the 1999 superhero comedy Mystery Men, what flatulent hero played by Paul Reubens drew his gas-based powers from a gypsy curse?
rows.n: His costume included a tactical ring pulled to release pent-up pressure with pinpoint aim.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Simba avenges Mufasa in the Pride Lands, then abdicates his throne to divide Britain among Cordelia, Goneril, and Regan.
rows.n: The Lion King itself drew heavy plot inspiration from Hamlet, not King Lear.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Simba belts Hakuna Matata in the savanna before crying ‘A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!’ at Bosworth Field.
rows.n: Jeremy Irons based his voice performance as Scar partly on Laurence Olivier’s Richard III.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Simba outruns a wildebeest stampede, then rallies an outnumbered English army on Saint Crispin’s Day at Agincourt.
rows.n: Kenneth Branagh’s 1989 film adaptation earned him Oscar nods for both directing and acting.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Simba returns from the jungle to overthrow Scar, then stages the Tudor pageant play that burned down the Globe in 1613.
rows.n: A cannon discharged during the performance ignited the Globe’s thatched roof.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Rafiki hoists baby Simba over Pride Rock before Henry Bolingbroke usurps this doomed monarch of the ‘hollow crown.’
rows.n: Shakespeare’s company was paid by supporters of the Earl of Essex to stage it before their 1601 rebellion.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Simba befriends Timon and Pumbaa, then carouses in Eastcheap taverns with the rotund knight Sir John Falstaff.
rows.n: Falstaff was originally named Sir John Oldcastle until descendants objected.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Buzz Lightyear rescues Woody from a greedy toy collector, then follows Proteus and Valentine to Duke Milan’s court.
rows.a: Toy Story Two Gentlemen of Verona
rows.n: Toy Story 2 was originally greenlit as a direct-to-video release before Disney upgraded it.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Elastigirl hunts the Screenslaver on a motorbike, then Proteus betrays Valentine in a romantic comedy set in Romeo’s hometown.
rows.a: The Incredibles Two Gentlemen of Verona
rows.n: It took 14 years for Pixar to release a sequel to Brad Bird’s original 2004 superhero film.

rows.q: Known for flashing a pale white mouth lining when threatened, what two-word pit viper is North America’s only venomous semi-aquatic snake?
rows.n: Young water moccasins have bright yellow tail tips that they wiggle as lures to attract frogs.

rows.q: Derived from the Irish Gaelic word bróg, what single-syllable noun describes the distinctive, lilting regional accent of English spoken in Ireland?
rows.n: A popular, though debated, theory claims the accent was said to sound like speaking with a shoe in your mouth.

rows.q: Sharing historical roots with tap and Irish step, what Appalachian percussive folk dance became the official state folk dance of both North and South Carolina?
rows.n: Dancers often wear special double taps that click against each other as well as the floor.

rows.q: Known for dissonant piano improvisations on standards like ‘Round Midnight’, what bebop pioneer shares his religious surname with a resident of an abbey?
Replacing Auckland in 1865 to be closer to the South Island, what coastal hub on the Cook Strait is the southernmost national capital in the world?
rows.n: Its notorious winds through the Cook Strait have earned it the nickname Windy Wellington.

rows.q: Derived from the Latin for ‘little stake’, what slender, needle-pointed dagger was developed in late medieval Italy to pierce through gaps in plate armor?
rows.n: The weapon’s narrow triangular cross-section was designed purely for thrusting, not cutting.

rows.q: Directed by Wolfgang Petersen and nominated for six Oscars, what claustrophobic 1981 German film depicts the doomed WWII patrol of submarine U-96?
rows.n: It was released both as a 149-minute feature film and as a six-part television miniseries.

rows.q: In 1830s American slang, what six-letter noun for a chronically idle bum or lazy vagrant was likely borrowed from the German Landläufer?
rows.n: Walt Whitman wrote an 1840 article titled ‘The Spanish Loafer’ about idle young men in New York.

rows.q: Abandoned in 1974 after its undersea coal ran out, Japan’s Hashima Island was used as cyber-terrorist Raoul Silva’s hideout in what 007 film?
rows.n: The island is also called Battleship Island because its high concrete seawalls give it the silhouette of a warship.

rows.q: In 1981, a boy plummeted into a steaming sinkhole in what Pennsylvania borough, finally spurring Congress to buy out the fire-plagued coal town?
rows.n: A trash fire set in an abandoned strip mine ignited an exposed coal seam in 1962 that may burn for another 250 years.

rows.q: German diamond miners built luxury mansions at Kolmanskop, now filled with blowing sand dunes, within what vast coastal desert in southern Africa?
rows.n: When richer deposits were discovered south near the Orange River in 1928, the town was left to the sand.

rows.q: Chile’s Atacama saltpeter town of Humberstone became a ghost town after the Haber-Bosch process let manufacturers mass-produce what pungent gas?
rows.n: Synthetic fertilizer collapsed the market for natural sodium nitrate mined across northern Chile.

rows.q: Deadly crocidolite mining in the contaminated Australian ghost town of Wittenoom inspired ‘Blue Sky Mine,’ a 1990 hit by what rock band?
rows.n: Australia officially degazetted Wittenoom in 2007 and removed it from all official maps.

rows.q: A 1982 flood spread lethal dioxin sprayed on unpaved roads across Times Beach, forcing a total federal buyout in what Midwestern U.S. state?
rows.n: The contaminated town along the Meramec River was demolished and turned into Route 66 State Park.

rows.q: When the Soufrière Hills volcano buried Plymouth in 1997, what Caribbean island was left with a ghost town as its official legal capital?
rows.n: Plymouth remains the de jure capital of the British territory, though government offices operate in Brades.

rows.q: Preserved by park rangers in a state of ‘arrested decay,’ what California gold-boom ghost town had over sixty saloons in its 1870s heyday?
rows.n: The town was abandoned as gold veins dried up and after a 1932 fire destroyed 90 percent of its buildings.

rows.q: Occupying HM Fort Roughs, a World War II sea fort in this cold body of water off the coast of Suffolk, the Principality of Sealand declared its independence in 1967.
rows.n: In 1968, a British judge ruled that because the fort was outside UK territorial waters, British courts had no say.

rows.q: In 1964, Leicester Hemingway founded the raft-based micronation of New Atlantis, bankrolled by a memoir he wrote about his older brother, author of this 1952 novella.
rows.a: The Old Man and the Sea
rows.n: Leicester earned 20,000 dollars from the book to construct his bamboo raft, which later sank in a tropical storm.

rows.q: Established in 2015 on an unclaimed pocket of floodplain called Gornja Siga, the micronation of Liberland sits on the western bank of this river dividing Croatia and Serbia.
rows.n: Croatian border police regularly arrest anyone trying to enter the land, which remains uninhabited.

rows.q: Established by squatters on an abandoned military base in 1971, the self-governing commune of Freetown Christiania is an enclave located inside this Scandinavian capital.
rows.n: Its famous Pusher Street openly sold cannabis for decades until residents voted in 2024 to dig it up.

rows.q: In 1982, Key West seceded to create the Conch Republic in response to a disruptive roadblock set up on Highway 1 by this federal enforcement agency.
rows.n: Secession lasted roughly one minute before Mayor Dennis Wardlow surrendered and requested one billion dollars in aid.

rows.q: Western Australia farmer Leonard Casley declared his land an independent principality in 1970 after the government slapped strict quotas on this staple cereal grain.
rows.n: Casley faced quotas limiting him to selling only a fraction of his harvest, sparking a 50-year tax feud with Canberra.

rows.q: In 1972, American real-estate mogul Michael Oliver built artificial land on Pacific reefs for his new Republic of Minerva, until this Polynesian kingdom sailed in and seized it.
rows.n: King Taufa’ahau Tupou IV personally led an expedition to tear down the Minerva flag and assert Tongan sovereignty.

rows.q: After buying the British island of Lundy in 1925, Martin Coles Harman declared himself king and minted unauthorized coins depicting this seabird, the island’s Norse namesake.
rows.n: Harman was fined by a British court for issuing his unauthorized half-puffin and one-puffin coins.

rows.q: In 1745, King Louis XV purchased an estate for his chief mistress Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson and officially elevated her to what aristocratic title?
rows.n: She lived at Versailles for nearly twenty years as the king’s most trusted political confidante.

rows.q: Due to its bumpy green skin and teardrop shape, 19th-century English speakers often referred to the avocado by what reptilian, fruit-based nickname?
rows.n: Sir Hans Sloane coined the name ‘avocado’ in 1696, but ‘alligator pear’ persisted well into the 20th century.

rows.q: Manufactured by Toronto’s Jem Rubber Company in the 1930s, what rubber novelty prank operates on the sudden expulsion of air through a flapped aperture?
rows.n: Prank maker S.S. Adams was originally offered the item but rejected it, calling it too vulgar to sell.

rows.q: Originating in 1782 as George Washington’s Badge of Military Merit, what U.S. decoration was revived in 1932 to honor service members wounded or killed in action?
rows.n: Washington’s original medal was made of silk; only three Revolutionary War soldiers were awarded it.

rows.q: In Arthurian legend, King Leodegrance of Cameliard gave what massive piece of hall furniture to King Arthur as a dowry gift when Arthur married Guinevere?
rows.n: Norman poet Wace first mentioned the table in 1155 to explain why no knight took precedence over another.

rows.q: Spanning decades of Afghan history, what 2003 debut novel by Khaled Hosseini centers on the fraught boyhood friendship between Amir and Hassan in Kabul?
rows.n: Hosseini wrote the novel while working full-time as an internal medicine physician in California.

rows.q: Promoted by a black-and-white video filmed in a single continuous take, what 1987 lead single from Bruce Springsteen’s Tunnel of Love explores romantic distrust?
At the height of hyperinflation in 2009, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe officially issued a single blue banknote bearing what astronomical face value?
rows.n: Despite its nominal value, the 100-trillion-dollar bill was worth around 40 U.S. cents when demonetized.

rows.q: Chosen by Athens in 621 BC to replace oral law, this harsh reformer prescribed the death penalty for even petty offenses like stealing a cabbage.
rows.n: He gave rise to the adjective draconian. Folklore claims he later suffocated under a shower of cloaks and hats.

rows.q: Developed by Israel’s NSO Group to infect smartphones via zero-click exploits, this spyware shares its name with a mythical winged steed.
rows.n: It could silently commandeer a targeted phone’s microphone and camera without the user ever clicking a link.

rows.q: Raised among Oxford scholars, this silver-tongued heroine uses the alethiometer to navigate the multiverse in Philip Pullman’s trilogy.
rows.n: Her shapeshifting daemon Pantalaimon eventually settles into the permanent form of a pine marten.

rows.q: Credited with saving its maker in 1985, this family car’s aerodynamic jellybean look ended Detroit’s obsession with boxy sedans.
rows.n: It stood as the best-selling car in the United States from 1992 until the Toyota Camry unseated it in 1997.

rows.q: Borrowed straight from the Latin word for a wooden torture cross, this four-letter noun now refers to the vital, decisive point of an issue.
rows.n: In textual analysis, the phrase crux interpretum denotes a passage that is virtually impossible to translate.

rows.q: Glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau feed this 2,000-mile waterway, the primary river that gave India its historic European name.
rows.n: Ancient Greeks derived their term Indos from the native Sanskrit word for the fast-flowing river, Sindhu.

rows.q: Marking the northernmost latitude where the sun shines directly overhead at noon, this line passes through Mexico, Egypt, and India.
Named from a Greek root meaning light due to its glowing eyes, this tufted-eared predator uses huge, furry paws as natural snowshoes.
rows.n: The Iberian lynx, once the world’s most endangered feline species, has made a steady population comeback in Spain.

rows.q: Now an informal word for any person, this common three-letter noun entered English as a term for grotesque effigies burned to mark the foiled 1605 Gunpowder Plot.
rows.n: The effigies depicted Guy Fawkes; over centuries, the word broadened from a ragged person to simply a fellow.

rows.q: Allan Pinkerton thwarted the 1861 Baltimore Plot against Abraham Lincoln; his agency’s unblinking logo later gave English what two-word slang term for a detective?
rows.n: The Pinkerton National Detective Agency used the slogan “We Never Sleep” beneath an open eye.

rows.q: In 1887, Aleksandr Ulyanov was hanged for a foiled bomb plot against Tsar Alexander III, radicalizing his teenage brother Vladimir, who later took what famous alias?
rows.n: Aleksandr helped manufacture the bombs using hollowed-out medical dictionaries packed with dynamite.

rows.q: In 1938, German generals prepared to depose Hitler if he invaded this neighbor, but their plot collapsed when the Munich Agreement ceded the Sudetenland.
rows.n: Plotters led by Hans Oster had an assault team ready in Berlin, but the peaceful annexation ruined their pretext.

rows.q: In 1800, Gabriel Prosser led a foiled Virginia rebellion that planned to take hostage which sitting governor, who later became the fifth U.S. president?
rows.n: A severe thunderstorm washed out roads, delaying the rebellion and allowing informants to warn Monroe.

rows.q: In 1806, Aaron Burr used Blennerhassett Island, now part of this “Mountain State,” as a staging ground for his foiled plot to carve out a Southwestern empire.
rows.n: Burr was arrested and tried for treason in Richmond, Virginia, but Chief Justice John Marshall acquitted him.

rows.q: On the eve of his ill-fated 1601 coup against Elizabeth I, the Earl of Essex’s followers paid the Lord Chamberlain’s Men to stage which monarch-deposing tragedy?
rows.n: Essex hoped King Richard’s on-stage deposition would incite Londoners to join his rebellion.

rows.q: Before his 1822 slave rebellion in Charleston was betrayed, leader Denmark Vesey bought his freedom in 1799 using money he won playing this type of wagering game.
rows.n: Vesey won a $1,500 prize in the East Bay Street lottery, purchased his freedom for $600, and worked as a carpenter.

rows.q: Featuring bizarre spoken lines about tanning butter and earplugs, what 1978 debut single became the signature party anthem for The B-52’s?
rows.n: John Lennon cited the song’s energy as the direct inspiration that prompted him to return to recording in 1980.

rows.q: Colin Farrell earned a Golden Globe nomination for what 2015 Yorgos Lanthimos satire, in which single adults are given 45 days to find a mate?
rows.n: Guests who fail to find a partner at the hotel are surgically turned into the animal of their choice.

rows.q: Created by Bill Barretta in 1996, what tempestuous, heavily accented Spanish Muppet character is famous for ending his sentences with ‘okay?’
rows.n: Barretta based the character’s fiery personality and cadence on a former boss at a California restaurant.

rows.q: Conceived during the Great Depression by Alfred Mosher Butts under the title Lexiko, what word game was trademarked under its current name in 1948?
rows.n: Butts determined the frequency and point values of letters by studying the front page of The New York Times.

rows.q: During the occupation of Boston in the 1770s, colonial residents hurled what derogatory, coat-inspired nickname at British redcoats?
rows.n: The slur mocked the British soldiers’ vivid red wool jackets, often shortened simply to ‘lobsters.’

rows.q: In Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, what Slytherin student accidentally destroys Ravenclaw’s diadem with Fiendfyre, dying in the blaze?
rows.n: Actor Jamie Waylett did not return for the final two films, so the scene was given to Gregory Goyle in the movie.

rows.q: After winning a 1932 Olympic swimming gold, what athlete starred on the silver screen as Tarzan, Flash Gordon, and Buck Rogers?
rows.n: He is the only actor to play all three of these legendary pulp-fiction heroes on film.

rows.q: A key face of 1960s Swinging London, what English model caused an international fashion uproar in 1965 by wearing a minidress in Melbourne?
rows.n: Her white shift dress ended four inches above the knee, scandalizing traditionalists at the Victoria Derby.

rows.q: Fronted by the late Bradley Nowell, this Long Beach ska-punk trio scored massive posthumous 1996 radio hits with “What I Got” and “Santeria.”
rows.n: Their breakthrough self-titled album was released two months after Nowell died of a heroin overdose.

rows.q: Launched in 2000 on the Gnutella network, this ubiquitous free peer-to-peer program plagued family PCs with malware disguised as MP3 downloads.
rows.n: A federal court shut it down in 2010; it was revived in 2022 as an AI-focused music creation platform.

rows.q: In Marvel Comics, this archenemy of Iron Man wields ten alien power rings recovered from a crashed spaceship in China’s Valley of Spirits.
rows.n: In the MCU film Iron Man 3, the character is initially portrayed as a front for a fake actor named Trevor Slattery.

rows.q: In Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, Jim Carrey undergoes a procedure to forget his impulsive ex-girlfriend, played by Kate Winslet and named what?
rows.n: Winslet wore several differently colored wigs so viewers could track the non-linear timeline by her hair.

rows.q: In the Glorious Revolution of 1688, this Dutch stadtholder crossed the North Sea to take the English throne, ruling jointly alongside his wife Mary II.
rows.n: His victory at the 1690 Battle of the Boyne is still commemorated annually by the Orange Order in Northern Ireland.

rows.q: Before electric lighting took over theaters, stages were illuminated by heating cylinders of calcium oxide with gas flames, inspiring this common idiom.
rows.n: Scottish engineer Thomas Drummond developed the illumination technique in the 1820s for surveying work.

rows.q: In Carol Reed’s 1949 film noir The Third Man, Orson Welles makes a famous doorway entrance playing this penicillin-racketeering fugitive in Vienna.
rows.n: Welles improvised the famous speech comparing Switzerland’s 500 years of peace to the invention of the cuckoo clock.

rows.q: Founded in West Berlin in 1967 by Edgar Froese, this pioneering electronic music group released landmark ambient synth albums like Phaedra and Rubycon.
rows.n: They later became prolific film composers, scoring movies such as Risky Business, Thief, and Legend.

rows.q: Invited to celebrate Zimbabwe’s official independence under the 1979 Lancaster House Agreement, this reggae icon chartered his own PA system to Harare to headline the ceremony.
rows.n: He performed his anthem ‘Zimbabwe’ amid clouds of tear gas when thousands crashed the stadium gates.

rows.q: Hours before the British Mandate for Palestine expired in 1948, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel not in contested Jerusalem, but in this coastal city’s art museum.
rows.n: The ceremony was held early at 4:00 PM to avoid conflicting with the Jewish Sabbath.

rows.q: Before reunification with West Germany in 1957, the Saar basin was famed for steep vineyards along the Saar River, known for prized, slate-grown bottles of this noble white wine grape.
rows.n: Saar wines were historically marketed as Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until the region was simplified to Mosel in 2007.

rows.q: Gaining independence from Britain in 1960, Cyprus is the culinary homeland of this brined sheep-and-goat milk cheese, prized for a high melting point that allows it to be grilled directly.
rows.n: In 2021, the European Union officially granted halloumi Protected Designation of Origin status.

rows.q: Following the 1990 treaty reuniting Germany, this British architect was chosen to redesign the Berlin Reichstag, topping it with a walk-through glass dome.
rows.n: Foster’s dome uses an inverted cone of 360 mirrors to funnel natural light into the parliament chamber below.

rows.q: After the 1993 Velvet Divorce dissolved Czechoslovakia, this six-time Vezina Trophy winner led the underdog Czech hockey team to Olympic gold at the 1998 Nagano Games.
rows.n: Known as ‘The Dominator,’ he allowed just six goals during the entire 1998 Olympic tournament.

rows.q: Though Hong Kong Island was ceded in perpetuity in 1842, Britain returned the entire territory in 1997 because this mainland region, comprising over 85% of its land, was on a 99-year lease.
rows.n: The 1898 Convention of Peking leased the New Territories rent-free until June 30, 1997.

rows.q: While shooting his 1961 Cold War comedy One, Two, Three on location, this director woke up on August 13 to find the Berlin Wall going up, forcing him to rebuild the Brandenburg Gate in Munich.
rows.n: It was James Cagney’s final film role before a twenty-year acting retirement.

rows.q: When a devastating leaf blight wiped out Sri Lanka’s coffee plantations in the 1870s, Scottish grocer Thomas Lipton stepped in to buy estates and plant this crop instead.
rows.n: By shipping Ceylon tea directly to his British shops, Lipton made what was once a luxury affordable to the masses.

rows.q: In the 1970s, the tiny Pacific island nation of Nauru briefly had the world’s highest per-capita GDP by strip-mining this resource, formed by fossilized seabird guano.
rows.n: When the deposits ran out by the early 2000s, roughly 80 percent of the island was left a barren limestone plateau.

rows.q: Invented near Santiago de Cuba around 1898, this classic rum, lime, and sugar cocktail takes its name from an iron mine and a beach where American soldiers landed.
rows.n: American mining engineer Jennings Cox allegedly invented it after running out of gin while hosting a party.

rows.q: In 1968, American singer Johnny Nash traveled to Kingston, Jamaica, where he met this reggae icon and scored a hit with his composition ‘Stir It Up.’
rows.n: Nash was among the first outside artists to record in Jamaica; Marley would record his own version on Catch a Fire.

rows.q: When Barbados named pop superstar Rihanna a National Hero in 2021, they honored a woman whose legal first name is not Rihanna, but this.
rows.n: Her full name is Robyn Rihanna Fenty; she used her middle name for music and her surname for her cosmetics empire.

rows.q: Ernest Hemingway wrote The Old Man and the Sea while living in Cuba. In the 1958 film adaptation, this two-time Oscar winner played Santiago.
rows.n: Tracy earned an Oscar nod for the role; the film won Best Original Score for legendary composer Dimitri Tiomkin.

rows.q: Madagascar’s apex mammalian predator looks like a small cougar, but this tree-climbing carnivore is actually a close kin of the mongoose.
rows.n: Known scientifically as Cryptoprocta ferox, it is endemic to Madagascar and feeds primarily on forest lemurs.

rows.q: Rising from the ocean south of Iceland during an eruption in 1963, this newly formed volcanic island took its name from a Norse fire giant.
rows.n: Named after Surtr, the island is strictly protected as a pristine laboratory to study how life colonizes bare rock.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Marcus Fenix saws through Locust hordes and straight into Tolstoy’s epic about the 1812 French invasion of Russia.
rows.n: Tolstoy fought in the Crimean War before writing his 1869 masterpiece.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Nintendo’s overall-wearing plumbers debate faith and patricide in Dostoevsky’s tale of Ivan, Alyosha, and Dmitri.
rows.n: Dostoevsky published the novel in 1880, shortly before his death.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Gordon Freeman’s crowbar-swinging sci-fi franchise drifts across the Pacific with an Indian boy and a Bengal tiger.
rows.n: Yann Martel’s 2001 novel won the Man Booker Prize.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Sackboy’s stitched-together platformer crash-lands in Pierre Boulle’s sci-fi novel about civilized simian overlords.
rows.a: Little Big Planet of the Apes
rows.n: Pierre Boulle also wrote The Bridge over the River Kwai.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Ubisoft’s exotic open-world shooter merges with Alan Paton’s 1948 novel of an apartheid-era Zulu pastor in Natal.
rows.n: Paton wrote the book while touring reformatories in Europe and America.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, BioWare’s dark fantasy RPG series infiltrates Edith Wharton’s high-society drama of 1870s Gilded Age New York.
rows.n: Edith Wharton was the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, Booker DeWitt’s floating city of Columbia merges with David Foster Wallace’s novel set at an elite tennis academy.
In this before-and-after, Capcom’s mansion-set zombie series becomes an Agatha Christie resort-island murder mystery solved by Hercule Poirot.
rows.n: Christie’s real-life Burgh Island Hotel inspired the setting.

rows.q: Scotsman James Taylor established commercial tea production in 1867 by planting 19 acres in the Kandy hills of what island nation?
rows.n: Taylor worked closely with Thomas Lipton, whose eponymous brand popularized Ceylon tea worldwide.

rows.q: Yul Brynner won an Oscar for 1956’s The King and I, a musical that remains strictly banned under lèse-majesté laws in what Asian nation?
rows.n: Thai authorities condemned the film for historical inaccuracies and portraying King Mongkut as a buffoon.

rows.q: The epic poem Shahnameh, or ‘Book of Kings,’ was completed by Ferdowsi around 1010 CE and remains the foundational national epic of what country?
rows.n: Ferdowsi wrote all 50,000 rhyming couplets in Persian, resisting Arabic influence during the Islamic Golden Age.

rows.q: Distinctive soapstone bird figurines found within the dry-stone ruins of a medieval trading city now grace the national flag of what African country?
rows.n: The massive curved stone towers of Great Zimbabwe were constructed without any mortar.

rows.q: Behind the dominant goaltending of Dominik Hasek, what underdog country beat Canada and Russia to win Olympic men’s hockey gold at Nagano in 1998?
rows.n: Hasek stopped all five Canadian attempts in the shootout, including shots by Theo Fleury and Eric Lindros.

rows.q: The endangered Irrawaddy dolphin, famous for cooperatively herding fish into local cast nets, is named for the chief river of what nation?
rows.n: Fishermen summon the dolphins using specific clicking sounds against the sides of their wooden boats.

rows.q: The 11,000-year-old megaliths of Göbekli Tepe, featuring massive T-shaped stone pillars carved with wild animals, stand in what modern nation?
rows.n: German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt led excavations at the site, which predates Stonehenge by 6,000 years.

rows.q: Spanning just 6,700 square miles between Mozambique and South Africa, Africa’s sole remaining absolute monarchy is what tiny landlocked nation?
rows.n: The country has two capitals: Mbabane serves as executive capital, while Lobamba is the royal seat.

rows.q: Sergei Eisenstein’s 1925 masterpiece Battleship Potemkin dramatizes a 1905 Black Sea mutiny, climaxing in an iconic massacre down a monumental flight of outdoor steps in what port city?
rows.n: The steps were officially renamed the Potemkin Stairs in 1955 to mark the 50th anniversary of the uprising.

rows.q: In October 1918, German sailors at Kiel and Wilhelmshaven mutinied rather than sail into a doomed final battle, directly triggering the revolution that forced which monarch to abdicate?
rows.n: Wilhelm fled across the border to the Netherlands, where he lived in exile at Huis Doorn until his death in 1941.

rows.q: The June 1905 mutiny aboard the Russian battleship Potemkin was ignited when crewmen refused to eat borscht prepared from beef crawling with what insect larvae?
rows.n: The ship’s surgeon inspected the meat and insisted the white specks were harmless fly eggs, enraging the crew.

rows.q: The 1789 mutiny on HMS Bounty erupted after months in Tahiti collecting over a thousand potted specimens of what starchy tropical fruit, intended as cheap sustenance for Caribbean slaves?
rows.n: Captain Bligh rationed precious drinking water to keep the breadfruit alive, further enraging his thirsty crew.

rows.q: In the acclaimed 1935 film Mutiny on the Bounty, what British actor earned an Oscar nomination for his snarling portrayal of the tyrannical Lieutenant William Bligh?
rows.n: The film earned three Best Actor nominations—for Laughton, Clark Gable, and Franchot Tone—an Academy record.

rows.q: In 1819, which French Romantic painter shocked the Paris Salon with a massive canvas depicting the horrific mutiny, starvation, and cannibalism among the shipwrecked crew of the frigate Méduse?
rows.n: Géricault interviewed survivors and visited hospital morgues to study the color and texture of dying flesh.

rows.q: Following a massive munitions explosion that killed 320 men in 1944, fifty African American sailors were convicted of mutiny after refusing to load ammunition at a naval magazine in what U.S. state?
rows.n: Located in the San Francisco Bay Area, the disaster and subsequent trial spurred the desegregation of the U.S. Navy.

rows.q: Cast adrift in an open launch by Bounty mutineers, Captain William Bligh navigated 3,600 miles to safety, landing at a Dutch outpost on what island now split between two nations?
rows.n: Bligh reached the settlement of Kupang on West Timor after an astonishing 47-day voyage with no charts.

rows.q: In 2012, a cat named Hank won 7,000 votes for U.S. Senate in Virginia, trailing Republican George Allen and this future 2016 Democratic VP nominee.
rows.n: Hank raised thousands of dollars for animal shelters and campaigned on job creation in mouse catching.

rows.q: In 1999, Billy Gumboot the goat was elected president of the Republic of Whangamomona, a rebellious micro-republic on this island nation’s North Island.
rows.n: Billy died in office after serving 18 months, and was succeeded in 2003 by a poodle named Tai.

rows.q: Since 1998, the historic town of Rabbit Hash, Kentucky has elected only dogs as mayor. The hamlet sits along this 981-mile river bordering Indiana and Ohio.
rows.n: The town charges one dollar per vote as a fundraiser, allowing residents to cast as many ballots as they can afford.

rows.q: During Rio de Janeiro’s 1988 mayoral race, over 400,000 protest votes went to Macaco Tião, an inmate belonging to this closest living ape relative of humans.
rows.n: Tião finished third out of 12 candidates and was notorious for hurling feces at visiting dignitaries.

rows.q: Clay Henry, the goat mayor of Lajitas, Texas, famously guzzled up to thirty longnecks a day of this historic lager, the ‘National Beer of Texas.’
rows.n: Tourists bought the bottles for the goat, who drank them unassisted by gripping the neck in his teeth.

rows.q: In 2015, teenagers registered a cat named Limberbutt McCubbins for U.S. President, organizing his viral bid on this forum site featuring the alien Snoo.
rows.n: Limberbutt’s paperwork was formally processed by the FEC, inspiring a wave of parody registrations.

rows.q: Mayor Max, a golden retriever elected mayor of Idyllwild, California, ruled from high in the mountains directly overlooking this iconic Coachella Valley resort city.
In 1988, a famous orange tabby ran for U.S. President on the Finicky Party ticket as a promotional gimmick for this Del Monte cat food brand.
rows.n: Morris was originally adopted from an animal shelter in Chicago before starring in dozens of TV ads.

rows.q: NASA’s Lucy mission is named for the 3.2-million-year-old hominid skeleton unearthed in 1974 in the Afar region of what East African nation?
rows.n: The fossil was named after the Beatles song ‘Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds’, played on repeat in camp.

rows.q: Rosetta’s comet lander, Philae, was named for a Nile island famed for its temple to which Egyptian goddess of magic, the wife of Osiris?
rows.n: The entire temple complex was moved to nearby Agilkia Island in the 1960s to save it from Lake Nasser.

rows.q: NASA renamed its NEAR probe for Eugene Shoemaker, the pioneering geologist whose ashes were carried by a probe to be buried on what celestial body?
rows.n: Shoemaker remains the only person whose cremated remains have been laid to rest on the Moon.

rows.q: NASA’s Stardust probe captured comet dust using what porous, ultralight synthetic material nicknamed ‘frozen smoke’ because it is 99.8% air?
rows.n: Aerogel was invented in 1931 by Samuel Kistler, who replaced the liquid in a gel with gas.

rows.q: NASA’s Psyche probe launched in 2023 to explore a metallic asteroid believed to be an exposed core, made mostly of iron and what other metal?
rows.n: Scientists believe 16 Psyche may be the stripped remnant core of an early planet that failed to form.

rows.q: In 2023, scientists analyzing asteroid samples from Japan’s Hayabusa2 probe found uracil, one of four essential bases in what genetic molecule?
rows.n: The discovery supported the theory that ingredients for life on Earth may have been delivered by asteroids.

rows.q: ESA’s Rosetta spacecraft was named for the stone slab that unlocked ancient Egyptian texts, deciphered in 1822 by which French linguist?
rows.n: Champollion famously fainted after realizing he had cracked the phonetic nature of the hieroglyphs.

rows.q: In 2023, NASA’s OSIRIS-REx probe dropped its sample capsule of asteroid Bennu dust into a military test range in what western U.S. state?
Hermione brews it in Moaning Myrtle’s bathroom using lacewing flies, boomslang skin, and a bit of the person you want to become.
rows.n: She accidentally adds a cat hair, turning herself temporarily into an anthropomorphic feline.

rows.q: Hawaii, New Zealand, and Easter Island mark the three vertices of a vast oceanic cultural triangle bearing what name?
rows.n: French scholar Charles de Brosses coined the name in 1756 from the Greek words for “many islands.”

rows.q: Wonder Woman co-creator William Moulton Marston helped invent an early systolic blood pressure test that led to this controversial device.
rows.n: Marston credited his wife Elizabeth with noticing her blood pressure spiked whenever she was excited or mad.

rows.q: In medicine, it is an abnormal projection growing from a mucous membrane; in marine biology, it is the sessile body form of a coral.
Odysseus blinds this son of Poseidon with a wooden stake after identifying himself as “Nobody.”
rows.n: Blinded, the Cyclops cried to his brethren that “Nobody is killing me,” so they ignored his pleas.

rows.q: An urban legend claims this fictional 1981 arcade game caused seizures and amnesia in Portland suburbs before Men in Black confiscated it.
rows.n: The myth likely arose from real arcade inspections in Portland by FBI agents investigating illegal gambling.

rows.q: John Waters directed this 1981 comedy starring Divine and Tab Hunter, which gave moviegoers scratch-and-sniff “Odorama” cards to smell along with the film.
rows.n: Scents on the scratch-and-sniff card ranged from roses and pizza to flatulence and model airplane glue.

rows.q: Born Marianne Joan Elliott-Said, this frontwoman of punk band X-Ray Spex chose a stage name she found in the phone book for its synthetic vibe.
rows.n: She wrote the feminist punk anthem “Oh Bondage Up Yours!” in 1977 after catching an early gig by the Sex Pistols.

rows.q: Before moving to Paris, a teenage Pablo Picasso held his first solo exhibition in 1900 at the bohemian cafe Els Quatre Gats in what Spanish city?
After being fired from Handy Dan in 1978, the founders of The Home Depot opened their first two orange-aproned hardware stores in what southern city?
Poached in honey water before baking in wood-fired ovens, dense and sesame-heavy bagels are a signature culinary staple of what Canadian city?
rows.n: Local legends Fairmount Bagel and St-Viateur Bagel have maintained a fierce rivalry just blocks apart since the 1950s.

rows.q: Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinicius de Moraes watched a teenager walk toward the beach from a seaside cafe in 1962, inspiring a hit song set in what city?
rows.n: The cafe where the song was written, the Veloso Bar, was later renamed Garota de Ipanema in honor of the tune.

rows.q: Betty White fed livestock to a thirty-foot prehistoric crocodile in a 1999 horror-comedy named for what Adirondack resort village?
rows.n: The horror-comedy was actually filmed in British Columbia, though its fictional lake was set in Maine, not New York.

rows.q: Steven Van Zandt starred as a New York mob capo who relocates through witness protection to Norway in a 2012 comedy series named for what resort town?
rows.n: The show was Netflix’s first-ever original content broadcast, premiering in 2012 as a co-production with Norway’s NRK.

rows.q: In Nevil Shute’s 1957 nuclear novel On the Beach, survivors stoically await deadly global fallout in what coastal capital of Victoria?
rows.n: A local journalist falsely claimed star Ava Gardner called the city the perfect place to film the end of the world.

rows.q: In 1899, Giovanni Agnelli co-founded an automaker whose acronym honors what northern Italian city, home to a factory with a rooftop racetrack?
rows.n: The rooftop test track at the historic Lingotto plant was featured in the iconic 1969 film The Italian Job.

rows.q: Boasting that its citizens formed its brick wall, which ancient Greek city-state famously went without defensive stone fortifications until the fourth century BC?
rows.n: Plutarch recorded King Agesilaus pointing to his armed citizens and declaring, “These are the Spartans’ walls.”

rows.q: In SpongeBob SquarePants, what microscopic owner of the Chum Bucket was saddled by creator Stephen Hillenburg with the ironically mundane first name Sheldon?
rows.n: Hillenburg was a marine biology teacher at the Ocean Institute before pursuing a career in animation.

rows.q: Bordered by Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia, which small African republic contains the continent’s lowest land point at the hypersaline Lake Assal?
rows.n: Lake Assal sits 509 feet below sea level and is ten times saltier than the open ocean.

rows.q: Joining the clavicles and the first seven pairs of ribs, what flat T-shaped bone of the chest consists of the manubrium, body, and xiphoid process?
rows.n: Its name derives from the ancient Greek word “sternon”, which Homer used specifically for the male chest.

rows.q: Which Hall of Fame right wing scored 86 goals for the Blues in 1991, but is best known for his controversial triple-overtime Stanley Cup clincher in 1999?
rows.n: His skate was inside the crease when he scored in 1999, prompting the NHL to scrap the crease rule that summer.

rows.q: Taking its name from a medieval site reserved for visiting northern royalty, what metonym has designated London’s police headquarters since 1829?
Georges Cuvier coined the name of what prehistoric proboscidean from Greek roots meaning “breast tooth”, noting the conical bumps on its fossil molars?
rows.n: Cuvier used its distinct teeth to prove for the first time that an animal species could vanish completely.

rows.q: Secretary of State for War John Profumo resigned in 1963 after lying to Parliament about his affair with which 19-year-old model, who also slept with a Soviet spy?
rows.n: Her iconic nude portrait sitting backward on an imitation Arne Jacobsen chair became an emblem of the 1960s.

rows.q: At the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition, Emperor Dom Pedro II of Brazil famously gasped, “My God, it talks!” after testing what brand-new acoustic apparatus?
rows.n: Alexander Graham Bell’s demonstration won him a gold medal and introduced voice transmission to the world.

rows.q: Delivering a dedication address at the 1939 New York World’s Fair, Franklin D. Roosevelt became the first sitting U.S. president to appear on what newly debuted broadcast medium?
rows.n: FDR’s speech was transmitted by RCA to an audience of only a few hundred television receivers in the New York area.

rows.q: In 1970, the Fuji Group pavilion in Osaka screened Tiger Child, the very first film presented in what Canadian-developed, high-resolution giant-screen cinema format?
rows.n: The system used 70mm film spooled horizontally through the projector, creating an image ten times larger than 35mm.

rows.q: Concessionaire Maurice Vermersch popularized what sweet breakfast pastry at the 1964 New York World’s Fair, dropping “Brussels” from its name because fairgoers could not place the capital?
rows.n: Served warm with strawberries and fresh whipped cream, they were sold from 24 irons running non-stop.

rows.q: Three years before its nationwide 1985 rollout, what fruity soft drink variation was test-marketed to parched attendees at the 1982 World’s Fair in Knoxville?
rows.n: It marked the first commercial flavor extension of Coca-Cola’s flagship recipe since the brand began in 1886.

rows.q: Blending the Latin word for “ladder” with the suffix of “elevator,” Charles Seeberger coined what commercial name for his moving staircase, which carried millions at the 1900 Paris Exposition?
rows.n: Otis lost exclusive rights to the name in 1950 when a federal court declared it a generic term for all moving stairs.

rows.q: Patented by Whitcomb Judson as the “clasp locker” to fasten high Victorian boots, what everyday closure debuted at the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair decades before B.F. Goodrich named it?
rows.n: B.F. Goodrich coined the snappy name in 1923 after using the slide fasteners on a line of rubber galoshes.

rows.q: Frustrated that servants kept chipping her heirloom china, socialite Josephine Cochrane won highest honors at the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair for inventing what mechanized home appliance?
rows.n: Cochrane’s enterprise eventually became the KitchenAid brand, which introduced home dishwashers to the mass market.

rows.q: Created in 1959 to promote Colombian beans alongside his faithful mule Conchita, what fictional mustachioed farmer became the face of the country’s coffee industry?
rows.n: Actor Carlos Sánchez portrayed the character in commercials and public appearances for over thirty years.

rows.q: Painted directly onto the walls of his Madrid home, Francisco de Goya’s terrifying Black Paintings decorated a farmhouse known as the Quinta del Sordo due to what physical condition?
rows.n: Goya lost his hearing in 1792 following an undiagnosed, near-fatal illness.

rows.q: The Cathedral of Seville houses an ornate 19th-century tomb where four heraldic figures, representing the historic kingdoms of Spain, carry the coffin of which navigator?
rows.n: DNA testing in 2006 confirmed that the remains inside indeed belonged to Columbus.

rows.q: Before entering Ukrainian politics, what dominant athlete broke the world record in the men’s pole vault 35 times, winning gold at the 1988 Seoul Olympics?
rows.n: He was the first pole vaulter to clear the six-meter barrier, achieving the feat in Paris in 1985.

rows.q: In 2012, Ecuador granted political asylum to WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange, who then spent nearly seven years confined inside the country’s embassy in what world capital?
rows.n: Ecuador revoked his asylum in April 2019, allowing British police to enter the embassy and arrest him.

rows.q: Purchased in 1987 by the Sultan of Brunei, which historic Los Angeles lodging on Sunset Boulevard is famously nicknamed ‘The Pink Palace’?
rows.n: Celebrities led high-profile boycotts of the hotel in 2014 and 2019 over Brunei’s human-rights policies.

rows.q: To escape Rome’s light pollution, the Vatican Observatory operates its primary optical-infrared research telescope atop Mount Graham in which mountainous U.S. state?
rows.n: The Vatican Advanced Technology Telescope was built in partnership with the University of Arizona.

rows.q: Flourishing without human interference, the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone in Ukraine has become a haven for what endangered, stocky equine—the world’s only true wild horse?
rows.n: Thirty-one horses were released there in 1998, and the Ukrainian population has since grown to several hundred.

rows.q: At age thirteen, this California kid had never acted before being scouted at a Boys & Girls Club to play John Connor in Terminator 2: Judgment Day.
rows.n: Casting director Mali Finn discovered him at the Pasadena Boys & Girls Club in 1990.

rows.q: Before winning an Oscar as Atticus Finch, he took Audrey Hepburn on a scooter ride through Rome in her breakout 1953 rom-com.
rows.n: Peck insisted Hepburn get equal billing above the title because he knew she would win an Oscar.

rows.q: Blended from Scotch whisky, heather honey, herbs, and spices, this golden liqueur forms the boozy backbone of a classic Rusty Nail cocktail.
rows.n: Legend claims the secret recipe was gifted by Bonnie Prince Charlie after his defeat at Culloden.

rows.q: The shipwrecked S.S. Minnow on this 1960s sitcom was named by creator Sherwood Schwartz as an inside insult to FCC chairman Newton Minow.
rows.n: Schwartz despised Minow for famously calling television programming a “vast wasteland.”

rows.q: Originally formed as a glam metal outfit called Sleze, this Seattle quartet broke into the mainstream in 1990 with the hit “Man in the Box.”
rows.n: Singer Layne Staley and guitarist Jerry Cantrell shared the band’s signature vocal harmonies.

rows.q: Founded in Lebanon, Tennessee in 1969, this highway restaurant chain features porch rocking chairs, a country store, and peg-jumping games.
rows.n: Founder Dan Evins originally conceived the concept to sell Shell gasoline to interstate drivers.

rows.q: In a 1968 picture book by Don Freeman, a department-store teddy bear named after this ridged fabric searches after hours for his missing button.
rows.n: Freeman’s wife suggested the name, which had been a childhood nickname for their son.

rows.q: John Cameron Mitchell created and starred in this 1998 glam-rock musical about an East German singer touring dive bars after a botched operation.
rows.n: Mitchell’s father was a U.S. Army general who commanded the American sector of West Berlin.

rows.q: Before and after: Upton Sinclair’s 1906 meatpacking exposé gets down with Kool & the Gang’s funky 1973 dance-floor anthem.
rows.n: Sinclair’s novel spurred the passage of the 1906 Meat Inspection Act.

rows.q: Before and after: David Fincher’s 1999 flick about an underground fight ring joins Flo Rida’s 2010 party track featuring David Guetta.
rows.n: Chuck Palahniuk wrote the 1996 novel after getting beaten up on a camping trip.

rows.q: Before and after: Richard Wright’s 1940 Chicago tragedy about Bigger Thomas runs into Dusty Springfield’s soulful 1968 classic.
rows.a: Native Son of a Preacher Man
rows.n: Springfield’s hit was originally offered to Aretha Franklin, who passed on it.

rows.q: Before and after: Alice Walker’s epistolary novel about Celie in rural Georgia pours into Prince’s soaring 1984 title track.
rows.n: Walker’s 1982 book won both the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award.

rows.q: Before and after: Leo Tolstoy’s Napoleonic epic rolls right aboard Cat Stevens’s hopeful 1971 acoustic chart-topper.
rows.n: Tolstoy drafted the massive manuscript by hand more than six times.

rows.q: Before and after: Sylvia Plath’s 1963 story of Esther Greenwood’s breakdown smashes into Christina Perri’s 2010 piano ballad.
rows.n: Plath first published the book under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas.

rows.q: Before and after: Charles Dickens’s legal satire of Jarndyce and Jarndyce crashes into The Animals’ 1964 blues-rock number-one smash.
rows.a: Bleak House of the Rising Sun
rows.n: Dickens’s novel was famously published in twenty monthly installments.

rows.q: Before and after: Frances Hodgson Burnett’s 1911 tale of a locked Yorkshire plot links with Ricky Nelson’s 1972 Madison Square Garden hit.
rows.n: Nelson wrote the song after being booed at a 1971 rock-and-roll revival concert.

rows.q: In 1799, Aaron Burr ostensibly founded a company to pipe clean water to this island borough, secretly using its charter to launch a rival bank to Alexander Hamilton’s.
rows.n: The Manhattan Company’s water business was neglected, but its banking side evolved into JPMorgan Chase.

rows.q: Locusts are not a separate family of insects. Under crowded conditions, a spike in serotonin triggers a swarming phase in certain species of this common jumping pest.
In 1919, this silent screen legend co-founded United Artists alongside Charlie Chaplin, D.W. Griffith, and her future husband, Douglas Fairbanks.
rows.n: Known as America’s Sweetheart, she won the second-ever Academy Award for Best Actress for 1929’s Coquette.

rows.q: In 1986, the CIA helped turn the tide of the Soviet-Afghan War by supplying Afghan mujahideen with this shoulder-fired, heat-seeking antiaircraft missile.
rows.n: The FIM-92 Stinger forced Soviet gunships to fly higher, drastically cutting their strike effectiveness.

rows.q: Gene Hackman won his first Academy Award playing rogue NYPD detective Popeye Doyle in this gritty 1971 crime thriller directed by William Friedkin.
rows.n: Its high-speed chase beneath Brooklyn’s elevated train was filmed without city permits on live streets.

rows.q: French naval officer Gabriel de La Landelle coined this noun in 1863, deriving it from the Latin word for “bird” to describe heavier-than-air flight.
rows.n: He coined it four decades before the Wright brothers flew, while promoting steam-powered helicopter models.

rows.q: Popularized in English by William Seabrook’s 1929 book The Magic Island, this undead figure of Haitian folklore is reanimated by a sorcerer called a bokor.
rows.n: Seabrook’s sensationalized account inspired the 1932 Bela Lugosi film White Zombie, cinema’s first zombie movie.

rows.q: Named for the dove her father drew for the 1949 World Peace Congress, this designer created signature scribbled “X” jewelry collections for Tiffany & Co.
rows.n: Her mother was painter Françoise Gilot, the only one of Picasso’s romantic partners to walk out on him.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the Home of the Whopper teams up with Robert Fripp’s prog-rock pioneers behind 21st Century Schizoid Man.
rows.n: Fripp has been the only constant member of King Crimson since their founding in 1968.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the fast food chain urging you to Live Mas recruits the New Edition spin-off trio who sang Poison.
rows.n: Ricky Bell, Michael Bivins, and Ronnie DeVoe formed the trio at the suggestion of producer Teddy Riley.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the soft-serve chain famous for the Blizzard shares a royal title with the star of Living Single.
rows.n: Born Dana Owens, she earned an Oscar nomination for playing Matron Mama Morton in Chicago.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the alt-rock piano trio behind Brick orders burgers from the chain known for brown bags of fries.
rows.n: Ben Folds Five was actually a trio; Folds joked that the name sounded better than Ben Folds Three.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the deep-voiced soul icon behind You’re the First orders square sliders from a 1921 burger pioneer.
rows.n: White Castle is widely recognized by historians as the world’s first fast food hamburger chain.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the falsetto singer of Tiptoe Through the Tulips buys coffee from a chain founded by an NHL star.
rows.n: Horton was an active Toronto Maple Leafs defenseman when he opened his first doughnut shop in 1964.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the mall pretzel giant joins hands with the Nova Scotia singer who took Snowbird to number one.
rows.n: Murray was the first Canadian female solo artist to earn an American gold record and a number-one hit.

rows.q: In this before-and-after, the smoothie chain founded in California shares a refreshing name with the Angel of the Morning singer.
rows.n: Juice Newton won a 1982 Grammy for Best Female Country Vocal Performance with Break It to Me Gently.

rows.q: Tom Hanks and Halle Berry each played six different roles across multiple eras in this ambitious 2012 Wachowski sci-fi film based on a David Mitchell novel.
rows.n: Mitchell’s 2004 novel was structured as a nested series of six stories that fold back on themselves.

rows.q: Italian dictator Benito Mussolini coined this geopolitical term in 1936 to describe the diplomatic line linking Rome and Berlin.
rows.n: Mussolini declared that all other European powers would rotate around the Berlin-Rome axis.

rows.q: Co-created by two former Microsoft executives in 1998, this party board game divides challenges into Creative Cat, Data Head, Word Worm, and Star Performer.
rows.n: The game was originally sold through Barnes & Noble and Starbucks rather than traditional toy stores.

rows.q: Developed by Sumerian scribes around 3400 BCE, this wedge-shaped script is widely considered humanity’s earliest known writing system.
rows.n: Scribes pressed cut reed styluses into soft clay tablets, which were then baked or sun-dried.

rows.q: Hector and Achilles clash outside the walls of this ancient citadel, which provided Homer with the classical Greek title for his Trojan War epic.
rows.n: Heinrich Schliemann excavated the site in northwestern Turkey in the 1870s.

rows.q: Located in modern-day Turkey, this ancient Cilician trade city was both the birthplace of Saint Paul and the meeting place of Antony and Cleopatra.
rows.n: Cleopatra sailed up the Cydnus River dressed as Aphrodite to meet Antony there in 41 BCE.

rows.q: Originally designating an ancient Greek tactical unit of infantry packed tightly with overlapping shields, this word now means any close-knit body of people.
rows.n: Anatomists later applied the plural form, phalanges, to the rows of bones in human fingers and toes.

rows.q: Named for the German physicist who calculated it in 1916, this measurement defines the radius of a black hole’s event horizon.
rows.n: Karl Schwarzschild derived his black hole solution while serving on the Russian front in WWI.

rows.q: In 1947, fruit flies became the first animals intentionally sent into space, launched aboard a V-2 rocket from this historic New Mexico testing ground.
rows.a: White Sands (or White Sands Missile Range)
rows.n: The flies reached an altitude of 68 miles and were recovered alive inside their ejection capsule.

rows.q: France launched Félicette, the first cat in space, from a military testing range in this North African country, just a year after its independence.
rows.n: The Centre interarmées d’essais d’engins spéciaux launch site at Hammaguir operated until 1967.

rows.q: In 1960, dogs Belka and Strelka safely completed 18 orbits aboard a prototype of this Soviet spacecraft, which carried Yuri Gagarin into space in 1961.
rows.n: The Korabl-Sputnik 2 mission proved the capsule’s life-support and re-entry systems worked.

rows.q: Miss Baker, a squirrel monkey who survived a 1959 Jupiter missile flight, lived to age 27 and is buried at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center in this Alabama city.
rows.n: Visitors regularly leave fresh bananas atop her tombstone outside the Huntsville museum.

rows.q: Reaching an altitude of 83 miles in 1949, Albert II became the first mammal in space aboard a modified version of this captured German ballistic rocket.
rows.n: Albert reached space safely, but tragically died on impact when his parachute system failed.

rows.q: Apollo 17 carried five pocket mice that orbited the Moon 75 times. Four were nicknamed after the giant’s rhyming chant from this classic English fairy tale.
rows.n: The mice were Fe, Fi, Fo, and Fum; command module pilot Ron Evans dubbed the fifth Phooey.

rows.q: After becoming the first living creatures to circle the Moon in 1968, two Soviet steppe tortoises splashed down and were recovered in this warm ocean.
rows.n: Soviet naval ships retrieved the Zond 5 capsule after it made a ballistic re-entry over Antarctica.

rows.q: Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev gifted a puppy named Pushinka to Caroline Kennedy. Pushinka’s mother was this canine veteran of Sputnik 5.
rows.n: Pushinka mated with JFK’s terrier Charlie, producing what Kennedy jokingly called ‘pupniks.’

rows.q: In April 1988, the U.S. Navy launched Operation Praying Mantis against Iranian forces in this strategic waterway after a frigate struck a mine.
rows.n: It was the largest surface-warship battle the U.S. Navy had fought since World War II.

rows.q: Declared extinct when Ned Maddrell died in 1974, this Goidelic Celtic tongue of an island in the Irish Sea has since seen a modest revival.
rows.n: Ned Maddrell’s speech was recorded by researchers in the 1950s and 60s to preserve the accent.

rows.q: Founded in 1733 by James Oglethorpe around a distinctive grid of public squares, this Atlantic port was the first colonial capital of Georgia.
rows.n: General Sherman spared the city in 1864, famously presenting it to Lincoln as a Christmas gift.

rows.q: In the 1925 serum run to Nome, Gunnar Kaasen and his lead dog Balto completed the final blizzard-swept leg driving a sled team of what breed?
rows.n: Balto’s taxidermied mount is displayed at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.

rows.q: Created by Steve Jackson, this 2001 card game parodies role-playing tropes with gear like the Chainsaw of Bloody Dismemberment. Name the game.
rows.n: Its success helped spawn spinoffs themed around everything from Cthulhu and zombies to Shakespeare.

rows.q: Set in the fictional outpost of Kyauktada, this satirical 1934 debut novel by George Orwell drew on his years in the Indian Imperial Police.
rows.n: Orwell resigned from the police force in 1927 while on leave in England, partly inspired by his guilt.

rows.q: Nationalized in 1960, this rum brand has been contested in a decades-long international trademark dispute between Pernod Ricard and Bacardi.
rows.n: Because of the U.S. embargo on Cuba, Bacardi sells a Puerto Rican version in the American market.

rows.q: Featuring a horn section and co-written with Jim Vallance, this 1987 Permanent Vacation single gave Aerosmith a major MTV-era comeback hit.
rows.n: Steven Tyler originally sang the placeholder line ‘Rag time, get that grease fire out of your face.’

rows.q: In 2006, Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman became the first person to turn down this prestigious quadrennial honor, mathematics’ equivalent of a Nobel Prize, after solving the Poincaré conjecture.
rows.n: Four years later, he also turned down the Clay Mathematics Institute’s million-dollar Millennium Prize.

rows.q: In the 2008 film 21, Kevin Spacey tests his student with the Monty Hall problem, where switching doors doubles the player’s odds of winning a sports car instead of these barnyard animals.
rows.n: The problem is named after the original host of Let’s Make a Deal, who launched the game show in 1963.

rows.q: Olbers’ paradox asks why the night sky is dark if the universe has infinite stars. In 1848, this American master of the macabre published the first correct resolution, in his essay Eureka.
rows.n: Poe deduced that the universe was not old enough for light from the most distant stars to have reached Earth.

rows.q: To argue that motion is impossible, Zeno of Elea imagined this swift-footed Greek hero from the Iliad giving a head start to a tortoise, doomed to mathematically never catch it.
rows.n: Because the runner must first reach where the tortoise was, Zeno argued the gap could never fully close.

rows.q: In computer science, puzzles like Minesweeper and Tetris share a mathematical classification with this 1996 Nintendo creature-collecting franchise, which researchers proved is NP-complete.
rows.n: If an algorithm could efficiently beat generalized Pokémon puzzles, it would instantly resolve P versus NP.

rows.q: In a 1989 episode of Star Trek: The Next Generation, Captain Picard laments that Fermat’s Last Theorem is still unsolved—a claim rendered obsolete four years later by this real-life mathematician.
rows.n: Wiles worked in secret in his attic for over six years to complete the proof of the 350-year-old problem.

rows.q: Braess’s paradox shows that adding roads can worsen gridlock. In 1990, NYC planners proved it when closing this Midtown cross street for Earth Day actually caused traffic to improve.
rows.n: The surprising traffic speedup helped inspire the permanent pedestrianization of Times Square in 2009.

rows.q: Also called hailstone numbers as values rise and fall, the unproven Collatz conjecture claims that repeated basic arithmetic on any positive integer will always end at this single digit.
rows.n: If odd, multiply by 3 and add 1; if even, divide by 2. It has been checked for all numbers up to 2 to the 68th.

rows.q: The armored scales and lobed fins of the “living fossil” coelacanth directly inspired the look of the Gill-man, the title monster of what 1954 film?
rows.n: Milicent Patrick designed the Gill-man, but makeup head Bud Westmore claimed sole credit for decades.

rows.q: New Caledonia’s predatory terror skink was named Phoboscincus after the Greek god of panic, who also names the larger moon of what planet?
rows.n: Phobos orbits closer to its parent planet than any other moon in the solar system, just 3,700 miles up.

rows.q: Rediscovered in 2019 after 113 years lost, the Fernandina giant tortoise is native to an island chain owned by what equatorial South American nation?
rows.n: DNA analysis confirmed the lone female found, nicknamed Fernanda, belonged to the lost species.

rows.q: Presumed extinct until 1981, the black-footed ferret made history in 2020 with Elizabeth Ann, the first imperiled U.S. animal born through what process?
rows.n: Elizabeth Ann was cloned from tissue samples frozen in 1988 at the San Diego Zoo’s Frozen Zoo.

rows.q: Eaten nearly to extinction by English survivors of the 1609 Sea Venture shipwreck, the Bermuda petrel nested on the island that inspired what play?
rows.n: William Strachey’s written account of the Bermuda wreck was read by Shakespeare before writing the play.

rows.q: In 2001, scientists rediscovered the Lord Howe stick insect on Ball’s Pyramid, a sheer volcanic spire in what sea between Australia and New Zealand?
rows.n: The entire surviving wild population numbered fewer than thirty insects, living around a single bush.

rows.q: Thought extinct until 1974, the Chacoan peccary is native to the dry scrubland contested in a 1930s war between Paraguay and what neighbor?
rows.n: The 1932 to 1935 Chaco War was fought over suspected oil deposits that turned out to be almost non-existent.

rows.q: A landmark statue of the rediscovered, flightless takahe stands in Te Anau, the gateway town to what fjord dubbed the “eighth wonder of the world”?
rows.n: Rudyard Kipling dubbed it the eighth wonder; the dramatic fjord receives roughly 250 inches of rain a year.
